en: (The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Month of Dhanus)
The dawn period lasts for thirty days; one should exclude any excess days.
O Śambhu, O Maheśvara, how is it that there are twenty-nine days?
By including [the time] from the previous month, there is one day for the worship of Śiva.
And the fruit of that is obtained by performing worship for a thousand days during the single junctions.
"On whichever day the sun should enter Capricorn at dawn, at evening, or at midday, on that very day the worship of the gods [should be performed]; such is the reason."
At dusk, the sun rises; these two are your suns.
Beyond twenty [degrees], one should worship that day as dawn.
The six-month period beginning with Capricorn is known as the day of the gods.
The period from Kaṭakāvranta is known as Devarātri for six months;
it lasts for five nāḍīs during one month, and likewise for six months in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
It shall be five nāḍīs in Āṣāḍha, and for six months in Mārgaśīrṣa.
When the sun is positioned at the bow [in the sky], one should worship Śiva at dawn;
at the twenty-fifth [muhūrta] of the dawn period, the highest [grade of worship] is prescribed;
at the twenty-seventh [muhūrta] of the dawn period, the middling [grade] is prescribed.
At the time of the twenty-eighth *muhūrta* of the dawn, it is called *adhamana*. Pure food mixed with curd, combined with *śuṇḍikā* powder,
along with *āmalaka*, *ādṛka*, and mustard powder, [should be offered].
One should especially avoid using condiments such as young tubers and the like;
for him, the fruit of twelve years is accomplished in a single day.
[The Ritual for Determining the Kindling of Kṛttikā]
Both [the sun and moon] ascending the lamp bring about destruction;
however, the ascension of the lamp on Wednesday, Friday, Monday, or Thursday is most excellent.
In Ajita...
In the month of Ūrja, under the constellation Śatabhiṣaj and with Vahni as the presiding deity,
one should offer the Kṛttikā-lamp at the time of dusk.
One should perform it only on the full moon night,
or at twilight, or on a Sunday, or under the asterism of Kṛttikā, or during a lunar festival, or on the fourteenth day.
That is said to be the most excellent lamp; the [planets] Saturn and Mars are middling.
In the Pauṣkara [treatise], [the asterisms] Kṛttikā and Bharaṇī, as well as the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī), on that same day [are auspicious].
If the occurrence of the eclipse should take place at midday or in the afternoon;
or if the occurrence should take place at midnight or when the moon is full—
one should not celebrate the festival of lights on that day, but rather observe it on the preceding or the following day.
If an eclipse should occur on the night of the full moon day, one should not perform the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava) then; rather, one should observe the festival with lamps on the following day.

One should celebrate the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava) on the first day of the bright fortnight;
or one should perform it when the Moon is in Scorpio or Cancer, during its period of exaltation, on the full moon day, under the asterism Kṛttikā, or in Taurus.
One should perform the kindling of the great lamp with saffron.
In the *Mṛgendra*,
it is said that whoever should perform a lamp-offering to the Kṛttikās conjoined with a lunar node (*parvan*) attains a middling state, equal to the progress of a king and his kingdom.
In the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*:

"If on that day the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*) is joined with the Kṛttikā constellation alone, one should not perform the Festival of Lamps (*dīpotsava*); if one were to do so, it would bring about the destruction of the kingdom."
One should cause a lamp to be lit on the full moon day during the asterisms of Kāraṇa, Rohiṇī, or Bharaṇī;
for if a lamp is lit on a non-parvan day, that village will bring about the destruction of the kingdom.
In the Kāmika [Tantra],
it is said that Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, and likewise Mṛgaśīrṣa constitute the primary festival; one should perform the offering of lamps at dusk.
The Sequence of Invocation (Āvāhanakrama)
The thirty-two forms reside on the top of the *liṅga*, on both its sides, and within the image;
the image resides in the heart by means of *śakti*; and the form [of the deity] is present in stone, water, and metal.

The life-force (jīva) of that [image] resides within the garment of the bust; on the chariot, it is at the top of the spire (stūpikā) or the nose, or established in the dome (vaṭa). Thus, in the Citraśnottara (Citraśnottara-praśnottara):
"On the head of the Lord, in the middle of the trident, and in the belly of the pinnacle."
The power (*śakti*) of Skanda resides in the head of the chariot; the bull and fire reside at the tip of the cow.
The *sañjīva* [plants] always dwell in the breasts of those born of stone, water, and iron, beginning with the *śakti*.
[The Lamp Festival Bath]. (Side Heading)
On the day of the lunar month corresponding to the Gaṅgādvīpa constellation, one should reside by the water of the Lakṣmī-taila;
for the sake of warding off misfortune (Alakṣmī), one should perform this rite for you.
During the other months beginning with Āśvina, on the fourteenth day of the fortnight at dawn, [one should likewise act].
A bath with warm oil in sand or water is equal to a bath in the Gaṅgā; indeed, it brings complete satisfaction.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, I do not request anything else:
men who fear hell must perform an oil massage and a ritual bath.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, at the dead of night,
one should perform an oil massage and a ritual bath after crushing the demon Naraka.
[The Procedure for the Navarātri Festival]
O Guha, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
worship and a hunting expedition are prescribed in the Śaiva Āgamas.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, on both the tenth and ninth days— these two days— the lunar day (tithi) is divided;
one should accept the subsequent [day] as the superior [time for the rite].
In the *Kāmika*,
it is stated that starting from sunrise on the tenth lunar day, during its nine *nāḍikās*,
hunting and travel on that day are most excellent.
In the month of Kanyā, during the bright fortnight of the yoga-born [period], one should worship Śamī on the tenth day;
either in the forenoon or the afternoon, whenever that lunar date occurs within the ten-day interval.

At that time, however, the preceptor should especially worship according to the rules. On the tenth day of the month of Āśvina (Ajita), one should worship the God at sunrise; it will be most excellent.
At midday it should be known as middling; in the evening, it becomes inferior.

Whether there is an increase or even a decrease [in the duration], one should worship the deity who is the cause of the *daśā*. However, if the [period] begins on the previous day, the preceptor should perform the worship on that prior day.
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"Whichever lunar day (*tithi*) the sun reaches at its rising—
that lunar day is to be known in its entirety for rites such as the worship of sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kanyā, or on the tenth night,
one should constantly recite the mantra and perform the vow of fire-oblations for the sake of the Āsura rite of destruction.

One who contemplates Gaurī, Īśa, Gaṇeśa, Guha, Abhicarasa, Śekhara, Sundara, or Śamīrūpa—these ten bring about auspiciousness; one is liberated through the grace of Śambhu. One who meditates on the supreme Śakti, joined with Siṃhāsura and Dhī, bestows victory.
One should worship the hand-weapon and the missile-weapon at the root of a *śamī* tree; this bestows victory.
One should also worship the celestial chariot, the horse, the spirit-being, the elephant, the bull, the wish-fulfilling cow, the tree, the swan, and the *sahama*.
Having adorned the peacock, the parrot, the lion, the palanquin,
and so forth, one should meditate upon the Root Power (mūlaśakti).
In the Svāyambhuva [Kalpa],
on the tenth day, there is the worship of the Śamī tree (fifth line); in the Sahasra [Kalpa]...
Beginning from the new moon, the worship of Guha was performed on the tenth day;
when that lunar date arrived in the evening, there was a hunting expedition on that very day.
Alternatively,
[the first] is on the crown;
in the month of Kanyā, during the bright fortnight, on the two lunar days that are the causes of the *daśā*.
One should perform the worship of the Śamī tree and likewise cause the tenth day (Daśamī) to be observed.
Except for the worship on the lunar day (*tithi-pūjā*), the king shall incur invincibility;
[otherwise], there will be the destruction of the village headman and the ruin of wealth and grain.
[The Ritual Procedure for the Skanda-Ṣaṣṭhī Festival]
Kauśika said: "O God of gods, Lord of the world, Sovereign of the gods, whose banner is the bull!
[Tell me] the sequence for Skanda-Ṣaṣṭhī and likewise the procedure for the festival."
"O Destroyer of Tripura, tell me how that holy site (tīrtha) arose when [it was] surrounded.
Śiva said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the festival of Skandaṣaṣṭhī."
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and destroys all diseases.
It bestows health, longevity, and fame, as well as the complete increase of wealth and grain;
it brings victory at the time of battle and destroys all enemies.
One shall properly attain royal fortune as well as excellent sons;
having experienced everything in this very world, one shall thereafter obtain liberation.
I shall proclaim the origin of the vow; listen with virtuous conduct, O Kauśika.
Formerly, by the evil-minded Asura named Tāraka, [the world was oppressed].

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods were oppressed for a long time by the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, due to cruel afflictions and calamities. At that time, for the sake of protecting the world, the Lord Ṣaḍānana was born.
Once, all the gods went to Kailāsa out of fear.
On the first day, the gods of Śiva consumed his splendor, thinking it to be their own;
on the second day, that splendor likewise entered the body of Pārvatī.
In the third [month], the fire was held in his hand; likewise, in the fourth, he ascended the throne. Having reached the Kṛttikās in the fifth, in the sixth, the six Kumāras were born.
From that time forth, the Kumāra became dear to Skanda and Ṣaṣṭhī;
at that moment, all the gods, having undertaken the great vow (mahāvrata), [honored him].
One should realize permanence and the attainment of one's desired goals through the majesty of the aggregates (*skandha-vaibhava*);
one should perform everything exactly as prescribed in the ritual manuals of the *kalpa*.
When the month of Tulā has arrived, on the first lunar day (tithi) which is pure,
this supreme worship of the six-faced one [Kārttikeya] ending with the sixth [day] should be performed.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Tulā, one should first observe the vow;
in the month of Vṛścika, one should observe the Skanda-ṣaṣṭi vow until the end of the sixth day.
Likewise, whichever month constitutes the vow, that month is the primary one;
if the commencement is made in another month, that worship shall be fruitless.
If the new moon occurs after twenty ghaṭikās, then [the following] shall be the first [lunar day].
From that time forward, one should observe the vow; however, if it is a *vṛddhi* (an auspicious domestic rite), it should be performed on the following day.
In all vows and at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the lunar day (*tithi*) is certainly determined by its pervading the midday;
it is not said to be defined by its pervading the evening, nor is the day so designated.
This vow has been fully described; it is honored in all undertakings.
Through its grace, one who is well-versed in the sacred word attains all desires.
O Kauśika of excellent conduct, listen as I shall describe the festival of the vow.
It should be surrounded by Skanda and the sixty [attendants]; thus, it becomes threefold and equal.
One should prepare a mandala with a pitcher surrounded by the principal image;
one should perform the fire-oblation in a hexagonal sacrificial pit and carry out the binding of protection.

One should perform only the *mañcaka* rite; this is proclaimed as the *kanyasa* (inferior) *savana*. However, in front of the image (*bera*), one should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) together with a water-pot (*kumbha*) and a mandala.
One should worship the sacrificial pot, the fire-pit, and the sacrificial hall.
For the purpose of the festival, there should be a [processional] image, and the rite of binding the protective thread (rakṣābandhana) should be performed.
One should carry out the fire-oblation (homa), the food offering (bali), and the sequence of rites; furthermore, the powder and the sacred water (tīrtha) are used on the sixth day.
The middle [mantra] is thus renowned; now hear the supreme one.
Following the very sequence previously described, that which is endowed with the Crest-Standard (Śikhidhvaja) is renowned as the supreme, the cause of all auspiciousness.
In the water-pot, in the mandala, and likewise in the image, there are three types [of forms]:
in the water-pot it is endowed with four arms, while in the mandala it is two-armed.
One should worship the image, twelve cubits in height, according to the prescribed ritual.
I shall now describe the sequence of the mandala, beginning from the eastern breast.
The mandala is sixteen finger-breadths in width and square;
each petal is six finger-breadths, and the pericarp is four finger-breadths.
It is said that the pericarp in the center is yellow, the six petals are red in color, and the tips are white; thus it is described as a black orb.
Alternatively, one should visualize the six-petaled lotus as dark blue in accordance with the petals.
Thereafter, one should draw the earth element surrounding the exterior of the lotus.
O Great Sage, it has been taught that in the four corners— namely, Agni, Rākṣasa, Vāyu, and Īśa— the colors are intoxicated-dark, black, white, and yellow.
One who is firm in his vows should fasten a cord of six threads— whether for a man or especially for a woman—
around the right or the left arm.
Having invited them, let them come with great honor; having provided a meal for the Brahmins, one should perform the daily obligatory rites day by day, even if they are performed without mantras.
When the sixth lunar day arrives, one should perform the first festival;
this vow is proclaimed as the bestower of success in all undertakings.
One obtains all desires through the propitiation of Subrahmaṇyā.
I shall describe the Vrata-festival that bestows the fruit of all desires,
specifically on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.

The wise one should raise the banner for the benefit of all the world. Having performed the rites for the sprout, the purification of the site, and the special worship, and having established the vow-vase and the mandala thereafter;
Then, having specially bathed the banner-cloth in front of the peacock,
one should subsequently strike the drum and worship the deity of the weapon (Astradeva). One should sacrifice to the Lord of the Festival and the Lord of Guha, together with their respective Śaktis.
And having tied a protective thread, one should perform a circumambulation of the village;
having invoked the deities of the directions, one should raise the banner in due order.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice and worship, the Guru should install the water-pots (kumbhas);
the principal pot in the center, and likewise the Śakti-pot at its side.
One should worship the eight jars of Viśveśvara in the center of the altar,
as well as the jars of Yāgeśvara and the jars of the door-keepers.
One should worship the groups of world-protectors (lokapāla) from the auspicious banner,
as well as the weapons, the archways, the sprouts,
and the sacrificial pit and altar; thereafter, one should worship them in sequence, offering incense and lamps.
A mirror, a full water-jar, a peacock, two chowries,
a cock, a lotus, and a lamp— these constitute the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala).
Likewise, there are a thunderbolt, a spear, a bow, a sword, and an arrow.
The cock, the one whose arrows have departed, the lotus, and likewise the discus—
one should thus place these ten weapons in the directions in their proper sequence.
Having prepared forty-nine sacrificial pits, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
One should carry out all the rites beginning with the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), as prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agni-kārya*).
[This applies] to the image, the mouth, the fire, and the *kubara* of the festival.

Having thus meditated upon the fivefold deity, one should worship with the mantra. One should offer oblations of fuel-wood with the Skanda-mantra, clarified butter with the root-mantra, sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Kumāra-mantra, and parched grain (lāja) with the Senāni-mantra.
One should offer mustard seeds with the Guha-mantra, sesame seeds with the Vai-kārtika-mantra, and other substances with the Skanda-gāyatrī-mantra;
one should perform one hundred and eight oblations of this [mixture] with the Kumāra-mantra.
One should perform the expiation with the *mātakumāra* mantra,
and likewise offer oblations in sequence for the rites beginning with *jaya* up to the *abhyādhāna*, ending with the *rāṣṭrabhṛt*.
The wise practitioner should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra and present the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
Thereafter, he should worship the Lord of the Festival and the Lord of Guha with ritual ablutions and other rites.
And having especially adorned it with various fruits, as well as perfumes, flowers, incenses, lamps, and food offerings;
One should worship with various kinds of offerings and well-adorned ornaments;

having thus performed worship twice a day, and having performed the occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), and daily (nitya) rites preceded by the fire-oblation (homa) and the offering of oblations (balidāna).

One should perform the circumambulation of the village, especially in the evening and in the morning. [The procession] shall be provided with various items such as an umbrella, chowries, banners, and fans,
and accompanied by various kinds of musical instruments.
It was joined by various devotees, accompanied by various dances,
and further adorned with many other services and royal insignia.
Thus, having performed the circumambulation of the village with many such [rites],
he should afterwards enter his residence, and thereafter proceed to his seat.
One should cause the offering of food (naivedya) to be presented to the deity, as well as the worship with lamps, accompanied by dance and song; thus one should perform [the rite].
In the first [instance], it is for all the gods; likewise, in the second, it is for the asuras.
On the third day, one should offer it to Brahmā; on the fourth, to the Yoginīs;
on the fifth, to Śiva and Śakti; and on the sixth, one should give to Guha.
A wise person should especially perform this bali offering every single day.
In the first [life], there was a palanquin; in the second, a hunting expedition;
in the third, the Śūrapadma chariot; and in the fourth, an elephant mount.

One should perform the Mayūra on the fifth day, the Rathotsava on the sixth, and likewise the Tīrtha and Ekadina, for the sake of accomplishing all goals. Having completed the fire-oblation according to the rules, one should conclude the festival.
One should perform the slaying of Tāraka and the others according to the prescribed ritual of divine play.
At the conclusion of the festival of the mountain peaks, during the bright fortnight of autumn,
the deity should be worshipped on the sixth lunar day at mid-afternoon.
For the purpose of destroying the enemies of kings, one should perform the ritual of withdrawal on the sixth lunar day;
beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Tulā, one should undertake the vow.
One should always perform the ritual up to the end of the sixty [days] according to the prescribed rules of the Kalpa;
the lowering of the banner should take place at night, followed by the dismissal of the World-Protectors (Lokapālas).
On the sixth day, the wise one should perform [the rite] for the sake of the welfare of the entire world;
and on the seventh, there is the dismissal of all the Pratikas.
One should perform the ritual of the vow (vrata-karman) at the base and the tip of the primary pitcher (kumbha).
On the seventh day, one should join the pitcher with the mandala.
Afterwards, one should worship the preceptor (ācārya), preceded by the offering of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus, whoever performs this with devotion shall attain a meritorious state.
[Thus ends the thirtieth chapter on the festival of the Skanda-ṣaṣṭī vow, from the Utsavapaddhati of the Kāmika Āgama.]
Hariḥ Om.
(Ṣide heading) || [Ekākṣaranikhaṇḍu] || May that Lord, at the arising of whose wisdom infinite beings are made like crest-jewels by the very shadow of his lotus feet, be for our supreme welfare. (1)
To you, whose [intellect] has been rendered free from impurity by the friction of various scriptural compositions, the goddess Sarasvatī acts as a mirror for your playful manifestations. 2.
Thus, the illustrious Nirañjanapaṇḍīśa has composed this work, beginning with the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, which is radiant with virtues, being neither too brief nor too extensive. (3)

It is described through six chapters (*kāṇḍa*) in sequence: one [chapter] characterized by four castes (*varṇa*), two [chapters] characterized by one, two, three, and four castes, and two chapters on mixed lineages (*saṅkīrṇānvaya*).
Furthermore, it is told through various meanings via the path of other systems of grammar (*śabdatantra*).

Furthermore, those [words] that exist through the distinction of having a gender marker (*saliṅga*), being without a gender marker (*nirliṅga*), or being both, are sevenfold according to their application (*vṛtti*) as feminine, masculine, or neuter: [the feminine] in the feminine, masculine, and neuter;
[the masculine] in the feminine and masculine; [the neuter] in the neuter and masculine; [the feminine] in the neuter and feminine; and [the feminine] in all three genders. (5–6)

I shall explain, for the most part in their proper order, words that are masculine, feminine, neuter, or of various genders and belonging to all three genders, starting from those with two syllables and so forth, according to their phonetic forms and by association.
One should also determine them through the context of the section or by the presence of other words.
One should recite those [verses] according to their gender, or that quarter [of the verse] together with the preceding one as distinct.
"In the three" means it should be understood as applying to the three genders; "in the case of *saṃjñā* and *itva*" here serves to prescribe the remaining gender while prohibiting other genders. (9)

The letter *a* [is used] in the sense of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa; in a tortoise, in a mark, and in battle; in respect, within the inner apartments, and in the sense of a cause; and in the sense of an ornament, a nose-ring, and a wise man. (10)
The letter Ā occurs in *pada*, *bhāva*, *paritāpa*, and *pitāmaha*.
The letter I occurs in *phaṇi*, *raktārcis*, the tip (*agra*), the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the planet (*graha*), and the half (*ardha*).
(11) It also occurs in *hari*, *kareṇu*, the end of a girth (*kakṣyānta*), the moon’s ray (*niśākarakara*), and *smara*.
The vowel *ī* is in the lotus petal of Lakṣmī, in the speech of Vāṇī,
in the filament of the lotus, on the tongue, in the rainbow, in the arrow, and in the hollow of the serpent.
The vowel *u* is in the Kṣatriya, in the eye, on the crest of Hara, and in Hari and Hara.
The letter *ū* is found in the word *puruṣa*, in the moon (*candra*), in the king’s eye, in the throat,
in a demon (*asura*), in the two ears, in a full jar, in a merchant, and in protection.
(14) The letter *ṛ* is found in the elephant (*kuñjara*), in a mountain (*śaila*), in a type of intelligence (*dhī-bheda*), and in the Mother of the Vedas (*vedamātṛ*).
One should employ the letter *bhā* here when there is enmity with a deity, or in the case of wine (*surā*) and the downward direction (*nīcī*).

(15) The letter *ḷ* occurs in the word for elephant (*dantin*), in the words for elephant-girth (*kuñjara*) and the wise (*kavi*), in one whose limbs are eternally smeared with celestial sandalwood paste (*svargādinityaliptagātra*), and in one who has gone beyond the reach of enemies (*gatanaptarirakṣas*). (16)
The letter *ḷ* is in the lizard, the moon, the cow-eyed one, and the sea-monster;
it is in the playful gait, the eye, the elephant, the mother, and the mother. 17.
The letter *e* is in splendor and strength at night, in the interior of a palace for Hari;
it is in the sky during the eleventh [tithi], at the beginning of the day on a jeweled floor. 18.
The vowel *ai* is present in the face of the quarters, in the hand, on the peak of Mount Haridri, and in the bark [of trees].
(3rd line) The vowel *o* is found in the lotus, a wall, water, Śrīda, a cloud, and the source of the moon. 19.
The letter *ca* belongs to Śiva and Viriñci; the letter *au* belongs to the son of Ambikā (Kārttikeya);
[the letters] *vi*, *śu*, *ddhā*, *ṅga*, *indu*, and *kalayoḥ* belong to Ananta, Siddha, and Puṣpaka. (20)
The syllable *aṃ* is recorded as being used in speech, in a long *añjali* gesture,
in the measurement of the seven musical notes (*svara*), and in the supreme light.

Aḥ is at the crest; when the mantra is perfected, it is placed upon the chariot of the fierce one (Rathārpaṇi), within the wheel, upon the cock-headed lunar orb, and in Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu. || 22 ||
What is the word for Brahmā, the self, wind, sun, fire, the peacock, and the peahen? It is *haṃsa*.

What is the word for Viṣṇu, the void, the penis, and the white color? It is *śaṅkha*. What is the word for the head, water, and the neuter gender? It is *kaṃ*. In that same sense, what is the indeclinable word for the discus? It is *cakrī*.

The word *kiṃ* is used in questions, objections, incantations (*kṛtyā*), and deliberation (*vitarka*), and it possesses various grammatical genders. However, as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it is used in the sense of reproach, as well as in alternatives and questions. The word *ku-* is an indeclinable used in the senses of a bad woman, the earth, sin, smallness, reproach, and concealment. (25)

The word *kha* denotes a man, Garuḍa, a sword, heaven, the peaceful aesthetic sentiment (*śāntarasa*), and a bird; (it also denotes) the senses, pleasures, the sky, a constellation, a field, and a city. 26.
* Kṛpā (mercy) is in the two protectors; Śuṣminya is in the cavities of union; Bindu is in the apertures.
(3rd line) Gā is in Gaṅgīta; Ga is in Gaṅgā; Go is in the Gandharvas and Gaṇeśa. 27.
The word *gauḥ* (cow/ox) is used for a bull, the moon, speech, the earth, the quarters, the sky, and the stars; it is used in the feminine for a cow.
(Line 4) However, in the masculine and neuter dual, it refers to rays, teeth, arrows, heavens, thunderbolts, water, and hair. 28.

The letter *gha* occurs in the words *megha* (cloud), *nidāgha* (heat of summer), *kiṅkiṇī* (small bell), *ghaṇṭā* (bell), and *ghaṭṭana* (striking). The letter *gham* signifies the Vedas and immortality (*amṛta*). Alternatively, it may signify the earth and news. It is used in three genders when denoting the seasons. The letter *ṅa* signifies the neuter gender and collyrium (*añjana*). As a masculine noun, it denotes Śiva, a day of the week (*viṣṭi*), and a person.
The word *ca* is used for the land of the Turks (*caṣṭuruṣka*), a sound, a crow (*cora*), a *coraka* plant, and also the moon;
(30). The feminine noun *cā* denotes beauty and blood; *kūrca* is neuter, while in the three genders it means "pure";
*ccha* is used for repetition (*īpsā*), covering (*cchādana*), and a lotus; as a neuter it means "in front," and as a masculine it means "arrival" (*saṃprati*). (31).

The word *jau* refers to the three [worlds], the stainless, the eternal, the impure, and that which causes division; it also denotes the syllable *oṃ*, the one who is free from envy, and the conqueror. (32) The word *jā* is used for a woman, a river, a source of birth, the ocean, and a wave.
The word *ja* occurs in the sense of a hut, an ornament, a lotus, and the act of wiping away water.

(33, second line) *Juḥ* occurs in the sense of fame, battle, decay, life, the sky, and a ghost. *Jū* occurs in the sense of a woman’s speech; the word *śabda*, however, is masculine and means a traveler or a swan. (34)
When the jewel of majesty has perished, amidst terrible storms, intoxication, the assembly of meditative absorption, the realm of pride, and when the cloud of arrogance moves upon the head; 35.
The root *jhiṣ* is used in the sense of yawning, being stupefied, and being impotent; it is also used with fear as its prefix.
The word *jña* means wise when used in the masculine; otherwise, it refers to the Moon’s son (Buddha), the Self, and the Creator (Brahmā). (36)

The word *ṭaḥ* is masculine when meaning a crow, smoke, a bow, a ray, or sound; it refers to a door-panel and a whirlpool, and to a son. However, *ṭā* is feminine when meaning a female elephant or a suffix. (37)
Ṭhaḥ is for Śaṅkara in the great meditation; ṭhaṃ is for the neuter [deity] in the lunar orb.
Furthermore, for paralyzing and daring acts, there are three [syllables]: śūnya, īśa, ṭha, indu, and ṭhe. (Verse 38)

The letter *ḍa* is masculine when meaning Vijayeśa, Śambhu, laughter, protection, a friend, sound, the sound of a conch, and the heroic sentiment (*raudrarasa*); it is feminine when meaning firm speech and a follower;
(39) it is neuter when meaning a thunderbolt, a fortress, a cloth, and a small drum (*ḍamaruka*).

The sound *ḍha* occurs in the word *andolanetu* (in the sense of "in the movement"), *triṣu* ("in the three genders"), and *dṛḍhe* ("in the firm"). (40) *Ḍha* is used for a pole with a projection (*viśaṅga*), in times of fear, and for one who is passionate (*rāgī*). *Nā* refers to the sound of a *pāṇḍu* drum. *Ḍhakkā* is feminine; *piḍha* is neuter and denotes knowledge as well as the mouth of a musical instrument (*tūryamukha*). (41)

The word *ṇa* (ṇakāra) denotes a man, a paramour, a bell, and a sound; it is used in the sense of the threefold restraint (*niyama*), that which is hidden, and that which is gentle, as well as for the left and right paths. 42.
The word *dhenu* is used for a female cow, a river, and compassion; *ṇam* refers to a lotus petal and knowledge; and *triṇu* denotes a thing that is free from husks. (43)

The word *ta* denotes masculine conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and certainty (*niścaya*); it occurs in the sense of "going" (*yātu*), foot-ornament (*pādavidhi*), and theft (*caura*). However, when meaning compassion (*karuṇā*), it is feminine.
The word *ta* is used in the sense of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtārtha*) in all three genders; as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it signifies cause (*hetu*).

The word *śabda* is feminine when it means "playing" (*krīḍana*), and [it is] like the base word (*abhidheyavat*) when it means "instrument of play" (*krīḍaka*). (45) *Tis* is feminine when it means "thirst" (*pipāsā*) or "water" (*payaḥ*); *tha* is masculine in the sense of "enemy" (*ari*), "mountain" (*giri*), and "moon" (*indu*);
this [word *ti*] is feminine when it means "river" (*taraṅgiṇī*), and neuter when it means "protection from fear" (*bhayanivāraṇa*). (46)
The word *vācya* (to be expressed) takes all genders; *dhavala* means white or grey; *prathula* means large.
The root *da* is masculine in the sense of giving and cutting; as a feminine noun, *dā* signifies patience and giving. (47)
The word *da* is used for a eunuch, drinking, dispassion, and the observation of one's wife;
it is a term with varying genders (*bhedyaliṅga*) when meaning mute, auspicious, beneficial, melting, and pure.
(48) It is used for vision, knowledge, eyes, and for women who have seen their menses.
The letter *dha* occurs in the words *puṃsindau* (the moon), *dhvani* (sound), *dhvāna* (roar), *śrīdeya* (a name), *anvantara* (another), and *ghaṭa* (a jar). || 49 ||
The word *dhī* denotes the end of a lute (*vyāmanidhana*), sound, and intellect; it is feminine when meaning "thought" or "wisdom.
The word *dhūḥ* refers to incense, trembling, wealth, a burden, and the front of a battle. (50)
The word *heramba* denotes a man and not a woman; it refers to the navel, wisdom, and the two increases (*vṛdhau*).

The word *vakṣyam* is used for the subtle, the unafflicted, the void, and the undivided, but not for women. (51) The particle *nu* is used in the sense of praise (*stuti*) and may denote a woman; *nau* signifies a boat and a place of crossing.
The word *paḥ* is masculine when it means wind, time, light, the Kaustubha gem, or a moment (52).
It is neuter when it means an auspicious planetary conjunction (*lagna*), a row, gold, water, or the act of drinking.
It is feminine when it means intelligence, nectar, or agreement (53).

The word *phā* is used for women, distress, and being pleased; *pu* is used for a city, a woman, a body, filling, and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (Line 54) *Pho* is used for a gale, clapping, the syllable *pha*, warding off, and battle.
And in the case of harsh speech from one's wife, as well as in the case of the peacock and the huts. 55.

Now, the word *pha* denotes the remote (*parokṣa*) tone and has all genders as its referent; *ba* denotes the neuter, Varuṇa, the ocean, and according to the opinion of Guru, it also denotes optionality. (56)
*Vibhūti* means ash; *kāra* means quarrel; *pakṣin* means bird; *garbha* means the interior of a womb; and *parvan* means a festival day. (p. 18a, F.
4b, 1st line) *Bāstrī*, *kāhlī*, and *vallī* mean a chain; *svamala* means one's own impurity; these three [words] are used in the feminine gender. 57.
The term *bha* denotes Śambhu (Śiva), the absence of passion (*arāga*), and in the sense of water, it is masculine when referring to Venus (*śukra*) and the moon (*añjala*).

*Bhā* signifies adornment (*alaṅkṛti*) and radiance (*dīpti*); as a feminine noun, it refers to light (*karaṇa*) and effort (*yatna*). In the neuter, however, it means the sky (*gagana*), a sign of the zodiac (*rāśi*), a father (*tātuya*), and the two types of *puṇḍra* and *cakra*.
The word *bhī* is feminine in the sense of fear; it is masculine when meaning a bird (*khaga*). Let there be *sthāna* (abode) in the neuter, and *bhrama* (error) in the feminine.
|| 59 || *Maḥ* is masculine when meaning Śambhu, Dhātṛ, or the Moon; *māḥ* is also masculine when meaning the month.
*Mā* is feminine in the sense of measure (*māna*) or death (*mṛta*). *Velā*, *medhā*, and *śrī* are feminine; *madhya* is of three genders. || 60 ||
The word *mā* is used in the sense of intoxication (*madya*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), and as a verb meaning "to produce" (*janetu*); it is not neuter.
It is also used in the sense of "man" (*pumsabandha*), and in the sense of the two colors *piṅga* (tawny) and *adhigala* (throatless). 61.
The word *yā* is used in the senses of abandonment (*tyāga*), treasure (*nidhi*), wind (*vāyu*), the son of Yayāti (*yāyāta*), and the Creator (*dhātṛ*);
it is also used for a journey (*yātrā*), a vehicle (*yāna*), and for non-decay (*ajaya*), as well as for beauty (*śobhā*), fortune (*lakṣmī*), and exit (*nirgamana*).
(62) The word *ya*, which is called a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), is used [as a relative pronoun] with respect to women; the indeclinable *yat* is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).

The word *yu* is used in the sense of "celestial sphere" (*nāka*), "day" (*diva*), and "fire" (*vahnih*); as a feminine noun, it denotes "one's own" (*sva*) and "heaven" (*dyau*). The word *ru* is masculine and denotes "fire" (*pāvaka*), "desire" (*kāma*), "destruction" (*īkṣaya*), "thunderbolt" (*vajra*), and "conduct" (*vṛtti*). 64.

The word *raṃ* is used in the neuter for blood, the head, meditation, the sky, and the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) in the eyes; [it is also used] in the royal golden hall and in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the time of sunset. 65.
The word *va* occurs in the sense of "mouth" and "fear"; *vi* in the three senses of "distaste," "effort," and "sharpness";
*ra* in praise, wealth, and gold; the sound *ri* denotes "well-examined";
*ru* denotes a woman, flame, desire, and beauty; and *ri* occurs in the sense of battle and sound.
O you who desire women, O you whose body is like that of a woman, O you who possess a beautiful form, O you who can assume any form at will! 67.

The word *śrī* denotes dress, arrangement, splendor, and prosperity; it refers to the *sarala* tree, speech, and the *lavaṅga* flower; and it is found in *viṣa* (poison) and *bilva* (the wood-apple tree), as well as in three genders. 68.
The syllable *ja* is used for matted hair (*jaṭā*), filling (*prāpūraṇa*), the female organ (*strīhṛt*), the moon (*soma*), a limb (*aṅga*), and the throat (*gala*)—it is feminine.
*Laṃ* is used for the ears and eyes (*karṇanetra*), taking (*ādāna*)—it is feminine—and for the lord of serpents (*indra*) and salt (*lavaṇa*). *Tula* refers to a balance scale (*tulā*). (69)
The term *saṃ* denotes a male (*pumān*) when referring to conciliation (*sāṃtvena*), wind (*vāyau*), time (*samaye*), Varuṇa (*varuṇe*), and Smara (*smare*).

The term *viḥ* denotes the eye (*cakṣuṣi*), the sky (*vyomni*), falling (*pāte*), the Supreme Self (*paramātmani*), and a bird (*pakṣiṇi*). The term *vai* denotes sprinkling (*secane*) and also a person (*puruṣe*). Furthermore, in sequence, these [terms] are used in the masculine (*puṃsi*) and the feminine (*striyām*).
The word *sva* is feminine when meaning "sister," masculine when meaning "kinsman" or "wealth," and is used in three genders when meaning "one's own" or "self. (71)
The words *svar*, *vyoman*, *tridiva*, and *tviṣ* are feminine when denoting "splendor" or "flame.
The terms *valka*, *elavāluka*, *elā*, *tvaca*, and *tvak* are feminine when referring to the "door" or its "adjuncts. (72)

It [the word *śiva*] is used for an anthill (*valmīka*), a tortoise (*kūrma*), the earth (*bhūmi*), one who has performed good deeds (*sukṛtin*), (line 5) one capable of ritual worship of the gods according to the scriptures (*śāstrīya-devapūjā*), power (*śakti*), beauty (*śobhā*), and tranquility (*avara*). ||73||
*Ramā* is used for the goddess Lakṣmī, the letter *śa*, the neuter gender, the Śāstra of Agni (the Āgama), and the auspicious planet Mars;
*śrī* is used for the season, the rainbow, and heaven. *Īśaḥ* has three genders when used in the sense of "beyond perception.
*Śam* is indeclinable and signifies happiness; *śi* is used for Śambhu, and for the words *śiva* and *śānti*.
The word *ṣa* is used in the senses of Nirvāṇa, injury, sleep, heaven, and sexual intercourse;
(75). It is feminine in the sense of a woman skilled in the arts (*śāstrīramā*), neuter in the sense of a womb, liberation, and conclusion;
it is also triliṅga (of all three genders) in the sense of endurance. The word *ravi* denotes the remote and the excellent. (76).
The word *sa* is used for "man," "the son of Umā" (Kārttikeya), and "wind"; it is used for "body" and "splendor" in the feminine;
and *sam* is used in the neuter for "cow," as well as for "knowledge," "sound," and "prohibition. (77)

The word *sat* is used in three genders: it denotes one who serves, the best, and the virtuous. (Second line) *Sat* is neuter in the sense of "truth. The root *sū* signifies impelling and the delivery of a fetus. 78.
The word *se* may mean "sacrifice" (*savana*), "woman" (*strī*), or "servant" (*sevaka*), according to its denotation.
*Ha* refers to Śaṅkara, Hari, the swan (*haṃsa*), movement (*raṇa*), horripilation (*romāñca*), and horses (*vājin*).
*He* denotes pride (*garva*) and Pracetas; as for *he*, it signifies abandonment (*tyāga*), movement (*gati*), and the lute (*vīṇā*).
The word *haṃ* denotes a eunuch, one who is not a woman, and one who is happy; it also refers to a sound and the rays of a jewel. || 80 ||
The syllable *bā* occurs with the mantra *barhāma*, while *yo* is used in the sense of "three," "earth," "intoxicated," and "laughter.
*Kṣaḥ* is used for "obstruction" and "opposition," as well as for "forgiveness" and "sleep. (81)
The word *kṣāstra* is used in the sense of patience (*kṣamā*) and sleep (*nidrā*); *kṣam* is neuter; *kṣetra* refers to a field and a Rakṣasa.
(5th line) The gender of a word's usage is sometimes disregarded when it has not been previously established. 82.
In the case of monosyllabic words, this should be inferred by those who know the intended meaning (*lakṣya*).
Hari Om. (Written by hand) (The year of Vikṛti; the month of Mārgaśīrṣa = 21st day). Hari Om.
(Ṣide heading) || [The Rākṣoghna Homa] ||

Now I shall explain [the procedure for] the preceptor and others: having bathed, one should perform the application of sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*). Having gone to the east, north, or south of the temple, and having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, one should worship Vināyaka. Having caused the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formula and having sprinkled [the site], one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*staṇḍila*) with sesame, rice, and *śāli* grains. Having drawn a lotus and adorned it with threads, cloth, and other ornaments, one should place a water-pot (*kuṃbha*) and arrange eight or nine jars starting from the east.
In the central jar: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Kālāgnirudra; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Kālāgni. (4th line) Meditation:
[He holds] a skull-bowl, a hand-drum, a trident, and likewise an axe.
Bearing a most formidable form, three-eyed and moon-crested,
with a face made crooked by a frown and terrifying with bared fangs—
may that Lord of great splendor devour the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the like.

The wise practitioner should contemplate [the deity] as resembling the fire of the submarine mare (*baḍavāmukha*), having a form like ten million suns, and similar to Kālāgnirudra. Having meditated thus, one should invoke [the deity] with the root mantra, and perform the rites of installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), sealing the sacrificial pit (*avakuṇḍana*), and the cow-seal (*dhenu-mudrā*), and so forth.

Having displayed the five mudrās, [one should offer] into the vases starting from the east: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅga Bhairava; obeisance to Ruru Bhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa Bhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Krodha Bhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Unmatta Bhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kapāla Bhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīṣaṇa Bhairava.*

(4th line) *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Saṃhārabhairava.* Having thus worshipped the eight Bhairavas, on both their sides (5th line), having consecrated two sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) and placed a cloth upon them, having set a coconut on the south and a sword on the north (6th line),
one should worship Śiva along with his retinue and the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) and so forth within the coconut; [then] the enclosure of the sword.
Oṃ, salutation to Mahādevī. Oṃ, salutation to Vāgdevī. Oṃ, salutation to Pārvatī.

Oṃ, salutation to Kṛttikāyinī. Oṃ, salutation to Mahocchiṣṭā. Oṃ, salutation to Raktaśakti. Oṃ, salutation to Kālikā. Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍikā. In the midst of the sword: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vīraśakti. Oṃ, salutation to Khaḍgāsanā.
Oṃ, salutation to the one whose form is the sword. (Meditation:
He who holds a formidable skull in his hand, is clothed in a tiger skin, possesses a face resplendent with a loud laugh, and has a voice as resonant as a thundercloud.
Having thus meditated upon Khaḍgeśa— who wears red earrings and armlets and resembles a blazing fire— the most excellent knower of mantras should offer worship.

Having performed the root-anuvāhana, āsthāpana, and other rites, together with the ancillaries, and having worshipped [the deity], one should touch the water-pot (*kumbha*) and recite the two *śānti* mantras. Having prepared a nine-square grid (*navakoṣṭha*) in front of the pot, one should worship Kālāgnirudra in the center with "Oṃ, obeisance to Kālāgnirudra," including his retinue (*sāvaraṇa*). Then, in the squares starting from the east, [one should worship] with "Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī."

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Māheśvarī; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kaumārī; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vaiṣ� red meat as an offering with their respective mantras. Then, having performed the rites beginning with the establishment of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) in that [fire] to its east—

Having worshipped Kālāgnirudra along with his retinue in the heart-lotus of the fire, and having then offered clarified butter while reciting the *anuvāka* beginning with "kṛṇuṣva vāja," (3rd line) and having again offered seeds of cotton mixed with sesame, [one should offer]: *oṃ dahāśaso svāhā*; *oṃ śarmasvāhā*;
*oṃ atratyāvāḥ svāhā*; (4th line) *oṃ bhuvasvāhā*; *oṃ atra svāhā*; *oṃ suvasvāhā*; *oṃ atra svāhā*.

"Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā. Having recited this three times and offered the *sampāta* oblation, he offers clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra beginning "ye devāḥ purasadaḥ" and ending with "rakṣoghne svāhā. Then, in front of the fire, he offers a bali of red food with the words "vṛṣṭivāhiradho dakṣiṇā svāhā. [Then follows] "devasya tvā... and so forth, up to the *bhūta*.

Having performed the protection as before with the *vyāhṛtis*, having recited [the mantra] three times, having offered the *sampātāhuti* oblation, having first offered [an oblation] with the root mantra, and having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with "Svāhā," having given the internal and external offerings (*antarbali* and *bahirbali*), having united the deity residing in the fire with the pitcher, having united the deity in the pitcher with one's own heart, and having united the *sampātājya* with the water in the pitcher, [one should offer] the sword and the trident.

Having placed [the offerings] in the hand of the attendant, [the officiant], standing before [the deity], sprinkles the entire abode, beginning with the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), with water from the jar while reciting the *pavamāna* mantra. [The ritual procedure for the fire-offering that destroys demons is completed. Hariḥ Om.
Regarding the *liṅga*, they say there are thirty forms (*mūrti*) and images (*pratimā*), whether made of stone, metal, or wood, according to one's capacity;

some say it has breasts, while others say its life-force (*jīva*) resides in the head, the *sthūpikā*, or the nose. This is the consecration of cloth paintings (*paṭa-pratiṣṭhā*), according to the *Citra-śrotra*.
On the head of Īśa, in the middle of the trident, on the peak, in the hollows, on the shoulders, on the spear, on the top of the chariot, on the horns of the bull, and at the tips of the banner—
on these parts of the stone, water, and iron [images], the breasts always reside as their vital essence; likewise, the Ganges resides in the water as the goddess Lakṣmī.

One should reside on the islands during the lunar days (*tithi*). For the purpose of warding off misfortune (*alakṣmī*), one should perform an oil massage and a bath. In the other months beginning with Āśvina, and during the fortnights, at the times of dawn (*aruṇodaya*), bathing in warm oil in waters of sand is indeed marvelous and equal to the Gaṅgā; it brings satisfaction. And on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Avayuj, [one should bathe] in both [types of water].
Men who fear hell should perform an oil-bath (abhyaṅga-snāna). On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, those two great men,
Narakāsura and Martya, should practice the oil-bath.

The preparatory rite (*pūrakarman*): [one should place] rice, grains, *śāli* rice, well-prepared *kuśa* grass, mung beans, the three salts, *kuśa*, and unbroken grains upon the belly, face, eyes, feet, navel, heart, throat, forehead, and head.
[This is] that which is produced from Śiva and Śakti, the cause of the world’s origin.
The sowing of seeds here is said to bring about the culmination of the activities of those who possess the intellect of a bull;
the gift of salt is declared to produce personal creation and happiness.
A daughter should be given in marriage, as well as gold and the gift of clothing.
Gold is for the protection of the world; clothing increases one’s progeny.
Therefore, the gift of a cow brings happiness to all living beings. (The cause is...)

Kṛsarā rice, along with salt and powdered sesame, served as an oblation for the Maghore [rite], and that oil used for sprinkling becomes a source of delight for Rudra. During the festival of consecration (*pratiṣṭhotsava*), such items are difficult to obtain in the absence of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
"And sesame oil should be prepared; one should especially offer it as a burnt oblation (homa). Thus, in the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa].
In the absence of ghee, sesame oil is pure for the purification of food;
likewise, that which is mixed with Marīci and Sindhu is said here to be pure.
(Kāmika-tantra)
One should have cakes and other foods cooked with ghee or sesame oil;
one should avoid coconut oil and any other oils.
At the time of the lamp-worship, one should carry the lamp [to the designated place].
Having recited the *aghora-astra* mantra ten times, one should again light the lamp.
(Seventh line) [Rumvari] That oil. [Pullaḍi] (P.23a, F.2b, 1st line) || The procedure for the food offering (*naivedya*).
I shall describe the two kinds of food offerings that are auspicious and pleasing to me;
listen with faith, O Goddess, for they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
May all undertakings be successful, and may this grant all forms of prosperity. (21)
To Īśāna, however, pure rice; to Puruṣa, rice with molasses.
One should offer *kṛsarānna* to Aghora and likewise *mudgānna* to the northern [face]; to the western [face], one should present *pāyasānna* to the five-faced [Lord].
At the end of the cooked offerings, salt, black pepper, and *muṇḍa* should also be offered.
Thus, pure food mixed with ghee has been proclaimed by the wise.
Half a measure of rice, half of that in split mung beans, half of that in galam, and half of that combined with ghee and salt—this is *gulodana*. ||24||
At the conclusion of cooking the *śivataṇḍula* rice, it is filled with salt;
there is half a *prastha* of sesame powder and an equal amount of sesame oil.
Thus, in the southern face, kṛsarānnam is prescribed here.
Half a measure of rice and half a measure of mung beans, combined with ghee, and salt at the end of cooking— this is mung-bean porridge (mudgānna), which is likewise offered in the northern face.
Three parts rice, one part milk, half as much water, and half as much split mung beans;
this is the *pāyasa* (milk-rice) food in the western direction.
(27) [In the north] there is the *śivataṇḍula* (Śiva-rice) food, the *tintriṇī* fruit, and the fruit of the directions.
One *prastha* of sesamum seeds yields [one] *kuḍuba* and a half of oil; [the same measure] for mustard seeds.

One should offer to the goddesses black nimba leaves, dried leaves, and salt combined; likewise, one should present the food of tamarind. Half a *prastha* of *śivataṇḍula* rice and powdered *māṣa* beans are thus prescribed.
Half of that, mixed with ghee and combined with salt.
In this way, *gaurī* is said to consist of *māṣa*-grains. (29) [The offering] for *jaṃbhīra* and *elaka* consists of curd-rice combined with ginger and sea salt, along with ginger.
One should offer to the God, at the time of sunrise and other such occasions, flowers that have not been used before, are not stale, and consist of eight types;
(201) as well as half a portion of *śivataṇḍula* rice and *mudga* beans that are neither split nor deficient.
Twenty pieces of sugar-candy and coconut mixed with powder,
along with ghee for the back-filling and combined with salt and cardamom powder at the end of cooking— this is called *citrānna*. 211.
One should avoid food that is overcooked or undercooked, excessively hot or excessively cold, as well as food containing hair, stones, or living organisms;
for such things cause disease of the stomach, abdominal tumors, and likewise diseases of the glands.
Consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, and the occurrence of fevers and other diseases [are thus prevented]. ||212||
Milk, molasses, honey, oil, curd, and ghee—these six flavors, together with food itself, are here called "food of the six flavors. (213)
One should extract its essence, which is endowed with five cobra hoods and equal to the Milk Ocean, as much as is required for the meal of the gods. (214)
Just as watering the root of a tree nourishes the leaves and the stalks, so too should one offer the root-liṅga that has been enjoyed by the deity. 215.
The essence of the wood-apple fruit lasts as long as it is consumed by an elephant;
one should grasp that essence until it is enjoyed by the gods.
216. [Characteristics of the Mudrās]
It brings joy to the gods and likewise puts the asuras to flight;
because it causes their delight (modana) and their fleeing (drāvaṇa), this is proclaimed as the Mudrā.
Having placed those two below, one should not bind the hand-gestures (kara-mudrā).
Then, O Śambhu, when presenting the gestures, one should display them at the region of the heart.
In the Siddhānta:
from the thumbs, both ears; with the index fingers, the two eyes;
and with the middle fingers, one should firmly bind the pair of nostrils.
This is indeed the "making six-faced" (*ṣaṇmukhīkaraṇa*); one should employ it in the rites of bathing.
Having released the right hand, the index finger is likewise bent.
The fist-mudrā of Aindra and that of Ākuśa are as follows:
in the Vīratantra,
one should place both hands palm-upward and join the wrists.
Then one should place the right hand above the left hand;
then one should place the right [hand] above the left thumb;
then one should place the right thumb above the left thumb.
One should make a hollow in the middle and have it [the width] of one finger;
this shall be the *kumbha-mudrā*, which one should employ at the time of bathing.
(Kālottara, P.25a, F.1b, 1st line)

Having placed both hands palm-upward, with the thumbs and both index fingers [extended] and the remaining [fingers] indeed clenched into fists, this is proclaimed as the food mudrā (*annamudrā*). (2nd line) Amśumati.
Having placed [the ring finger] of the left hand upon the navel-mandala,
one should join that very [finger] with the thumb of the right hand.
Having extended both hands, one should place the right thumb in the mouth;
this is declared to be the *pariyā* [mudrā], which destroys the burden of evil.

Bhojadeva states that the *utthānamudrā* consists of the hands being turned upward with the fists clenched, as in the case of the *vahni* (fire) and other gestures. In the *Suprabheda*, however, it is described as the bases of the palms being joined together at the region of the heart.

Having formed the lowest *yantā* with the hand, this [mudrā] becomes the *śodhanī*. (5th line) Having joined both hands together and likewise leaving a hollow space in the middle, this *mudrā*, shaped like a lotus bud, is known as the *mukulī*. (6th line)
The two index fingers should be bent and placed upon the fire;
the thumbs should rest on the heads of those two, while the remaining fingers are level and joined at their tips.
Having formed the wrist-bands on the left, one should likewise place them on the right;
this mudrā, known as *śaśikarṇa*, is to be employed in the ritual of sacrifice.
All [fingers] are interlaced with one another, joined at the tips over the backs of the hands.
One should make a hollow space between the fingers and the thumb within the hand;
one should employ this in the ritual of worship with the Gāyatrī,
for the sake of the cause.
Having formed a fist with the fingers pointing upward, one should encircle it with the left hand;
this is renowned as the *liṅgamudrā*, and it should be displayed when [the enemy] has been cut down.

Having formed a *añjali* with both hands, one should join the two ring fingers at their tips; the remaining fingers are said to be extended. This is the *dravya-mudrā*; one should display it in the absence of the actual substance, or when the substance itself is unavailable.
Having placed the two hands palm-upward with the little fingers and thumbs joined,
the index and middle fingers extended and positioned crosswise,
with the left hand turned over the right— this is proclaimed as the Vajra-mudrā.
The two index fingers extended and long, proclaimed as being in the position of a staff;
one should display the two index fingers pointing upward.
From the joining of the other thumb with the other index finger.
This shall be the *pāśa-mudrā*; if it is the *pāśa*, it is the cause.
Having placed both hands face-up, with the two middle fingers extended and joined, and the other fingers joined together facing inward, this is proclaimed as the *gadā-vyodha*.
The mudrā is proclaimed when the little finger and the thumb are joined;
when blazing,
the two little fingers are bent, while the left hand goes elsewhere.
The left thumb and little finger are positioned on the right [hand],
and the right thumb is likewise positioned there; the index, middle, and ring fingers of both hands are bent inward.
The supreme teacher, having formed the lotus [mudrā], should display the pericarp (karṇikā). Having placed the two hands palms upward and specifically formed fists,
he should insert the two thumbs into the middle and join the two little fingers extended outward.
The seed-seal (bījamudrā) has been fully explained; one should display it to one who possesses power.
Having turned the two hands palms upward, the wise one should bind them at the base of the palms;
having placed the tips of the thumbs upon the head, he should extend the two index fingers.
The tips of the two ring fingers are joined together, especially at their faces;
the two little fingers are said to be joined, and the two middle fingers are then extended.
This is declared to be the *āsani* (seated) mudrā; those who know the procedure for the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) should wrap the tip of the left index finger with the right [hand],
place the thumb upward, and join it at the heart.
One should place the middle finger at the tip of the ring finger and rest it upon the left thumb;
with the little finger extended from the mouth, this is proclaimed as the Dhvaja-mudrā.
One should manifest the presence of the deity during the hoisting of the banners,
having formed a fist with the tips of the fingers specifically turned upward.

And the two [hands] joined at the tips of the thumbs, with the *kālakarṇa* [finger] applied, are the *varā*. Bhojadeva says: having formed an *añjali* with both hands, by joining the ring fingers, the little fingers, and the thumbs, it is the *āvāhinī*. This same [mudrā], when placed face down, is the *eḍā* and the *sthāpinī*. When the two hands are in the state of fists with the thumbs joined, those very same [hands] with the thumbs inside are the *garbhāṅguṣṭha*.
It is the complete cessation [of breath].
In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
when the middle and little fingers are interlaced and placed upon their own palms.
Having joined the tips of the ring fingers and the index fingers,
and having raised the tips of the thumbs from the root-joints [of those fingers], [the mudrā] is called Manorathā when it is blazing.
Having placed the fingers of both hands interlaced behind the back,
one should lay them across horizontally and join the two thumbs together.

The two index fingers joined at the middle joints, with the ring fingers extended like a flowing stream and joined by the thumbs—this is known as the "five-faced" (pañcamukhī) mudrā; one should display it during the ritual of the faces.
It is bound like a lion (mṛgendrabaddha).
When the two little fingers are touched to one another, and the palms are heard [to be joined],
the two ring fingers and the two middle fingers are extended with their tips joined;
the two index fingers are attached to the backs of the middle fingers and curved at their ends.
The *mudrā* known as *sṛgī* is formed by joining the two thumbs with the tips of the middle fingers. When the two index fingers are well-aligned, the two ring fingers are bent,
and the two thumbs pass behind them, it becomes the *sṛgī* of the left hand.
When the two index fingers of the hands are bent back and joined behind the pair of little fingers,
and when the three [remaining fingers] are pressed together and extended, it is the *śūla* [mudrā].
In the *Kālottara*, one should contract the little finger and the thumb, while extending the remaining fingers;
this is the incense mudrā (*dhūpamudrā*). Now hear the lamp mudrā (*dīpamudrā*) that follows.
One should press the ring finger and middle finger together with the thumb;
then, holding the index fingers upward, one should display the lamp mudrā.
In this [rite of] cause,
one should join the palms; having grasped a handful of flowers with the right hand bent at four finger-breadths, one should offer it at the base of the feet.
O Prajāpati, at the end of the creation, that which is known as Cibukodaka is located on the right wrist of Aṃśumat and above it on the left hand.
One should join the three fingers, beginning with the middle one, at their centers.
One should avoid three flowers joined with the thumb and forefinger;
having avoided those flowers, however, one should [offer] with the *nirodha* mudrā.
In this way, one should perform the *visarjanī* mudrā with the palms joined at the head.
In the *Suprabheda*, having formed the *añjali* with both hands, one should place the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers together.
Then, O Goddess of divine form, one should extend the remaining [fingers] upward;
O Mistress of the Gods, having joined the two hands together with their palms facing downward in this manner within the lineage.
Placing the palms upward with the middle of the thumbs resting [on each other],
it is called *udvāsya* (the rite of dismissal); it accomplishes the purpose of all rites,
as stated in the *Kālottara*.
Having placed both hands palm-upward, with the thumbs and index fingers [extended] and the remaining two fingers joined in a fist,
this is proclaimed as the food mudrā (annamudrā).
Having placed the *Aṃśumatī* [finger] upon the circle of the little finger of the left hand,
one should join that very same [finger] with the left thumb of the right hand.
Having extended both hands, one should place the right thumb into the mouth;
this is declared to be the *paridheya* [mudrā], which destroys the burden of evil.
Bhojadeva states that *mudrā* arises from the casting of fire and other substances into a loose, open fist;
this is found in the *Suprabheda*.

Having joined the bases of the two hands together at the region of the heart, and having made the thumbs [pressed] against one another, this hand-mudrā, when performed, becomes purifying. Having brought the two hands together as one, with a hollow space between them...
This mudrā, shaped like a lotus bud, is known as the Mukula. One should bend the two index fingers and place their tips upon the heads of the two thumbs;
the remaining fingers should be held straight and level.
Having placed [the hands] at the wrists, one on the left and the other on the right,
this mudrā is to be known as the *karṇatī*, which serves for the purpose of sacrifice.
All [fingers] are interlaced, with the tips joined against the backs of the hands.
One should make the thumbs and fingers hollow; the others are said to be the bringers of death.
In the rite of worship, one should employ the Gāyatrī with the Gāyatrī mantra. As for the mudrā: having formed a fist with the thumb pointing upward, one should encircle it with the left hand.
This is renowned as the *liṅgamudrā*; when asked, one should display it.
Having formed the *añjali* with both hands, with the thumbs and ring fingers placed together at the mouth, their tips joined, and the remaining fingers extended outward from them.
This is the *dravyamudrā*; one should display it during the distribution of the sacrificial substances (*dravyabhāga*).
Having turned both hands palm-upward, the little fingers and thumbs are joined;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are extended and positioned sideways.

The Vajra-mudrā is proclaimed as being performed with the right hand moving to the left; the index finger is extended behind [the thumb], which is proclaimed as being like a staff. Having placed the palm facing downward, one likewise moves the arm.
Known as the Sword Mudrā, one should display it at the beginning of worship and other rites;
having turned the hands upward, one should specifically form a fist.
Extending the thumb and index finger, one should display [the gesture] upwards;
the other thumb and index finger [are joined] through the union with the other thumb.
This shall be the *pāśa-mudrā* if it is intended for the purpose of binding.
Having placed both hands face upwards, with the middle fingers extended and joined together, this is declared to be the *bīja-mudrā*; one should display it when conceiving of the *śakti*.
Having turned the hands upward, one should bind them at the base of the palms;
placing the tips of the thumbs upon the head, the wise one should join the tips of the ring fingers together,
especially so that they meet at the mouth.
When the two little fingers are turned upward and joined, and the two middle fingers are extended,
the wise know this as the "seated" (āsīna) pose in the ritual of the lion-throne (siṃhāsana).
One should wrap the tip of the left index finger with the right;
having placed the thumb upward, one should join it at the heart.
One should place the middle finger upon the tip of the ring finger and rest it on the left thumb;
with the little finger extended from the mouth, this is proclaimed as the Dhvaja-mudrā (Banner Seal).
One should display it in the presence of the deity during the hoisting of banners.
Having formed a fist with the palms turned upward,
specifically with the tips of the fingers joined together at the tips of the thumbs— this is the excellent *kālakaṇṭha* [mudrā], according to Bhojadeva.
Having formed a fist with the two hands joined face-to-face with the thumbs, it is called *kālakaṇṭhaka*.
(4th line) Having placed the two hands palm-upward, the fingers are interlaced; here, the right ring finger is placed obliquely across the left ring finger. (5th line)
The tips of the ring fingers are extended toward the palms, while the two index fingers are distinguished [by being raised];
the middle fingers are joined together, as are the little fingers. Placing the thumbs at the sides of the bases of the index fingers, they form the añjali gesture.

This shall be the Śaṅkha-mudrā; one should display it at the time of bathing. Having placed the two hands palm upwards, one should form a braid (*veṇi-bandha*). With the two middle fingers extended and joined, it is proclaimed as the Śiva-mudrā.
Having turned the hands palm-upward, one should form the *veṇībandha* (braided) gesture.
Then, with the little fingers and index fingers extended and joined together,
one should display this *Sadāśivāvyāsa* mudrā at the conclusion of the invocation.
Having turned the hands upward, one should form the *veṇibandha* (bamboo-joint) position;
having extended the middle fingers and thumbs, the little fingers should be joined together.
At the conclusion of the installation, one should display this mudrā of Maheśvara:
having placed the two hands palm-upward with the thumbs positioned in the middle of the palms,
one should interlace them so that the two index fingers are joined and slightly bent.
This shall be the Paraśu-mudrā, which crushes all enemies.
Having turned the hands upward and specifically formed the fist-bind,
one should draw [the hand] toward the left ear with the right hand.
This is the Dhanurmudrā, which crushes all enemies;
having turned the hands palms-upward, one skilled in binding should form fists.
Having extended the two middle fingers, one should direct them downward and upward;
the tips joined together, the left [hand] upward and the right [hand] downward.
The remaining [fingers] and the two bent ones are proclaimed as being in the position of the arrow-mudrā. Having placed both hands palm-upward, one should form the bond of the bamboo (veṇibandha).
Then, having extended the two middle fingers, the remaining [fingers] should be made into earrings (kuṇḍala).
This shall be the Ghaṇṭā-mudrā, which destroys and dispels their obstacles.
Having turned the two hands palms-upward and interlacing them, one should bend both thumbs; this is proclaimed as the Sṛk-mudrā.
Having turned the hands upward and joined the little fingers with the thumbs,
while interlacing the remaining fingers, this is proclaimed as the Śiromudrā (Head Mudrā). Having turned the hands upward and pressed the index fingers against the thumbs...

The remaining [fingers] are pressed against one another; this is proclaimed as the *śikhā-mudrā*. Having placed the two hands palms-upward, with the index fingers and thumbs concealed, the remaining [fingers] joined and pressed together, one should form the *veṇibandha* (flute-binding).
With the thumbs tucked in between, the little fingers extended and joined together—
this shall be the Vāmamudrā, which wards off all enemies.
Having turned the hands upward, the index fingers are joined with the thumbs.

From the remaining [fingers], the *jughānā* is likewise proclaimed as the *netramudrā*. (7th line) Having placed the two hands face upward with the two palms joined together, and by joining the thumbs and index fingers, it is proclaimed as the *astramudrā*. (P.31a, F.7b, 1st line)
Having turned the hands palm-upward, one should form the *veṇibandha* (bamboo-knot) gesture;
with both thumbs extended halfway, this is proclaimed as the *mudrāprakīrttagatā*.
Having placed both hands palms upward, one should form the *veṇībandha* (braided) gesture;
extending the two middle fingers halfway, it is declared to be the mudrā named Aghora.
Having turned the hands palm-upward, one should form the *veṇī-bandha*;
extending both index fingers halfway constitutes the *tatpuruṣa* mudrā.
Having turned the hands upward and placed the *veṇibandha* behind the back,
with the two little fingers extended halfway, this is proclaimed as the mudrā of Īśāna.
In the Svāyambhuva [mudrā],
the tips of the index finger and thumb are joined; this is proclaimed as the *śānti* (pacification) mudrā,
which the wise practitioner should employ for the installation of mantras.
In the *Kālottara*, having placed the two hands palm-upward, with the index finger and thumb joined together,
one should form a fist with the remaining fingers and display the Śaśāṅka mudrā.
Having turned the hands palms-upward, one should join the wrists;
having extended both thumbs, one should extend the little fingers.
This shall be the Bull Mudrā (*vṛṣamudrā*), which bestows the fruit of all ritual actions (*sarvakarmaphala*).
O Six-faced One (*ṣaḍānana*), having turned the hands upward and formed fists, [this is it].
One should extend the right hand over the left back and the left hand forward;
this is the Khaḍvāṅga mudrā, which destroys all sins.
Having placed both hands palm-upward, one should place the left hand upon the other.
Having slightly bent both arms, one should display the *kapāla-mudrā*. Having placed the two hands palms upward, one should form the shape of a lute (*vīṇā*);
having extended the little fingers and thumbs, the tips should be like earrings.
O Six-faced One, this is the supreme mudrā of the Nāgas known as Ḍāmavyākhyā;
O Six-faced One, when both hands are extended with the tips slightly bent,
the wise know this to be the Bhikṣā (alms-begging) mudrā on the right side.

O Six-faced One, by extending the right [hand] while keeping it slightly bent, this becomes the Grāma-mudrā; it accomplishes all desired aims for these [deities]. And whatever mudrā is prescribed for the right [hands] of those beginning with Dhvaja, it should be performed in that very manner.
For a Śūdra it is in the left hand, but never for those of the lowest castes (antyaja).
Having placed both hands with palms upward, the thumbs are concealed between the fingers;
the fingers are extended and slightly bent.
This mudrā, which causes all grains to increase,
is formed by placing both hands palms upward, with the fingers and joints [joined].
With the tips of the fingers slightly bent, it is proclaimed as the water mudrā (*udakamudrā*);
likewise, there are the ghee mudrā, the milk mudrā, the curd mudrā, and the honey mudrā.
Extending both hands from the index finger to the little finger so that they face each other,
one should place the right thumb upon the index finger and likewise the [left] thumb upon the [right] index finger;
this *akṣasūtra* mudrā is especially recommended at the time of recitation.
Having turned the hands upward, one should extend those two remaining fingers. (4th line) Having raised them upward, one should cast down the "Parasenā-stambha" (army-paralysis) mudrā;
and having raised the "Jaya" (victory) mudrā, the mantra-practitioner should cast those [down]. (5th line)
The thumb and index finger joined together are proclaimed as the golden mudrā;
through the joining of the middle finger and the thumb, it is proclaimed as the silver mudrā.
The thumb and ring finger joined together—this is proclaimed as that mudrā.
The mudrās of the diamond, ruby, emerald, and pearl are thus proclaimed.
Having extended the fingers from the index to the little finger while the thumbs are bent,
one should then open both fists and conceal the tips of the thumbs within them.

When the thumb and middle finger are joined together and the remaining fingers are bent downwards, this becomes the *vrihī-mudrā*; when combined with the mantra, it becomes inexhaustible. This is the *paśu-mudrā*, which [is used for] all four-footed animals in every respect.
The middle of the thumb and index finger, while the remaining fingers are bound in a fist.
This shall be the fragrance mudrā, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
having formed the hands like buds, with each pair [of fingers] interlaced with one another.
This shall be the *arghyamudrā*, which accomplishes all desires and goals;
it consists of all the fingers joined together at their tips like a mantra.
The *nivedya-mudrā* should indeed be formed, and one should display it during the offering (*naivedya*).
One should bind the left and right thumbs together.
This shall be the *śayanamudrā*; one should display it at the time of sleep.
Even those of little merit and *piśācas* are all skilled in [the ritual of] cutting and so forth.
One should join the middle of the thumb with the middle of the index finger;
O Six-faced One, this is the mudrā for sexual union with one's own wife. The wise one should remain positioned with the left thumb at the base of the little finger.
One should place the index finger on the right, and likewise the ring finger on the left; one should properly join all the fingers of the courtesans in this manner.
This may indeed be the Kāmamudrā; one should bring about entry by means of the Guru.
Having placed the two hands in the *uttamāñjali* position, one should press them against the left and right [sides].
With the middle fingers merged into the thumbs, this is the *nidhi-mudrā* for accomplishing one's aims.
Having turned the two hands palms-upward, one should press the two thumbs;
likewise, one should properly press all the fingers together.
One should perform the Dhenu-mudrā, but one must not reveal this secret.
Having turned the two hands palms upward, one should form fists with the little fingers;
by pressing the thumbs on top, it becomes the pustikā-mudrā.
One should show all eleven Rudras the *liṅga-mudrā*,
and one should show the *śūla-mudrā* to the Vasus and the Muktipas.
One should perform obeisance to Gaṇeśa; for the Lords of Knowledge, the trident;
and for the World-Protectors, one should display their respective weapon-mudrās here, each to their own.
He should display the seven classes of attendants along with their own weapons,
as well as the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, and the hosts of Maruts, who are slightly agitated.
Homage is offered to the Asuras, Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, one's own and others' attendants (caraṇas), as well as to the Bhūtas, Piśācas, and Kṣetrapālas;
and specifically to the Liṅga-mudrā, the wives of the Ṛṣis, and the Ṛṣis themselves.
Homage! [There are] the *mudrā-liṅga* (1), the supreme *mudrā* in every respect (2),
the six-faced *mudrā* (3), the hook *mudrā* (4), the jar *mudrā* (5), the ash *mudrā* (6),
the triple-clapping (7), the binding of the directions (8), the triple arrow *mudrā* (9), the great *mudrā* (10), and the purification of the hands (11).
(10) the purification of fragrant substances through mudrās; (11) the visphura-mudrā; (12) the presence of the deity.

The five-faced mudrā (-21), the *sṛk* mudrā (-22), the makara mudrā (-23), the trident (*śūla*) mudrā (-24), the incense (*dhūpa*) mudrā (-25), the lamp (*dīpa*) mudrā (-26), the water-offering with cupped hands (*culukodaka*) mudrā (-27), the dismissal (*visarjana*) mudrā (-28), the substance (*dravya*) mudrā (-29), the rising (*utthāna*) mudrā (-30), the food (*anna*) mudrā (-31), the moat (*parikhā*) mudrā (-32), the purification (*śodhani*) mudrā (-33), and the ear (*karṇa*) mudrā (-34).
