(The Sixteenfold Service)
First is the incense lamp, second is the flower lamp;
the third is the male deer, and the fourth is the serpent.
The fifth is the Vṛṣabha-lamp, and the sixth is the Kuṃbha-lamp;
thereafter one should perform the Ārātrika rite, and likewise the eighth is the Ṛkṣa-lamp.
Ash is the ninth, and the mirror is the tenth;
the parasol is declared the eleventh, and likewise the fly-whisk is the twelfth.
The palm-leaf fan is the thirteenth, and sacrificial altars are the fourteenth.
The directions, the lamps, the ten, the five, and the sixteen with collyrium;
then the three principles (*tattva*) by way of the foot, the head, and the belly, and the ninefold sequence of power (*śakti*);
the stalk and the power in the blazing fire—these three proceed in this order through the two sequences.

Having displayed the *mudrās* of gazing and so forth: at the incense, "Oṃ, homage to Śaṅkara. (6th line) Having whirled it before the tip of the nose with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra: at the lamp, "Oṃ, homage to Brahmā. Having performed the four consecrations (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*) with the *mudrā*: having whirled the lamp over the eyes with the eye-mantra (*netra-mantra*), and having whirled the four consecrations over all the lamps, thereafter [offer] the deer-lamp, the deer-lamp. (P.35b, F.12a, 1st line)

Oṃ, salutation to Sārasvata. Having offered a flower upon the serpent-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to the King of Nagas. Upon the elephant-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Vighneśa. Upon the tiger-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Śāstṛ. Upon the swan-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Caturmukha. Upon the horse-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabhadhvaja. Upon the banner-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Ketu. Upon the trident-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Astrarāja. Upon the bull-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabhadhvaja. Upon the banner-lamp: Oṃ, salutation to Ketu. (Fourth line)

Above the *kukkuṭa* lamp: *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Above the *siṃha* lamp: *oṃ sānduvapakṣirājāya namaḥ*. Above the *sṛk* lamp: *oṃ trimūrttaye namaḥ*. Above the *śakti* lamp: *oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*. Afterwards, the *kuṃbha* lamp, accompanied by the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*): *oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*.

Having worshipped the nine powers of the three principles (*tatvas*) and having caused it to be whirled three times, following the sixteen lamps—whether five, three, or one—with fire: inspection with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkling with the *astra-mantra*, striking with the *astra-mantra*, and sprinkling with the *kavaca-mantra*.

Having performed the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) with [the mantra] ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having worshipped [the deities] together with the five Brahmās and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), as well as the world-protectors (*lokapāla*); having first fully honored Brahmā;

and having worshipped the eight forms beginning with Bhava, accompanied by their respective powers (*śakti*) and joined with fire, [with the mantra] *oṃ raṃ agnaye namaḥ*; and having worshipped the eight powers beginning with Vāmā and the digits (*kalā*) beginning with Nivṛtti.

Having worshipped the five elements beginning with earth and the causal lords beginning with Brahmā; having displayed the great mudrās of the cow, the lotus, the trident, the crocodile, and the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) together with the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth; having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*); having presented incense and lamps; and having caused the lamps—along with camphor and other substances—to be waved three times before the head of Śiva using the five *Brahman* mantras beginning with Īśāna; one should worship in a pure vessel the neem leaf, cotton seeds, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the five *Brahman* mantras and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

Having displayed the *triśūla-mudrā* and having whirled [the ashes] three times around the base of Śiva’s head, one should cast them into the *nimba* vessel. Afterwards, having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to Śakti" at the rim of the ash-vessel, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva" in the ashes, and "Oṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara" at the foot [of the vessel], and having displayed the *śūla-mudrā* and whirled [the ashes] three times around the head of Śiva with the *tryambaka-mantra*, one should cast them into the lamp-vessel. Afterwards, [one should take] the ashes with the thumb and ring finger...

Having performed the protection rite with the *Bṛhatsāman* mantra from the crown of the head down to the feet, one should thereafter install the five Brahma-mantras, beginning with Īśāna at the head, upon the sixteen locations. Having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the *arghya* offering, one should then perform the following: on the handle of the mirror, *Oṃ śaktaye namaḥ*;
in the center, *Oṃ tejodbhavaśivāya namaḥ*. Having displayed the lotus and the five-faced mudrās, on the umbrella-staff, *Oṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*; on the ring, *Oṃ sāratvikāya namaḥ*.
[The Statement on Substantial Offerings (*dravyāhuti*):
The *brahmajajñānam* [verse] bestows fruit and the first increase;
the *khādira* [verse] destroys enemies; and by means of the *suparṇa* mantra, one attains the Nagas.
With the mantra "āpyāyasva," the lord of the earth should obtain an *aśvattha* tree;
with the mantra "yo rudra," he should obtain a *plakṣa* tree, which destroys his enemies.
Reciting "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should offer *udumbara* wood, which bestows happiness; with the mantra "indraṃ viśvāḥ," sandalwood becomes a source of prosperity.
The *vaṭa* tree, when consecrated with the *tryambaka* mantra, is a cause of satisfaction for Viṣṇu;
the *śamī* tree, consecrated with the *śanno devī* mantra, is said to be dear to the Son of Bhaya (Yama).
By means of the Umā-mantra, the sacred fig tree (śrīvṛkṣa) becomes a cause for the presence of Rudra;
by means of the "hiraṇyavarṇā" mantra, it becomes dear to Vaṇu and Kṛṣṇa.
The mantra beginning with "yā te rudra" is declared to be dear to Rudra, while that beginning with "arka" is dear to Bhānu.
The mantra known as "pitaraḥ pitāmahāḥ" is for Apāmārga, which brings about fame. Furthermore, by means of the mantra "hiraṇyavarṇā," one should offer mung beans, which likewise remove disease.
"O fathers, O grandfathers," [he said], offering wild rice as a means for great merit.
With the mantra "gaṇān tvā," sugar is for the destruction of enemies;
that which is called "vāyuśveta" is molasses, which bestows the essence of fruits.
"Viśvambhūta" is said to be barley (*yava*), which bestows happiness upon all living beings;
"Indraṃ viśva" refers to wheat (*godhūma*), which brings about the increase of wealth.
With the mantra "kadrudrāya," wheat (godhūma) which removes sin [is offered];
with the mantra "imaṃ me varuṇa," horse-gram (kuluttha), which bestows an increase of cattle, is proclaimed.
The hymn beginning with "yā te rudra" is proclaimed as one that removes evil and bestows prosperity upon the bride;
with the mantra "niśīrya," one should crush the *tarala* grain, which accomplishes many purposes.
The hymn beginning with "somodhenu" is proclaimed as one that yields an *āḍhaka* measure of wealth.
With the mantra "apsume," it bestows the growth of the priyaṅgu crop;
with the mantra "madhuvātā," it shall grant honey-like sweetness and happiness.
A piece of sugarcane, beloved by the gods, with the *rājādhirāja* mantra;
white mustard seeds, which grant all desires, with the *jātavedas* mantra.
With the mantra *hiraṇyagarbha*, one [uses] rice that removes defects caused by fire;
with the *suparṇa* mantra, one [uses] *śimba* for the destruction of agitation.
With the mantra "yo rudra," the auspicious *kuśa* grass is prescribed;
with the mantra "viśvataścakṣuḥ," the *ucūka* is used, which increases the growth of the stalks.
With the mantra "uddhṛtāsir varāhaḥ," the very young *atibāla* is offered, which is dear to the gods.
With the mantra "marmāṇi te," one should perform the subjugation of the *sūraṇa* root;
with the mantra "adhyavocaḥ," the *bālakanda* for the destruction of enemies;
and with the mantra "śrīśca te," the beautiful *padmakanda*.
The *nīkanda* root, which bestows victory, is consecrated with the mantra of Yama, the lord of the southern quarter;
and the *śāka* herb, which grants all happiness, is declared to be that which was spoken [by Brahmā] as "yatovāca."
With the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," the *raṃbhā* tree bestows the fruit of liberation;
with the mantra "avatatya," the mango tree bestows the happiness of sons.
That which is called "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" is the *phanasa* fruit, which bestows royal enjoyment; that which is called "suvar jyotiḥ" is the *kapittha* fruit, which originates from the horse.
With the mantra *agna āyāhi*, one accomplishes the essence of dates (*kharjūra*);
with the mantra *hiraṇyagarbha*, one bestows the increase of wealth through pomegranates;
and that which is proclaimed as *suvar jyotiḥ* grants the fruit of oranges through its recitation.
The hymn beginning with "Agnimīle" is declared to be the Jambhīra, which destroys death;
that beginning with "Suvar jyotiḥ" is declared to be the Drākṣā, which brings about subjugation. That beginning with "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" is declared to be the Kṣīrānna, which removes divine defects.
With the mantra of the Lord of Yama, sesame-rice destroys enemies.
Food offered with the mantra "Tryambakam" bestows wealth;
food offered with the verse "Dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam" shall be a remover of disease.
With the mantra "vibhūr asi," one should offer cooked rice (*odana*) which bestows auspiciousness;
with the mantra "śukram asi," one should offer black gram (*māṣa*) food which grants sovereignty.
Milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered with the Kṣīra-mantra for the sake of pleasing all the gods;
honeyed food should be offered with the mantra "yaḥ prāṇaḥ" to bestow a torrent of eloquence.
With the verse *haṃsaḥ śuciṣad*, one offers pure food as a means for worldly success;
with the verse *oṣadhayaḥ saṃvadante*, one offers mustard seeds for the fulfillment of desires.
With the verse beginning "annaḥ prāṇe," the food-oblation is dear to the gods;
by this, this entire universe is declared to be like fragrant black aloe-wood, beloved by the gods.
The "Soma-cow" is said to be the moon in the sky, which brings pleasure;
the "Moon-mind" is said to be the sweetmeat (laḍḍuka), which grants many desires.
Having recited "vayaṃ somavrate," one should offer rice gruel (*sūpa*) which accomplishes all aims;
with the verse "saṃvatsarīṇām," one should offer flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), which destroys obstacles.
With the mantra *asmāirudra*, one should offer a cake (*apūpa*) for the attainment of Indra;
with the mantra *adhvavoca*, one should offer a dense cake that bestows victory.
In this great [work], victory is granted through various verses;
by the mantra "tvanno agne," there is a beautiful and great fruit.
With the verse "manojyotiḥ," one should offer a piece of *kāmadantu* wood that is bright and solid;
with the verse "yajjākṛto dūram," one should offer a piece of sesame (*tila*) that is sharp-pointed.
By means of this, the entire universe is explained as the destroyer of the fever of the six families (ṣaṭkulī).
It is proclaimed as the goddess Śanodevī, the cool water that bestows happiness.
Suvarjyotis is said to bestow wealth, while hrībera grants the earth;
Agnihotṛ is said to be the deer that bestows happiness and joy.

The substance known as Kailāsaśikharākhya, when applied with the mantra "ya ātmadā," bestows victory; musk, when used with the mantra "agnir vā apām," grants liberation; and gorocana, with the verse "agnir vā apām," bestows happiness.
With the verse beginning "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," one obtains nutmeg (*jātīphala*) and the destruction of enemies;

with the verse beginning "saṃvatsaropāma," one obtains jasmine flowers (*jātīsumanas*) and victory; and with the verse beginning "nakṣatrāṇi sapta," one obtains cloves (*lavaṅga*), which bestow auspiciousness.
By the mantra of Rājādhirāja, saffron bestows wealth;
by the mantra of Saptate agne, it subjugates people in an instant;
and by the mantra of Puṣpāvatī, flowers grant auspiciousness.
The betel leaf known as *śrīścate* is a means for attaining liberation (*mokṣa*).
By means of the *pūrṇā* mantra, men attain the state of union (*sāyujya*) with the Fullness.
Thus, having offered these ninety-six substances into the fire with devotion—
Having prepared sacrificial fuel, grains, clarified butter, various fruits,
and other materials for the oblation in the auspicious rite of Śiva, he performed the homa.
Through these substances and oblations, one becomes present with Śiva;
those who perform this rite attain liberation—so say all the scriptures.

Thus, one who possesses a discerning mind should, with compassion, perform what ought to be done in the auspicious sacrifice; that which might otherwise be done through force or delusion must instead be performed with full conscious awareness.
But the poverty of the Ālaya is the non-manifestation of Sadāśiva;
therefore, a wise person should cause [the temple] to be constructed according to the rules with every effort.
"Let them perform the Śivadharmas; by doing so, a person attains union (*sāyujya*).
For the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, it bestows all auspiciousness. Thus [it is said].
[The Chapter on the Ritual for the Oblation of Substances in the Fire-Sacrifice of Śiva, from the Compendium of the Essence of All Āgamas] (7th line). The Guru: Om.

[Subheading: Material Oblations (*dravyāhuti*)] First: [the syllable] *(-)*, [the mantra] *phalāśam* (*-*), [the mantra] *brahmajajñānam* (*-*), [the invocation] *sadyojātena* (*-*), [the direction] *vāruṇe* (*-*); he offers into the golden-tongued [fire]. Second: [the wood] *khādiram* (*-*), [the mantra] *nāgeṣu suparṇa* (*-*), [the invocation] *vāmadeva*; this is the thirty-second oblation. It is offered in the center into the golden-tongued [fire].

Third: [the tree] Aśvattha; [the mantra] “Āpyāyasva same”; [the mantra] “Aghora”; twenty oblations; [the direction] Vāruṇa; [the material] gold. Fourth: [the tree] Plakṣa; [the mantra] “Yo rudro”; [the mantra] “Sadyojāte”; [the direction] Vāruṇa; sixteen [oblations]; [the material] gold. Fifth: [the tree] Audumbara; [the mantra] “Idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame”; [the mantra] “Kavacāya”; twelve [oblations]; [the material] gold.
The sixth: *candana-kāṣṭham* (sandalwood), *indram* (O Indra), *viśvā* (all), *sadyojāta* (Sadyojāta), twelve [syllables], gold.
The seventh: *vaṭam* (the banyan tree), *tryambakam yaja* (worship Tryambaka), *tatpuruṣa* (Tatpuruṣa), twelve [syllables], gold in the center.
The eighth: *śamī* (the śamī tree), *śanno devī* (May the goddess be auspicious to us), *vāmadeva* (Vāmadeva), ten [syllables], gold.
The ninth: *(-) bilam (-)*; *gaurīmimāya (-)* with the *astra* [mantra] (*-*) makes twelve;
*(-) kanaka* (7th line). The tenth: *(-) veṇu (-)*; *hiraṇyavarṇā (-)*; *hṛdayā (-)* makes ten; in the *āgneya* [direction], it is one redundant [syllable].
The eleventh: *(-) arkaṃ (-)*; *yāte rudra (-)*; with the *kavaca* [mantra] (*-*) makes twelve; in the east, it is *suprabha*.
Twelve: *apāmārgam*; eleven: *pitaraḥ prapitāmaha*; ten: *netre*; ten: *yāmya*; thirteen: *kṛṣṇaji*; thirteen: *jātavedase*; nine: *astrāya*; eight: *īśāna*;
fourteen: *āmram*; nine: *madhuvātā*; nine: *hṛdaye*; nine: *kanaka*.
Fifteenth: *pāṭalī*, *asatye*, *tatpuruṣa*, ten, gold.
Sixteenth: *panasam*, *viśvaṃ bhūtam*, ten, sixteen; he offers these in the center upon the golden tongue.
Seventeenth: subsequently, first, *palāśa-vabrahmajñānam*, ten, gold.
The second [offering] is rice (*anna*); with the *haṃsaśuciṣad* mantra, by means of the *aghora* mantra, five [times], in the center on gold.
The third [offering] is clarified butter (*ghṛta*); with the *brahmajajñānam* mantra, by means of the *sadyojāta* mantra, one hundred [times], in the center on gold.
The fourth [offering] is sesame (*tila*); with the *sugandhannasya panthāḥ* mantra, by means of the *aghora* mantra and the *mṛgamudrā*, five [times], in the south on black [ground].

The fifth [offering] is white mustard seed (*śvetasarṣapa*); with the mantra *agnim īle*, the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), ten syllables, and the eastern [direction], it is offered upon the tongue of blood (*raktajihvā*).

The sixth is black gram (*māṣa*); with the mantra *iṣetvorjetvā*, the head-mantra (*śiras*), ten syllables, and the eastern [direction], it is offered upon the tongue of beautiful radiance (*suprabhajihvā*).

The seventh is parched grain (*lāja*); with the mantra *agna āyāhi*, the crest-mantra (*śikhā*), twelve syllables, and the southern [direction], it is offered upon the tongue of blackness (*kṛṣṇajihvā*).
The eighth: *saktu*, *asatye*, *vāmadevena*, *daśa*—gold.
The ninth: *kṣīram*, *āpyāyasva*, *daśākṣareṇa*, *pañca*—gold.
The tenth: *dadhi*, *krāviṇo*, *tatpuruṣāya*, *daśa*—gold.
Eleven [beads] of *mudga* (third line), [the verse] "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" for the heart; twelve [beads] of gold (*kanaka*) on the tongue.
Twelve [beads] of *nīvāra* grain, [the mantra] "pitaraḥ pitāmahāḥ" for the head; five [beads] of gold (fourth line).
Thirteen [beads] of sugar (*śarkarā*), [the mantra] "gaṇānāṃ tvā" for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*); seven [beads] of gold.
The fourteenth [syllable] is *gulam*, the fifteenth is *vāyuśvetasi*, the sixteenth is *kavacā*, and the seventeenth is *pañca*; in the east is *suprabhā*.
The eighteenth is *yavam*, the nineteenth is *viśvaṃbhūtam*, the twentieth is *netrā*, and the twenty-first is *īśāne bahurūpa*.
The twenty-second is *godhūmam*, the twenty-third is *indraṃ viśvā*, and the twenty-fourth is *hṛdayāya*; the twenty-fifth is *dvādaśa*, and the twenty-sixth is *kanaka*.

The seventeenth [syllable] is *vaiṇava* (—), the eighteenth is *kuluttha* (—), and the nineteenth is *niṣpāva* (—). For the head (*śiras*), there is *kadrudrāya* (—); for the fire (*agni*), there are five [syllables], which are redundant. For the weapon (*astra*), there is *imaṃ me varuṇa* (—); for the armor (*kavaca*), there are ten [syllables], which are golden (*kanaka*).
Having crushed twenty *tarala* [pearls], twenty-two *śalya*, *astra*, and *kanaka*;

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the Navarātra:
on the first and ninth days of the bright fortnight joined with the Aśvinī nakṣatra.
Beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight, when the pavilion has been beautifully decorated—
either in the northeast or the north, as well as in the previously described pavilion.
Having established a sprout, or a pinnacle, or a *pālikā*,
with materials for the sprout-worship during an auspicious rising; and likewise,
in the middle [ritual], with pitchers possessing the stated characteristics and with sprouts.
Having invoked the Goddess into that pitcher, which is covered with a red cloth,
one should tie a protection-thread (rakṣāsūtra) at the front of the pitcher during the fire-sacrifice (homa),
having fastened it to the left hand of the Śakti with the mantra "Tryambaka."
Starting from that very day, the wise one should perform the recitation of various mantras according to the procedure for sacrifice and worship as prescribed for festivals.
Every single day, one should perform festivals, offerings, and oblations,
as well as the presentation of nine types of food offerings (naivedya), according to one's means.
For nine days, seven nights, five nights, three days,
or beginning with a single night, one should worship the elephant, the horse, and the weapons; likewise,
one should perform the worship of the Goddess and her limbs every single day.
It was accompanied by various musical instruments and endowed with diverse songs.
Adorned with various dances and accompanied by various Vedic hymns,
one should worship those possessed of all powers, beginning every night.
Then, on the tenth day at dawn, one should worship the water-pot (kumbha).

Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then gradually join the pot [to the ritual]. All [the rites], including the procession, the giving of gifts, and the dismissal of the sacrifice (yāgodvāsana), [should be completed].
Having performed a circumambulation of the watchtower accompanied by various musical instruments.
All the various devotees should perform the consecration of the jar;
one should then offer the food oblation, incense, and lamps, and dismiss the protective thread.
Then, having offered blessings as well as sacred ash and betel leaf—
now the worship of the Śamī tree shall be described—
it is considered twofold: at dawn and at midday.
Or indeed, when he has spoken thus, standing either in the east, the south-east, or the south-west; |||
We shall decorate Śamīyāma, equipping it with four gates, canopies,
archways, and various ornaments.
The wise one should visualize the form of Induśekhara mounted upon a horse,
adorned with various ornaments, and accompanied by various devotees.
Then, having entered the sanctuary of the Śamī tree, he urged the horses forward with speed;
having performed three circumambulations, he stood facing the east.
Having performed the ritual worship of the Śamī tree and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), he then caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited.
A sword, a shield, an arrow, and a bow, along with a śamī branch.
Having worshipped with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), along with food offerings, incense, and lamps,
and having performed worship with Mahiṣāsura, one should likewise cause the Śamī tree to be worshipped.
Having bathed [the deity] with water for ablution and other offerings, one should present the food offering (naivedya), incense, and lamps;
then, one should worship the four Śaktis in the four directions and the eight Śaktis.

Oṃ, obeisance to Kālī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kālarātri; Oṃ, obeisance to Yamā; obeisance to Yamadṛśī. (Fifth line) Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī; Oṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī; obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī; obeisance to Vārāhī; obeisance to Māheśvarī; obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā. (Sixth line) Obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. Having thus worshipped and offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and incense (*dhūpa*):

Having taken hold of the bow and arrow, he should touch the hand of the deity while reciting, "Thou art Agni... and specifically taking up the weapon. Having recited the hymn: "O Śamī, for the destruction of enemies; O Śamī, destroyer of sin; O Śamī, bestower of prosperity—to the Śamī, salutations, salutations!"—and having performed the rites beginning with the taking of the spear, he, being well-pleased, [honors] the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, as well as the village-founders and kings, while wearing his turban.
The mantra beginning with "sarvādi" has been declared, as well as the fixing of the arrow;
by means of four arrows in the four directions, the wise one proceeds.
Therefore, one should quickly take a leaf of the Śamī tree and place it upon the head;
indeed, all devotees of Śiva should especially offer it.
"Long life, health, and victory—may you be protected throughout the three worlds."

Henceforth, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the festival.
One should perform the Śiva-sacrifice for the purpose of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
[and] the great festival of sacrifices through the ascetic penances of Indra and the others.

For the sake of world conquest, he performed the Śivayāga, the great Vajra, as a circumambulation; and for the purpose of piercing the quarters, he performed the Kāmya sacrifice in the ancient time of the Kali-līlā. He [performed] the Dakṣayajña, which produced Indra, and the Śivanetraka.

From him was born Vīrabhadra, who destroyed the Prajāpati Dakṣa. Those who possess the form of sacrifices, such as Indra and others, and those who exist in the form of trees— by the grace of Vīrabhadra, one may traverse through Yakṣas, Daityas, and other beings.
Having transferred his great dexterity, he wandered for ten thousand years.
Subsequently, by the power of their asceticism, the gods led by Indra and rich in penance brought about the destruction of the Daityas and others,
and the dismissal of the Yakṣas and others.
For the sake of sacrifice to all the gods, the entire world is its foundation. Having achieved victory for the purpose of sacrifice, one should increase prosperity within that realm;
for the protection of the king, the kingdom, and so forth, one should perform a festival.
This letter "u" which has been spoken of, and the letter "sa" established in sacrifice, along with the bindu of the letter "va"—
for the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), this festival has been described by me.
I observed that the asterism was Berana, the lunar mansion of the village, the month was [such-and-such], and it was the birth asterism of the king-maker;
both the king and the asterism were pure.
On the primary auspicious day following death, let there be a Maṇḍa-tīrtha for Śiva;
beginning from the eastern direction, whatever constellation [was] at his birth, let it be endowed with all [the lunar mansions].
One should protect that great sacred site (tīrtha) and perform [the rites] every year,
especially during the solstices, the equinoxes, the new moon days, and both types of eclipses.

On the sixth lunar day of the month of Māgha, or likewise on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha; or on other auspicious lunar days, on [auspicious] weekdays, at sacred fords (tīrtha), or during festivals and the like.
When two lunar mansions fall within a single month, it is not desirable for them to be mutually [conflicting]; however, one may perform a pilgrimage at the first asterism or at the final asterism.
The commencement is said to be threefold: first, the raising of the banner, and afterwards, the striking of the drum; likewise, the first three are described as being liberated.
Then, having performed the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the commencement (*ārambha*) is declared to be complete;
thereafter, having struck the drum in the east, one should raise the banner.
At its end, there is the sprout (*aṅkura*), which constitutes the middle of the commencement;
having first made that sprout, one should afterwards strike the drum (*bherī*).
At its conclusion, having hoisted the banner, one should likewise begin the festival with the maiden;
during the day and night of the festival, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) at night.
The festival is said to be of six kinds, beginning with Ghorā and ending with Paitṛka. One day is called Ghora, and three days likewise constitute Vikrama.
A five-day [rite] is declared to be *tīvara*; a seven-day rite is remembered as *śrīkara*.
A nine-day rite is called *tava*, while a twelve-day rite is *paitraka*.
The wise man should celebrate two kinds of festivals, Vijaya and Puṣkala,
in sequence on the days of Śiva (11), Veda (4), Gaja (8), Āditya (12), Kalā (9), and Dvāviṃśati (22).
The "number of the balance" (balisaṅkhyā) refers to the victory [of the breath] from the Ghoras to the end of the Pitṛs;
it consists of the Aśvinī, the moving nāḍīs, Manu, and likewise Smṛti.
The number of offerings (*bali*) beginning with the *ghora* [rite] is twenty-four; this is the *puṣkala*.
Regarding the victory of the *puṣkala*, listen now to the festival beginning with the *ghora*.
Having placed the drum-beating for the sake of the spectacle in front of him, at his very forefront—
The worship of the sacrifice has been declared; one should perform it during the first part of the night.

One should perform the offering of the *bali*, the festival, and the powder at the conclusion of the sacred site (*tīrtha*). Then, after the ritual bath with the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*), there should be silence, the *bali* offering, and circumambulation during the night.
O Ambikā, hear now of the extensive victory known as Balimeketa;
all the rites spoken by Dvija should be performed especially during the first part of the night.
Having performed the morning twilight worship and offered the bali-oblation, one should then carry out the festival of that twilight.
The two offerings of the *bali* are indeed called the "Terrible" (*ghorāhuti*).
In this very manner, according to the sequence heard in the scripture, the wise one should proceed with valor.
The wise one should cause [the disciple] to hear the sequence up to the end of the Tīrtha according to the number of *balis*.
Śrīkara, listen to the three-fold festival of *tapas* and *pitṛ*.
First is the offering of the flag-staff, followed by the consecration of the banner;
third is the hoisting of the flag, and fourth is the beating of the drum.

Next, the sprout of the festival; then, in the sixth [day], the tying of the marriage-thread (kautuka-bandhana); the seventh is the sacrificial hall, followed by the sequence of the Vāstu-bali offering.

Having worshipped the ninth pavilion, one should worship the tenth as the site of the sacrifice; the eleventh for the sake of the bali offering, and the twelfth for the vehicle itself. Afterward, one should worship Naṭeśanāyaka, as well as the mounting of the horse and other [mounts].
Then, on the fifteenth day, there is the consecration (*āropa*); on the sixteenth, the *kautuka-tīrtha*;
on the seventeenth, the *cūrṇa-tīrtha*; and on the eighteenth, the *tīrtha* [of the water-pitcher] occurs.
On the nineteenth, there is the bath with the water-pitcher (*ghaṭasnāna*), followed by the lowering of the banner (*dhvajāvarohaṇa*).
Then, O Ambika, listen to the sequence of their festival rites, including the offering of silence (*maunabali*), which lasts for twenty-one days.
"Listen thus to the indication of the festival regarding the offering of the banner and the sprouts. Thus it is to be contemplated.

[Side Heading] [The Planting of the Banner-Sprout] Therefore, I shall now explain the auspicious planting of the banner-sprout (*dhvajāṅkura*),
both for its installation and consecration (*prokṣaṇa*), as well as for the various forms of festivals and the like.
In the performance of auspicious rites for others, one should not perform the ritual of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa);
if done, that rite will be fruitless.
[This applies] before the designated day, whether nine days or even seven days prior.

The sowing of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) may take place five days prior, three days prior, or on that very day. Since the Moon is the lord of seeds, one should sow them at night. The preceptor, together with the disciple, should perform the ritual bath according to the rules.
One should wear a bright cloth as a turban and an upper garment;
one should duly perform the purification of the body through ash-baths and other rites,
[and serve] one endowed with the characteristics of a teacher and adorned with the five-fold ornaments.
One should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and so forth; perform the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa).
Having received permission through a command or an authorization, one should collect a coconut;
thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa and again the Supreme Lord.

"O Lord of the hosts, foremost among the Skandas, together with the Goddess, the beloved of Śiva— be gracious so that this performance of the Śiva-sacrifice may proceed without obstacles. Thus he should petition, and thereafter again address the Supreme Lord:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, cause of the world’s joy;
may the Tantras proclaim you, O Maheśvara, through your grace.
Having made this request, at the conclusion of the worship,
one should offer permission for the sake of the deceased's house, or [offer] Caṇḍeśa or the trident.
A small vessel, an axe, sacrificial oblation, and a new cloth,
accompanied by the sound of conchs and joined with the resonance of musical instruments,
provided with an umbrella and chowries, and adorned with great lamps.
Adorned with various banners and joined by various devotees,
having performed the circumambulation of the site (vāstu), one does not perform circumambulation for others;
[this should be done] on a riverbank, at a pond, in a field, or at the root of *darbha* grass.
One should cause it to enter a field, a flower grove, a place outside a thicket of creepers, a cow-pen, a mountain, or a pure location.
In the west, above Dakṣa, one should install the King of Weapons (Astrarāja).
Vighneśvara is to be worshipped with flowers, and one should offer coconut.
Having worshipped the King of Weapons (the bow), he should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
thereafter, the most excellent of preceptors should duly place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound at the tip of the weapon, one should smear it with nine squares;
having sprinkled it with the Heart-mantra, one should worship Brahmā in the center.
Ananta, Vinatā, Bhadrā, Jayantā, Bhramarī, and Bhrama—
Prasthitā and Parijṛmbhī are the mantras for Indra and Īśāna respectively.
Having worshipped the fourth form according to the rule, beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should offer the bali-oblation at the end of the word *svāhā*.
Thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered, accompanied by incense and lamps.

First, one should sprinkle the sacrificial mandala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Having worshipped the ground with the mantra "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and with perfumes and other offerings using the heart-mantra, one should proceed.
Having sprinkled the axe itself, one should hold a cloth-wick;
one should brandish it with the weapon-mantra while the corpse is held on the left. One should fill the vessel in the northern direction with the skulls facing north.
One should take three kinds of nectar and make the ground level.
Having worshipped with the heart, one should protect [the deity] with garments;
[one should place the image] upon the head of an attendant, like an elephant or even a palanquin.
Having performed the circumambulation of the site (vāstu-pradakṣiṇa), accompanied by all auspicious sounds and joined with dance and song, he should enter the temple.
At the top of the palace, or in the northeast,
the north, or the south— in a pure place— one should smear it with cow dung.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the shallow bowls (*śarāva*) should belong to the woman.
The length should be eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the lip should be one finger-breadth.
The mouth and the base of the handle should likewise be three parts in length.

One should extend the opening of the mouth in sequence by one *kalā*, one *āra*, one *rasa*, and one *vasu*. The width of the feet is said to be eight, nine, and four [units] respectively. Furthermore, for others, there is a five-faced [liṅga], while for the rest, it is single-faced.
One should avoid a staff that is split in time, hollow, cracked, or broken.

A wise person should fasten to the middle of the staff a tip of *darbha* grass or a tip of *kuśa* grass that is without holes or hollows, as well as branches of the *śirīṣa*, *aśvattha*, and *bilva* trees.
The wise one should prepare the Śrīkara and Śrīpaṅka rites, as well as the two kinds of Aṅkura; one should sow eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice and half that amount of husked grain.
There, one should worship Vighneśa and then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
likewise, one should [lay down] the eastern thread, the Nāga thread, and the northern thread.
In the center, the wise one should take nine squares, [forming] an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
having left three squares in the intermediate directions,
and having left one square for the door in each of the four cardinal directions in due order.
One should place a new, auspicious moon-pitcher in the center of the pericarp;
these pitchers, along with their threads and lids, should be filled with water.
Having worshipped them according to the rite while reciting the Vāruṇa mantra.
After that, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and then present betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*).
One should place two *pālikā* vessels on either side of the four gates.
The wise one, having placed the *ghaṭikās* in the side compartments of the *pālikās* and in other squares according to the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
should fill the *pālikās* and the rest with sand, cow dung, and water.
And Sahasrāṅgī, Puṣpā, Bhūṣaṇī, and Māviṣū;
Puṣpā, Uttarā, Icchā, Bhrakūṭī, and Caṇḍī—these are the deities of the Pālikās; thus the wise one [knows] the eastern doors.
Tantrī, Vaiśākhī, Śāntinī, Maulinī, as well as Śātanī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Paurṇamāsī, and Śravaṇī.
Thus, one should worship them in sequence within the divine bowls:
[beginning] from the weapon-limbs (astrāṅga) up to Pūṣan and Īśa, as well as Uṣā and Aśvinī;
likewise Bhakṣaṇī, Kṛttikā, Nīcā, Śaṅkhinī, and Ādityāyaṇī.
The wise one should state the Ghaṭika-deva starting from the southeast (Agnikoṇa) and so forth.
One should sprinkle sesame, mustard, mung beans, black gram, śibāḍaka, padma, and kulattha— these seven seeds— as well as milk.
One should sprinkle [the vessels] with water from the Moon-vessel (somakumbha), facing either east or north, using the Heart-mantra alone; one should thus sprinkle the *pālikā* and other vessels.
Now listen as I describe that which is renowned as Śrīkara, the bestower of prosperity.
First, the eastern thread, then the thread of the elements (the southern), and likewise the northern thread.
In the center, one should take a four-legged stand with lotus petals and a pericarp;
in its middle, the wise practitioner should place a moon-pitcher as before.
Having arranged the Kriyākoṣṭha and so forth with the Heart-mantra as the twelfth,
[one should worship] Sahasrāṅgī, Pūṣaṇī, Puṣyāṇī, and likewise Bhrakuṭī.
Tantrāṇī, Śāntinī, Cāntinī, and likewise Harṣaṇī;
Astrāṅgī, Uṣādevī, Bhakṣiṇī, and likewise Śākhinī.
The wise one should establish the seed-syllable of the twelve Āditya-śaktis, beginning with Śara-vādī-tī, as a deity, using the heart-mantra as before.
One should take water from a lunar pitcher and sprinkle it upon the bow-wielder (Śiva).
Even when [the ritual] has concluded, one should release the mouse and other [offerings].
Having placed [the deity] in a suitable location, one should protect it; perform the characteristics [of the rite] with turmeric and so forth.
[The omens are] smoky and very crooked, occurring according to the lunar days;
[this causes] disease in the village. One should perform peace rites by offering a hundred oblations with the Astra mantra.
One should worship daily at the two junctions [of day and night] until the end of the specified period.
On the designated day, having offered Soma into the jars, the wise practitioner should sacrifice;
he should worship the deities of the Tantra with grains, unbroken rice, and Dūrvā grass.
The offering of the flagstaff and the germinating of seeds has been described; thereafter follows the consecration (adhivāsana) of the banner.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the offering of the germinating seed in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
[Side Heading] (6th line) [The Consecration of the Bull] Henceforth I shall explain the consecration of the bull-bannered deity.
The ritual procedure for the consecration takes place during the three periods prior to the mounting. (7th line)
The cotton cloth should be white, marked with auspicious signs, fine,
eight hundred and four fingers long, and one-fifth of that in width.
The tail should be equal to the width, and half of the tail is known as the crest;
in the middle of one-fifth of that, the wise man should draw a white bull.
Her ears are like antelope horns, her hooves are shaped like those of a deer, and her lips are like red coral;
her hair is as radiant as gold, and she is adorned with a garland of tinkling bells.
The two eyes are white, and the middle [face] is likewise black;
he is situated either seated upon the pedestal of a red lotus or reclining.
Above that, having drawn an umbrella, one should draw a pair of chowries on the sides;
above that, one should draw a lamp, and above that, the Śrīvatsa and a mirror.
Then, one should draw a full water-pot and a trident above that lamp.
On the surface of the bull’s back, one should draw a lamp upon the upper part of a svastika.
Below that lamp, one should draw the syllable and a conch shell.
Having performed the purification according to the rules, perform the opening of the eyes.
For the purpose of obtaining permission for the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*), one should worship the Supreme Lord;
either in front of Śiva or in a pavilion, one should smear it with various kinds of cow-dung.
One should sprinkle the auspicious day and the five products of the cow with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having eaten rice upon the ground, one should draw a lotus beneath it.
One should strew it with rice, sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and flowers;
having placed a new water-pot upon a bull, one should worship it in the west as well.
Thereafter, one should worship the Bull with the names Vṛṣa, Vipreśvara, and so forth,
as well as Ukṣan, Gopati, Balivarga, Anadud, and Adhvaga.
One should likewise worship Śaṅkhakarṇa, Mahodara, Aṅgī, Cakragupta, and Īśvara as a bull, beginning with Māgra. Having meditated upon Śiva within Sadāśiva, one should worship the Bull in his center.
Then, having offered food consisting of mung beans, one should present incense and a lamp with the heart mantra;
taking his water-pot, one should do so without the breaking of the seal.
Having invoked the bull of Śiva, one should worship the pitcher in the center.
O wise one, the invocation of Vṛṣavidyeśvara is for the sake of the sacrifice;
the preceptor should then place the pitcher as before, using the seed-syllable of the bull.
And the world-protectors were placed in their respective positions within the eight covered jars.
Having worshipped them according to the rule— with kuśa grass, sprouts, cloth, and lids— one should afterwards place them before the bull-bannered Lord.
Having placed [the mantra] with the heart-mantra, one should sprinkle it with water from the ritual vessels;
having worshipped the wise one who knows the Vṛṣagāyatrī at the base of the bull.
We know that mantra for Maheśa;
we meditate upon the one who possesses sharp horns and whose feet are the Vedas; may that Bull inspire us.
Having thus worshipped with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should worship Indra and the other deities for the sacrifice and so forth;
having thoroughly honored the mirror and other items with perfumes, flowers, and the like, one should perform the sacrifice.
Having performed the rites beginning with the taking of fire, the wise one,
having worshipped [the deity] at the front of the bull and the pitcher with the Agni-Gāyatrī mantra, should worship Indra and the others through sacrifice.
Having worshipped the mirror and other items with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
the wise one, having performed the rites beginning with the taking of fire, should worship at the front of the bull and the pitcher.
The preceptors, having meditated upon the fire in the center by means of the seed-syllable *VṚ*,
should offer clarified butter at the base of the bull with the *Sannidhāpana* mantra.
One should offer the *caru* oblation with the heart-mantra one hundred times for each [deity] while meditating;
from the bull [image], one should offer the *sparśāhuti* (touch-oblation) with the six-limbed mantra upon touching the water-jar (*kumbha*).
Having offered the *sparśāhuti* upon touching the banner (*dhvaja*), one should then perform the rites up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having worshipped [the deity] within the water-pot (kumbha), one should offer the sacrificial cake (naivedya), incense, and lamps.
One should likewise wrap the water-pot of the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) with a single cloth.
At dawn, perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) around the enclosure wall.
The consecration of the bull has been declared; one should now begin the hoisting of the banner.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for hoisting the banner in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* within the *Cintya*].
(5th line) (Sidebar heading) [The Ritual for Hoisting the Banner]:
Hereafter, I shall explain the purpose of hoisting the banner.
But for the sake of traveling to the realms of the yakṣas and others, all the gods employ their respective vehicles.
This initiation of the Śiva-sacrifice is proclaimed for the purpose of world-conquest;
one should commence the hoisting of the banner for the sake of illuminating all the worlds.
In the morning, at midday, or at night— at a favorable moment (*sumuhūrta*) and under an auspicious lunar division (*suvāṃśaka*)—
one should perform [the rite] either between the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the gateway (*gopura*), or in front of the pedestal, or on the tip of the bull.
The middle [measurement] and so forth, as well as the great-middle and so forth, have been declared as the measure for the location of the banner; now hear concerning the banner-pole (*dhvajadaṇḍa*).

Sandalwood, *devadāru*, *campaka*, *agaru*, and *bilva*— *Note: The original text contains orthographic variants (e.g., *camba* for *campaka*, *gāru* for *agaru*). The translation reflects the intended botanical names.*
The *panasa*, the *khadira*, the *tāla*, the *phalāśa*, and likewise the *vakula*.
The preceptor should take up a staff made of bamboo, coconut, madhūka, or likewise of bamboo;
it may be made of the outer bark or the inner pith.
It should be joined with curved joints, free from worms and hollows,
and it may be level with the temple or even with the gate-tower (gopura).
Similarly, the height of the *daṇḍa* is said to extend either up to the neck, or equal to the bull of the temple,
or ending at two or three storeys (*tala*). It may be made eight cubits in measure, or even thirty-five cubits.
Beginning from twelve cubits,
this is the height of the staff for the goddesses of good vows,
up to the maximum limit; its base is twenty-four finger-breadths and its tip is likewise twenty finger-breadths.
The root [of the staff] shall be twenty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, and the tip eighteen finger-breadths;

alternatively, the root may be eighteen finger-breadths and the tip sixteen finger-breadths. The best and other [grades] are determined by the proportions of the hand-span (nirvapāṇi), the forearm (bhānu), and the cubit (hasta). The tube (nāḍikā) should be of appropriate length.
Among all festivals, it is considered the most excellent; by it, one is liberated.
One should place three *skandas* at the tip of each staff, each having the form of a *cāṭuka*;
and within those *cāṭukas*, one should join a great staff into the great opening.
In the covering of the suitable place, Skanda has a width of three finger-breadths;
it is equal in thickness and sixteen finger-breadths in length.
Two [parts] are provided with hollows, and half of them consists of apertures.
The bamboo staff should be thirty-six finger-breadths in length, and one should attach a cord to it.
The binding of the bamboo staff should be eight, six, or five finger-breadths [in thickness];
in the middle, from joint to joint, it should be provided with twelve finger-breadths.
Above that [pedestal], upon the middle of the bamboo staff,
there should be an iron ring facing northward.
One should join the cord for the threefold girdle with a measurement equal to the tip of the little finger;
likewise, the cord attached to the base of the staff should be twice that length.

At the top of the *skanda* [staff], which is a great pillar, there should be a long [finial] shaped like a cow's ear (*gokarṇa*). Above that, one should place a bull made either of metal or wood. The location for the banner (*dhvaja*) should be solid and measure exactly one cubit (*hasta*) in height.
One should place a golden tortoise adorned with jewels upon its center;
above that, one should set up a staff and fill it with sand.
As for the staff made of bamboo, its natural quality should be joined with a girth of three [units].
At its base, having constructed a pedestal two cubits in width and either one cubit in height,
provided with three girdles;
Having constructed a pedestal at its base measuring two cubits in width,
Devakarmā should summon [the artisan] adorned with ornaments consisting of five parts.
Wearing a pure white upper garment, adorned with perfumes and garlands,
his limbs smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste, and beautified by golden rings.
Taking hold of the tip of the banner of endurance, one should perform a circumambulation of the village,
which is filled with various banners, including the principal banner, and is crowded with many flags;
it is provided with various umbrellas and endowed with various peacock feathers.
It was filled with various devotees and accompanied by the sound of Vedic chanting.
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, and joined with dance and song,
one should circumambulate the site clockwise and cause [the image] to enter the place of the banner.
There, one should worship Gaṇeśa and then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, having worshipped Astranātha with the permission of Dhānanātha.
Having consecrated the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) through the sequence of the five purifications,
one should worship the deities of the archway (toraṇa) and the gate at the direction of the staff.
Then one should worship Bhūmidevī upon the lower girdle;
having worshipped Śrīdevī in the middle, one should worship Sarasvatī above the girdle.
One should likewise worship the staff as consisting of Viṣṇu and worship the five elements.
During the auspicious moment (sumuhūrta), one should attach the rope to the top of the banner (dhvaja) and to the heart [of the deity] with the Indra-mantra;
having taken up the bull, the jar, and so forth— provided it is not joined by day—
one should place them in that location and install the bull at the base of the banner.
The wise man should worship the Vṛṣagāyatrī according to the rules,
accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and joined with all [auspicious] elements.
On the fourteenth day, accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, dancing, and singing,
the wise man should quickly raise the banner with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
The Lord of the Earth, the garland of *darbha* grass, and the staff should be placed in a counter-clockwise direction.
At the base, it should be joined with a mango-wood vessel bound with a girdle of darbha grass.
Having sprinkled the bull, the pitcher, and the other items, one should consecrate them at the base of the staff.
One should worship the bull at its base, surrounded by the guardians of the world.
Having worshipped Varuṇa and the others, one should offer cooked mung beans,
accompanied by incense and lamps, and provided with dance and song.
The supreme preceptor should perform all the ritual services;
whether for the preceptor or for the disciple, O beloved, listen to [the description of] the garland of jewels.
Accompanied by auspicious songs, he should bestow sacred ash upon the devotees.
Whether it be Caṇḍeśa or a devotee,
having purified the path and performed the circumambulation of the village, one should enter toward the temple;
this is declared to be the hoisting of the banner, and then one should begin the beating of the drum.
[Thus ends the chapter on the hoisting of the banner in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
(Side heading) [Beating the Drum] Hereafter I shall describe the beating of the great drum.
O lords of the Gaṇas, this is the vehicle for one who has commenced the Śiva-sacrifice.
One should give a portion of the sacrificial offering (havis) for the purpose [of the rite], and then begin the striking with the *bharī* drum;
this should be performed before Śiva, or at the top of the banner, during the time of night.
Having prepared a leveled altar within the hall, likewise in the western and eastern sections,
one should draw lotus petals adorned with sesame seeds and parched grain;
having strewn them around with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should sprinkle them while reciting the Heart Mantra.
Above that, one should place a trident and a drum to the west and to the east.
One should first worship Gaṇeśa and then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, having duly honored the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), one should place Rudraka in the central vessel.
One should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu on the right and left petals;
likewise, one should worship Skanda and Varuṇa upon the base of the trident and the water-pot.

The wise practitioner, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite, should worship Tāṭikā, Agnirāja, and the Vāmā and other Śaktis at the Pīṭha. Afterwards,
he should sprinkle the drum with water while reciting the mantra beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Having wrapped [the image] with a new cloth, one should worship Brahmā in the center.
Upon that, one should worship Rudra on the left and Viṣṇu on the right.
On the bracelets, one should worship the Sun and the Moon, and on the leather cord, Vāsuki.
One should cause the seven stakes to be purified with the mantra of the Mothers;
having recited the Nandi-mantra, [one offers] the food offering, incense, and lamps.
Having offered [oblations] with the Tryambaka mantra, one should strike in the eastern corner;
having struck twice with the Viṣṇu mantra, one should strike three times with the Brahmajajñāna mantra.
Having struck [the drum] with this mantra while facing either east or north,
one should cast a flower, offered with reverence, into the center of the *bherī* drum. Then,
using the *carcapuṭa* rhythm and tempo, one should lift the *bherī* and strike it.
Having heard [the mantra] for the invocation of the deity from either the preceptor or the disciple, |||
For the purpose of invoking the deity and offering the bali-oblation, one should bring either a vehicle or an image of Candraśekhara,
provided with offerings of food and a liṅga, and accompanied by the resonant sound of bells.

The wise man, [offering] the five products of the cow, jaggery, cooked rice, and so forth, along with *darbha* grass and flowers— without [the need for] days— and provided with incense and lamps, adorned with a parasol and chowries.
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and the ringing of bells,
the wise man, having placed an offering upon the tip of the banner while reciting the *Vṛṣagāyatrī*,
[should likewise place] the most excellent serpent on the side of the gateway of the city gate.
From Brahmā up to Īśāna, and from Indra up to Īśāna, [are the respective mantras].
Having heard the invocation of the deity of the offering (*balideva*), the preceptor should then place the offering toward the direction indicated by his disciple,
or toward the direction indicated by the rhythmic beat (*tāla*).
Having performed a slow circumambulation, one should enter toward the temple.
[Thus ends the chapter on the beating of the drum in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
[The Tying of the Auspicious Thread] Hereafter, I shall explain the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*).
It is for the sake of accomplishing one's desired wishes; it is not [performed] for the sake of a maiden.
Therefore, one should maintain single-minded mindfulness, just as in the rite of tying the auspicious thread (*kautuka-bandhana*).
The preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) should take place on the day previously specified, or during the first watch of the night;
O Vāsuki, if that is not possible, the ritual should be performed on that very day, preceded by the preparatory rites.
It shall be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Then, in front of the deities mentioned in the Tantra, one should have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) made.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with *śāli* rice, one should draw a lotus in its center.
One should strew sesame seeds, parched grains, flowers, or even *darbha* grass;
in the center of that, one should place a jar filled with water and containing excellent gems.
One should arrange them together with their mouth-covers and lids;
thus one should perform the *adhivāsana* rite for the *kumbha*, and then carry out the fire-oblation (*homa*) for Indra.
All rites beginning with the installation of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) should be performed in that [fire] according to the prescribed path;
having invoked the independent deity, one should worship him in the midst of the fire.
In that [fire], one should offer sacrificial fuel (samit), clarified butter (ājya), and the oblation of boiled rice (caru) to the deity by means of its root mantra.
The most excellent of teachers should offer one hundred oblations, or fifty, or twenty-five.
He should perform the fire sacrifice beginning with the *jaya* offerings and the *āghāra* libations, ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having thus established the jar, he should then join it to the door of the jar.
One should employ the sprinkling water for the image, as well as the food offering, incense, and lamps;
having offered these, one should fill the vessel within the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
[One should also offer] threads of gold, linen, and cotton, whether of the highest or other qualities.
One should place that thread and the sacred ash upon the rice.
The worshipper, having filled his palms with rice mixed with fruit,
should perform the binding of the protective thread on the right hand of the deity.
The wise man should maintain what is prescribed for the heart with the mantra beginning "bṛhatsāmā";
then, for women, [he should do so] on the left hand with the Tryambaka mantra and the [mantras] beginning with the heart.
Having recited the mantra as a refuge, one should consecrate the water-jar and other items, wrapping them in a new cloth with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
This is known as the "excellent" [method]; the "middling" [method] is accomplished by means of fire-oblation (*homa*).
One should perform the *homa* without a water-pot (*kumbha*), and the architect (*sūtradhāra*) should be of the lowest rank.
For the deities who are part of the festival, one should wear a protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*);
the wise man should place the auspicious thread (*kautuka*) on the southern petal of the trident.
Thereafter, one should cause the sacred ash to be applied and wrap [the image] in a new cloth;
this is declared to be the binding of the *kautuka*. Now hear the procedure for the sacrificial hall.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for binding the protection in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
The pavilion should be situated in the northeast direction or in the four directions from the fire;
it should be square, measuring nine, eight, seven, six, or five cubits.

Having drawn the "Nanda's joy" (nandananda) footprint in the center, one should make nine divisions for the altar (vedī). The height of the altar should be three times the measure of a cubit, a ratna, or a muṣṭi. For the sake of the nine or five Śivas, the pit (kuṇḍa) should be made in the middle portion.
The fire-pits in the cardinal directions are square, while those in the intermediate directions are circular; furthermore, the primary circular pit is located between the northeast and the east.
From the corner of the direction toward the principal deity, the primary [measurement] is one cubit,
or a fist, or nine fingers in width and height;
the three girdles (mekhalā), starting from the top, are four, four, and two fingers [in width] respectively.
The shape of the girdle should correspond to whatever form the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possesses.
Above the girdle, there should be a fire offering (homa), adorned with garlands of flowers,
and beautified with betel leaves, areca nuts, fruits, and foliage.
Having smeared it with cow-dung and performed purification, the wise one [should proceed];
thus has been declared the characteristic of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), or else the sequence for the offering to the site-deities (vāstu-bali).
[Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the pavilion in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
(Side heading) [The Vāstu-homa]:
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of offerings to the deities of the site (vāstudeva).
For the purpose of purifying the locations beginning with the site, the frog-step (maṇḍūkapaḍa) is supreme.
Having strewn the sacrificial ground with *śāli* rice— either two *droṇas*, or one and a half, or half a *droṇa*—
and having drawn the footprint of a frog, adorned with sesame seeds and parched grain,
one should place *darbha* grass in each square; such is the measure for a woman.
Having first made it square or in the shape of a womb (yoni), the wise one [should proceed].
Having placed the vessel made of *aśvattha* leaves upon a tripod (*trimekhala*) and touching it,
the Hotṛ priest should offer it into the fire, facing northward toward Indra.
In the southwest [is] Varuṇa, and in the northwest [is] Vāyu; in the north, it should face the east. The pavilion should have four doors and be adorned with four archways.
One should place a plank above with a width equal to its height;
there, one should insert a peg according to the measurement of a *mātrāṅgula*.
One should draw the vehicle of Indra and other deities and place banners in the eight directions;
it should be adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass, grains, parasols, and other ornaments.
The unique arrangement of the syllables and the measurement of the squares is as follows: each square shall be four finger-breadths in size.
Having marked eight by eight squares, one should draw two lines at each corner.
In the center is the four-footed Brahmā (*), [situated] in the portion of the qualities of those faces:
Sūrya, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Bhūdhara.
Outside of that, with six squares each, starting from the east and ending in the north;
outside of that, with half-squares, starting from the northeast, one should place the excellent Īśāna in the corners.
Āpa and Āpavatsa, Savitṛ and Sāvitra,
Indra and Indrajaya, as well as Rudra and Rudrajaya;
[these constitute] one half-veda and one āgama, according to the sequence of the middle words.
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Mahendraka; Āditya, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Antarikṣa, who holds the eastern quarter;
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, and Yama.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛgarāja are in the south; Niṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Varuṇa [are in the west].
Asura, Śoṣa, and Rogas are in the west;
Vāyu, the chief Nāgas, Bhallāṭaka, and Somaka [are also there].
For the sake of *ṛta*, one should offer to Aditi and Diti in the northeast;
likewise, to Śarakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā,
and the evil Rākṣasī, according to the sequence of offerings in the northeastern corner.
Skanda, Adhamanyā, Jambha, and Balipiñcaka—
thus one should offer the circular-line oblation (*vṛttarekhābali*) in the four directions starting from the east.
Immediately after [the offering] ending with *sānta*, one should worship the gods, each by their own name followed by the word *ananta*.
One should offer the bali-oblation beginning with *oṃ*, ending with *namaḥ*, and concluding with *svāhā*;
thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be given, accompanied by incense and lamps.
From Sūryadāpa, from his own lord Īśāna, and from Śarakya-skanda and the others,
one should worship the fivefold Brahmā deities in their proper sequence.
Likewise, the wise one should duly install the Vāstu-pitcher and other vessels;
he should worship the Vāstu-pitcher and the others among the deities within the central pitcher.

One should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the previously mentioned procedure; then, preceded by the offering of oblations (bali) and the mandala, one should perform the Vāstu-homa. All rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) should be carried out according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
The gods, along with Brahmā and the Vāstudevas, should be established in the center of the fire.
One should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seeds, barley,
and sesame seeds— all these together— each by its own name, according to the sequence prescribed in the fifty-third [chapter].
One should perform the *jayādi*, *abhyādāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, as well as the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having invoked [the deity] into the center of the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should present food offerings (*naivedya*), incense (*dhūpa*), and lamps (*dīpa*).
Having fashioned a crest from a *palāśa* leaf, one should touch that fire to the ground;
then, having rotated it clockwise, one should sprinkle it with water from the ritual jar (*kumbha*).

Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and having performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), one should perform the bath. Thus has been declared the offering for the site (*vāstubali*); now hear the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the sacrificial offering and fire-oblation to the site-deities in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
(8th line) (Regarding the sacrifice and worship:
Hereafter, I shall explain the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Having strewn the sacrificial ground with rice grains, one should proceed in order from the east through the eight directions:
[the squares] of five, eleven, four, three, six, seven, two, and four.
Having thus placed [the deities] in the pitchers in sequence, the wise one should hear the Veda:
Mahākāla, Śānti, Nandin, Indra, and likewise Ravi.
Agni, Vighnarāja, the Brahmins, Bhṛṅgin, and Yama;
Viṣṇu, Nairṛti, Vāstu, Brahmā, Kāla, and likewise Guha;
Nivṛtti, Vṛṣa, Nandin, Vāruṇa, and Vināyaka.
Vāyu, Caṇḍa, Pratiṣṭhā, the Goddess, Soma, Brahmā,
Īśāna, and Guru— these twenty-eight in number [are worshipped] in the pitcher (kumbha) according to the sequence of the deities, O twice-born one.
One should worship the Sun in the pitcher situated between Indra and Agni;
then, having risen and gone outside, perform the washing of the feet.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
one should accomplish the half-syllable *praṇava* at the eastern gate of the pavilion, in due order, for the two deities of the archway (*toraṇa*).
Śānti is on the auspicious archway of Catur, Bhūti likewise on Vijaya;
Bala is on the archway of Vajra, and the Nīlalohitas are on Ārogya.
One should worship the two deities of the archway (toraṇa) with their respective names. Furthermore,
at the eastern gate and the others, one should worship the kalās— Śānti, Vidya, Nivṛtti, and Pratiṣṭhā— in the pitchers (kumbha) of the gates.
Furthermore, O beloved, one should worship the two jars at the eastern gate, namely Nandika and Kalaka, as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā, along with Śakti, in due order.
In the pitcher at the southern gate are two Vināyakas for Bhṛṅgin;
and likewise Śakti, Vaikartī, and Nirmadā, respectively.
At the western gate, one should worship two jars, as well as Skanda and the Bull;
Sarasvatī and Siddha are also there, for the deity possesses two powers.
At the northern gate, however, one should first worship the goddess at the jar.

One should worship Caṇḍeśa in the western pitcher of the door, and likewise Pauṣṇi in the [western] pitcher; furthermore, at the western door, one should worship the door as if it were permanent (nityavat). Above the door, on the left side of the umbara-post, one should worship Vighnarāja.
One should place Sarasvatī on the left side, and Lakṣmī in the middle of them;
then, at the sides of the bull’s shoulders, one should place the two jars, Nandin and Kāla.
In that very same way, one should strike the bell with the weapon-mantra while shaking the other doors— the power of the deities being Gaṅgā and Yamunā as well.
One should worship Astradāsa at the side of that door;
upon entering, one should worship Vāstubrahmā in the Nairṛta pitcher.
One should meditate upon the principles beginning with earth in their proper sequence by means of the three supports, the bonds, the bamboo-staves, and likewise the strings.

Between the garland of *vāsukī* and the *darbha* grass, one should likewise place the Ganges; having worshipped the moon upon the canopy with the vehicles of the banners and the guardians of the directions, one should arrange the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) on the altar in the four directions.
Having worshipped [the disciple] in due order and being seated comfortably facing north,
the Guru— holding the sword of knowledge in his right hand and having consecrated the "Hand of Śiva" (śivahasta)— should contemplate himself as Śiva with sandalwood paste applied to his left hand.
Combined with thirty-six blades of darbha grass and joined with a braid of knots,
it is one tāla in length and is known as the Sword of Knowledge.
One should bind it at one side and fix it very firmly;
the wise man should scatter it in a clockwise direction with the weapon-mantra.
Having recited "Bhūmirbhūmnā," one should perform the sprinkling with the Heart-mantra while gazing [at the site]; one should strike it with the Īśa-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ."
Sprinkling, digging, sweeping, and likewise smearing—

by means of the mantras "Astra," "Astra-varma," and "Netra," one becomes pure in regard to the site. Having strewn a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with *śāli* rice to the west of the northeastern pit (*īśakuṇḍa*), [one should proceed].
Having drawn a lotus in the center of that [mandala], one should cover it with *darbha* grass and flowers.
Above that, one should place a jar containing the embodied form of Śiva mounted upon a bull—
four-armed, three-eyed, and with dark-brown hair tied upward.
Having meditated upon the Lord Pāśupata, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who holds a noose and a sword, and who is measured [in form], one should place the *vardhanī* vessel on his left.
One should meditate upon the Mistress of Weapons (Astreśvarī), who has blazing red hair, holds a sword and a shield,
and rides upon a lion with the courage of the great Indra.
The mantra is: Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya namaḥ.
With this Pāśupata-weapon mantra, one should join [the weapon] to the female or male organ.
One should worship the two deities facing west with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the world (*lokapālakas*) in the jars of the pavilion,

the wise practitioner should then take up the weapons as prescribed by Viṣṇu and Viriñca in their proper order; thereafter, he should increase the *vardhanī* vessel with water by means of another jar.
Having consecrated the unceasing streams of milk with the root mantra, one should cause them to flow from Indra to Īśāna, saying: "Make it very firm!
Then, as before, one should establish the food offering, incense, and lamps in their respective places.
Having thoroughly worshipped the sword of knowledge at the junction of that water-pot.
Having worshipped the Guru in the pitcher located in the northeastern direction,
the twice-born [should perform] the offering of the cloth as prescribed in the *Rathātantra*, and likewise the festival according to the *Tantra*.
One should worship Vighneśa in the pitcher to the left of the pitcher of Māruta.
The worship of the pavilion has been described; now hear the procedure for the installation of the pitchers.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the worship of the pavilion in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
(Side heading) [Śivayāga] (3rd line):
Therefore, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual procedure for the Śiva-sacrifice,
which serves as the sacrifice for all the gods and is the destroyer of all enemies.
For the sake of Indra and the other deities, for the purpose of the jar-offering (ghaṭa-homa),
and for the sake of the object of perfect satisfaction, one should perform the Śiva-sacrifice for the benefit of all the world.
Having gazed upon the Great Goddess above the altar with the heart-mantra,
one should perform the sprinkling and anointing with the left eye of the mantra.
One should then proclaim an auspicious day and sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow using the heart-mantra.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with *śāli* rice— either eight *droṇas* or half of that—
one should draw a lotus in its center, adorned with sesame seeds and parched grain (*lāja*).
Having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should then sprinkle it with water.
In the center of that, one should place a water-pot while recollecting the Śiva-mantra;
one should then place the Vardhanī vessel and eight other pots around it.
One should fill the water-pots with water using the mantra "āpo vā".
One should encircle each weapon with the heart mantra.
In its center, one should place the *kūrca* (bundle of grass), and worship the mango leaf with the *śikhā* mantra;
then the preceptors, having established the coconut, [should worship it] with the *śiras* mantra.
Having condensed gold and gems with their respective seed-syllables,
the wise one should meditate upon the form of Sadāśiva in the center of the Śiva-kumbha.
Having addressed Sadāśiva with the water of Śiva, may he be auspicious;
having worshipped Sadāśiva according to the rite, let them increase the state of Manonmanī.
[For the sake of sacrifice,] the world-protectors, who are superior even to the eight Vidyeśvaras, [should be invoked].
Therefore, one should place jars for the satisfaction of Indra and the other guardians of the directions.

Having performed the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth, the wise practitioner should worship according to the rules. Then, upon the altar in the northeast, he should install the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*).

One should install, in due order, the mantras beginning with Vajra and ending with Śūla, starting from the east and extending to the northeast; and one should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
This *astrayāga* has been proclaimed; thereafter, one should perform the *homa*.
All rites pertaining to the fire, such as the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and so forth, should be performed according to the path taught for the fire-ritual.
In his tantra, one should worship the deities and establish the fire in the center;
having worshipped according to the rule, the wise one should meditate as before.
The *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees are [to be planted] in the directions starting from the east;
and the *śamī*, *khadira*, *bilva*, and *arka* trees are [to be planted] in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast.
One should offer the leaves of the *palāśa* tree at the end of the substances and perform the *vyāhṛti* oblation;
then, one should offer *bilva* leaves according to the rule of that mantra. [The mantra:

oṃ namo bhagavate āryyāvalokiteśvarāya tadyathā oṃ kaṇe kaṇe kuru kuru sarvvaduṣṭān bandha bandha sarvvaśatrūn hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | 1 || oṃ namo bhagavate āryyāvalokiteśvarāya tadyathā oṃ kara āryyāvalokiteśvarāya tadyathā oṃ kala kala kuru kuru bandha bandha hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | 29 || o
We know that Great Lord; we meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may that Śiva inspire us.
This is declared to be the Śivagāyatrī; at the conclusion of the substances, one should perform the oblation with the Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered ghee with the root mantra, one should offer it all with the root mantra of Manonmanī.
One should offer oblations with their respective names to Indra and the other guardians of the world;
one should perform the homa for each one in sequence, either a hundred times, fifty times, or half of that.
One should offer ten oblations for Śiva and one oblation for others;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the offering with the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne."
One should perform the Jaya and other rites, the kindling of the fire, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings in due order;
having worshipped the sacrificial pitcher with equal devotion, one should present the food offering, incense, and lamps.
Having offered [the oblation], the wise one should worship the King of Weapons according to the rules;
at both twilights, evening and morning, the wise one should cause the flow to reach the end of the sacred site (tīrtha).
This Śiva-sacrifice has been proclaimed; now hear the offering of the sacrificial oblation (bali).
[Thus ends the chapter on the Śiva-sacrifice in the Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra.]
[The Sequence of the Bali Offering] Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the bali offering for the Śiva-sacrifice,
for the protection of the great sacrifice, for the sake of attaining wisdom, and for the benefit of the twice-born.

One should perform the offering of the sacrificial oblation for all the lords who are the embodiments of sacrifice, taking half of that portion; furthermore, one should present a food-offering for the protection of the three worlds.
Having made the wise foundation for the joints of the Vāstu-Brahmā and so forth,
the width of the pedestal should be one cubit, and its height half of that.
Each of the three girdles (*mekhalā*) should be four finger-breadths wide; this is declared to be the high pitch (*tāra*). It may be made of silver, copper, or even clay.
Now hear in due order about the offering deities (*balideva*) at the junctions of the temple site and the enclosure walls.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Brahmā and the other world-protectors in their respective places.
Having taken recourse to those various lords of the two worlds at evening and morning,
[one honors] Vighnarāja, Gaṇādhīśa, Śakti, and Vināyaka.
And Heramba, the one with a single tusk, the elephant-faced one, the destroyer of demons,
Vīra, Vighna, Guha, Agra, and on the first [day], Dinādhipa.
Piśāca, Śabala, Dhīra, Guhyasiddha, Ūrdhvakeśaka,
Dīrghānghri, Naratveṣibhūta, and Īśma Dinādhipa.
The great nāgas Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka,
Kārkoṭaka, Padma, and likewise Mahāpadma;
Śaṅkhapāla and Gulaka are the deities of the third day;
likewise Gandharva, Kinnara, Yakṣa, Siddha, Vipura, Adhara,
as well as Nārada, Mahānāga, Cāraṇa, and Stambaru.
May the deities, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśa, accept the offering. Bhūteśa, Śyāmadanta, Saṃvarta, Dīrghakāyaka,
Kuṇḍakukṣi, Sṛsvāṅgin, Siṃharūpa, and Vṛṣānana.
And those who have become ornaments for the Nāgas, the leader of the five-faced ones (Pañcamukhanāyaka),
Guha— the son of the Kṛttikās, the son of Gaṅgā, and the son of Umā.
Viśākha with spear in hand, Krauñcaka, Tārakāntaka— these,
along with Subrahmaṇya, are the six who should be grasped as offerings in the battle against the Nirandhras.
The king of sages Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Kāśyapa, Agastya, Pulastya, Bhāradvāja, Gautama,
and Kaiśika were present at my sacrifice on the seventh day for the sake of Bali.
Indra, Śatakratu, Vajrin, Sahasrākṣa, Purandhara; Jambhahā, Cakrin, Drivitojas, Aṣṭadinnādhipa;
Brahmā, Sarasvatikrānta, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Caturmukha.
The Self-Existent One, the Lotus-born, Vajrahasta, and Prajāpati—
these embodied beings were restrained by the Grandfather or by me.
Viṣṇu in the form of the Tortoise, Varāha, Narasiṃha,
Vāmana, Balabhadra, Paraśurāma, and Rāma.
And Kṛṣṇa himself was the leader of the forces at the festival of Daśarātra;
so too were the Rākṣasas, the Suras, the Iṣis, the Dānavas, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
He who has consumed much food, whose limbs resemble the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri),
who fought battles with Indra, and who is Nīla for eleven days;
