he is Śiva, the womb of all existence, whose form is the void, and who is the soul of the world.
And on the twelfth day, the Lord Svayambhūsthāṇu is the presiding deity of the day.
On the first day, one should know there are nine [offerings], while on the twelfth day there are one hundred and eight.
Alternatively, one should cast the bali offering for the principal deity toward the left of Īśa.
In the Ekāha sacrifice, however, there is one principal [deity]; in the twelve-day sacrifice (Dvādaśāha), there are twelve;
the third is the one who creates obstacles, and the second is the Paiśāca.
The third is the Night of the Nagas, while the fourth is that of the Gandharvas;
the fifth is the Night of the Bhutas, and the sixth is the Night of the Guhas.
The seventh shall be Ṛṣirātri, and likewise the eighth Indrarātri;
the ninth shall be Brahmarātri, and the tenth Viṣṇurātri. (The eleventh is) Rākṣasarātri and Raudrarātri, and the twelfth is Śivarātri.

Having resorted to the asceticism of the Gandharvas and others, one should obtain the *Śrīkara* and other [mantras]. In the *Vikrama* [kalpa], during the nights of Viṣṇu and Viṣṇurātra, and on the day of Ghorāha, there shall be Śiva; now hear the sequence for the consumption of the sacrificial offering (*balibhojya*).
Mudga-rice mixed with sesame, coconut fruit, ghee, punnāga,
and two red flowers— while recollecting the mantra for removing obstacles—
one should offer red rice, kṛsarā, cakes, and meat accompanied by clarified butter.
Combined with a hibiscus flower, it brings pleasure to the lord of the Piśācas.
Milk-rice and flour of *śāli* rice combined with jaggery and sugar-candy,
along with the flowers of the black sunflower (*kṛṣṇārka*), jasmine (*mallikā*), and the *nāga* tree, will be dear to him.
Rasa-rice with powdered turmeric mixed with clarified butter,
curd-soup, and *vakra* flowers— these are dear to the Gandharva as offerings.
Rice mixed with sesame (*kṛsara*), horse meat, and *kulattha* beans combined with sweetmeats (*modaka*)— [these are for the Yakṣas].
One should offer the *campaka*, *utpala*, and *puṣpa* flowers, as well as *bhūta*, O beloved;
(4th line) one should cause to be given *gulānna*, coconut, and together with the fruit of the plantain, the *kadaṃba*, *utphala*, and *puṣpa* flowers to Guha’s beloved. (5th line)
The great Ṛṣi is very fond of bamboo shoots mixed with curd, combined with jackfruit,
white lotuses, and the tips of *kuśa* grass.
An offering of turmeric rice mixed with ghee and combined with pieces of meat,
along with *pāṭala* and lotus flowers, is a bali that brings delight to Brahmā.
Rice mixed with ghee and combined with the fruit of the bṛhatī plant,
along with tulasī and yavāgū— these are dear to Viṣṇu.

One should offer black gram food mixed with śambara fish, combined with curd and honey; all red flowers and the favorite oblation of the rākṣasas. Pure food, milk, cow’s milk, and combined with plantain fruit.
The *karavīra* and *droṇa* flowers are for the pleasure of Śiva;
such is the sequence of food offerings, and then the wise one should perform the *bali* offering.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the rules, both the preceptor and the officiating priest [should proceed].
Then the wise preceptor, having worshipped the banner,
should subsequently worship the drum while recollecting the Nandi-mantra.
The wise one should place rice cooked in a vessel as a symbol of food;
its height is twelve finger-breadths, and twice that is said to be the depth of the navel.
Having worshipped this emblem of food (annaliṅga) in due order— beginning with the foremost, the secret of the digits, and likewise the emaciated one— by means of the Pāśupata weapon-mantra.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
he grants boons with his right hand, while in the left [he holds] a rosary and a trident, and [bestows] protection from fear.

Having meditated upon this form of Annapūrṇā, who is endowed with a fierce gaze and adorned with all ornaments, one should worship her according to the prescribed ritual. One should fill the vessel for the bali offering with water from the heart-mantra and with food, along with the [other] offerings.

One should not maintain a perpetual fire, but should perform the oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rules. Having invoked the Goddess there, one should worship her as the Root-Liṅga; having meditated upon Sadāśiva as Śivā, one should then worship her within Śiva, the Moon-crested Lord.
The invocation must be performed, especially when there is an abundance of offerings;
the two attendants, taking up the weapon and the food-marked emblem, [should proceed].
One should visualize the uṣṇīṣa, the upper garment, the ornaments, and so forth;
then the consecration, the five products of the cow, the perfumes and flowers, and thereafter the water.
Accompanied by incense and lamps, and joined with the sound of sugar-cane sugar;
likewise accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, drums, and other instruments.
Adorned with umbrellas and chowries, and equipped with the bull-umbrella and banners,
one should offer bali-offerings to Nandin and Kāla at the right and left of the door;
[one should place] the bull and Durgā in the southeast, and [the cow] in the northeast.
In the south is Bhṛṅgarāja, accompanied by the hosts of Mātanga;
in the southwest is Vighnarāja; in the west is Varadaivata;
Skanda is in the direction of the wind (the northwest); and Caṇḍeśa is in the domain of Soma (the north).
In the northeast, one should place Kṣetrapāla, and in front of Śiva, Bhāskara;
at the gateway (gopura), there should be the sound of musical instruments accompanied by the blare of conchs.
On both sides of the gateway door, moreover, are Daṇḍin and Muṇḍin.
One should offer an oblation to Vṛṣabha in the eastern quarter, each by its own name.
Indra, as well as Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti;
likewise Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna.
For Indra and the others, a dance and song are performed as offerings for each one individually.
Having again performed a circumambulation from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*), one should present the offering to Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu is in the south, in the southwest (*naiṛta*); Prajāpati is in the north, in the northeast (*īśa*).
Afterwards, one should offer the *bali* for the bull-mantra at the tip of his banner.
Then, one should proceed to the serpent situated beside the gateway of the city gate.
Now listen to the sequence for offering the *bali*, beginning with the twilight rites, for the site of the village.
The offering of the bali-oblation is of two kinds: one made of flour and the other of silver.
Having smeared it with cow-dung, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should then sprinkle the flower with scented water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

One should offer the *bali* on a single pedestal with the respective mantras of their own names: Brahmā at the junction of the quarters (*brahmasandhi*), and the deity of that [direction] on the left;
from Indra up to Īśāna, each is the lord of his respective quarter on the left.
Having reached the great seat (mahāpīṭha), perform the washing of the feet after offering oblations and songs of dance to Viriñci and the other deities of the sacred seats.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, and the goad,
as well as the mace, the trident, and the discus, [are placed] at the bases of the seats starting from the east.
One should offer oblations (bali) to Īśa with the words "cakraṃ padmena nṛtau" and by their respective names.
On the upper pedestal, at the tips of the petals, one should [place offerings] in the four directions starting from the east.
Āmoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, and likewise Durmukha;
[these are placed] in the northeast as the absence of obstacles, while Vighneśa is in the pericarp above.
For the fourth form, however, one should use its own name preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*;
having offered the *bali* at the end of *svāhā*, one should apply the formula "to all" (*sarveṣām*).
Having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should enter the temple.
Having established the crescent-moon crest, one should properly join it to the Śivaliṅga.

Thus has the procedure for the brahminical [installation] been declared; now listen attentively to that which pertains to the silver [image], including the temple enclosure, the gates, and so forth, up to the gopura.
Having offered the bali oblation as previously described, especially at the junctions of the village,
one should place the four-faced Brahmā upon the Brahma-pīṭha and the deity of that day on the left.
And first, one should offer an oblation to the sages in the middle of the girdle;
on the seat of Indra, there is the great vajra, and on its left, the deity of the day.
In the middle of that uppermost girdle, one should offer oblations to all the gods;
on the pedestal, as before, [one should worship] Agni, the wielder of the spear, and the deities of the day.
For the protection of the house and all else, [this is done] in the middle of the uppermost girdle.
One should place Yama, the wielder of the staff, in the south, and the presiding deity of that day in the north.
For all the ancestors, [the deity] should be in the front, at the girdle, and in the middle;
and in the southwest (Nairṛta), one should place the wielder of the sword, with the deity of that day in the north.
The *stuparākṣa* [is the form] of all; the middle girdle is the foremost.
In the western direction, he holds a noose in his hand, and on the left is the deity of that day.
The Gandharva is for all [the fingers] at the middle and tips of the girdle;
likewise, the Lord of All Nagas is at the front of the girdle and the middle of the girdle. The sprout of the abode of Vayu is on the left hand, which is the deity of that day.
To all the Gandharvas and Khecaras, [offerings are made] at the middle and the tip of the girdle; Gadādhara is in the north, and Dinadeva is on the left.
To the Mahātapas and Rakṣases, at the front and in the middle of the girdle;
to the wielder of the trident in the northeast, and on the left, the deity of that day;
to all the Bhūtas and Piśācas, at the tip of the girdle and in the middle.
One should offer the bali-oblation from the front of the Creator (Brahmā) toward the left,
or [from the right]. Caṇḍarudra is at the city gate, Sarasvatī is in the assembly hall,
Śasta is in the place of Ārya, and Durgā is in the place of Durgā.
In the Kālikoṣṭhas there is Kālyā; on both banks of the river is a tīrtha;
on the mountain is Bhūtarāja; at Kuṇḍodara is Taṭārka; and in each sacred field (kṣetra), as well as in those joined with the outer boundary, resides Kṣetramūrti.

Having especially offered the *bali* oblation as before at the great seat (*mahāpīṭha*), and having performed the circumambulation of the shrine, one should enter the temple. This has been declared as the offering of the *bali*; now listen to the Mahāyāna.
[Thus ends the chapter on the extensive ritual of the *bali* offering in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
(The sequence of the *bali* offering:
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the sacrifice and other rites; listen!
The subduing of wicked beings such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and yakṣas;
the protection of the virtuous, including the Gaṇas, gods, and ṛṣis;
and for the purpose of world conquest, either equal to a sacrifice or consisting of the circumambulation of a village.
At the time of commencing the festival, however, one should fashion the vehicles of the deities, beginning with the rat and ending with the chariot,
endowed with their characteristic features.
To the east of the Bherītāḍya [temple], however, is the cause for purifying the pathway; Caṇḍeśa is at the end of the pathway, while Vāyanāga is to the right of the village.
It was provided with various musical instruments, accompanied by parasols and fly-whisks,
joined by various devotees, and its streets were pure, though uneven.
One should prepare a cushioned covering, as well as perform sweeping and sprinkling;
having constructed a beautiful water-shed for the city and for all people,
it should be provided with various arrangements and adorned with umbrellas and cloths.
It was adorned with garlands of gold, garlands of red cloth, and garlands of flowers; the palace was completely furnished with door-pitchers,
as well as plantains, betel-nut trees, various archways, and banners.
The palace was gradually adorned with gifts of gold and other riches, as well as lamps;
at the conclusion of the offerings, the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) was the preeminent feature of the festivities.
O Ambikā, one should perform the sacrifice for Śiva’s power (Śivaśakti) at every festival for the god Umāskandeśvara, who is established in the Śivayāga.
Thus, the empowerment of the Śakti occurs during the two junctions of the Mahāyāna;
thus, seated in divine bliss, she becomes the first among the Rudras.
His limbs were anointed with fragrant sandalwood, he was adorned with all manner of ornaments,
endowed with the splendor of flowers, and beautified by variegated garments.
One should present the offerings of food (naivedya) in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa).
For the sake of protecting the Śiva-sacrifice, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion;
at the time of observing the sacrifice, the wise one should perform worship.
Accompanied by incense and lamps, endowed with the sound of musical instruments,
provided with various parasols, and furnished with various peacock-feather fans.
Adorned with various banners and accompanied by various hymns,
one should place Rudra at the front— either all three, or two, or even just one.
First, [he is] seated comfortably; second, the moon-crested one;
third, the king of dancers, O King; and the fourth is for the sake of the Goddess. Fifth, however, is he mounted upon the bull, the destroyer of the cities of the bull’s minister.
The seventh is Ākālahārī, and Dakṣiṇāmūrtti is the eighth.
The ninth is Hari and the tenth shall be Śrīkaṇṭha;
the eleventh is Śūlapāṇi, who is remembered as the eleventh Rudra.
In a chariot, a flower-palace, and likewise upon a jeweled lion-throne; in a palanquin and on a bull, as well as on a horse, [one should visualize] the Lord of Beings.
In the theater, during the festival of the lion,
the lordly elephant, and the horse, the primary song and dance of Rudra should be performed in due order at the front of the procession.
Before him were the attendants of Rudra; before them were the Brahmins and others;
before them were the ten Rudras and the moon-crested Īśvara.
At the very front was the Subrahmaṇyā priest, and at the head of him was the leader of the troop;
and at the head of him, in particular, arose the sound of great musical instruments.
O Ambikā, the principal vehicle of Rudra followed behind him.
And at the end of all those [sections], one should subsequently proceed to Caṇḍeśvara. There, one should meditate upon the forms of the vehicles day by day;
and for Gaṇeśa, before the fire, one should perform all the services and so forth.
On the first [day] of Guhya, one should meditate on the vehicle (*yāna*) as the summoning (*āhvāhana*);
on the second day, that of Gaṇeśa, as the cause of the youngest (*kaniṣṭha*).
One should meditate upon his form as Mahāyāna, mounted on a five-headed vehicle;
one should meditate upon Tripurāntaka, who brings delight to the Gaṇas and Bhūtas.
On the fourth day, after the day of the Destroyer of Tripura (Śiva), compassion arises;
through his form and the bull-vehicle, the joy of the worlds shall be accomplished.
On the fifth day, however, at the morning twilight, there is indeed a cause for the impairment of power.
In former times, during the Kali age,

for the sake of the prosperity of the worlds and for the purpose of sacrifice at the time of victory, Gaurī was taken by him, the enchanting one, for the sake of the people's desire for spiritual attainment, according to the prescribed ritual.
"One should later abandon any deficiency; thus Bhuvaneśvarī is well-pleased.
In this manner, one should perform the *līlā-yāga* for the sake of Gaurī’s satisfaction.
On that day, however, traveling during the two subsequent twilights will be the cause for future success.
Having heard this, O Brahmin of the city of Brahmā, knowledge shall arise;
may Umā and the lotus grant the milk of the two sciences of the wife and the husband.
"May you two, beloved of Śiva, ascend the path of destruction of your own [sins].
Thinking thus, he [approached] the garden, which was like the very form of the end of the world.
On the sixth day from that of the sacrifice, she who is very dear to Indra and the other gods should meditate upon the god who bears no fault and has an elephant as his vehicle.
In other sacred places where the divine play of Śiva occurs,
the wise man should perform all the rites for him and contemplate the festival day by day until the conclusion of the festival,
including the rites for the images that are part of the festival.
One should offer coconut fruit, pieces of sugarcane, and other fruits as the food offering (naivedya),
followed by incense, a lamp, and betel leaf in due order;
accompanied by dance and song, and with hymns and auspicious recitations.
Thereafter, having bathed [the image] with cow-products and other substances, one should consecrate it with the respective water-pots (kumbha).
One should worship the food offering (naivedya), incense, lamps, and so forth, according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise, one should honor the preceptor (deśika), the officiant (pūjaka), and the consecrator (sthāpaka) with ornaments.
And the cook—these five one should worship in due order according to the prescribed rule.
And on the seventh day, one should perform the festival of Naṭeśa. [Thus ends the chapter on festivals and processions in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
[The Festival of Naṭeśa] Hereafter, I shall describe in due order the festival of the King of Dance (*nṛttarājotsava*),
which bestows the fruits of penance upon all those who have attained the form of the sacrifice (*yāgamūrti*).
May this desired [work] lead to success, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the teaching for the purpose of sacrifice and desire, which destroys faults such as the killing of a Brahmin.
In the first part of the night, however, one should perform the rite and wear the protection cord;
or else, one should worship [the deity] according to the rules in the assembly pavilion.
Having prepared all the bathing substances, perform the ceremonial bath at the conclusion of the rite;
clothe [the deity] in variegated garments and adorn [him] with all the ornaments.
Camba (or campa), kothphala, hrīvera, sukha, āmbuja, pāṭalī, ketakī, vakula, nandyāvarta, and mallikā.
One should cause these to be offered with fragrant flowers according to one's ability;
having constructed a pavilion before it, provided with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers, he should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made;
thereafter, the most excellent of preceptors should duly install the vessel of peace (*śāntikuṃbha*).
On its southern side, having performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule,
one should perform all the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna), as described in the Agnikārya.
One should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame, bilva leaves, blue lotus, bulbous roots, plantain, and breadfruit.
Having placed [the image] in a water-pot before the fire, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the *kṛṣṇapiṅga* mantra.
Then, having taken that mixture of mahiṣī and other fragrant substances such as camphor,
the wise one should place it along with black perfumes in a vessel.
He should purify it with the Astra mantra and encircle it with the Varma mantra.
One should consecrate with the Brahma-aṅga mantras and display the Dhenu-mudrā.
The water for rinsing the mouth and the water for sipping (ācamana) should be rendered sinless by means of the Hṛdaya mantra alone.
One should apply black sandalwood paste and recite the Ghora mantra upon the forehead.
One should cause the *śikhā* [mantra] to be placed on the right arm with the mantra. One should duly establish the sacred ash (*bhasma*) and offer incense and lamps, O Kurus;
thereafter, one should present Sadāśiva and then cause the [other] forms (*mūrtis*) to be offered.
Then, one should cause the Śaktis to be placed upon the forehead and the throat;
[one should meditate on] the God seated upon a jewel lion-throne in the midst of the radiance.
On the left-hand seat of the deity, the preceptor takes a comfortable seat;
on the left side of the deity, however, is Gaurī, adorned with ornaments on all her limbs.
Either a king in the region of the left, or a devotee behind,
while the dancer and the wrestler are stationed on the right;
and on both sides, the attendants of Hara and the courtesans are situated.
In front of the deity, one should especially perform a dance accompanied by song.
Having performed a circumambulation of the temple compound, one should enter the sanctuary;
having offered water for the feet and other honors, one should present fruits and other offerings.
Provided with incense and lamps, accompanied by dance and song,
and having placed the five products of the cow and other substances there, [one should perform the rite] with all the mantras beginning with those of Rudra.

One should perform the consecration with nine jars using the mantras beginning with the *Pañcabrahma*. Then, having offered garments, a sacred thread (*upavīta*), ornaments, and likewise a mirror, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other items while reciting the *Īśāna* mantra and the *Hṛdaya* mantra respectively.
One should place the garland on the head with the *Śiras* mantra, the incense with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra,
the lamp with the *Netra* mantra, and the collyrium with the *Varma* mantra.

One should display the *liṅgamudrā* and likewise the *bījamudrā*; with the mantra "devasya tvā," one should present the food offering (*naivedya*). Having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should dismiss the floral remains (*nirmālya*).
Afterwards, one should cause the offering of faded flowers (nirmālya) to be given, and one should also cause incense and lamps to be offered.
The wise one should cause all the ritual offerings to be presented in due order to the Lord seated upon the lion-throne, accompanied on his left by Gaurī.
Seated comfortably on the left in the Śiva posture, free from the halo,
the wise one should thus contemplate the Lord situated as described, especially within the vehicle (yāna).
When the world-protectors and their devotees have been circumambulated in due order,
one should perform the circumambulation of the discus by moving to the left, accompanied by recitation, hymns of praise, and austerities.

In the midst of that inner assembly hall, one should offer a circumambulation of the vehicle-wheel (yānacakra) according to one's desired wishes; then, with the vehicle proceeding in its course, one should offer [oblations] until it is satisfied. Afterward, there is a hymn of praise (stotra), and at its conclusion, the rite of the vehicle (yānakāraṇa).
Accompanied by dancing and the sport of Kumārdaka, joined with song and dance,
endowed with various umbrellas and banners, preceded by conchs and black [trumpets],
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, and provided with peacock-feather fans and chowries.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should enter toward the temple.
Then, the festival of Naṭeśa is declared to be the same [as others], followed by the mounting of horses and other mounts.
[Thus ends the chapter on the festival of Naṭeśa in the Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra.]
[Side Heading] [Mounting the Horse] Henceforth, I shall explain the procedure for mounting horses and other mounts.
For the sake of sacrifice, the twice-born may mount a horse for their own desired purpose.
At that time, one should contemplate the Śabara’s purification through austerities,
as well as Śambhu’s arrival on a hunting expedition and his commencement of battle,
accompanied by parasols and chowries and the sound of musical instruments.
I believe that [force] was joined by Kirātas and equipped with spears;
some were mounted on horses, some had elephants as their vehicles,
some were bowmen, and others likewise held nooses.
Some were indeed named Kundadhara, and some were known as Ūrdhvamukha;
in ancient times, they were worshipped by the Kirātas when the lotus had but a single petal.
Therefore, having worshipped the Eye, one should bestow auspicious light;
in that place, O Earth-holder, hold that Liṅga-form in your hand like a deer.
At the time of his entry, he [beheld] the lord of Ūcāpada on that land,
together with the Kirātas of great speed and others, equipped with weapons, umbrellas, banners, and so forth.
In all systems, the king should subsequently be joined with the heart-mantra and the single form;
he should always manifest that form to him through the service of Śambara.
Śambara, being well-pleased, shall always grant Śiva’s proximity;
thus, one should perform the eight-day festival dear to the Śabaras on the eighth day at the beginning of night,
or during the final junction of the seven-day period.
Resorting to a hunting expedition, one should roam about during the time of night.
During the day, until the end of the eighth twilight, and at the twilights and other junctions of time,
one should mount a vehicle or a horse to go to the Lord who bears the skull-weapon.
At the proper time, he should perform the circumambulation of the village, inquire about the alms-round, and engage in conversation.
During the inquiries, the offerings, and the gathering of alms, he should then meditate.
Afterwards, by means of the two junctures, Hari [is perceived] as half-lion (siṃhārdha).
Just as the half of Hara was taken by Hari through their conversation,
so too, for the sake of achieving the welfare and joy of the worlds, one should meditate upon Maheśvara as having two joints with the half of the Goddess, mounted upon his bull.
On the eleventh day, at its conclusion, one should begin the mounting of the chariot.
[Thus ends the chapter on the mounting of horses in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]

[Side Heading] [Mounting the Chariot] Henceforth, I shall explain the reason for mounting the chariot. In ancient times, by the command of Śiva, for the purpose of world-conquest and the suppression of the wicked—
Accompanied by all the Rudras and endowed with the fourfold army,
one should perform the mounting of the chariot during his very festival.
It destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, increases the king and the kingdom,
brings about the affection of all the world, and annihilates all enemies.
On the eleventh day, during the two twilights, one should perform the rite of the chariot procession;
at night, however, one should duly maintain the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*).
Then, when the morning has become clear, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
One should don a new garment with the mantra "yuvam vāsaḥ.

Having placed the upper garment upon the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should worship according to the prescribed rule. Then, in front of the Śiva-fire that has been produced, one should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) according to the path described therein.
One should offer clarified butter with the *samīdīśāna* mantra and the root mantra;
one should offer the *caru* with the *hṛdaya* mantra and the parched grain (*lāja*) with the *vāma* mantra.
One should offer the sesame seeds with the *varma* and *netra* mantras, and likewise offer the *gulā*.
One should offer twenty-five bilva leaves individually for each deity.
The wise one should offer the weapon-mantra once; at the end of the substances, he should offer the *vyāhṛtis*.
With the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," the most excellent preceptor should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation.
One should perform the *jayādi* oblations and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, and sacrifice with clarified butter (*ājya*).
Having offered the first oblation to the head, one should worship Śiva in the northeast.
[One should also offer] the gift of a cow, the peace-vessel (*śāntakuṃbha*), a bronze vessel, and a cloth.
Having placed a sesame seed at the tip [of the tongue], one should show the body together with its calf;
then, having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one should cause incense and lamps to be presented.
One should place silver, bracelets, and gold upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in front of Śiva.
Saffron, agallochum, camphor,
and sandalwood mixed with hot water should be combined and placed in a cauldron along with mud and other such materials.
One should respectfully place flowers such as the pāṭalī, utpala, jasmine, punnāga, and campaka, as well as the ketakī and bilva, upon the banner.
Having worshipped the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), the wise one, with a mind intent on the mud of the Ādrā constellation,
should provide the mud of Ādrā for the sake of performing the sacrifice and for the preceptor.
Before three muhūrtas have passed, one should perform the purification of the chariot;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then cleanse it with water.
Having sprinkled the flow [of the chariot] with water consecrated by the root mantra, one should touch it;
then, having performed the purificatory rites for the chariot, one should install the presiding deity.
On the two staffs of Hari and Vajra, the Moon and the Lord of Day (the Sun) were fashioned;
around them, the lords of the [eight] regions and the hundred Rudras are proclaimed to have been placed.
In the various limbs, beginning with the dharma [element], that which pertains to the deceased is remembered;
from one limb to another, it is endowed with qualities such as the coolness of wind and so forth.
Upon the pinnacle of the temple's spire, one should always install Sadāśiva,
as well as Skanda, Indra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Having taken his stand at the edge of the chariot, he stationed the world-protectors;
then, having worshipped the cords and the architect (Vidhi), he [placed] the earth and the serpent in the four directions.
The supreme preceptor should install these very [deities] in their proper sequence,
adorning them with variegated cloths and canopies, and embellishing them with ornaments of gold and jewels.
Having decorated the silver crescent moon, he should further adorn it with banners and parasols.
One should cause it to be hung with golden chains and strings of jewels;
it should be adorned with various flowers, fruits, and leaves, such as plantains and other [offerings].
At the conclusion of that, however, one should especially perform the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a yogin who is absorbed in meditation and who knows the knowledge of Śiva.
One should cause gold, weapons, and other such items to be offered in the presence of Śiva,
having taken one's station upon a chariot at an auspicious moment and under a favorable planetary division (aṃśaka).
Having recited the Svastisūkta, O Lord, the mounting upon the chariot [should take place];
likewise, the preceptor, the worshipper, and the installer—these six or seven [should be present].
And having adorned it with a *pācaka* ornament, one should likewise place it upon the chariot;
with the forms of the *upanāyana* [initiation] rites, one should lead it to the mounting of the chariot.
Having placed Śiva upon a lion-throne on a swing fixed atop a chariot-seat,
and having embraced him with the heart while he is moist with water, one should [apply] that [liquid] as the limbs of the deity throughout all [the parts].

One should offer perfumes, garlands, and a paste for joining [the lips], adorned with all ornaments; thereafter, one should cause an offering of food consisting of excellent fruits and the like, as well as betel, to be presented.
O Śambhu, one should offer incense and lamps, and afterwards cause the sacred ash (bhasman) to be given. At the front of the chariot, there should be the meeting of the banners of valor;
and right before that, there should be the gathering of the great sound of various musical instruments.
At its end is the swing-mechanism (ḍolayantra), and at its end the horse-mechanism (vājiyantra);
then the balance-mechanism (tauliyantra), and at its conclusion the elephant-mechanism (gajayantra).
[This constitutes] the mounting of all the fire-mechanisms (śikhiyantra) and so forth for the two Rudra-maidens.
At the end of that, one should worship Vighnarāja upon a mouse or even on a chariot;
Guha mounted upon a peacock; the Lord who wields the trident (Śiva) upon a dog;
Śrīkaṇṭha mounted upon an elephant; and Hari [mounted] upon half of a lion-king.
One should cause Dakṣiṇāmūrti to expand [in the east], Bhūtanātha in the south, and Yamāntaka in the west.
On a horse, [he worships] Tripurāhārī; likewise on a bull, Vṛṣārūḍha;
on a bull, the half-body of the Goddess; and Naṭeśa on a lion-vehicle.
On the next lotus, Candra-ardhaśekhara;
at its end, Mahāśaiva; and likewise, at its end, Bhūsura.
At the end of that is the king (*bhūpati*), and at the end of that is his mantra;
at the end of that is Rudragaṇikā, and at the end of that are Nṛttikā and the others;
at the end of that the singers (*gāyaka*) are declared, and at the end of that the offspring of the dancers (*nṛttaka*).
The festival of the Lord [Śiva] and the chariot procession take place at its conclusion.
At the end of that, Goddess Umā arrives in her chariot procession;
then follows Caṇḍeśa, and finally the Śiva-festival procession itself.
And for all these forms, [the chariot] is provided with parasols and chowries,
joined with various banners and endowed with various peacock feathers.
Equipped with all musical instruments and provided with incense and lamps,
having thus performed the circumambulation, one should enter the temple.
Now hear the excellent and well-established procedure for this abundant festival of Vijaya.

Thus, on the twelfth day, at the two junctions of the day, the festival of victory (*vijayotsava*) is celebrated as before. Alternatively, the extensive procession of the chariot (*rathayāna*) is prescribed for the stability [of the kingdom]; the mounting of the chariot has been described. Now hear concerning the collection of sacred sites (*tīrthasaṅgrahaṇa*).
[Thus ends the chapter on mounting the chariot in the Pratiṣṭhātantra, which is to be contemplated.]
(Side heading) [The Compendium of Holy Sites] (7th line) Henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequence for the compendium of holy sites;
on the very day of the powder-offering, one should collect the great holy site.
During the first part of the night, one should duly fasten the protection-thread (*rakṣāsūtra*).
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should then have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited.
One should then duly place the *dṛṇḍhra* water-pot in the center of the pavilion.
In the central jar [representing] Manonmanī, and in the jars starting from the east (Indra’s direction),
are Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Nirmadā, and Sarasvatī.
The Sindhu, the Godāvarī, the Kāverī, and the Tāmraparṇikā—
having thus established these sacred sites in sequence, one should offer the food offering (naivedya), incense, and lamps.
Having placed the jar upon a *śivara* (pedestal), it should be provided with a trident;
it should be completely equipped on all sides and joined with incense and a mirror.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, he should cause him to enter a sacred bathing place—
a river, a stream, a lake, or a holy site frequented by men.
Having made the bank level, the wise man should prepare cakes.
Having prepared a mound of rice on the ground, one should place the trident and the water-pot (*kumbha*).
Then, having established Gaṇeśa in the west as before, one should worship him;
and after having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should invoke all the deities.
Having consecrated the water-pots, one should especially bathe the trident in the middle of the northern door,
and then enter the temple with full restraint.

The collection of sacred sites (*tīrthasaṅgrahaṇa*) has been proclaimed; now one should perform the *cūrṇotsava* festival. [Thus ends the chapter on the collection of sacred sites in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
[Side Heading] [The Powder Festival] Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the Powder Festival (*cūrṇotsava*),
beginning from the day following the gathering at the sacred site (*tīrtha*) and continuing through the subsequent days.
Having performed the Baliyāna festival, one should thereafter observe the Cūrṇotsava,
either at the front of the temple, or on its right, or even on its north side.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should then have the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) proclaimed;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on a double-layered surface, one should draw a lotus in its center.

Having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, the wise one should worship the trident as having a single womb (*ekayoni*); others, however, consider it to have the same womb as the aforementioned [deities], while the mortar and pestle are likewise [worshipped].

One should know that the *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha* [woods] are for the mortar; the pestle should be made of *khadira*. One should sprinkle them with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having worshipped Vighneśa, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, having duly honored the Trident-form (Śūlamūrti), one should strike the drum.
One should carry dūrvā grass, sahadevī, and cloth upon the mortar;
Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the mortar, while Rudra is the presiding deity of the pestle.
One should worship Śūrpa with the mantra "Brahmā is the presiding deity," using each respective name.

One should perform the offering of clarified butter upon the head with gold, dūrvā sprouts, and unbroken rice grains. Having placed the śukā plant in the middle of the mortar and touching the middle of the pestle, one should meditate upon the Guru as the all-pervading Vyomavyāpin.
Then the devotees should touch [the image] with auspicious hymns of praise,
while the courtesan, together with her attendants, should grind the powder separately.
Having collected the powder, one should cause the root-sign to enter [the heart]. Having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, one should display the lotus-mudrā.
And the best of instructors [should employ] the spear, the measuring-line, and the trident.

A Brahmin or a Kṣatriya should give [the remainder]; the rest should be collected in a vessel. That powder, combined with mercury and joined with trident-mercury, should be given to the people of the village after performing a circumambulation.
Afterwards, one should enter the abode and perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford.
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the powder festival in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha),
which serves to purify all forms of contact and is beloved by all sacred fords.

For all devotees, the fulfillment of the temple is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). For the sake of destroying all defects, it grants the same fruit as the world of Indra. One should perform the ritual bath at this sacred ford of Śiva, which bestows happiness.
The most excellent preceptor, having duly performed the rite of the "sprout of the sacred ford" (tīrthāṅkura),
[should perform] the "auspicious thread" (kautuka) as instructed by the preceptor, accompanied by the King of Weapons (astrarāja),
provided with incense and lamps, and joined with a parasol and chowries.
Accompanied by dance and song, and joined with the sound of musical instruments,
he should proceed together with his devoted followers and enter for the ritual bath at the sacred ford.
Likewise, having placed the image in the middle of a water-shed (*prapā*) on the bank,
one should prepare a ritual platform (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice— either eight *droṇas* or half of that—
and specifically place a perforated jar (*randhrakumbha*) before each image.
Then, one should duly install the jar with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Having established the sacred water (tīrtha) and the jar, one should place Manonmanī in the center;
the seven sacred waters (saptatīrtha), starting from the east and ending in the northeast, should be arranged together with Durgā.
One should especially worship the jar according to the rules in the midst of water;
likewise, one should perform the ritual bathing at its sacred site, as well as the offering of incense and lamps.
Furthermore, there are eighteen groups and thirty-three presiding deities.
One should invoke Indra and the other guardians of the world in the vicinity of the trident,
from the hands of both [the officiant and the disciple], as they move toward the two images [of the deities] with clarified butter.
Having established [the image] in the midst of water, one should perform the threefold ablution;
having bathed the preceptor, the wise man shall emerge from the sacred ford.
As before, one should cause the images to be bathed within the light;
then, having consecrated them with their respective jars, [one should offer] food offerings, incense, and lamps.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should enter the temple;
having placed [the image] in the assembly pavilion, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas (brahmaghoṣa).
Then, with the consecrated grains (*akṣata*) of blessing upon the hands of the preceptor,
and having honored the preceptor with those very grains of blessing,
one should join each [deity] to its own respective place, and all the *beras* as before.

This is declared to be the ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrthasnāna); one should perform the ritual bath with the water-pot (ghaṭasnāna). [Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the Ghaṭasnāna in the Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra.]
[Side Heading]: *Ghaṭasnāna* (The Vessel Bath).

Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the vessel bath (*ghaṭasnānavidhi*), which serves as the preliminary for the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*) and is the cause of stability for the worlds.

One should perform the ritual bath of the jar (ghaṭasnāna) for the sake of attaining the grace of the knowledge of Śiva, which further bestows the accomplishment of proximity to the forms of the deities such as Indra.
Afterward, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the supreme preceptor should establish [the deity];
he should worship the deity in that jar with food offerings, incense, and lamps.
Having honored the preceptor, one should cause the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given;
then, having summoned the cook, one should adorn him with garments, gold, and other ornaments.
One should carry the jars placed upon the *vedī* on top of the head,
accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and provided with incense and lamps.
Having performed the circumambulation, the wise one should place [the vessels] before Śiva;
first, he should bathe the Liṅga from the jars of the four Vedas in sequence.
Having bathed it with the jar of the Great Sacrifice (mahāyajña), he should proceed in order to the pedestal of the Liṅga.
One should indeed perform the ritual bath with a jar for the guardians of the quarters (Lokapālas).
Then, one should grant the position of the Lord; this is recorded as the fourth enclosure.
Having established the half-measure of the bath, one should place Sadāśiva in its center.
One should place the Vardhanī vessel on the left side as Manonmanī;
one should also place [the vessels] for the eight Vidyeśvaras upon the eight jars that form the enclosure.
When the Śivāgni has been generated, one should duly establish everything;
then, with the head [of the vessel], one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and after the sviṣṭakṛt, one should offer the final oblation.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the fire-pitcher (agnikuṃbha), one should then dismiss that fire.
Having placed that *kumbha* [vessel] and the *vardhanī* [overflow vessel] upon the pedestal of the *liṅga* in due order,
one should bathe it with eight jars all around and install the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*).
One should then perform the respective ablutions for the deities of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) of Śiva and worship them.
Because of the abundance of the sacrificial oblation, one should cause incense and lamps to be offered;
specifically for the image, one should perform the ritual bathing according to the prescribed procedure.
This is declared to be the ritual bath with the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*); after that follows the lowering of the banner (*dhvajāvarohaṇa*).
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the ritual bath with the jar in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
[The Hoisting of the Banner] Hereafter I shall explain the hoisting of the great banner:
the hoisting on the third, fifth, seventh, or ninth day.
Whether it be the Ghoratriguṇa, the Vikrama, or the Triguṇa;
whether it be the Śivarātriguṇa or the Śrīkaratriguṇa;
whether it be the Stavāhatriguṇa or the Paitṛkatriguṇa.

The wise man should again commence the festival and perform the rites as before. This same procedure prescribed for the best [type of flagstaff] applies also to the hoisting of the banner. Having placed the bull upon the flagstaff, one should install the image of the Bull-form.
Once the water-pot has been established, one should place the banner and the bull within the opening;
one should know that the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be placed in the eight pots surrounding it.
Having bathed the water-pot of that king of bulls,
one should bathe the pots of the directions of the bull with hair [from its tail] in villages and other such places.
Having bathed [the deity] with the seed-syllable of the bull (vṛṣabīja), one should worship him with its mantras;
having worshipped Vṛṣavighneśvara according to the procedure in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Having worshipped the two bulls at the gates, one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas), such as Varuṇa and Yama, along with their respective directions,
guardians, and scriptures in the third enclosure;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.
One should offer incense, lamps, and food, and perform worship in the proper sequence.
The lowering of the banner and likewise the offering of bali for the sake of silence have been declared.
[Thus ends the chapter on the lowering of the banner in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
[Side Heading] *Maunabali* (The Silent Offering) Henceforth, I shall explain the procedure for the offering (*bali*) intended for the purpose of silence (*mauna*),
[dedicated] to Brahmā and the other guardians of the world (*lokapāla*s), as well as Indra and Īśāna.
The offering of the *balikāra* is for the sake of fulfilling the specific purposes associated with each respective name;
furthermore, the offering of the *balimāna* is for the purpose of protecting the village and for the sake of maintaining silence.
Furthermore, one should present the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), accompanied by the insignia of food,
joined with a sword and shield, and provided with perfumes and flowers;
this should especially take place at midnight, accompanied by many lamps.
The wise one, having removed the long vowel from the direction [of the letter] joined with the sound of the hot [letter], [remains].
Having offered food mixed with red rice and meat, along with molasses, ghee, and curd,
and having all maintained the practice of silence, one should bid farewell to the Siddhidevas.
Having cast the offering (bali) for Maunārta at the junction-seat of the village,
and following the sequence of circumambulation, one should enter toward the temple.
As before, one should install the trident and cast the food-liṅga into the water;
then the wise man should worship the form of Caṇḍa according to the rules in due order.
There, he should worship the preceptor and cause sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
One attains satisfaction through the mind regarding the teacher; from that, one attains supreme Śiva.
From the commencement of the rite up to the final offering of the sprouts and the vow of silence, there are twenty-one festivals.
By reciting this and practicing it, one shall attain union with Śiva.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the silent offering in the Pratiṣṭhātantra, which is to be contemplated.]
[The procedure for the Śivotsava festival, written by the teacher Kālīśvara, is completed. Hariḥ Om.
(Side Heading): [Expiation for Festivals;
The Rite of Planting Sprouts] Henceforth, I shall proclaim the expiation for the festival of Śiva:
regarding the failure to perform worship after having granted permission to the Gaṇas and the God of Gods.
If diseases afflict the preceptor and his sons,
the deity should be provided with a ritual bath and twice the usual amount of sacrificial oblation should be offered.
One should recite that great mantra two thousand times;
if the offering of sprouts is omitted, the festival will become fruitless.
Auspiciousness perishes in the village; one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
The Goddess should cause the sprout to grow, and then one should perform the ritual action.
In a field of clay that is devoid of offerings and lacks the sprinkling of cow-products,
there will be the destruction of the rice and the destruction of the cattle.
Having relied upon the *śānti*-oblation, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should present an offering (*bali*) before the weapon-mantra (*astra*) for the deities of the field and the [other] deities.
If it lacks a covering of clay, there is the danger of the destruction of clothing;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should recite the Pāśupata mantra one hundred times.
If the moon-pitcher (candrakumbha) is missing, there is no doubt that the patron will suffer misfortune;
therefore, having performed a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma), one should install the moon-pitcher.
If the worship of the moon-pitcher is omitted, or if it is missing, or if the opening is deficient and devoid of water, [the rite fails].
If death should occur for the officiant (sthāpaka), one should perform a pacifying fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
Having properly selected another [officiant], the wise man should install him according to the rules.
After having arranged the autumn and other seasons, [one should proceed] when the ritual is deficient or has been omitted.
If there is agitation caused by enemies in the village, one should recite the terrible mantra a thousand times;
then, relying on the sequential conjunction (*saṃdhāna*), one should offer a hundred oblations at the root of the moon.
One should offer ten oblations for each of the attendants and the Jayās.
When there is a loss of the Moon-vessel (*candrakumbha*), or upon contact with a Vaiśya or others,
and when drought occurs in the world, one should perform the propitiatory *homa*.

Then, having discarded the *pālikā* and other vessels, one should collect the clay remaining there. Alternatively, one may place it in a new jar; having poured that clay into a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or similar vessel, one should fill it.
Having cast seven sprouts along with unbroken rice grains (akṣata) and combined with dūrvā grass and akṣata,
one should first generate the Śiva-fire and offer a hundred oblations at the base of the moon.
One should offer ten oblations each for the vessels and other items belonging to the wives;
furthermore, the blood of a rat, a maiden, and so forth, as well as sprouts and unbroken grains, are to be taken.
One should perform a pacifying homa even for a hundred children;
having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place *ūrvā* grass, *kūra*, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having offered one hundred oblations with the heart mantra, one should offer one hundred at the base of the moon;
for each of the wives in the retinue, one should likewise offer one hundred.
One should worship the deity prescribed in the Tantra with sprouts, unbroken rice, and dūrvā grass.

Having worshipped the deity prescribed in the Tantra—even if the sprouts and unbroken rice are deficient—one will suffer from headaches in the village; therefore, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
Having worshipped the sprouts and the unbroken grains, one should then perform the dismissal of Soma.
[Thus ends the chapter on the offering of sprouts and expiation in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
If the Śrī-kara, Tapa, or Pitṛ asterisms occur, or if the rite is devoid of the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga), death will befall the performers; therefore, one should cause the bull to be bathed.
One should then offer food consisting of mung beans and perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*).
Having performed the consecration of the bull, one should begin the hoisting of the banner.
If the banner is bitten by a rat, it should be taken down and replaced with a new one using vermilion, a virgin, and other such means.
If [the fire] is extinguished by fire in Daṇḍaka, Kandū, Vṛṣa, Citrāṅga, or Hīnaka, the destruction of the performer will occur; therefore, one should perform a propitiatory homa (śāntihoma).
Having resorted to rekindling, one should perform everything as prescribed from the beginning.
If the *pācaka* is devoid of its subsidiary limbs (*upāṅga*) while the *amṛta* is present,
one should perform a hundred oblations at the base of the *vṛṣa*, relying upon that reconstitution (*sandhāna*).
At the time of circumambulating the village, one should touch the banner with *vaiśvādi*.
There may be sorrow and disease in the village; one should perform the remaining rites in a clockwise direction.
Taking recourse to the site of the banner (dhvaja), one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having kindled the Śiva-fire there, one should offer the "touch-oblation" (sparśāhuti) upon the banner.
If the water-pot of the bull-sacrifice is broken, cracked, or becomes empty of water, it is declared that the destruction of the cows will occur; therefore, perform the ritual bathing of the bull.
Having set aside the inferior and the last [vessels],
the wise one, having offered a hundred oblations at the base of the bull with the *parivāra* and the *gāyatrī*,
should perform the cutting and joining upon the jars of the *parivāra*.
To destroy diseases in that direction, one should recite its mantra one hundred times.
The installation of the bull-sacrifice should be touched by a Vaiśya or others from a water-pot;
otherwise, diseases will quickly afflict the people in that village.
Having performed the pacification of the bull (*vṛṣaśānti*), one should perform the re-consecration (*punassandhāna*);
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform everything with the *sadyas* [rite].
[Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for the bull-sacrifice in the Cintya.]
In the Śrīkara and Tapapaitra rites, when the hoisting of the banner has been omitted,
one should perform the Mūrtihoma after encountering something difficult to overcome for kings.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars according to the prescribed rite;
having duly hoisted the banner, one should perform the Bharī-tāḍana.
If another person sees the characteristics of the staff and the altar during the raising of the banner, death shall occur for the teacher; he should recite the terrible [mantra] one thousand times.
Having fashioned a pedestal for the staff,

the wise one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and worship it as before, using a vessel marked with auspicious signs. The flagpole should be mounted during rain, and it must be devoid of a garland of *darbha* grass.

If [the snake] moves in a counter-clockwise direction, or if it holds a staff, or if it is bound by a rope; (3rd line) or if it is devoid of *darbha* grass or clothing, one should have it swallowed by a young girl or others.
If the rope is cut, [one should perform] foot-strikes in the courtyard of the temple and at the city gate.
When a planet falls upon a pure *deśaka* belonging to a king or a brahmin,
it brings grief, disease, and fear to the people of that village.
Relying upon the *śāntihoma* rite, one should recite the *Śiva-mantra* one hundred times;
having sprinkled [the flagpole] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), perform the hoisting of the banner.
If a merchant [is born] in the house of a Śūdra, or even if the banner falls, there will be defects as before; one should perform propitiatory rites and fire oblations.
Having performed the consecration of the flagstaff, the wise man should erect it as before,
even if it falls upon a tree, a river current, or the ocean.
If a dead child is born in another's house, a cremation ground, or similar places, or during an inauspicious planetary period (*aśuci-graha*),
or when a banner falls, the death of kings is certain; therefore,
one should perform a *mūrti-homa* (image-offering rite) for the sake of pacifying those evils.
One should have forty-nine pots made for the Supreme Lord;
having taken another as the ninth, one should perform the immediate joining.
When the staff falls, breaks, or is cut, great winds arise.
If death is imminent for the king, one should perform the *diśāhoma* (the oblation of the quarters).
Having performed the *punassandhāna* (re-consecration), one should immediately perform everything with the *sadyas* rite.
Afterwards, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with a thousand jars.
[This applies] when it is devoid of the secondary staff (*upadaṇḍa*) and devoid of the Skanda-staff (*skandayaṣṭi*);
also when there is no bull above the staff, and even when there is an iron ring.
If [the bell] is inferior, fallen, or broken, there is no doubt that the maker will perish. One should perform a propitiatory *homa* and carry out a re-consecration;
for if the bell is fallen or inferior, it brings about the destruction of children.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should recite the Astra-mantra a hundred times;

having sprinkled [the objects] with that very mantra, one should perform the re-consecration (*sandhāna*) once more. This applies to the three Skandas, the bell (*ghaṇṭā*), the flagstaff (*dhvajadaṇḍa*), and the banner (*dhvaja*) as well.
In particular, the penance involves cutting, piercing, and so forth.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound at the top of the banner, one should place the jar with the apertures;
having invoked the Bull in the center, one should invoke the world-protectors in their surrounding circles.
The wise man should duly place the Veda-pitcher in front of that;
having summoned [the deity] from the Viṣṇu-staff, he should properly join it to the central pitcher.
One should install Śrīdevī and Bhūmidevī at the two feet of Viṣṇukumbha;
others should install Sarasvatī at the two jars (kumbhas).
Above the staff (daṇḍa), one should perform the appropriate expiation (prāyaścitta) and the respective reconnection (sandhāna).

Thereafter, perform the sprinkling of the jar and the staff (*keśavakumbha* and *daṇḍa*). Having bathed in the Sarasvatī river situated between the Goddess of the Earth and the Goddess Śrī within this enclosure, the wise man [should place] the jar upon the top of the staff-altar (*daṇḍavedi*).
One should bathe the bull-vessel (vṛṣakuṃbhaka) above the altar and at the base of the staff;
one should then consecrate the jars of the world-protectors and the surrounding enclosure. Having offered rice mixed with mung beans, one should then cause incense and lamps to be presented.
The coming and going is said to be constant; one should place the bull upon the banner.
On the banner and on the staff, as well as at the altar, the offering of oblations should be made.
[This applies] even when the rites of invocation and dismissal are omitted, and likewise when the worship is deficient.
One should offer praise to the Lyaghañca and Garuḍa above the staff of the crow;
others, such as monkeys and the like, one should indeed touch, while those of the Vaiśya class and so forth should be touched.
Fear of enemies shall arise in the world, and there shall be the destruction of cattle;
having resorted to a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should mutter the Ghoramantra a thousand times.
Having performed the sprinkling of the banner according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the wise one should then mutter the Gāyatrī mantra a hundred times with the root of the Vṛṣa mantra.
If one observes other marks on the flagstaff of a mountain (*rohaṇa*),
there may be negligence in the world, and the destruction of the craftsmen shall occur.
At the base of the bull, one should offer all [oblations] and perform a hundred oblations with the *gāyatrī*.
One should offer one hundred oblations for each [deity] with the mantra of the World-Protector (*lokapāla*).
One should recite the mantra a thousand times and perform the *mūrtihoma* (image-oblation).
At the conclusion of the festival, especially, one should perform the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*).
Thereafter, one should perform the application of the staff as described in the characteristics;
one should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars.
Having resorted to the Mūrtihoma, perform the consecration (samprokṣaṇa) of the staff.
[Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for the hoisting of the banner in the *Cintya-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
(P.86a, 1st line) [Side heading: The expiation for the omission of beating the drum.
If the festival is held without the beating of the drum, it shall be fruitless.
If [the drum] grows dull in the village, one should perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*).
One should recite the *Nandi-mantra* a thousand times and strike the drum.
When a corner is broken or has fallen off, the drum should be struck at the time of the proclamation.
In the case of the *carma* and the *saptakīla*, the musicians shall play inferior instruments;
having recited the *astra* mantra one hundred times, one should then recite the *nandi* mantra one hundred times.
The wise practitioner, having formally accepted another [disciple], should strike him according to the rule;
when the *vadaka* has fallen upon the ground at that time, during the period of the *balikālaka*.
If there should be trouble in the village, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *Nandin-mantra*.
Day by day, before that [trouble arises], one should strike the drum (*bherikā*) as prescribed for the leather-worker.
At that time, one should strike the Goddess; thus the village will become most peaceful.
Relying upon the *śāntihoma* (peace-offering), one should recite [the mantra] over the wooden stakes made of leather and other materials.

Having selected another [stake] according to the prescribed characteristics, the wise practitioner should bind it; furthermore, he should strike the drum (*bherī*) a thousand times while reciting the *Nandin-mantra*.
If the worship is deficient, the great drum causes the splendor of the site to perish;
having recited the Nandi-mantra a hundred times, one should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should offer double the amount of sacrificial oblation and recite the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) one hundred times.
When [the body] is bitten by a rat or the like, or when it is cut or pierced, one should apply the ointment.
For one who has played a musical instrument, one should mutter the Mṛtyu-ghora mantra a hundred times;
having offered oblations a hundred times with the Nandi mantra, one should perform the ritual of reconnection (*saṃdhāna*).
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), perform the sacrifice as before.
[Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for striking a drum in the section on what is to be contemplated.]
[Side Heading] [Expiation for the Tying of the Auspicious Thread] (3rd line) When the tying of the auspicious thread (*kautukabandhana*) is performed for the God of Gods during a festival,
it causes mental distress for kings and brings about the ruin of the kingdom.
For the sake of pacifying those defects, one should perform the *mūrtihoma* sacrifice;
the wise practitioner should bind the protective thread (*kautuka*) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
If a silver *pratisara* from the hand is lost, there is destruction of the maker;
therefore, having performed a *mūrtihoma*, one should perform the re-joining.
O best of Brahmins, having performed the kautuka-rite, perform the immediate sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa).
Therefore, when the thread of the arrow has been severed, one should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma).
Having performed the reconnection (*punar-sandhāna*), one should recite the *hṛdaya* mantra one hundred times. [Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for the binding of the *kautuka*.]
If the festival is devoid of sacrifice and worship, it shall be fruitless;
both the king and the kingdom will perish. Therefore, one should perform the *mūrti-homa* (fire-offering for the image).
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars.
One should recite the Śiva-mantra one thousand times and then commence the festival once more.
The most excellent of preceptors should perform [the rites] according to the sequence of sacrifice and worship,
even if the sacrificial pavilion is lacking, the altar is missing, or the ritual characteristics are absent.
Having established [the image] in a good village, endowed with the proper characteristics,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*) and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should perform each respective rite according to the previously stated procedure;
having strewn the sacrificial ground with *uṣṇīṣa* grass, one places the water-pot upon the altar.

If destruction of grain should occur in the village, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the rite and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Then, having placed the jars in sequence, one should establish them in the sacrificial hall (yāgaśālā), which is free from punishment (nirdaṇḍaka).
The king’s death will occur swiftly, and there shall be danger from fire within the kingdom.
Having extinguished all the coals, one should perform the re-consecration;
O best of Brahmins, one should sprinkle the God of gods with streams of milk.
Having bathed with one hundred and eight jars, one should begin the festival again;
if [the pavilion] was burnt solely by fire, construct the pavilion as before.
If there is danger from fire in the village, one should perform a propitiatory *homa* according to the *Śāta* [tradition];
having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should offer a hundred oblations with the *Śiva-mantra*.
If the site is devoid of gates and archways, there will be fear of enemies;
having recited that mantra a hundred times, one should offer oblations a hundred times with the Astra-mantra.
Then, after causing the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, one should perform the re-consecration.
And in a village devoid of garlands of darbha grass, there shall be danger from serpents.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should perform the respective reconnection;
and when the kingdom is devoid of the eight auspicious signs, it is "devoid of auspiciousness."
Having performed the pacification of the elements (*bhūtaśānti*), one should sprinkle the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having performed the respective reconnection (*sandhānaka*) for each, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *Śiva-mantra*.
If the worship of the pavilion is deficient, men will suffer loss, grief, and fear;
therefore, a wise person, relying upon the *saṃhitā-homa*, should worship the pavilion.
Having offered one thousand oblations with the root mantra, one should offer one hundred in the retinue;
O best of Brahmins, having offered with the Astra-mantra and performed one hundred recitations, one should offer again.
When the principal jar of the altar is broken or when it becomes waterless, [one must act].

Upon the imminent death of the king, one should swiftly perform the *mūrtihoma* (the fire sacrifice of the image). A wise person should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars, and having taken another new one, he should install it according to the prescribed rites.
Then, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a thousand times with the root mantra;
thereafter, [one should perform] the *vardhanī* for the sacrifice, as well as the eight vessels (*ghaṭa*) surrounded by the enclosures (*āvṛta*).
If the *pāśupatāstra* and the two jars are severed, pierced, or rendered waterless,
the king, his women, and his ministers shall meet with immediate death.
Having established a jar that has been broken, one should offer a hundred oblations with its root mantra.
Having finally performed the pacifying oblation, one should offer a hundred oblations into the root of Śiva.
O Brahmin, that number [of oblations] should be performed with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) according to the ritual manual;
having worshipped in the pavilion of the sacrifice, one should perform twenty-eight pot-offerings (*kuṃbhaka*).
When [the vessel] is broken or even when it is devoid of water, there shall be confusion in that region and its kingdom;
one should cause the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) to be proclaimed there and install a new, inferior jar.
Having recited [the mantra] a hundred times at its base, one should offer a hundred oblations at the base of Śiva.
In the sacrificial jars used for propitiation, those lacking jewels and gold,
(5th line) those lacking the *kūrca* grass and flowers, those lacking the coconut, those lacking mango leaves, and those lacking the thread-wrapping; (6th line)
O best of Brahmins, when the fourfold army of the king is deprived of its clothing and armor, it will swiftly meet with death born of grief.
Then, having performed the *śānti*-oblation, one should carry out the respective reconnection (*sandhāna*);
at its root, one should offer a thousand oblations and recite the mantra five thousand times.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars,
having offered oblations and recited the Śivagāyatrī mantra one thousand times.
If the sacrificial altar, the water-pots, the fire-oblation, the coconut,
or the cloth should be lost, or if the initiated person is touched by a Śūdra or others,
the king’s kingdom shall perish; therefore, one should perform the rite of re-consecration.
Relying upon the *mūrtihoma*, perform nine oblations for the Trident (*śūla*).
One should offer a thousand oblations to Śiva-mūla, and that same number to Sadāśiva. O best of Brahmins, one should offer one hundred oblations to each member of the retinue (*parivāra*).
If a water-jar or a coconut is broken even when devoid of water, head disease shall arise; one should perform a propitiatory fire sacrifice (homa) for the Lord of the Village.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having placed another coconut at its base,
one should mutter the *Śiromantra* a thousand times at its root and perform a hundred oblations (*hunet*).
If the propitiation of the trident (*triśūla*) is lacking, there will be fear of the weapons of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*).
O Śambhu, have the ceremonial bath performed; perform the bathing with the Astra-mantra.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should offer oblations one hundred times with the Astra-mantra;
for without the fire-ritual (agnikārya), the Śiva-sacrifice is fruitless.
The king will soon meet his death, and there shall be danger from fire in the world;
to pacify those evils, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* sacrifice.
Furthermore, one should maintain the Vedic fire (*vedavahni*) and practice the five-fire ritual (*pañcāgni*).

O Brahmin, enjoyment and liberation may occur [only when it is complete]; otherwise, there is a fault as previously described. If the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) lacks its characteristics, is broken, or is split, the destruction of the performer occurs; therefore, one should have it constructed according to the prescribed characteristics.
Having resorted to the *mūrtihoma* and having established the fire as before,
if it is devoid of the *brahmakūrca*, the death of the preceptor (*deśika*) will occur.
Having eaten and performed the wonderful propitiation (*adbhutaśānti*), one should place the *brahmakūrca* [mixture] down;
having recited the *brahma-mantra* one hundred times, one should recite the *astra-mantra* one hundred times.
If the *praṇītā* vessel moves or is damaged, one will encounter rain and famine;
therefore, one should resort to a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śānti-homa*) and have the *puṇyāha* recited.
One should set down the *praṇītā* with the sacred formulas and offer a hundred oblations with the Viṣṇu-mantra.
If the darbha-grass enclosures are missing, or if the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are lacking,
or if the village prosperity (*grāmaśrī*) is otherwise impaired, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*).
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should then perform the respective reconstitution of those [missing parts].
When the materials for the fire sacrifice are lacking, famine will certainly arise;
therefore, resorting to the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should offer a hundred oblations at the root of Śiva.

Having offered substances in their specific order, one should offer a hundred oblations, starting from the *Sadyojāta* mantra up to the end of the scriptures, and likewise eleven times for each mantra.
If there is an interruption in the sacrificial fires or the ritual staffs, men shall suffer from abdominal disease and fear.
Having extinguished the fires and deposited the ashes as before,
one should offer the Śiva-mantra one hundred times and the Sādākhya-mantra one thousand times.
If [the ritual] is deficient in mantra or deficient in action, the king and his kingdom will perish.
Having resorted to the *mūrtihoma*, one should offer the root-mantra (*mūla*) one thousand times;
having offered the root-mantra of Śiva one hundred times, one should then offer the Gāyatrī.
If the sacrificial lamp is lacking, men will suffer from eye disease;
having offered a lamp, one should perform a hundred oblations with the Astra mantra.
[Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for the sacrificial pavilion in the Cintya.]
[Side Heading]: [Expiation for the Omission of the Bali Offering] If the Śiva-sacrifice is devoid of the *halidāna* offering, it becomes fruitless;
there will be affliction by minor spirits (*kṣudrabhūta*) for both the village and its inhabitants.
Having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should again conduct the festival;
however, during the festival, the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*) is excluded from the single transitional period (*ekasandhi*).
Then all the inhabitants of the village will suffer from abdominal diseases.
One should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), recite the *dinadeva* mantra a hundred times,
and perform the *yānāntabali* offering according to the previously mentioned procedure.
If the *bali* offering is deficient, men suffer from hunger for a day and night.
Having performed the *mūrti-homa* by offering a thousand oblations according to the root mantra,
and having bathed with one hundred and eight jars of water, one should recite the *Aghora* mantra a thousand times.
One should then bathe the one who has the crescent moon as his crest;
having sprinkled him with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform everything [else] with the *Sadyojāta* mantra.
If the sacrifice is deficient in offerings, the death of the king is certain.
Having resorted to the *diśāhoma*, one should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having installed the sacrificial jar (*yāgakuṃbha*), one should perform the sacrifice once again.
Furthermore, one should perform festivals such as the beating of drums and other similar rites.
There will be a great rain, and the fortress wall will face destruction;
there shall be fear from a foreign enemy on the earth, and one should perform the *mūrtihoma* sacrifice.
One should offer the Vāstu-Brahmā-bali at the center of the village rampart;
however, for the Vāstu of the world-protectors (lokapālas), it is offered during the watch (yāma) between the directions and outside the guardians of the quarters.
Having offered the oblation on the ground according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the wise one should subsequently perform the *śāntihoma* once the dissolution [of the ritual] has taken place.
One should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity] with the mantra of the Lord of the World-Protectors (*dikpālādhipa*).
One should cause the Goddess Vāstu to be enclosed by a wall and perform the *bali* offering as before.
As before, one should consider the merits and defects when the dissolution (*pralaya*) occurs at the end of the ritual procedure.
Then, one should offer the *bali* at the edge of the water for those two divine [deities], Gaurī and [the other]. Alternatively, one should perform the *bali* on the path of the *brahmasūtra*.
Having performed the *pūrva-īśānti-homa* and having offered oblations a hundred times to Śiva, [one should proceed].
If the sandals are indeed lost, destroyed, or likewise broken, there will be disease of the feet in the village; one should then perform the re-consecration.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
At the time of the offering (bali), during the other twilight (sandhyā), one should employ the sandals (pāduka).
One should sprinkle the sandals with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should mutter the Ghoramantra a thousand times and perform the remaining ritual of the bali offering.
One should perform the rite of the sandals (pādukā) at the time of the offering,

during the twilight, and at the time of departure for the sake of the oblation, O Bull-bannered One; however, if the vehicle is devoid [of these], and if the umbrella is without chowries, men will suffer from grief and disease.
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred times, one should perform the respective reconsecration (sandhāna).
Furthermore, in a village devoid of offerings and lamps, one should [perform this] for the resident Jyeṣṭhā.
Having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred times, one should perform the lamp ritual twice as many times at the gateway of the gopura,
free from the sounding of conchs.
One should perform the ritual for the Rākṣasas in the village and carry out the fire-oblation (homa) for peace;
if it is devoid of the sound of the bell, the same faults as mentioned before will arise.
