One should recite the weapon-mantra (astramantra) one thousand times accompanied by the sound of the bell.
For those who neglect the daily fire-ritual, there shall be affliction from the fires for men.
Having resorted to the ritual of oblation to the image, one should perform the fire-ritual at the conclusion of the offering;
and in the form of Candraśekhara, one should worship the fearless Śiva known as Sādākhyā.
If [the deity] is inferior, it should be placed behind; in the case of one who is both inferior and weak, it should be applied as before.
However, if the preceptor should die, one should perform the image-oblation (mūrtihoma).
Having offered a thousand oblations with the Śiva-Gāyatrī mantra starting from the root syllable, the wise one,
having established the Śiva-pitcher, should bathe the Supreme Lord.
When the offering is deficient in hymns, or devoid of song and dance;
when, at the time for dancing, the courtesan has fallen away and the rhythmic beat is lost.
A day for the Daityas and others is said to occur when the creator is in the water-sign;
at the conclusion of the offering (bali), one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) within the sacrificial image.
In that case, having offered oblations with the mantra of the deity and having recited it a thousand times,
[one should perform purification] upon touching a prostitute or others, or being touched by a dog, a pig, or a monkey.
If there should be an affliction caused by negligence in the village, one should perform a rite of pacification there;
having performed the sprinkling over the image, one should perform the homa for pacification.
Having touched the preceptor and bathed, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
then, perform the ceremonial bathing upon the image of Candraśekhara. Upon touching the trident-weapon as well, perform the bathing and the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
In the case of touching [the vessel] or when there is a defect in the food, one should perform re-consecration;
having resorted to a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma), one should mutter the Astra-mantra a thousand times.
Having performed the re-consecration of the substance, one should mutter the Ghora-mantra a thousand times.
If the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are lacking, there will be the destruction of the cows;
therefore, relying upon the *śāntihoma*, one should mutter the formidable [mantra] one thousand times.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) at the time of the *bali* offering during the junctions [of day and night],
[one should know that] the absence of *bali* substances brings about sorrow, delusion, and fear.
Having recited the great mantra of Dinadeva one hundred times,
one should cause that substance to be given back double its amount to another person who has entered into a secret agreement.
When food falls from the vessel, or when a morsel falls from the mouth, Garuḍa becomes a crow.
If one recites [the mantra] of the Lord of the Day (the Sun) one hundred times, there shall be a destruction of grain in the world.
Furthermore, one should take the ninth [syllable], *agni*, and perform the offering with the remainder of the *bali*.
If it is devoid of the characteristic of food, a famine will certainly arise.
Relying upon the pacificatory oblation (śāntihoma), one should perform the rite with food as the emblem;
if [the image] is lost, broken, or fallen, the fault shall be as previously stated.
One should accept a new vessel marked with the sign of food and perform a *śānti* oblation;
at the base of the vessel marked with the sign of food, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred times.
If the *śūla* weapon is missing, men will suffer from the affliction of weapons;
having resorted to a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should offer a hundred oblations with the *astra-mantra*.
Having resorted to the *astrayāna*, one should perform the remainder of the *bali* offering.
As for the fault previously mentioned, perform the ritual bath (*snapana*) for one who has fallen from grace.
Having offered the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) one hundred times, one should perform the ritual offering of the remains (bali-śeṣa).
When the staff of the weapon is severed [by this rite], the king shall become invincible.
Having taken up another weapon, one should perform the *mūrtihoma* (image-oblation).
If [the original image] is made of wood, one should draw the weapon there and install it;
then, relying on Sadyojāta for everything, one should perform the *mūrtihoma*.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should perform the ritual of the remaining offering (bali).
Having fashioned the weapon (*astra*) as previously described, one should install it made either of wood or of metal.
One should install the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) according to the previously stated ritual procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
[Thus ends the chapter on offerings and expiation in the *Cintya*.]

[The Expiation for the Binding of the Auspicious Thread] When the auspicious thread (*kautuka*) and the image of the offering (*balibimba*) fall to the ground while the king is capable [of preventing it],
it brings grief, delusion, and fear to the king and his subjects.
One should invoke Paraśiva within the heart of the preceptor;
there, one should perform the ceremonial bath and carry out the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
Having offered one hundred oblations to Śivamūla, one should perform the remaining rites of the vehicle;
likewise, if there is a deficiency in the limbs, death occurs for oneself and one's ancestors.
Having performed the immediate reconnection (*sadyaḥsandhānaka*) and having established [the image], one should proceed with the rite;
for there is no waiting for days, fortnights, or auspicious moments (*muhūrta*).
Relying upon the *mūrtihoma*, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra;
then one should again bind the *kautuka* and perform whatever remains of the ritual procedure.
It has been stated that for one who is deficient in the limbs [of the ritual], there is another vehicle consisting of mere words;
relying upon the image-homa (mūrtihoma), one should offer a hundred oblations at the base of Śiva.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars;
however, a wise person should cause a deficient image to be properly restored according to the rules.
One should perform all the rites prescribed from the sowing of the seed up to the final sprinkling;
then, having tied the protective cord (*pratisara*), one should abandon the other image.
Then, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should proceed with the ritual of the vehicle (*yāna*).
When the movement of the machine is interrupted, the king’s vehicle brings about destruction.
Having performed the reconnection of all [parts], or if there is no [reconnection] or if it is pierced by a needle,
one should install his image and perform the remainder of the ritual according to the vehicle.
Having performed the ritual bathing (snapana) and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should offer a hundred oblations to Aghora.
When the time for mounting the vehicle has passed, one should indeed gather the image from a Vaiśya or others.
In that [period], there will be both enjoyment and liberation; however, in that kingdom, fear shall arise.
But at another time, through arrogance, one should touch the image of a Vaiśya or others.
One should bathe the kings with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) to alleviate their grief;
at the conclusion of the procession, one should perform the ritual bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa).
At the time of marching, when there is a great wind accompanied by constant rain,
especially at the mouths of rivers or when a wall is in a state of collapse,
and when there is fear on the ground from an enemy army, one should perform the *mūrtihoma* sacrifice.

Circumambulating the site (*vāstu*) clockwise is not desired; rather, circumambulating the temple (*dhāma*) clockwise is desired. Furthermore, if the sequence of time and so forth for the great sacrifice (*mahāyāga*) is transgressed, that is said to bring ruin to the village; one should therefore perform a propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should perform the rite of departure (yāna) in due order;
for if the departure is omitted on a single day, the death of kings is certain.
Relying upon the Mūrti-homa, one should offer oblations one hundred times with the root mantra alone.
And one should bathe the Supreme Lord with one hundred and eight jars.
One should duly and swiftly employ the two vehicles in their proper sequence;
however, if the vehicle is lacking during the marriage ceremony, the king and his kingdom will perish.
Having performed the Diśāhoma and offered a thousand oblations of the Aghora mantra,
and having performed the ablution twice a hundred times, one should perform the festival once again after bathing.

Having sequentially established the sequence of the various types of machines, beginning with the *āhva* and ending with the chariot (*ratha*), as their prior support; however, in the case of a deficient [support], their station is destruction.
Relying upon the *mūrtihoma*, one should recite the formidable mantra a thousand times;
meanwhile, one should perform the ritual of the vehicle (*yāna*) for the image (*biṃba*) that was previously established in its place.
If the encircling thread is missing, the prosperity of the village will be otherwise [diminished];
having performed the ceremonial bath and the propitiatory fire-oblation, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If there is a fire encircling the staff, people will suffer affliction from fire;
in that case, the wise man should scatter embers there and then have it performed as before.

Having bathed, one should perform the bathing (*snapana*) of the image and carry out the *mūrtihoma* (the fire-offering for the form). One should offer clothing to the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśas*), and likewise place [garments] upon their heads.
Furthermore, if [the image] is not burnt by fire, the death of the king is certain.
Having performed the sprinkling with water, one should perform the image-oblation (mūrtihoma).
One should offer everything with that mantra; one should offer the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
If [the offering] is burnt by fire alone, there is no doubt that the performer will perish.
Then, having scattered coals there, one should perform the pacifying fire-oblation (śāntihoma);
having done so, one should recite the root mantra a thousand times and the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
If a village is devoid of water and collyrium, there shall be danger from fire;
having performed a hundred [recitations] based on that root-mantra, one should perform the rite of sprinkling with water and applying collyrium.
If the preceptor falls to the ground from his seat before the deity, there will be fear of enemies in the village; one should perform the ritual bath for the teacher.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, perform the ceremonial bath upon the image;
having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Ghoramantra a thousand times.
If the upper garment, the turban,
or even the clothing of the guide is not burnt by fire, people will suffer from diseases caused by heat.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, perform the sakalīkaraṇa;
then, having taken up another [image], the wise one should bring it forward as before.
At the conclusion of the bath, however, one should specifically perform the śāntihoma.
When the staff of fire has quickly reached the support-pavilion (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*),
others should station themselves in the pavilion and recite a hundred times the terrible mantra. If there should be an obstruction of the fire in the world, one should perform the reconnection again.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should enter its pavilion.
[Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for the tying of the marriage-thread in the Cintya.]
If the rites beginning with the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) are omitted prior to the mounting of the chariot, death shall befall the preceptor; he should then recite the Ghoramantra one thousand times.
Having placed one hundred and eight water-pots so that there is no gap between the chariots, the wise one,
having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, should perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).

If the pinnacle of the chariot falls to the ground at the time of the journey, the king will suffer from illness; if it is broken or shattered, death is certain. Having performed the rejoining, one should then sprinkle it with water.
One should recite the Ghoramantra one thousand times and recite the Śatamantra one hundred times.
At the conclusion of the journey, one should especially perform the Mūrtihoma (image-oblation) for the rejoining of chariot wheels and the like, as well as for what is broken or split.
Fearing an invasion by a foreign army on earth, or the outbreak of disease caused by the king,
one should quickly perform the Santānaka rite at a great sacred ford (tīrtha). Then,
perform the sprinkling of cow products and other substances upon the various deities associated with that site.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should perform the oblation to the deity's form (mūrtihoma).
Therefore, when [the enemy] has entered another sound, one should perform the *hīna* [mantra] and lead the movement;
the king and his kingdom shall perish. One should mutter the terrible [mantra] one thousand times.
Having prepared a vehicle for the Lord of Chariots (Ratheśvara) on a colored cloth or in a palanquin,
one should perform the ritual bath at the conclusion of the procession with one hundred and eight jars.
One should offer ten oblations for each [verse] with the Śatarudriya mantra,
or one should perform the Mūrtihoma with a thousand recitations of the Śiva-mantra.
When cattle, humans, and even chariot-wheels cease to exist, there shall be fear of enemies in the world; one should then recite the terrible mantra a hundred times.
In that specific place, perform the ritual sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*) of the image;
having performed the sprinkling of the chariot, one should carry out the fire-offering to the directions (*diśāhoma*).
Having relied upon the *sadyah* [penance] for all [offenses], one should perform the remainder of the journey;
at the end of the journey, however, one should perform the consecration with the *brahmakūrca*.
One should perform a thousand-fold oblation with the Śiva-mantra and a fire-offering to the deity’s form (mūrtihoma). This applies in the event of the death of a fallen person, a prostitute,
or the wives of artisans, occurring through negligence or accident.
Having offered Śiva, a sacred site, ash, perfume, garlands, clothing, and so forth, one should adorn the deceased and quickly go to the cremation ground; there,
one should dig a pit in the burial site and fill it with sand.
Having sprinkled [the materials] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the sprinkling of the image (berasamprokṣaṇa), one should carry out the oblation to the form (mūrtihoma).
Likewise, during festivals, in a multitude of men, and similarly in the case of elephants, horses, food, and divisions [of the army].
There will be fear from foreign armies on the earth, and the king will experience the outbreak of disease.
Having quickly performed the ritual reconnection at the eastern part of the great sacred site (mahātīrtha),
perform the sprinkling with cow products and other substances for each of those divine reconstructions.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should perform the *mūrti-homa*.
Then, when [the deity] has entered the chariot (*ratha*), having performed [the ritual], one should lead it forward.
One should recite the "Ghoram" mantra one thousand times over the king and his kingdom so that they may be destroyed.
Having fashioned a vehicle from either cloth or a palanquin, with the lord of chariots as its driver.
At the conclusion of the journey, one should perform a bath with one hundred and eight jars;
for each one, one should offer ten oblations with the Śatarudriya mantra.
Or one should perform the Mūrtihoma with a thousand recitations of the Śiva-mantra,
provided that cows, humans, chariots, and footprints [of the deity] are present.
If there be fear of enemies in the world, one should recite the terrible mantra a hundred times;
in that specific place, perform the special sprinkling of the image.
Having performed the sprinkling of the chariot, one should perform the oblation to the quarters (diśāhoma).
Relying entirely upon the Sadyas [rite], one should complete the remainder of the journey.
At the conclusion of the journey, however, one should perform the consecration with the Brahmakūrca.
One should perform a thousand-fold recitation of the Śiva-mantra and the Mūrti-homa. For those who die by falling from a tower or similar heights, for those who die as courtesans,
and for the wives of artisans who meet death through negligence, [one should perform these rites].
Having offered sacred ash from a holy site (tīrtha-bhasman), perfumes, garlands, garments, and so forth to Śiva,
one should adorn the deceased and go quickly to the cremation ground (śmaśānaka).
One should dig a pit in the ground where the corpse lies and fill it with sand.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), perform the rite of circumambulation by fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the sprinkling of the image (bera), one should carry out the oblation to the form (mūrtihoma).
During festivals, in human assemblies, and at the gathering of elephants, horses, and so forth—
If, at the time of the procession, death occurs due to the negligence of humans, there shall be fear of enemies in the world; however, the expiation is as previously stated.
If death occurs among the people in that village where the procession takes place, [the same penance applies].

A great disease may arise in the village; the wise man should quickly abandon the deceased. Relying upon the Mūrtihoma, one should offer the Astra-mantra a hundred times, and the Śiva-mantra a thousand times, and then sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the world is devoid of the sprouts of sacred fords (tīrtha) and lacks the gathering of holy sites, a drought shall occur; one should then perform the Mūrtihoma.
On the day of a great tīrtha, Gaurī should perform everything with the Sadyas mantra.
If the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) is omitted, and likewise if the oil-bath and anointing are omitted,
disease shall arise in the bodies and heads of both wives and men.
One should offer a thousand oblations with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and one hundred oblations with the *śiras-mantra*.
Having offered the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) one hundred times, one should perform the respective rite.
Taking the water-pot for the purpose of bathing, and when the jars have fallen to the ground,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*) before Śiva and strew it with *darbha* grass and flowers.
Having set aside the remaining jar, one should take up another that is superior;
the best of preceptors should duly install the inferior jar. Then, having generated the Śiva-fire in front, its root-mantra should be recited a thousand times.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and the oblation (*homa*), one should especially offer the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) one hundred times. Afterwards, one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and then carry out the ritual bath with the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*).
During the interval of the jar-bath, one should perform the fire-oblation for the image of Gaurī (*gaurīmūrtihoma*).
If the descent is performed first, it causes a great agitation of the winds; likewise,
if the staff supporting the banner is broken, or if the banner is tied by its top,
or if the banner is mounted too low, there will be disorder in the kingdom.
O Goddess, one should place the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) at the tip of the banner;
one should worship it according to the rules and recite its root mantra one hundred times.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before that, one should place the jar with the nine apertures (randhrakumbha).
Having summoned the bull, one should place it in the central jar.
One should summon the world-protectors (lokapālas) into the eight jars surrounding it;
and the wise one should install the other deities upon the banner in their respective places.
Having performed the ascent of the cooking vessel, perform the ascent of the banner.
One should consecrate the jar placed upon the banner at the base of the bull.
One should also consecrate the jars of the bull and the guardians of the directions within the enclosure.
Then, having offered cooked mung beans, one should cause incense and lamps to be presented.
Relying upon the *śāntihoma*, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times.
One should offer oblations to the deities of the junctions by their respective names, omitting the *śrībhūtabali*.
If untimely death should occur in the village, one should perform the *mūrtihoma* (image-oblation).
Having offered the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*) with three times the usual quantity of materials,
if the *Caṇḍayāga* is omitted, the people will face fear from enemies.
Relying upon the *śāntihoma*, one should perform the *caṇḍayāga*.
If [the rite] is deficient, there is expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the ritual bath with the jar (*ghaṭasnāna*), and the total destruction [of the defect];
[one should also perform] the *mūrtihoma*, the *diśāhoma*, and the consecration with the *brahmakūrca* [mixture].
Having performed this, O Mahādeva, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times;
for the sake of expiation, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with water from jars.
If the teacher’s fee (*ācāryadakṣiṇā*) is omitted, one should bring about the fruit of the Śiva-sacrifice;
however, the performer and the devotee will meet with destruction, so one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*).
One should recite the Śiva-mantra twice a thousand times and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
If a dog or a Śūdra and others should touch the sacrificial hall, one must enter [the rite again].
Taking the essential substance with his core [mantra], the king shall attain invincibility;
having removed the water-pots and other items for the purification of the sacrificial pavilion.
Having performed the sacrifice as before, one should carry out the concluding festival (śeṣotsava). The preceptor’s image shall be the *balibera*; there should be a distinction between these two.

Having established [the deity] in that place, one should then perform the ceremonial bathing, the pacifying fire-oblation (śāntihoma), and the festival ascent; otherwise, the king will meet his death.

Then, at the end of the fortnight, the wise one should perform the ceremonial bath for the Lord and cause the festival ascent (*utsavārohaṇa*) to be conducted during the month in which it falls. In this world he shall attain the status of a king, and he shall obtain union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*).
[Thus ends the chapter on the expiation for festivals in the Cintya.
Written by the hand of Ayyāsvāmin himself. It portends rain during the month of Mithuna.
(P.99b) Now I shall describe the ritual for the festival, which brings benefit to all the world;
it is joined with the thought "all is auspicious," and it brings happiness to all living beings.
But because it has arisen from that very [source] along with its vitality, it is called a festival (*utsava*);
its ninefold division is prescribed here in due order.
The Śaiva [initiation] is the first, the gauṇa (secondary) is the second, the bhautika is the third,
the bhāva is the fourth, and the śākta is indeed the fifth.
The sixth is proclaimed as Raudraṣaṣṭha, the seventh as Saura,
the eighth as Mānava, and the ninth as Pakṣa.
If there is only one [day] of the week, it is called the primary; if two, it is said to be secondary.
Five days are designated as such, but seven days are not traditionally recorded for Mars.
The ninth day is joined with Śakti; the eleventh day belongs to Raudra;
the twelfth day belongs to Saura, and the fourteenth day to Mānava.
A fortnight consists of fifteen days; these names are derived from their connection [to the lunar phases].
Since it marks the end of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and the commencement of a festival, it is therefore called a *tīrtha*.
In Caitra, the Aṣṭaka is prescribed; in Vaiśākha, it is called Śūrpa;
in Jyeṣṭha, Mūla; and in Āṣāḍha, it is remembered as Vaiśvadeva.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, there is Śraviṣṭhā; in the month of Bhādrapada, the asterism is Pūrvāṣāḍhā;
in the month of Āśvina, it is Aśvinī; and in the month of Kārttika, it is Kṛttikā.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Raudra constellation (Ārdrā) is declared;
in Māgha, the constellation Puṣya is said to belong to Bṛhaspati.
In the month of Phālguna, when the moon is in the constellation of Āryaman (Pūrvaphalgunī), it becomes a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
O Janārdana, thus have the months and constellations been declared for the purpose of [attaining] the merit of a tīrtha.
Even when the lunar mansions are not conjoined with the full moon,
a place such as a riverbank is called a *tīrtha* even when these [planets] are separated from them.

Whether engaged in worldly affairs or free from them, one who goes to the seashore on the day of the full moon for the sake of the month [of Mārgaśīrṣa] is said to attain a sacred ford that destroys all sins.
In all months beginning with Cakra, there will be a Raudra-kṣataṃdhaga;
likewise, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in Āṣāḍha and Jyeṣṭha.
At the edge of the sacred ford (tīrtha), at the time of the prescribed lunar day (tithi) which bestows the fruits of all desires,
and on both fortnights, that is the festival (parvan) in the four directions.
In all months, perform the ritual up to the conclusion of the *tīrtha* according to the knowledge of the *kalpa*;
likewise, [perform it] for the birth-star (*janmarkṣa*) of the patron (*yajamāna*) and for the *śrāma* and other [constellations].

The lunar mansion for the installation of the *liṅga*, as well as the two solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and the birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*)— these are especially [auspicious] for kings.
In the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) regarding a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one should not perform [the rite] at the actual ford and so forth;
rather, the primary [designation] should be "lunar mansion" while the ford and so forth are merely secondary.
Therefore, when there is a conjunction of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), a sacred ford (tīrtha) and the like do not constitute a true tīrtha.
If one should perform [the rite] out of delusion, that performer becomes the author of all faults.
When the conjunction of a lunar mansion and a tīrtha occurs repeatedly within a single month—
The rites beginning with the hoisting of the banner and ending at the sacred ford are praised when performed within a single month.
The commencement of the sacrifice and so forth constitutes the middle; otherwise, for one who worships at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), it is a *pala*.
During new festivals, such as those of Śiva and others, it should be three [palas].
Then, the first triad is likewise [governed] by the three beginning with Bhauvana;
the middle triad is said to be [governed] by the three beginning with Saura.
Regarding the first mantra among those [mantras] addressed to Uttaṃtra, it is not prescribed as being for mounting the goat;
rather, it is intended for Manyu alone.
Even for one who has performed the first consecration, there should be a festival for five days or three days;
having offered the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) and struck the drum, he should cause [the deities] to enter.
Alternatively, the wise one may cause them to enter for a single day, preceded by the striking of the drum.
From the Bhauvana heaven until the end of the fortnight, let there be great festivals here for those who dwell therein.
These indeed become threefold: those preceded by ascending [the throne], those preceded by the beating of drums, and those preceded by the planting of sprouts.
Among those three types that have been proclaimed, that which is called *tīrtha* among the six festivals mentioned shall now be distinguished. (6th line)
Then, when the threefold [measure] has been determined as three times the former,
having placed the goat there, the sounding of the kettledrums (bherī) is performed for the sake of the sacrifice.
Once that has been attained, one should rise for festivals and celebrations day and night;
this procedure, beginning with the hoisting of the banner, is now declared.
When it has been determined as before that the drum was previously struck,
the beating [of the drum] shall take place at night on the day three times the number of days [previously elapsed].
Having fashioned the drum, one should have a goat mount it immediately thereafter;
then, on the night of the appointed day, the commencement of the festival is declared.
And having first beaten the drum, he was addressed by Vajranārda; but at night, having first offered his finger, he was addressed by Bhasmāsura.
Having offered the finger-gestures (mudrās), one should mount the vajra;
thereafter, one should cause the drum and the deities to begin the ritual.
This [offering] preceded by the gesture of the fingers is declared by me according to the prescribed rule.
The raising of the banner, the beating of the drum, the erection of the platform, and the offering of the *añjali*—in this [context], a reversal of the sequence of all these festivals is intended:
for those lasting one day, it occurs on the first night; for those lasting three days, on the fourth.
For the festival of Pañcāha, it is on the night of the sixth day; for Niśiṣaṣṭha and Janārdana, it is on the eighth night; for Bhaumana, it is on the tenth night;
for Raudra, it is the cause of his own period (daśā); and for Saura, it is the thirteenth day of the Pitṛs.
On the night preceding the fourteenth day, it occurs on the fifteenth.
The commencement of the fortnight on the sixteenth day at night is declared [the beginning];
the festival begins at night itself, while the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is said to take place during the day.
In the [period] of Mars, thirty [balis] are prescribed; for Mānava, twenty;
for Saturn, twenty-four; and indeed, for Rāhu, twenty.
For Śakti, eighteen are indicated; and in the period of Bhuvana, fourteen.
Know that this offering to the spirits is called the secondary *bali*;
in the Śaiva tradition, one should likewise arrange this *bali* at night.
Thus, the procedure for the banners and so forth, which is the extensive mantra-ritual, is now described:
the best [measure] should be ten cubits, and the middling nine cubits.
Now, for the banner and weapons, it is taught that the cloth should be eight cubits long;
its width should be one-fourth, one-fifth, or one-sixth of its own length.
That best [measurement] should be half of the distance between the two stars; the head should be that much. From the measurement of the head, one should fashion the two arms on both sides.
Equal to the width, or one-quarter, three-quarters, or even half [of it],
it shall respectively bestow victory, peace, subjugation, and nourishment.
One should make three lines on the feet, or three lines below the ears;
[the cord] should be made from cotton thread, well-strung, very fine, and firmly fastened.
Neither too thick nor too thin, and free from the discoloration of hair—
one should thus prepare [the thread] and firmly draw the lines in the middle of the cloth.
When [the measurement] is subtracted by one-sixteenth of an *aṅgula*, it is called "released" (*mukta*).
Furthermore, the finger-gestures (*aṅgulīkṛti*) are as many as there are sun-fingers (*bhānu-aṅgula*) when calculated.
Then, having first released the thread, one should cause the height to be divided into nine parts according to the rule;
thereafter, one should have a pinnacle made that is exceedingly white.
Its horns, hooves, ears, dewlap, testicles, and lips should all be red; its eyes should be white and black.
The hairs are said to resemble yellow; the dung is like red-yellow.
One should fashion a garland for him that is yellow at the base and black at the top.
Adorned with whisks and chowries, seated upon a lotus-cushion; for the sake of pacification, it is reclining, and for the sake of nourishment, it is standing, provided with lamps and incense;
accompanied by a full water-pot and decorated with garlands and other ornaments.
And having closed his eyes according to the prescribed rite, he beheld Praṣabheśvara.

Having brought him and placed him upon his head— either on the south or the north side of the decorated and beautiful pavilion— once the ritual ground (*sthāṇḍila*) has been prepared, one should perform the rite.
In the center of that, one should place the excellent pitcher presided over by the Bull (Vṛṣadevatā),
filled with sixteen prasthas [of water] and possessing the luster of a ripe bimba fruit.
It should be consecrated with wrathful mantras and washed, beautifully adorned with a white thread,
properly filled with scented water, and accompanied by gold and cloth.
And one should place eight similar jars, provided with handles and lids and measuring half that size, upon the tips of the petals and the spokes.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) half that size, one should place a banner right there.
In front of that, having made a mound of sand about the size of a fist, [one should proceed].
There, having taken up the fire according to the rite seen in the scriptures and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, one should worship the Bull in the bull-pitcher.
Having prostrated, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective places;
then, having offered mung-bean rice to the lordly bull situated within the water-pot.
One should perform everything for him with the mantra beginning with *vṛṣamūla*;
then, one should worship the banner with the *vṛṣagāyakrī* mantra.
Then the mantra-practitioner should perform the oblation in that fire according to the prescribed rite,
[offering] sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, and mung beans, black gram, and horse gram.
The preceptor should offer sesame seeds and mustard seeds individually, either one hundred times each,
or half of that, or half of that again, using the root of the *vṛṣa* plant.
Or else, the wise practitioner should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*),
or sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with ghee, using the *vṛṣagāyatrī* mantra; then,
he should offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root-mantra of the deity.
Then, [he should worship] the preeminent bull standing before him, whether it be immovable or indeed moving.
Having established [the deity], one should cause the sacrificial oblation (havis) to be offered to it with perfumes and other offerings;
thereafter, one should apply the protective cord (pratisara) either to the image (bera) or to the ritual stake (śūla).
One should perform the special worship and the installation of the two [deities] upon the limbs;
then, having performed the consecration of the banner (dhvajādhivāsana) at night, one should thereafter carry out its festival (utsava).
At the clear dawn, the Creator himself appears;
then, having adorned the banner with garlands, ornaments, garments, and so forth.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, the wise and diligent devotee, placing [the image] upon a chariot or a palanquin, should lead it forth for the festival.
Alternatively, it is said that the attendants should carry the trident alone;
there, one should worship the trident, fully adorned with all ornaments.
Or else, one should bring a banner from that place where a sacrifice has been performed;
and that banner, together with its base and fully equipped with all ornaments.
One should summon you, O Caṇḍeśa, to the villages and other places in due order,
accompanied by song and dance and provided with all musical instruments.
Having entered the abode, one should thereafter raise the banner;
O youth, I shall also describe to you in due order the procedure for its hoisting:
first the *sāla*, then the *tamāla*, the *kramuka*, the *umayuka*, and then the *paka*.
Furthermore, bamboo, *aśoka*, *punnāga*,
*śirīṣa*, *bilva*, and *daśāpyami* are suitable for flagstaffs.
Those that are crooked, defective, marked by cracks or hollows, grown in unsuitable places, or naturally withered should be rejected.
The *vajra* and other [ornaments] should be split open; all of them must be avoided in the *prakṣa*.
The height of the temple should be equal to its width, extending up to the pinnacle.
One should fashion the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) so that it reaches as far as the nose, or even up to the gate-tower (gopura), or up to the cornice (prastara), or up to the neck (gala).
In this regard, the measurement of the flagstaff for the [three] classes beginning with the *kanyasa* has been stated by increasing it by one cubit at each stage;
however, for the middle and superior [classes], he says that its length at the base should be twenty finger-breadths more.
Then, having measured out the expansion by three finger-breadths, one should fashion the *śauna* [measure] from that;
there, having joined together three sections of bamboo including the stalks, one should apply them.
In this case, the flagstaff should be known to consist of four, five, or six parts;
the best of experts in ritual should fashion the subsidiary staff with one part.
One should fashion the neck of the staff with a circumference of seven and a half finger-breadths;
one should determine the circumference of the lower part [the base] as one-third of that.
Furthermore, its three sections should be shaped like a horse's neck and a mango fruit.
Alternatively, it may be made from madhūka wood, or from the wood of daṇḍa, upadaṇḍa, pratibandhana, anyaśodha, or produced from panasa;
the length of the shaft for the *skandhakraka* is said to be twenty finger-breadths.
There should be a reduction of one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for the middle and the lowest [types];
its width, however, should be one part of the length.
One-sixteenth part of that [measurement] shall be the width of the eye;
the lotus, the bud, and the stalk are declared to be three parts. The hollow should be equal in measure to the staff, and its position should be level above that.
One should descend by the side of the staff where the secondary staff (upadaṇḍa) is situated.
Due to the placement of the secondary staff, that cavity should be of the same measurement.
In the location of the secondary staff-house, one should leave a firm space of five finger-breadths.
One should insert a straight iron pin into an iron ring;
the position of the iron ring should be at the tip of the flagstaff.
A very firm ring should be made from the wood of the *mūpadaṇḍāgra* tree;
a rope should be fashioned from *kāryāsī* fibers, which must be strong and even.
Its length should be three times that of the staff, round, and free of knots.

The action is also prescribed when [the hand] is struck by the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb... (P. 106a, 1st line). It is encircled in a clockwise direction with a garland of *darbha* grass, joined with the sprouts of the garland, and provided with the cords of the ritual diagram (*yantra*).
Having prepared a flagstaff endowed with all the auspicious characteristics,
the wise man should then erect it either at the front of the temple or within the enclosure wall.
Either at the front of the *pīṭha*, or at the front of the *gopura*, or on the head of the bull, or on the back of the bull,
or between the *pīṭha* and the *gopura*, or between the bull and the *gopura*.
Having designated the *vaṭa* [pillar] as measuring four *tālas* in that [space], which is like the middle of the middle and the great middle of the beginning, (4th line)...
In the midst of that, the wise man should place either a bull made of gold or one consisting of gold-work;
it should be fashioned from gold by a skilled artisan, with its tail encircled by a cord.
One should place [the vessel] facing the deity with offerings of strength (balivardha).
At its base, one should fashion an altar (vedikā) measuring four tālas in height;
it should be lower at the back by six finger-breadths (aṅgula).

One should construct the altar made of baked bricks from the middle of the *muktā* and *kāñcī* lines up to the *karmya* line. In the absence of baked bricks, the altar may be made of unbaked ones; it should be half as wide as its height, extending to the end of the third part, and adorned with ornaments.
Alternatively, having made it stable with stone, one should establish the staff upon it;
then, having smeared it with cow-dung, one should cause the Puṇyāha ceremony to be performed there.
Having prepared a sacrificial altar at the head of the city with rice and *vīnala* grass,
and having strewn it around, one should then place the banner upon a slender post.
The wise practitioner should place upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) situated near the base of the banner the jar that was previously consecrated, having Vṛṣarāja as its presiding deity;
having placed it within the [specific] body, he should thereafter arrange the other jars.
Having worshipped [the deities] with the two *akṛti* mantras as before, the best of preceptors,
while recollecting the root mantra of the Bull (*vṛṣa*), should fill the jar with water from the *kūrca*.
O Lord of Maruts, one should employ that mantra which is the very life-force;
one should arrange its limbs in their proper places according to the form of the mantra.
Then, having indeed raised the banner, one should fasten it with a yak-hair rope while reciting the *praṣagāyatrī* mantra, provided it is equipped with small bells.
When the auspicious moment and the favorable lagna have arrived,
one should properly hoist the banner, accompanied by music and dance, and endowed with all the auspicious signs.
Then, the wise one should wrap it clockwise with the cord itself;
having offered worship to that which has been raised, he should do so with the *Sarvatathāgata-hṛdaya* mantra.
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, who is bowed to by the lord of bulls,
one should sprinkle the base of the flagstaff with water from the *kūrca* grass bundle.
One should place the pitchers representing the lords of the directions in the locations designated for the mantras;
or else, one should place the deities Caṇḍa, the eight Vasus, and the Vasudevas at the base of the flagpole.
Having established them as before starting from the pitcher, the knower of mantras should then perform their worship.
And one should place [the deities] around the base of the staff in successive order:
Caṇḍeśa at the base of the staff, Dhruva in the middle of the staff, and likewise Sūrya, Soma, and Agni on the shoulders; and Nala on the tip of the staff.
On the banner (the fifth line), having worshipped that bull-emblem in due order,
one should offer mung-bean rice or milk-rice to the lordly bull.
That which has been offered into the fire and submerged shall grant sons to women;
or else, having fixed it with the flagstaff, one should worship it.
Having thus raised [the image], at night the wise one should strike the drum on the roof of the palace, or else in a pavilion that has been decorated.
Once the base of the banner has been smeared, one should perform the fire-oblation according to the rule;
then, having prepared three altars with pure śāli rice.

There, one should first place the King of Weapons (the *astra-rāja*) facing the *liṅga*, and then the banner (*dhvaja*) facing that; furthermore, one should place the kettle-drum (*bherī*) in front of it.
Standing facing the drum, one should wrap it with a cloth;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should sprinkle it with that water.
Next, the worship of the trident-weapon is now being described:
one should worship Maheśvara on the middle petal of the trident.
One should worship Brahmā on the right petal and Viṣṇu on the left;
Bhavānī in the *pālikā* vessel, and Vighneśa in the water-pot (*kumbha*).
At the tip of the staff is Ṣaṇmukha; likewise, at the middle of the staff is Ravi;
at the base of the staff is Īśaśāṅka, and its end is Caṇḍa.
One should worship the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) in their respective places upon the trident;
having thus worshipped the trident according to the rules with perfumes and other offerings, [one should proceed].
Having offered the food offering, water for sipping, and betel to the deity in the center, the worship of the drum follows; that is now being described.
Having worshipped Nandin in the center, one should worship the Sun and the Moon on the right and left sides respectively; there, according to the prescribed rite,
one should worship Bherī in the corner and then offer oblations to the guardians of the directions (Lokapālas).
One should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented there, especially to Nandin; then, having offered betel-leaf, the invocation of the deities should take place—
namely, Śiva and all the other gods, as well as the eighteen classes of attendants.
Having specifically gathered together the constellations and the planets, as well as the oceans and the mountains, the continents, the worlds, and the nether regions (pātāla),
he subsequently caused all the people to dwell in a state of festivity.
Having summoned the musicians and sprinkled them with water immediately thereafter, one should cause water and flowers to be placed in his hand. He,
too, having cast down the flower, should strike the drum.
Having played the *krādi* rhythms accompanied by song and dance,
one should then conclude with the *vṛṣatāla* for all of them;
and the dance should be performed by those stationed in the eight directions.
Accompanied by women from Śithāyatana and provided with all kinds of musical instruments,
there were four types of primary musical instruments, which are proclaimed as follows:
the stringed (tata), the percussion (vitata), the solid (ghana), and the wind (suṣira).

Stringed instruments such as the vīṇā are called *tata*; those with membranes, such as the muraja drum, are *vitata*; solid instruments such as cymbals (*kāṃsyatāla*) and the like are *ghana*; and wind instruments such as the flute (*vaṃśa*) are known as *suṣira*.
Now hear from me that sound produced by these four instruments joined together in song;
it is the "Great Fivefold Sound" (pañcamahāśabda), which is always dear to the deceased.
With that [instrument], the preceptor should cause it to be sounded at the three junctions of the day during festivals in the temple of Śiva;
likewise, having struck the kettledrum, he should do so in villages and other places.
There, one should perform the offering of the bali-oblation, accompanied by a trident,
or else together with the image and the protective thread of the victim.
Or else, provided with the appropriate gender-markings and endowed with all ornaments,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the quarters, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna.
And having stood in their respective directions, he first established his position;
then, on the day of the Tīrtha festival, he summoned and addressed the people as well.
Then one should offer the *bali* with mantras accompanied by their respective names;
furthermore, having offered a single *bali*, one should not exclude the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*).
One should perform the aforementioned ritual of offerings (balikriyā) in the temple,
especially at the time of the commencement of the festival during the evening.
And having worshipped Vighneśa for the sake of pacifying all obstacles,
one should adorn Vināyaka with garlands, ornaments, garments, and so forth.
Having respectfully placed [the image] upon a chariot or a palanquin,
adorned with all ornaments, one should carry it in procession from the village to the temple.
In front of that [deity], one should bring Śūla and Astra; behind it, Sacāpī;
and to the left, Sacāṇḍeśa, or Vināyaka alone.
One should cause the seed-substances of Vināyaka, Aya, Ut, and so forth to be given;
then, in due order, [the portions for] Utkuṇḍamarasa, Mudārdha, and Caṇḍeśa.
O Janārdana, I shall describe the method for obtaining pearls; listen to that.
[They are found] on the shore of the ocean, on the banks of rivers, and on the shores of lakes.
Having reached a pure location on the bank of a lotus pond, or at a grove, or even in a garden,
one should perform purification upon the ground.
Having sprinkled the ground with the Astra-mantra and having offered oblations according to one's name,
and having dug [the pit] again with a hoe consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
and having strewn it around with Kuśa grass, one should face either the east or the north.
Or [he should fashion] a clay or wooden [image] with his own hands by means of a man.
Having placed the vessel upon the kuśa grass while reciting the mantra,
one should sprinkle it again and then place flowers within it while reciting the mantra.
With the sounds of conchs and drums, and filled with song and dance,
having thus performed the seizing of the clay, one should likewise celebrate the festival.
Alternatively, one who desires liberation should begin this [rite] at the conclusion of a festival;
having entered the temple afterwards, Vināyaka [should be worshipped] with edible offerings and other such items.
Having performed the worship of the half-germinating seeds, one should carry out the sowing of the seeds.
For the sake of the *tīrtha*, the germinating seeds should be placed in that location within the sacrificial pavilion;
using the *Śiva-mantra*, one should sow them either to the south or to the north.
Then, according to the path prescribed by the rules for that [rite],
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for all the mantras within the pavilion of the Śiva-yajña,
either in the northeast, in the region of the fire, or on both sides.
The best [size] should be ten cubits, the middling seven cubits, and the lowest five cubits;
it should be square and pleasing to the mind.
It is joined with four squares (the fifth line), adorned with four archways,
and provided with sixteen pillars, or perhaps twelve pillars.
Endowed with the ritual actions for completion, and possessing the highest mental exertion,
one should construct a pedestal in the center of that [area], measuring one part out of nine parts.
Its height is half its width, and it resembles the surface of a mirror;
and all around it, in the cardinal directions, are eight sacrificial pits for the four fires.
In the intermediate directions, there are forms of fire; the principal sacrificial pit (patmakuṇḍa) is situated between Īśāna and Śaṅku in that region.
The highest [method] has been described for the triad of sacrifices, especially for the *utsava*;
the procedure for the five fires (*pañcāgni*) is now stated for the middle triad as well.
There are four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the cardinal directions, with the lotus-shaped one in the northeast as the principal;
furthermore, for the three mantras, a single pit is prescribed.
In all four directions, one should perform the sprinkling as desired;
however, for all festivals, it is said that a single oblation (homa) suffices.

Then, having smeared the pavilion, which is provided with an altar and a sacrificial pit, with cow dung, and having adorned it with canopies, banners, and flags, one should encircle it with garlands of *darbha* grass.
Adorned with strings of pearls, beautified by fruits and sprouts,
joined with auspicious flowers, and graced by the eight auspicious symbols;
provided with golden jars and endowed with the splendor of gold.

Having constructed the pavilion (maṇḍapa) joined with pillars and enclosures, the wise man should first cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) and perform the Vaivāstu-homa sacrifice. Then,
upon the altar (vedikā), he should prepare a level sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains.
O best of beings, the superior [mandala] is made with eight droṇas; the middling should be with half of that;
and another is likewise with half of that again; in its center, one should draw a lotus.
It is endowed with a pericarp and eight petals, beautifully adorned with rice grains,
and further graced by sesame seeds, parched grain, and kusha grass, making it most delightful.
Having worshipped Manonmanī with perfumes and other offerings in the space between the ears,
one should worship the powers beginning with Vāmā on the eight petals beginning with Śaka.

One should worship Śarva and the others, who have the inner dissolution as their banner, all around; having worshipped the ground on the altar, one should place the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) all around it.
Having worshipped [the deities] in the directions starting from the east with their own names, the most excellent of teachers should worship the eight Vasus in the jars beginning from the east.
Then, having worshipped Bhava and the others in due order around the Kṛṇyas and in the directions starting from the east, one should worship Śiva as the principal deity.
In the procedure for the five oblations, however, one should offer to the five Brahmās in sequence:
to Puruṣa in the eastern fire-pit, and likewise to Ghoratattva in the southern one.
One should worship Sadyojāta in the western pit, Vāmadeva likewise in the north,
and Īśāna in the principal [central] pit, according to the prescribed rite.
In the case of one who has not performed the single oblation, one should worship Śiva alone in one place—
namely Bhadra, Vijaya, Vijrambha, and Lohita.
Having worshipped these in sequence upon the banners and arches, [one should proceed].

One should worship Vaikartana and the others on the exterior; one should perform the rite of immobilization (stambhana) in the east. Having worshipped the moon in the canopy (vitāna), one should then worship the world-protectors (lokapālas).
And having worshipped Vāsuki in the garland of darbha grass according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].
Having thus worshipped the deities, one should then perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa).
O Janārdana, for the jar of power (śakti-kumbha), the measurement should be half of that.
The remaining [deities] should be known as equal to them, and they are of the nature of Vidyādharas;
they have been washed, awakened, and sprinkled with the water of the funeral pyre (kamaśavāri).
Properly wrapped with thread and further adorned with clay,
filled with scented water, containing gold, and provided with cloth.
Having gathered together all [the vessels] along with their lids and their bases, which are smeared with fragrant unguents,
while pronouncing the *sarvātmāna* mantra.
One should place the jar of Śiva in the middle and likewise the jar of Śakti to the north;
on the eight petals, starting from the east, one should place the jars of the Vidyēśvaras.
Having thus arranged the jars, one should then worship the deities.
Having meditated upon the god Sadāśiva, one should worship the auspicious water-pot.
And one should worship Ādiśakti and the Vidyeśvaras in that pitcher,
having honored them thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, up to the presentation of food.

One should worship all the world-protectors (lokapālas), together with their weapons, each in their proper place; thereafter, the preceptor, with a tranquil mind, should establish the fire according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, the image-protectors (mūrtipāḥ) shall be instructed to perform half of the fire-oblation (homa) in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
Being pure, they should wear a turban, an upper garment, and new clothing.
In the case of the preceptor (*deśika*), there may be as many as all the *sāyaka* [initiates], or the *putrakas*;
or indeed, there are four *aśauca-hotṛs*. Even in the procedure for a single *ekāha-homa*, the principal [officiant] himself should perform it.
Furthermore, one should perform the path-ritual (adhvayajana) at the end, beginning from the east in the sequence of four and three [directions],
starting with the Ṛgveda and ending with the Sāmaveda.

Then the wise and accomplished master, having performed the ritual actions prescribed for the fire-rite (agnikārya), should offer that [oblation] along with the image-bearers (mūrtipas) and the practitioners (sādhakas).
One should offer into the fire sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame, mung beans, śāli rice,
bamboo shoots, and black gram.
The Udumbara, Pukṣa, and Vaṭa trees are placed in the east and other cardinal directions in sequence;
the Śamī, Bilva, Khadira, and Arka trees are assigned to the intermediate directions.
Thus, the palāśa wood is proclaimed as the primary material for the sacrificial fuel;
with those same woods, the four enclosing sticks (paridhis), equal to the grass mats (viṣṭaras), are prescribed.
Having thoroughly purified all the impurities with those who are wise and experienced,
one should offer the sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials in due order, accompanied by the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga).
The best of mantra-knowers should perform seven oblations beginning with Īśāna and ending at the head, and then offer oblations starting from Sadyojāta and ending with the weapon-mantra.
Then, at the conclusion of each substance, one should perform the Vyāhṛti oblation a thousand times,
or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations, or half of that, or even a quarter;
this is prescribed for all [mantras] during the medium rite over a period of seven days.
Now, regarding the performance of the [rite] with the mantras... (text missing).
And having uttered the mantra according to the Samhitā, while it is being recited with the prescribed mantras.
In the middle [fire], one should first perform the oblation with the [mantras] beginning with "la...";
in the lowest [fire], however, it should be done by the Brahmins according to the sequence starting with the fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
Then the preceptor should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra;
thereafter, having worshipped the fire, sprinkled it with water, and completed the rite.
Then, having brought the trident, it was placed upon the sacrificial mound by Śaṅkara or Māruti; and the deity was then worshipped with perfumes and other offerings.
One should bind the protective thread (*kautuka*), and its ritual procedure according to the mantra is now described:
having first prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) at the tip of the trident with pure *śāli* rice.
Having drawn a lotus in the center of that [mandala], one should place a vessel right there;
then, having filled that vessel with a *āḍhaka* measure of rice,
one should draw a lotus upon it, made either of gold or silver.
One should place cotton thread and silk thread right there.
The best of teachers should then place the ash and the bowstring there;
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, he should worship the threads as before.
Having worshipped the *kautuka* and proclaimed oneself as the soul of all (*sarvātmāna*),
the wise one should bind this at the base of the middle petal situated between the weapons (*astra*).
If there is an image, one should likewise bind it on the right side;
then, having bound the consecrated object with the *abhyastra* mantra, one should place the ashes upon it.
And one should install that very deity in the festival image;
even in other [regular] forms, one should conduct the festival according to the specific [tradition].
In each of those respective locations, one should first establish a connection;
through the singing of the *madavī* [songs], there shall be the binding of the festive rite (*kautilkabandhana*).
One should place the *tāva* upon the *lapaṇa*, and [place] the *kautuka* [therein].
For others, the procedure for the *apratisara* is said to be according to their respective names.
At the conclusion of the binding, all [the deities] are satisfied without distinction;
thereafter, there shall be an offering of oblations (bali), and its procedure is described here.

One should worship the weapons, beginning with the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), together with their presiding deities; these may be installed according to the specific instructions for each deity along with their ancillaries, or otherwise as solitary entities.
Having fashioned them from iron or wood according to the prescribed rule, one should worship them.
One should also perform the worship of the Balla for half the duration, and likewise the Cañcacakriya.
Then, the wise one should cause [the disciple] to go toward the food-linga,
having gratified him with boiled śāli rice and with water from a cavity.
Endowed with the characteristics previously described, situated in the midst of the desire-realm (kāmadhātu),
and measuring ten finger-breadths in width, it should be known as being here at the end.
The middle [pillar] should be one finger-breadth less than the first;
its width and height from base to top should likewise decrease in that same sequence.
Therein is the Lord of the Pāśupatas, the destroyer of all defects,
three-eyed, four-armed in form, with a mass of matted hair like ten million suns.
With his right hand granting boons and his left holding a trident,
having thus meditated upon him and worshipped him in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—
then all those deities who have been worshipped by the attendants...
And having had [the image] carried in due order by those who have applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), |||
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, the practitioner,
with curd in hand and established in meditative concentration, should go before the weapon-mantra.
Having thus [proceeded] with the vajra and other [mantras], he should finally recite the armor-mantra.
Upon their completion, the Liṅga should be consecrated, characterized by the previously described marks;
it should be provided with canopies and banners, accompanied by chowries and peacock feathers,
endowed with incense and lamps, and furnished with all musical instruments.
One should bring half a *bala* of *balārdraka*; its power will also be described. When prepared with pure rice, it is more effective than even *śivā*.
[In the section on] "The Subtle Festival of Śiva":
O Prabhāñjana, listen as I describe the ritual procedure for that festival.
It bestows fame and victory, is meritorious, and increases longevity and health;
it grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is holy, and accomplishes all desires and purposes;
it is complete, purifying, peaceful, and auspicious in its fourfold nature.
The entire sequence from the raising of the banner (dhvajāroha) up to the end of the pilgrimage (tīrtha) is thus proclaimed;
however, one may omit the single banner, while the remainder remains exactly as before.
This is declared to be the *pāvana* [rite]; now hear about the *śāntika* [rite].
Having omitted the *bali*, *homa*, and so forth, it should be performed either in the forenoon or in the afternoon.
One should perform a festival in the evening, as well as a rite for pacification (śāntika);
at times, one may also perform a festival for Śiva according to the wish of the patron.
Now hear about that which is renowned as the auspicious [calendar], consisting of four types: the solar, the lunar, the sidereal, and the Savana. (6th line)
One should arrange this festival during each of the four types of months;
in the solar month, the purifying festival should be performed with full completeness.
During the months of the solar, lunar, and nakṣatra reckoning, when they are peaceful and auspicious, one should perform a festival; or else, perform the "All-Festival" (sarvotsava) of the Sun.
In the month of Puṣya, it ends with Puṣyā; in the month of Māgha, it ends with Maghā;
in Phālguna, it ends with Uttarā; and in Caitra, it is said to end with Citrā.
In the month of Vaiśākha, [the period] ends with Viśākhā; in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it ends with Mūla; in Āṣāḍha, it ends with Uttarāṣāḍhā; and in Śrāvaṇa, it ends with Śravaṇā.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā is [the asterism] in the month of Hita (Caitra), and Aśvinī at the end of the month of Āśva (Āśvina).
Indeed, Kṛttikā is at the end of Kārttika, and Śiva (Ārdrā) is at the end of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Whether joined with the full moon or not, the asterism of the month is the primary one.
On the fourteenth day, the new moon, and especially on the sixth and eighth days; at the time of a king’s consecration, one’s birth star, or at the beginning and end of a battle;
and on other auspicious days—on such occasions, one should perform a festival.
The Śaiva, the Gauṇa, the Vibhūti, the Bhauvana, the Daivika, the Paitṛka, the Kāmāra, the Sāvitra, and the Ābhruma;
[these] are declared to be for two days or one day, while the Gauṇa is said to last for three days.
Five days are declared to be elemental (*bhautika*); seven days are known as pertaining to the elements (*bhautika*).
Nine days are declared to be divine (*daivika*); eleven days are known as ancestral (*paitṛka*). Thirteen days belong to the youth (*kaumāra*), and the fortnight belongs to Savitṛ.
The Cāndra [observance], beginning with the *uduttamā* and ending after seventeen days,
along with the Śaiva, Gauṇa, and Vibhūti, are said to be the triad of the lowest (kanyasa).
The Bhauvana, Daivika, and Paitṛka constitute the triad of the middling (madhyama).
The Kaumāra, the Sāvitra, and the Cāndra—these indeed are the three highest [stages].
Thus the wise one has described the ninefold festival in due order;
O Prabhajana, listen as I shall now explain their sequence.
It is proclaimed as threefold: bestowing prosperity, victory, and happiness;
one should commence it at the time of evening, joined with the first part of the night.
At the time of dawn, there should be a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), and on the same day, two offerings (bali).
Thus, this is declared to be the bestower of prosperity; now hear concerning victory.
Then, on the night of that day, one should hold a festival;
having performed a single bali offering, one should perform the pilgrimage at dawn.
Thus has Vijaya been described; now hear about Brāhmika.
It occurs on that day during the forenoon, at midday, and at dusk.
Having undertaken the single vehicle, one should practice for the ultimate goal.
For one day it may be for the sake of growth and so forth; listen, O well-conducted one, regarding the three-day [rite].
One should perform it in the evening prior to the designated day.
One should perform the festival of the three gifts according to the number of *kauśikas* for the offerings.
When the fourth day has arrived, one should perform the pilgrimage to the sacred ford at dawn;
on that same day, the wise and most virtuous person should perform the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*) in the evening.
Having commenced the festival, one should perform the offering of the bali on the fourth day and likewise carry out the rites at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
At the conclusion of the daily worship, however, perform a festival for three days;
during those three days, one should carry out the rites at the end of each vehicle.
Thus, having performed it for three days, listen next to the five-day rite:
beginning at evening time, it is joined with the preceding day.
One should prepare a vehicle and especially perform the tenth offering;
then, on the morning of the sixth day, the preceptor should perform the rite of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
One should begin at sunset on the day specified;
one should offer the oblation eight times and perform the rite at the sacred ford for five days.
Starting from that day, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform a festival for five days and carry out the procession to the sacred site (*tīrtha*).
This is called the "lesser" [ritual]; now hear about the "middling" one.
Beginning on the night prior to the day specified,

one should perform the fire oblation (*homa*) during that night and offer the fourth *bali* offering. On the eighth day, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*), the tying of the protective thread (*kautuka*), and the pilgrimage to the sacred site (*tīrtha*).
Having been instructed at night, one should perform the consecration (utsava) on the day [of the ritual];
a wise person should cause the fire-oblation (homa) and the food-offering (bali) to be performed during that night.
One should present the food-offering according to the number of suns (twelve), and perform the pilgrimage (tīrtha) during the week.

On the day specified and so forth, one should perform either the morning or the afternoon rite; one should perform the mere circumambulation first, and at the conclusion, one should perform the *tīrtha* rite.
This is known as the *bhauvana*; now hear about the *daivika*.
On the evening prior to the designated day, one should perform the rites;
one should offer oblations according to the number prescribed in the Smṛtis, performing them ten times over.
Listen now to that which is renowned as Vṛddhidanta and Vijaya;
on the day specified, the learned man should perform it in the evening.
One should perform the bali offering on the ninth day and observe the rites at a sacred ford;
at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform a single journey.
At its end is the Kautuka Tīrtha; it is known as "Kautuka" (the Auspicious).
It is renowned as the Daivika (pertaining to the gods); now hear about the Paitṛka (pertaining to the ancestors).
On the day preceding that [day], one should perform the *astrayāga*;
on the thirteenth day, one should offer twenty-four *bali* oblations at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Listen now to [the rites] known as Vṛddhidanta and Vijaya.
On the three specified days, one should perform the festival.
On the twenty-second day, the Kautuka-tīrtha [should be performed], and one should offer the twenty-two-fold bali.
Perform the festival exclusively by means of the vehicle-path previously described;
one should practice the final rite known as the Brāhmika at the sacred ford.
The third [rite] is declared to be middling; perform the third as the highest.
On the preceding day, the wise one should perform the *astrayāga* (weapon-sacrifice).
On the fourteenth day, it shall be the *tīrtha*; one should offer the *bali* twenty-six times.
This indeed has been declared to be the bestower of prosperity; now listen, O observer of good vows, to the *Vijaya*.
On that day, there should be a ritual sacrifice (*yāga*) with weapons, and one should offer twenty-four oblations (*bali*).
On the thirteenth day, it is proclaimed as the *tīrtha* of the *Vijaya*.
One should perform only the circumambulation; at the end, one should perform the rite at the sacred site (tīrtha).
Listen now to the well-known Kaumāra and the Sāvitra rites.
Beginning from the previous night, one should then offer thirty oblations (bali).

On the sixteenth day, however, the rites of the sacred ford (tīrtha-karma) should be performed specifically; on that day, there shall be the sacrifice of the weapon (astra-yāga), and one should offer twenty-six oblations (bali). On the fifteenth day of the fortnight, the auspicious thread (kautuka) for victory and the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Prabhañjana should be prepared.
One should practice a single vehicle until the end of one's life;
at the conclusion of that rite for the sacred ford, it is proclaimed as the Brāhmika.

The wise one should perform the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*) on the day preceding that which is renowned as the *sāttvika* lunar day, known as *cāndra*, during the wind-constellation (*prabhañjana*).
One should offer thirty-four oblations on the day of the pilgrimage site;
this is indeed declared to bestow prosperity. Now hear concerning victory.
On the evening of that day, one should conclude the festival;
there shall be thirty-two offerings of oblations, and the pilgrimage to the sacred site on the seventeenth day.
Having mounted the single vehicle, one should perform the final rite at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
This is declared to be the "Festival of Brahman" (*brahmotsava*); listen, O observer of noble vows, to its beginning and end.
The mounting of the vehicle and the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) are remembered as three constituent parts of the festival.
Each one is said to be threefold: beginning, middle, and end.
The festival is said to be threefold, consisting of the flag, the drum, and the sprouting of seeds.
One should first hoist the flag, and afterwards strike the drum.
Thereafter, one should offer the sprouts preceded by the hoisting of the banner;
first having struck the drum, one should then raise the banner.
Thereafter, one should offer the sprouts preceded by the striking of the drum.
First, one should offer the ritual sprouts (*aṅkura*), and after that, the sounding of the drum.
Following this, the hoisting of the banner (*patākāropaṇa*) occurs, preceded by the offering of the sprouts.
Regarding these three [rites], the worship of the flagstaff (*dhvaja*) will now be described.

On the day prior to the ritual of the *astrayāga* and other ceremonies, the wise one should raise the banner (*dhvaja*). On the day prior to the day of raising the banner, or even two days or three days before,
on the fifth day, the seventh day, or the ninth day, the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should be performed.
First, the Ketu-rite; second, the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga);
the third is the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa); the fourth is the purification with the staff (daṇḍaśuddhi);
the fifth is the Ketu-karma; and the sixth is the ceremonial bath with the water-pot (kalaśasnāna).
The seventh is the worship of the staff, and the eighth is the worship of the weapon;
the ninth is the sacrifice of the drum, and the tenth is the invocation of the deity.
The eleventh is the daily worship; the twelfth is the circumambulation with offerings;
the thirteenth is the purification of the site (vāstu-śuddhi); and that which follows is the ritual for the festival sprouts (utsavāṅkura).
Then, the sixteenth act in the sacrificial rite is declared to be the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha);
know that the seventeenth is the oblation (huta), and after that follows the offering of bali.
The nineteenth [day] shall be the procession; the next is the ritual of serving food.

The twenty-first is the rite of the collyrium-water (nīrāñjana), followed by the viewing of the dance. After that is the ceremonial bath for the journey, and finally the special sacrifice (viśeṣayajana).
The sprouting of the sacred site (*tīrthāṅkura*), the twenty-fifth, the twenty-sixth which is the sacred site of the *Kautuka*,

the consecration of the sacred site (*tīrthādhivāsana*), and thereafter the ritual of the powder (*cūrṇakarman*); then the ablution (*avabhṛta*), the nineteenth, the thirtieth, and then the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then follows the consecration with the sacrificial pitcher, the supreme sixteen-fold ablution,
the great oblation and other offerings, worship, and the subsequent giving of priestly fees.
Having lowered the banner, one should afterwards offer the supreme oblation (*bali*) for the Piśāca;
thus is the festival proclaimed as consisting of thirty-six constituent parts.
The wise man should worship Vighneśa at every ritual action;
thereafter, he should offer the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure.
[The rice should be] white, fresh, fine, and free from being broken or split.
The best [measure] should be nine cubits, the middling seven cubits, and the lowest five cubits; that is doubled for the two feet. Therein, one part is said to be the width of the cloth.
The wise one should encircle it with middle-sized reeds, joined by two rings, and bind them together with thread after having smeared everything all over with lime.
White, red, yellow, dark (śyāma), black, and saffron;
cow’s milk and the luster of a conch shell—these are proclaimed as the colors of the banner.
Among all colors, the white color is preeminent.
Having divided that cloth into nine parts, one should draw a bull in the central section.
The bull should have the appearance of a white color, according to the characteristics and methods of a bull.
Its two horns and its ears are said to resemble the color of rubies;
the tip of its tail is black in color, while the eyebrows possess a combination of colors.
Its eye is of a smoky hue, with a black circle in the center.
The seat is dark green in color, with a red lotus in its center;
the pericarp is yellow, and the filaments are of that same color.
Having fashioned a seat and drawn a square all around it with five colors, one bestows prosperity by means of red flowers.
The wise one, having drawn the *śīkāsūtra* and the *pādadhāra-sūtra* in the form of a band using five colors, [should proceed].
And the bell should have the luster of gold, and its cord should resemble a jewel;
it should be painted with red flowers and provided with a neck-ornament.
Having stood thus endowed with these characteristics, one should draw a bull;
then, one should draw the remaining auspicious forms around it in due order.
Having drawn a lotus in the lower portion, well-rounded and white in color,
[one should draw] a mirror white in color, a full water-jar, and a myrobalan fruit; likewise,
a fly-whisk white in color, and its handle yellow in color.
And at the tip of the stalk, it has the form of a blue lotus, with petals that are red and yellow in their interior.
The Śrīvatsa should be reddish in luster, and the Svastika should be tawny;
the conch should indeed be white in color, while the tip of the tail is joined with yellow.
The lamp should indeed have the luster of gold, and its base should be of the same material;
the incense should be of five colors, and the bell should resemble silver.
One should draw a full water-pot in the lower portion from the middle section;
however, one should fashion a white parasol in the upper portion of the middle section.
A bell for the neck, a lamp on both sides of the pitcher,
a mirror at the front of the bull, and the Śrīvatsa mark on the upper portion at the back.
One should draw a conch shell joined with a pedestal between the two feet;
and on either side of the white parasol, one should draw two chowries.
On both sides of each square, one should draw the respective limb;
in the spaces between those two, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus.
Thus the sequence of the banners has been declared; now hear the ritual procedure for its sacrifice.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, one should perform the rites up to the final offering of food. Thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa and offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
