Having prostrated before Śiva according to the rules and announced the supreme festival,
the excellent preceptor, being well-disposed, should adorn [the deity] with ornaments and the like,
and perform the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The wise man should have a sacrificial ground prepared with very white *droṇa* rice;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in the center,
he should take nine jars and encircle them with three threads.
One should wash [the vessel] with the *astra* mantra and fill it with scented water.
One should place the bull and the pitcher in the center, and the *vardhanī* to its left;
one should then arrange eight jars all around, starting from the east.
Having placed the water for washing the feet (pādya) in the east and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) in the south,
one should place the water for respectful offering (arghya) in the west and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the north.
Then, one should place the remaining vessels, starting from the east, with pure water;
they should be provided with a *kūrca* grass-bundle and a lid, joined with cloth and sprouts,
equipped with golden horns, and accompanied by dark-green *dūrvā* grass.
One should install them in sequence, starting from the east and ending with the northeast.
Afterwards, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and then,
saying "with pure, uplifted [waters]," he should sprinkle the arghya-vessel and other items in sequence with water from a conch shell.
One should worship the gatekeepers on the four sides of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*):
Nandin and Mahākāla in the east, and Bhaṅgī and Vināyaka in the south.
In the west, Vṛṣabha and Skanda; and likewise Caṇḍa to the north of the Goddess.
Āditya is in the direction of Agni (the southeast), and the deity of the site (Vāstu-devatā) is in the southwest.
One should place Gaṇanātha in the northwest and the lineage of gurus in the northeast;
in the center of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should place Ananta, who is known as the Support (Ādhāra).

Having mentally conceived the lotus posture (padmāsana), the wise one should contemplate it according to the prescribed ritual; he should worship it with perfumes and other offerings using the seed-syllable of Vṛṣa (*HRĪM*). One should bathe the deity Vṛṣa with jars containing the five products of the cow and the five nectars (*pañcagavyāmṛta*).
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should then cause moong-rice (mudgānna) to be given.
Afterward, one should cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered and then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited.
One should then prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there and worship according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped the Vṛṣecala-āsanam, one should worship it within the central pitcher (kumbha).
To its left, on the vardhanī vessel, one should perform worship according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Afterwards, the wise one should raise the pitcher and place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having placed the *vardhanī* vessel to the north, he should worship the firm seat (*āsana*).
Having worshipped the bull in the center, he should worship the female bull (*vṛṣāṇī*) to its left.
On all sides, one should worship the eight vases and the eight world-protectors:
the Bull, Śṛṅgī, Nandin, Vedapāda, and Gopati.
One should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Ugraśṛṅga and ending with Vṛṣeśvara, starting from the east up to the northeast, each by their own name.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of that, one should bring forth the Śiva-fire according to the prescribed rite.

Having invoked the Bull (Vṛṣa) in the center of that, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) as before. One should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and sesame seeds (*tila*)—
each individually for a number equal to the elements (*bhūta*)— beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna.

Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the substances, the wise and most excellent preceptor should place that cloth upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
The sagacious one should then gaze upon the banyan tree while reciting the *gaur-dhenu-bhidhāna-mantra*.
One should sprinkle [the area] from behind with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra using water for the arghya offering.
Having swept [the area] with two blades of kuśa grass while recollecting the root of the bull,
the preceptor [should apply] the *kulikā* together with the colors using the tips of the two blades of kuśa grass.
Therefore, the wise one, having performed the consecration of the bull, should perform the opening of the eyes with the Vṛṣagāyatrī, having Sūrya and Soma as its presiding deities.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow while reciting the Pavamāna hymns,

[he should pray: "O Lord of Cows, O Consort of Ambikā, you who are affectionate toward your devotees— by virtue of being beheld, may you become manifest as the Bull-Lord, whose enjoyment is entirely favorable."
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, the wise one should mentally visualize himself as standing upon the king of bulls; he should then perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa),
which is proclaimed as the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), extending from the head down to the soles of the feet.
One should designate the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) from Gulādvāra up to Sthalāṭa;
and that which extends from Hṛdaya up to Khura is proclaimed as the principle of the self (ātma-tattva).
Having worshipped each principle (*tattva*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship the Lord of that principle.

Then, having approached the fire-sanctuary, the wise one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) preceded by the drawing of a lotus, and taking nine jars, he should place them upon the mound as before.
One should fill [the vessel] with scented water, provided with a cloth and a bunch of grass (*kūrca*).
One should worship the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) and the pitcher (*kumbha*) with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *prāsāda* mantra.
Having offered one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, or ten oblations for each substance specifically, he should touch the cloth.
Having caused the jar to move upon its seat, the supreme instructor should take hold of it.
One should perform the recitation according to the number of oblations and sprinkle [the offerings] in the proper sequence.
As before, one should place the pitcher and establish the seat upon the head;
the wise man, having worshipped the banner and the pitcher with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
On the tip of the banner-reed, the wise man should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha).
He should place a water-filled pitcher containing gems upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, especially including the offering of food (naivedya), [he should proceed].
"Salutations be unto you, O Lord of all, O Protector, O you of excellent luster!
Having offered this oblation, one should protect the sacrificial hall.
Thus the learned man should announce, and he should perform the night vigil.
The sequence for victory is thus; now hear that which brings increase:
a wise man should have a pavilion constructed with eight *droṇas* of rice.
Having invoked the Bull according to the prescribed rite, one should establish him upon the sacrificial mound;
having worshipped him according to the rules with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
Then one should worship the pitchers belonging to the world-protectors, such as Vṛṣa and Kumbha;
thereafter, one should perform all rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should offer the *bali* oblation to the Kṣetrapāla around that pavilion.

Listen to the installation of the banner, renowned as the "Bestower of Prosperity. The most excellent of preceptors should take hold of either *kramuka*, sandalwood, *khādira*, coconut, *tvaksāra*, or *antaḥsāra*.
Alternatively, one may construct a roof using trees mentioned in the context of the *śūla* (spike), or a thatched covering with ropes;
it may extend over one, two, or three stories, or be level with the top of the *vṛṣasthala*.

One should determine the length of the flagpole as reaching to the end of the dome, the end of the pinnacle, the top of the great nose (mahānāsa), the edge of the platform (saman), the top of the stūpa, or the top of the gateway (gopura).
As before, one should have the rites for pacification and so forth performed using the measurement of finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*):
thirty-four, thirty-six, and thirty-two [finger-breadths].
The flagstaffs are prescribed at six, seven, and five *tālas*.
Then, having divided that into three parts, one part is made square.
One should fashion the remainder into the shape of a discus, adorned with various ornaments. Two [parts] should be provided with hollows, with a hole in the middle and one at the bottom;
it should be joined with a short staff, and one should place a ring at its tip.
In the middle of that, the rope is connected, resting upon its double root.

Between the pedestal and the gateway, or even upon the tip of the back of the bull, the wise man should install [the image] according to the prescribed rite; at its base, he should construct an altar.
Having first performed the purification of the staff, he should worship it according to the rules.
Having performed the morning bath and other rites, perform the sakalīkaraṇa;
then, worship the cloth and the jar in due order with perfumes and other offerings.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by all auspicious rites, he,
wearing a turban and an upper garment, summoned his attendant.
Having duly taken up the pitcher and the banner, which is the embodiment of the Weapon-mantra (astramūrti),
together with the Lord of Gods, perform the circumambulation of the village.
One should enter the place of the banner, equipped with all musical instruments;

there, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and bathe that cloth-painting (*paṭa*) with the bull-vessel (*vṛṣakumbha*) according to the prescribed rite. Then the learned one should worship it in due order.
Thereafter, one should bind it with a rope while reciting the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
Having equipped it with a garland of *darbha* grass and small bells,
the preceptor, having informed the Lord of the Gods of gods, prostrated and worshipped him.
The mantra-practitioner, recollecting the multiform [deity], should perform the rite of mounting [the deity] upon the cloth-painting,
together with the garland of *darbha* grass and the masters who represent the forms of the deities.
One should quickly perform the descent of the disciple upon the knot in the western part, binding it with *kuśa* grass at the base according to the sequence of the staff on the left. Then,
one should consecrate [the disciple] above the altar with the jars of Vṛṣa and Vidyeśa.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should then cause mung beans to be offered.
Having given water for drinking and for rinsing the mouth, one should present incense and a lamp.
One should cause betel-leaf to be given there; they say this is "pleasing to Śiva."

Having gratified the Bull-bannered Lord with hymns of praise, music, dance, and so forth, one should say, "May there be victory! Now, listen to that which is known as the "Victory" [mantra] and which bestows prosperity.
Having placed him upon a chariot or a palanquin adorned with the bull and the thunderbolt,
and having performed a circumambulation of the village, he was led into the presence of Daṇḍa.
The wise one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) there and raise the banner;
having bathed the deity known as Ādhāra with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, he should worship it.
Having again offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and gathered the jars,
the preceptor should perform a circumambulation of the night-watch and bathe [the deity] upon the altar.
The wise man should cause an offering of food to be presented with molasses, curd, and side dishes;
whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform according to what was prescribed for Vijaya.
Listen to the account of the drum-beating known as Vṛddhiddanta;
on that very day, during the night at the conclusion of the evening watch.
One should perform the invocation of the deity either in front of the gods or at the base of the banner.
Having prepared two sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place the trident on one of them.
Having placed a drum together with a nose-shaped ornament in front of it, to the right.
One should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day there, and then worship the Lord of the Weapon (Astra).
Bhava-Rudra is on the middle petal; Brahmā is on the southern petal;
Viṣṇu is designated as being on the left; and Pārvatī is on the Valakā.
Senāni is at the frontal globe (kumbha), and likewise Vighnanāyaka is in the mouth;
Madana is to be known at the tip of the staff, and Bhāskara is in the middle of the staff.
Caṇḍeśa is at the base of the staff (daṇḍa), while Lakṣmī is at the tip of the eastern petal.
The seven Mothers are on the right, Jyeṣṭhā is on the western petal,
and Kātyāyanī is considered to be at the base of the trident (śūla) in the direction of Kubera (the north).
Having worshipped the eighteen groups— Rudra, Arka, Vasu, and Aśvinī— with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, according to the sequence ending with the Tāṇḍava dance,
one should then worship the drum and wrap it in a new cloth.
In their midst, on the right and left, are Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and the four-faced Brahmā;
likewise the seven Mothers, Kāla, Āsyu, and the lords of the Moon, Sun, and the Earth-lotus.
Having worshipped [the deity] whose arms are leather straps and whose presiding deity is the nose,
with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, by means of their respective mantras, the preceptor—
First, the wise one should strike one [target] with the *trayambaka* mantra;
then he should strike [the others] in order from the end.
One should strike the third [syllable] three times with the mantra *brahmajajñānam*.
Then, having worshipped the King of Weapons (the Astra-mantra), one should invoke the Four-faced One (Brahmā) at its base,
as well as all the gods and the eighteen lords of the Gaṇas.
The most excellent preceptor should worship each of these with its own respective name-mantra.
Then, having summoned a musician and applied ashes to him, one should employ him;
taking that [ashes], together with the permission of the preceptor and while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Having placed the drum upon his neck, the wise one should strike it;
thereafter, he should play the musical instrument, especially according to the *balitāla* rhythm.
Afterwards, with a verse, he should cause everyone to hear the conclusion of the festival.
First, one should bring the lord of the asterism, joined with all the current [planets] from every side;
the wise man, standing before the deity, should perform the entry of the watch,
having offered the formal announcement (*sannivedya*) to the deity along with the festival.
One should offer oblations (bali) to the attendants beginning with Vṛṣa by their respective names, joined with the syllable *balibera* and combined with *sarvato'dya*.
One should perform all these rites daily, from Indra up to Īśāna.
Or else, it may be the station of Brahmā and so forth, or indeed the station of Indra and so forth.
Having invoked the deities of the junctions, one should perform the bali offering in this manner;
having thus invoked the deities, one should enter the temple.
The procedure for victory has been declared; now hear that which brings prosperity.
Having worshipped the weapon and the drum according to the previously mentioned rite, one should play it with the *carcapuṭa* rhythm, employing all rhythmic measures (*tāla*).
And having summoned all the gods, beginning with Śiva, he worships them in due order.
Having taken up the king of weapons, accompanied by all [attendants] today,
one should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim as promised in the temple.
In places where space is cramped, especially within enclosures such as walls,
one should offer the bali wherever it can be obtained.
Having washed one's feet, one should enter the temple.

One should worship the Lord of Gods there according to the procedure for the daily ritual (*nityapūjā*). The sounding of the kettle-drum has thus been described; now hear the rule for the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*).
It is prescribed that this should take place on the day prior to sunset.
Having first performed the Vāstuhoma, perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Then, for the sake of the festival, one should perform the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) in the proper sequence.
The wise practitioner should especially bind the auspicious thread (kautuka) before the Great Lord (Maheśa).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound with śāli rice, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
One should fill a small bowl with rice, accompanied by *darbha* grass and flowers;
it should be joined with a betel nut (*kramuka*) together with its fruit and provided with betel leaf (*nāgavallī*).
Then, one should place the auspicious amulet (*kautuka*) in the midst of the ashes and grains;
it may be made of gold, silver, or even linen or cotton,
provided with a new cloth and accompanied by perfumes and garlands.
Having placed the protection-thread (rakṣāsūtra) upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should recite the mantra over it.
Afterwards, the preceptor, having bathed the Lord of Sacrifice with scented water and worshipped Him with perfumes,
flowers, and so forth, should offer incense, lamps, and other offerings.
The master should cover [the image] with a cloth while reciting the mantra "yuvam vastrā," and having sprinkled the thread with ashes while reciting the Tryambaka mantra.
One should place rice in the hand [of the deity] with the mantra "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe";
the wise one [should do so] in the right hand of the god and in the left hand of the goddess.
One should bind the protective thread (kautuka) with the mantra beginning "bṛhatsāmā," and then one should cause the sacred ash to be given with the mantra beginning "yau brahmaṇā."
With unbroken rice grains as before, they uttered words of blessing for the Brahmins;
then, upon the middle petal of the trident, they placed an offering for the sake of the *bali*, without the *kautuka*.
Then, for the sake of the festival of the deities, one should tie the auspicious thread (kautuka).
To the east, northeast, or even the north of the ashes,
one should have a sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) constructed, endowed with the characteristics previously described.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and [covered it] with a thread sprinkled with flour,
one should lay down ten threads with their tips pointing east and likewise ten with their tips pointing north.
Then, having entered the sacrificial hall, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion;
one should thoroughly worship the pavilion, beginning with the Sun and ending with the Guru.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) above the altar with eight droṇas of śāli rice,
one should cover it with rice grains, sesame seeds, parched grain, darbha grass, and flowers.
Having taken nine jars, one should wrap them with thread;
one should wash them with the weapon-mantra and fill them with pure water.
One should place upon the altar vessels provided with water-pots, accompanied by sprouts and coconut fruits, and joined with jewels and garments.
In the center, one should worship the Lord of the Festival, and to his left, Manonmanī;
then, one should fully worship the Vidyeśvaras in the eight jars starting from the east.
One should worship the ten weapons all around, excluding the water-pot;
outside of that, the wise man should worship the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) on every side.
He should honor each one with its own name-mantra, using perfumes and flowers.

Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the prescribed rite, one should properly prepare the fire. One should perform the oblation (*homa*) for each of the following— fuel-sticks (*samit*), clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), black gram (*māṣa*), śāli rice, barley (*yava*), and sesame (*tila*)— extending from the beginning of all directions up to the crest of the flame.

Having offered one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, nine, five, or even just one oblation at the conclusion of the materials, and having performed the *vyāhṛti* oblation, one should then perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.

Therefore, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and likewise offer incense, lamps, and so forth. This is declared to be the ritual of the weapon-mantra (astrayāga); now hear the sequence for the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna).
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should offer the *bali* in due order, both morning and evening.
For the sake of the *bali*, one should cook a *droṇa* or half a *droṇa* of rice.
One should wash the cauldron or the small vessel with a hundredfold [amount of] water.
One should place the end [of the offering] into that vessel, together with the materials for the bali-offering.
For the sake of the inner liṅga, one should cook rice-grains equal in number to the vessels;
having placed them inside a small bowl, they should be accompanied by fruit and the ocean [of milk].
The height should be twelve finger-breadths, and its circumference should be double that;
the tip is said to be one fire-finger (three finger-breadths), and from the base to the tip it should gradually taper like a blade of kuśa grass.
Having fashioned the *liṅga*, one should cast the remainder of that food into water;
then, in the center of that *liṅga*, one should worship Raudra-Pāśupata.
Then, having summoned the decorator and caused him to provide garments, flowers, meat, and so forth,
O knower of distinctions, one should thereafter enter the inner sanctum.
Having informed the God of gods, one should perform the offering of the *bali* accompanied by mantras;
one should produce the five great sounds together with the *balitāla*.
[One should provide] the Lord of Weapons (*astreśa*), the food-emblem (*annaliṅga*), and the *baliberas*.
Equipped with parasols and fly-whisks, accompanied by the sound of bells,
joined with all kinds of musical instruments, surrounded by courtesans and others,
provided with offerings and lamps, and furnished with vessels for the sacrificial oblations.
Having offered the bali-oblation accompanied by the Svasti-sūkta, the wise man [should worship] Nandin,
Kāla, Vṛṣa, Bhānu, Muṇḍī, and the Mothers.
One should worship Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, Vighneśa, Acyuta, Guha, Durgā,
and Caṇḍeśvara in the first enclosure;
and in the second enclosure, Daṇḍin, Bhṛṅgin, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
Having circumambulated the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha), the Bull, and the Trident three times,
one should offer oblations to the kings of the gods at the front of the Great Seat:
to Agni, Vaivasvata, Sṛkpa, the Lord of Waters, and Māruta.
The Lord of Yakṣas, the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), Īśa, Viṣṇu, and Viriñcaka—
having thus entered the second enclosure, the city and so forth—
one should provide the door-guardian (Dvārabali) at the exit door from the temple.
One should offer the Kuṃbhodara bali on the northern side of the entrance.
On its southern side, one should offer bali to Mahodara;
between the two [other deities], one should especially offer bali to Mahāvegin.
Starting either from the Brahma-position or from the Indra-position in sequence,
one should fashion the offering pedestal (balipīṭhaka) out of bricks or clay.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
O Jvālājihva, whose hair blazes, great-treasury, and possessed of great strength;
O eater of mortals, of fierce speed, guardian of the site, and lover of offerings!

The great elements (mahābhūtas) are to be understood in order from the station of Brahmā; having first abandoned them, one should then offer bali to the gods starting from the station of Indra. Having thus given the bali to the elements, it shall bring peace to the village.

One should offer the daily deity-oblation (*dinadevabali*) either at the front of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), or at the front of the gateway (*gopura*), or in the northeast, to the left of the pedestal; this offering of the daily oblation is to be performed every day.
And for the sake of appeasing all the gods, one should offer the bali-oblation to Īśa, Īśāna, and Trāyambaka;
having offered the bali with the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra), the wise man [should proceed].
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp,
the presentation of the bali-offering, and the display of the bali-mudrā.
The offering of *arghya*, prostrations, hymns of praise, the sounding of kettledrums,
dance, song, and instrumental music— each performed in turn before the sacrificial altar (*balipīṭha*).
The song of Megharājābjavarta, accompanied by the *brahmatāla* rhythm and joined with the *malagirī* melody, is intended for the pleasure of Brahmā in the region of Brahmadeśa.
(It is) joined with the Ṇdhāra-svara; and as for the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) … [it is] joined with the Ṇdhāra-svara.
In the region of Indra, the Rāṭīs are the cause of delight for the deity.
Combined with Kollīsvara, one should perform the *pratyālīḍha* stance and the *maṭṭaya* dance;
likewise, singing on the coral mountain in the southeast is for the sake of pleasing the beloved.
The Naṭṭabhāṣā, the Bhujaṅga, the Tāla, and likewise the Puṭa,
combined with songs of the spring season, are for the sake of pleasing those in the southern region;
as well as the Kauśika and the Maṅgalāvarta, accompanied by the Ekatala rhythm.
Gānanda is joined with Īśa in the south-western direction, while Priya is in the western direction.
One should perform the Śrīkāmarāga, the Svasāvarta, the Tāla, and likewise the Ācapuṭa,
accompanied by the Somagiri melody, in the western direction.

The song, characterized by the *takkeśī* and the *bhujagālīḍha* [rhythm], accompanied by the *balitāla* [meter], and joined with the *mālava* [rāga], is for the sake of pleasing one's beloved in the region of Vāyu.
It is characterized by the fifth *utghaṭṭita* and accompanied by the *kumbha-tāla*;
joined with the *śuddha-gauḍa* [rāga], it is pleasing and meaningful in the Saumya region.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, one should enter toward the temple.
After washing one's feet, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) upon the great pedestal.
By virtue of the circumambulation of the watch, one should enter the pavilion of the deity.
Then, having performed the rite of sprinkling (nīrājana) for the central deity of the bali-offering, the preceptor [should proceed].
Having cast the linga into the water and [worshipped] the Lord of Weapons (Astra-īśa) in the sacrificial pavilion,
one should offer three handfuls of flowers in the presence of the primary image (mūlabera).
One should perform the remainder of the twilight rites according to the procedure previously described.
Then, at the conclusion of the twilight rite, one should have the Lord of All (Sakaleśvara) placed upon a stage,
a palanquin, or a chariot.
Having swept the pathway, one should sprinkle it with water alone;
[one should offer] plantains, sugarcanes, and full jars containing fruit,
as well as variegated cloth, incense, and pleasant cool water.
A mirror, hair, saffron, black perfume mixed with collyrium,
uśīra, giribera, kalhāra, jasmine, and campaka.
At every door of the house, one should offer betel leaf together with coconut, areca nut, a hundred-petaled lotus, and a lamp.
It was provided with various lamps, accompanied by various devotees,
endowed with various umbrellas, and furnished with various banners; it was accompanied by various musical instruments and attended by various women.
One should cause chowries and palm-leaf fans to be presented by female attendants.
After us, the great Śaivas [should be seated], and after them, the Brahmins;
after them, the Rudra-prostitutes, adorned with all ornaments.
At its end, those mounted on vehicles [should follow], and at its end, those making the sound of musical instruments;
[the image] adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by every kind of musical instrument.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village and entered the assembly pavilion,
the wise one, having seated [him] upon the lion-throne, played various musical instruments.
Water for rinsing the mouth should be given in a quantity that fills the palm;
one should discharge it once, three, or five times while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Then, having performed the purification of the ground, [one should offer] coconuts and other fruits.
Then, one should cause water to be offered to the deity who has been presented [with the oblation].
Next, the learned practitioner should offer betel-leaf together with camphor.
At the conclusion of the incense offering, he should indeed perform the lamp-offering using a piece of camphor.
One should indeed perform the Nīrāñjana rite for the welfare of all living beings;
at the conclusion of the pure dance, one should perform the Bahurūpa rite.
Adorned with various ornaments, it should be carried out by my female attendants.
Through stories of various lands, musical performances, and spectacles such as religious rites and battles.
By means of other entertaining words, by the display of great nets and the like,
and by the beauties of musical instruments such as the lute, flute, and drum.
The teacher sits on the right side, while the king sits on the left;
behind them, the disciples and the attendants are stationed.
Mardaka and Narttaka are stationed on the left side,
while the Gaṇikās stand on both sides of Rudra.
All the remaining people should assemble on the left side;
specifically, they should perform the *bahurūpa* rite before Maheśa with all manner of songs,
instrumental music, and hymns of praise to Maheśvara.
One should place perfumes, garlands, and descending [ornaments] upon the bathing altar;
the wise one should bathe [the deity] with ritual ablutions and offer pure food. Then, taking up the deity while reciting the Svasti-sūkta, [one should proceed].
Having performed the entry into the sacred abode accompanied by the sounding of conchs,
one should apply a coating of cow dung in front of the abode, or to the north, south, or west, and decorate it with various flour-powders.
In this manner, one should place the central image together with the daily icons;
the best of preceptors, having summoned all the materials for the water for the feet and so forth intended for the following day, should set them before the deity.
The materials for the lotus-water, sipping water, the arghya offering, and the bath should be prepared with aindras (soma-juices).
One should place clothing, ointments, substances, and ornaments in the southern direction;
one should arrange incense and other materials for the lustration ceremony in the western direction.
The wise man should place mouth-perfume and water mixed with substances to the north, and rice for the purpose of the *naivedya* offering near the fire.
One should place marīci, salt, asafoetida, cumin, and ginger in the southwest (nairṛta) direction; the parasol and fly-whisks in the northwest (vāyavya);
and tattered cloth, oil, and a lamp-stand in the northeast (aiśaka).
Then, one should place all other substances before the deity.
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) for the purpose of consecrating the substances.
Having worshipped them with the *praṇava*, perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).
In this manner, one should cause all the sacrificial implements to enter the sacred abode;
at the conclusion of the entry into the abode, [the deity] is joined with various ornaments.
Furthermore, having purified [the image] with fragrant flowers and other offerings,
one should place it upon a palanquin or similar vehicle and enter the temple of Bhavānī.
Having adorned the temple, which is fit for a bed, with canopies and other ornaments,
one should place within it a suitable bed provided with mudrās and flowers.
Having spread a cloth over it, one should install the Lord facing the east.
On his right side, one should worship Gaurī and the Guru.
Rohiṇī and the Gaṇas are in the east, tripled [in number];
the Guhya and Mātṛgaṇas are in the south; and Viṣṇu and the Mothers are in the west.
One should place Brahmā along with the three qualities (guṇas) in the northeast; Madana and Rati in the southeast;
Vasanta in the southwest; and the Lord of the Nakṣatras in the northwest.
The wise man should place the sandals and the royal insignia upon the cloth, beginning from the east and proceeding clockwise; he should worship each with its respective mantra.
There, one should cause an offering of food to be presented according to one's devotion;
then, having offered incense and a lamp, one should subsequently cause betel-leaf to be given.
Having worshipped the ten weapons on all sides, one should protect [the area] with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Then, according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the closing of the door with a cloth.

At the end of the night, having bathed and performed the salutation to the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) and other rites, the Guru, surrounded by skilled attendants, should enter the temple of the deity. Then, having performed the inner sacrifice (*antaryajana*), which is enriched by the offerings of the attendants...
Having caused Śakuni to enter and having closed the door, [he said:
"Having drawn aside the concealing curtain and bowed to the Lord of All, [he spoke]:
'Oṃ! Salutations to the Lord of the gods, the sole leader of all the worlds!'"
"Arise for the purpose of the bathing rite, for the prosperity of all the worlds! Having been addressed thus, he took the god, who was endowed with his former power.
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, adorned with all ornaments,
one should then perform a circumambulation of either the village or the residence.
Having constructed an assembly pavilion, one should perform the worship in due order;
having completed it with fragrant oils and the like, as well as ground *āmalaka* and sandalwood.
The preceptor should bathe the God of gods with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the nectars, and with coconut water and other such substances; at the conclusion of that,
he should bathe the Lord with musk and saffron from a casket.
Then, having wiped it with a cleaning cloth, one should discard the loincloth and other such items.
Wrapping [the image] in a pure cloth, one should carry it to the pavilion for the purpose of sacrifice;
specifically, upon the altar, on the right side or the north side.

Having placed [the deity] upon a lotus seat, one should worship the water-pot and other items with water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya), using water infused with flowers and other substances appropriate for the day.
The wise one should offer the oblation with devotion, as if performing the royal service;
he should perform the worship of the Śiva-fire, which has the seed-syllable of the Lord of Days (the Sun).
One should perform the sacrificial oblation according to this previously mentioned procedure;
having offered it, one should satisfy the Lord of All at the end with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
There, upon the altar in the northeast, one should worship the weapons.
With the respective mantras of their own names, [one should worship] the seed-syllables presiding over the deities of the days.
(4th line) In the presence of the deity, one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Then, one should perform hymns such as the Vedas, as well as song, dance, and instrumental music.
Having applied a tilaka with ashes along with the benedictions of the Brahmins, the wise man should offer the bali-oblation before the Lord of Gods and make his formal request.
Then, taking up the King of Weapons (the Trident), accompanied by the sacrificial vessel (balibhara),
provided with the mark of food (annaliṅga), and equipped with the bell and the small hand-drum (ḍamaru).
Equipped with umbrellas and chowries, provided with various lamps,
and accompanied by the offering of oblations (bali), one should then perform the circumambulation.
At the conclusion of the oblation, one should conduct a festival adorned with all ornaments.
And he was seated in the midst of that radiance upon a divine jewel lion-throne.
One should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the guest-offering (arghya), as well as fruits, edible foods, and so forth;
having offered incense, lamps, and the like, one should perform the visualization of bliss.
Then, at the time of midday, one should worship the Lord of all;
having performed the ceremonial bath for the sake of the procession, and having offered it, one should worship Him thoroughly.
One should perform the entire worship of the root image according to the previously stated procedure in the northeast,
the north, the east, or especially in the west; or alternatively,
one may perform the occasional worship in the assembly hall.
Having further adorned it, he rendered it free from all stains.
In the latter half of the evening, for the sake of diversion and observation,
having performed a circumambulation of the village in accordance with the sequence of the ritual offerings.
Whether it be a fight between goats and pigs, or a fight between fish,
or even a fight between tigers, or indeed a fight between a goat and a tiger.
Or a cockfight between two equal roosters, or [a fight] between dogs and pigs;
or a dog with a heap of rabbits, or a tiger with dogs and jackals.
One should arrange various amusements for the sake of diversion by means of elephants, men, or all [of them together];
one should display many kinds of mutual diversions.
Having entered the assembly hall, one should offer incense and lamps;
then, having performed the rite of eye-anointing (*nīrāñjana*) according to the protective ritual for the evening,
the wise one should once again bathe Maheśvara with the bathing rites and other ceremonies.

There, one should present the sacrificial offering and perform the fire-oblation (homa). Having offered the bali according to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise preceptor should offer incense, lamps, and other offerings to the primary image (mūlabera).
The wise man should worship for the sake of the vehicle, and at its conclusion, [he should worship] Utsaveśvara,
having placed him upon Garvikā and the like, adorned with all ornaments.
Then, one should perform a circumambulation in a clockwise direction following the sequence of the serving;
one should place [the vessel] upon the lion-throne in the center of the assembly pavilion.

Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, perform the viewing of the dance. The wise one should bathe [the deity] with ritual ablutions and then cause the offering of food (naivedya) to be presented.
Then, having performed the remainder of the twilight rites,
one should enter the temple of Bhavānī, which is adorned with garlands of perfumes and where Utsaveśvara resides.
The procedure for victory, which bestows prosperity, has been declared; now listen to it from me.
Then, according to the previously mentioned rite, [the ritual] from the germination of seeds (*aṅkura*) up to the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed.
When the following day arrives, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) at the conclusion of the *homa*.
One should perform the offering (*bali*) and the festival (*utsava*), endowed with the proper sequence.
Listen now to the daily rites and so forth, renowned as the "Vṛddhi" [observance]:
the first shall be Vighnarātri, and the second Bhūtarātri.

The third night shall be the Night of the Sages (Ṛṣirātra), and the fourth is the Night of Indra (Indrarātrika). The fifth night is the Night of the Gandharvas, and the sixth is the Night of the Moon (Candrarātrika).
The seventh is Guharātri, and Rāga-viṣṇurātrika;
the eighth is Pañcāgnirātri, and the tenth is Nāgarātrika.
The eleventh [night] belongs to Raudra; likewise, the twelfth is for the Mothers at night.
The thirteenth day is for Āhuka-kūrmaṇḍa, and the fourteenth is the night of the Pitṛs.
The fifteenth day is for Bhānu at night, while the night of the Kalās belongs to the Rākṣasas.
One should know the seventeenth as Śiva; these are the deities of the days.
[Then there are] the Vāruṇa, Yogapādya, Brahmacandreśapādya, Śaśiraṅgaurapādya, Dhauta, and indeed Śuddhapādya.

The auspicious foot-water, the water for the feet that brings happiness, the royal foot-water, the foot-water for removing impurities, the digestive foot-water, the perfected foot-water, and the pacifying foot-water consisting of water for the feet.
One should especially offer water for the feet (*pādya*) beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva;
and thereafter, [offer] Śa, Bhoga, Vīra, and Śāśvata in sequence.
The six-limbed [rite], the universal pacification, the sipping of water for the worlds,
then the sipping of water for the sun, the auspicious, the beloved, and the nectar;
the mental sipping of water, the fragrance, and the sipping of water for Soma.
The bliss that illuminates the self is the ultimate mental satisfaction.
From Gaṇeśa up to Īśa, the sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed for each day;
likewise, the offering of restraint (nirodhārghya), the lotus, and the release from bonds (pāśamocana).
The portion for the gods, the exclusive portion, the portion for Śaśin,
the portion for Śrīyāvaka, the portion for Śrībhoga, the portion for the mantra, and likewise the special portion.
Furthermore, there is the destroyer of bad dreams, the *arghya* for Śiva which liberates from sin,
the *arghya* for those who have turned away, Gaṇeśa, and the end-maker of Śiva;
then the seed, the bark, the tuber, and the water within the center of the tuber.

One should take water for the purpose of bathing, including supreme cleansing substances, sour juices, mineral salts, red dyes, astringents, perfumes, flowers, missiles, betel leaves, and so forth, as well as [the deities] beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva.
Śaphara, piṅgalam, dhānya, kapotaka, carīmadhu,
lohitvam, bujavarṇa, karpūra, and likewise vakula.
The tawny, the dark-colored, the blackish-red, the smoky, the yellow,
and the white— these are the [deities] beginning with Vighneśa and ending with Śiva.
An ornament of emerald, a forehead mark (tilaka), and a conch shell; crystal, puṣpomedaka, drujaṭa, and the seed of the lotus.
Adorned with golden ornaments, lapis lazuli, coral, pearls,
rudrākṣas, rubies, sapphires,
and emeralds in their proper order, [the liṅgas] begin with Gaṇeśa and end with Śiva.
One should especially offer the perfumes Kapila, Brahmagandha, Śrīgandha, Vimala,
as well as the eight perfumes dear to Śiva, namely Śrīgandha and Padmagandha,
beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva.
The *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, and the *punnāga* four finger-breadths [in size],
as well as the *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *mandāra*, and others.
O Lord of Obstacles, one should arrange the vakula, the lotus flower, and likewise the karavīra,
as well as the jāti, white arka, cāmpeya, pāṭalī, and utpala, and the droṇa flower, reaching to the end of the directions.

"O Priyānanda, prepare incense for the Madas that brings joy to loved ones, delight to the beloved, and is pleasing and beautiful to all; it is proclaimed as the 'Bestower of Prosperity and Desire' (Śrīkāmadam). Furthermore, O Aṅga, worship with incense that possesses a beautiful fragrance."
One should offer the incense of Varadhūpa, Śrīdhūpa, Śītārī, and Śivapriya,
as well as the incense beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva, day after day.
Nāgadīpa and Śivānta, with Śikhā as the auspicious lamp;
in the letter Śī, Nāradī, and Indrakānta as the five earth-lamps.
Bhadradīpa, Śikhānandīpa, and Śekhara;
Mantradīpa, Rudrarūpa, Rājadīpa, and Śivapriya; Indrāvapraṇadīpa, and those beginning with Vighneśa and ending with Śiva.
Food with ghee, food with curd and honey, food for enjoyment, fruit and water, royal food, food from which pearls have been removed, food from a dark-skinned woman,
rice mixed with sesame and peas, milk-rice, pure food, and rice with mung beans and molasses.
The wise one should offer as oblation flour-cakes, turmeric, *kaṇṭvanna*, and cooked rice (*siddha-modana*),
beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva;
likewise, cold water, *vātabhedin*, and the fragrance of the six ingredients (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
The water from the feet of Śrī possesses a beautiful fragrance, is cooling to the body,
and indeed removes all distress with its auspicious scent.
Śrībhadra, Citta-santoṣa, and Śitaśekhara; Varuṇa, Mārdava, and Mantrasantāna.
The Illumination of the Seated (sittasandīpana), the Pinnacle of the Water of Mental Bliss (cittānandāmbuśekhara),
known as the Water (pānīya), extending from Gaṇeśa up to Śiva; likewise, the Altar of Oblation (hutavedī), the Joy of Oblation (hutānanda), and the Divine Oblation (hutānāda).
Kriyāsandhānaka, Hutavāsa, and Hutāmṛta;
The enjoyment of the sacrificial fire, the awakening through ritual action,
the binding of karma, and the bestower of desires.
One should perform the oblation of the ritual substances, beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Īśa: Karmapūraṇikā, Kola, Vikaca, Hutaśekhara, Vidhipūrṇāmṛta, Siddha, and Hutadīpaka.

An oblation (*puroḍāśa*) filled with sugarcane, a bamboo vessel, and white water-lilies (*kumuda*), which are dear to Śiva; camphor, parched-rice flour, groats, and fried cakes (*pūrika*); along with lotus stalks, silk, cow products, and peacock feathers—all of which are beloved by Śiva.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva, [using] barley, nectar, and that which bestows strength, sustains strength, and indeed produces strength.
Tarkke, Naṭṭarāga, Megharāga, Kauśika,
Saindhava, and Tādhava as the fifth, [these are] in the Naṭṭa language.
Antālikāmara, Gāndhāra, and likewise Pañcama;
Tarkkeśī, Naṭṭarāga, Vyālāgreṇī, and Kauśika; Antālikāmara, Kolī (or Kollī), Gāndhāra, and Pañcama.
The Gāndhāra, the Tarkarāga, the Meghanāda, and the Kauśika;
the Pūrvapañcaraka hymn beginning with Vighneśa and ending with Śiva;
the Āditāla of Śrīraṅga, the Raṅgadyota, and the Tarpaṇa.
The *Jharjhari*, the *Haṃsanāda*, and the *Mallikāmoda*;
the *Maranda*, the *Kīrtiśatāloka*, the *Saṃsanāda*, and the *Gāruḍa*.
The Kīḍātāla, Karītāla, Janaka, Kumbhatāla, Jhampā,
Pañcavarṇatāla, and Lakṣemītāla— in this sequence,
the best of those skilled in ritual construction (kalpavittama) should arrange [the deities] from Gaṇeśa up to Īśa.
Then [he worships] Kālāgni, Kāmanāśa, and Caṇḍeśānugraha.
The form of Gaṅgādhara, the one who took away the elephant [from Indra], the friend of Umā;
the wandering mendicant Kaṅkāla, and Hari who is half-and-half woman.
Kalyāṇasundara, Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
Nṛtta, Sukhāsana, Kirāta, and Tripurāntaka.
The determination of the [deities] beginning with Gaṇeśa and ending with Śiva has thus been stated:
Gabdhika, Amṛgarāsi, Ratnadhāman, and Śekharī.

The Makara, the Bhūtayāna, the palanquin (śibikā), the Puṣpikaprapā, the Mauṇḍiratna, the Prapāyāna, the bull, and likewise the Raṅga; then the Puṣpadhāma, the chariot (ratha), the elephant (nāga), the horse (turaṅga), and finally the Kheṭaka.
One should imagine the vehicles (vāhana) starting from Gaṇeśa and ending with Īśa.
From Śiva down to Candra, one should abandon the preceding and take up the succeeding;
likewise, the best of teachers should collect the musical instruments and other such items.
First, the circumambulation of the shrine; after that, the daily worship (nityārcana);
then the ceremonial bathing for the festival procession (yātrārthasnapana); and finally, the fire sacrifice (homa) and the offering of oblations (balis).

Then follows the rite of *nīrājana* and the viewing for diversion; thereafter comes the midday worship, followed by the occasional (*naimittika*) worship. After that is the evening worship, and finally the re-entry for the fire-oblation (*homa*).
And likewise, the festival of the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna), as well as the pitching of camp for the march.
At the time of the half-watch remaining [of the day], every single day;
but especially on the sixth day, one should perform the festival of Śambhu.
In the eighth month, one should undertake a hunting expedition;
otherwise, by failing to act at the proper time, one brings about the destruction of immortality.
Afterwards, for the sake of the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform the binding of the auspicious thread (kautuka-bandhana),
the consecration of the ford (tīrthādhivāsana), and then carry out the festival of the powder (cūrṇotsava) before the deity,
in the assembly hall, or on a delightful bank of the ford.
Then one should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) and engage in water sports;
having then offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the consecration with the sacrificial jar (yāgakuṃbha),
conduct the ceremonial bathing, and there offer abundant sacrificial food (havir).
One should perform the lowering of the banner and carry out the silent sacrifice (*maunayāga*). Listen now to the renowned *Vijayantī*, the prosperity-bestowing *Prabhañjana*.
At the conclusion of the water-play, one should then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* offering;
perform the consecration with the sacrificial jar and the lowering of the banner.
Then, having performed the *caṇḍayāga*, one should cause the ritual bathing (*snapana*) to take place.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods, he offered abundant oblations.
Next, listen to the [mantra] known as Vṛddhidantiviti and the Brāhmika;
thereafter, one should worship Vighneśa, and after that, the formal petition.

The purification of the image is the third; the consecration of ornaments is the fourth; then follows the rite of binding the protective thread and the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi). Next is the procedure for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and finally, the ritual for daily worship.
Then follows the sacrifice to Utsaveśvara and the midday worship.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship at dusk, followed by the rite of Nīrāñjana;
having performed the rite of the food-offering, one should engage in the play with water-jars.
At the conclusion, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed and offer the drinking of wine (ja-bhū-pāna).
This is renowned as the Brāhmika [rite], following the sequence of festivals.
Indeed, there is some slight distinction even among the three types of small [festivals].
The sprout, the drum, and likewise the invocation of the deities.
One should perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga), the offering of oblations (balidhāna), the pilgrimage site (tīrtha), the worship of Caṇḍeśvara,
the ritual bathing (snapana), and the abundant drinking (bhūripāna) in their proper sequence.
He should diligently dismiss all others as well;
perform the festival for the devotees at the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Thus, whatever mortal performs this shall attain a meritorious state.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for festivals in the Sukṣmāgama.]
Oṃ. Karavarṣa, the twenty-first day of the month of Kalyāma. Written by the hand of Ayyāsvāmin himself.
(Side heading) [The Crown and the Festival of Śiva]:
Prior to the festival of Śiva and other rites, the excellent offering of the sprout (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should first be performed.
Initiated practitioners and sādhakas should likewise perform bathing and sprinkling;
one should worship during the bathing at different times and at the commencement of battles.
[One should also worship] during the plowing and when entering the stone slab that serves as the form of the image.
On the occasion of the *navabhojana*, the *kalyāṇa*, and likewise the *kṛttakāmāsaka* (3rd line), as well as during the *pavitrārohaṇa* and indeed the *prāyaścitta*,
the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) is performed on the fifth, the seventh, and the ninth [days].
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva* should each be of three kinds:
made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
The *pālikā* [vessel] is eight finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in length;
the width of the mouth of the *pālikā* is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
Half of that is the width of the base; the thickness of the *oṣṭaka* is one-sixth of the [base] width;
and one-third of the width is said to be the projection (*bali*).
Thus the sequence of the feet has been declared; now the staff (daṇḍa) is described here.
One-third of the width is said to be the width of the staff.
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the characteristics of the *ghaṭikā*:
the width of the *ghaṭikā*-jar should be eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and it should have a beautiful base.
The staff (*daṇḍa*) should indeed be four finger-breadths wide, fashioned auspiciously like a *pālikā*.
Then one should have a water-clock (ghaṭikā) constructed, joined with five openings.
The width of the mouth of the bowl (śarāva) is declared to be eight finger-breadths;
its middle width at the base should be [the same], and its height should be eight finger-breadths.
From the nāraṅga [measure], the *pālika* and other [units] are established by half the width;
they are distinct, hollow-based, without division, cornered, and dark blue.
The most excellent practitioner should avoid both the *āpa* and the *jharjhara*.
The *śūli*, *mukundadhārā*, and *pālikā* are presided over by deities.
In this manner, ten [vessels] should be placed, each held by its handle;
[they are to be arranged] in the east, northeast, south, and likewise in the north of the temple.
Having meditated on the application of cow-dung for purification during the triple practice,
and having thoroughly adorned the pavilion, one should take the eastward thread and the northward thread;
taking the central point of space, the wise practitioner should apply the plaster.
And having abandoned the three internal [factors], listen now to the sequence of actions.
The wise one should have a sacrificial mound prepared with eight *droṇas* of rice;
in its center, he should draw an eight-petaled lotus together with its pericarp.

One should place in the center of the pericarp a beautiful, pure moon-vessel together with a thread; and the thread, along with the gems, should be prepared as before. Having worshipped it according to the rule, it is called "with the purifier" (*sopavitraka*).
Afterwards, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and then cause the food offering (*naivedya*) to be presented.
For three days, and for each single day during which the preceptor (*ācārya*) recites [the mantra],
one should perform the rite at dawn and commence it again in the evening.
Prior to the commencement of the festival, the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) are described:
one should dig it there to the measure of one cubit, provided with a girdle (mekhalā).
The girdle (mekhalā) is said to be fashioned similar to the pit;
having adorned it with girdles, it should be provided with a single girdle.
Its height is nine finger-breadths according to the measurement of its width.
Above that, it should be four finger-breadths high and extended by a single girdle.
I shall describe the sequence of the three girdles (*trimekhalā*), and Maheśvara [will explain] the specific details:
the upper [girdle] should be four finger-breadths wide, while the middle one should be three finger-breadths.
The other two [lines] should be two finger-breadths wide and raised;
one should place the womb (yoni), shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha), above the girdle (mekhalā).
Its height is one finger-breadth and its width four finger-breadths;
above that, it is seven finger-breadths. Now hear regarding the days:
in the month beginning with Kṛttikā, [one should perform it] starting from Kṛttikā and ending with Kṛttikā.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it ends with Ārdrā; in the month of Puṣya, it is Puṣya;
in the month of Māgha, it ends with Maghā; and in Phālguna, it ends with Uttarā-phalgunī.
In Caitra, it is Citrā; likewise, in Vaiśākha, it is Viśākhā.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the auspicious day at the conclusion of the Mūla festival,
one should subsequently cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented and offer betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
One should first place two small earthen vessels (pālikā) on either side of the doors.
One should place two *ghaṭikās* on the eyes and two on the two feet;
on the remaining parts, one should place *śarāvas* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
With the tips of *kuśa* grass and *darbha* blades, make the *nicimra* porous.
One should fill the small pots and other vessels with sand, cow dung, and earth;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should worship them with the *Śakti-mantra*.
Then, one should especially cause betel-leaf to be offered;
furthermore, one should place the seed of milk-rice and mung beans in a golden vessel.
Sesame, mustard, mung bean, black gram, rice, and *ambaḍha*—these are the seven seeds; for these seven, there are seven maidens as presiding deities.
The preceptor, facing either east or north, should scatter the seeds;
he should then sprinkle the *pālikā* vessels and the others situated within the *soma*-vessel.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
The festival is said to be of three kinds: nine days, seven days, or five days.
The best [festival] lasts for nine days, while the middling lasts for seven;
the middling should be known as lasting five days, which constitutes the strength of the festival.
This occurs in Āṣāḍha under Uttarāṣāḍhā, and in Śrāvaṇa under Śravaṇā.
Likewise, in the month of Pūrvabhādra, the end of Pūrvabhādrapadā is declared.
Likewise, on the full moon day of Āśvayuja and the auspicious final day of the festival for the Aśvattha tree,
the Śiva-festival should be performed in all months, concluding with the month of Āṣāḍha.
The sacrificer [should perform it] on the day of the sun, and likewise the king on his birthday.
(Third line) I shall describe the characteristics of the banners; listen now to the characteristics of the staff.
It is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
The staff should be level at the edge of the temple and extend to the end of the temple's summit;
the staff should be equal in size to the *mahānāsī* (great nose), and this is the sequence for the three types of superior [measurements].
[The measurements] up to the chest region, up to the pinnacle (kuṭa), and likewise up to the gateway (gopura)—
listen now to the threefold classification of the middle and the inferior in due order.
Alternatively, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may be situated in the very center, or it may be on level ground or even among trees.
Then, construct a staff equal in length to a five-cubit pavilion;
it is said that for a three-cubit pavilion, the staff shall be double that length.
One should employ a staff of four cubits, two and a half cubits, or even half a cubit;
above that, however, the staff for the middle [deity] and others is five cubits.
Nirvāṇa and Ṛju, free from worm-holes and hollows;
likewise Candana, Dāru, Bilva, and Campaka;
as well as Kramuka, Veṇuka, and the Panasa and Āmra trees.
The *kundapannāga*, *khadira*, and likewise the *ketakī* [wood] are used for the cleansing.
A circumference of six or eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is prescribed as the best;
a circumference of twenty-four finger-breadths is prescribed as the middling.
One should construct the lower [measure] there with a circumference of twelve finger-breadths;
this superior [measure] is proclaimed to have a circumference of twenty-four finger-breadths.
The root [of the handle] should be ten finger-breadths long, extending up to eighteen finger-breadths;
this is called the superior, the middling, and the inferior circumference.
It should be made with the inferior finger-breadth, or one should have it fashioned with the middle finger-breadth.
The best [size] is one cubit (hasta), provided with five planks;
its length is prescribed as twenty finger-breadths (aṅgula) for the superior type,
while that which is eighteen finger-breadths long is twelve finger-breadths wide.
Having performed the middling rite, one should then arrange the inferior one;
it should be one cubit in measure and four finger-breadths in width.
Having made the staff three parts, then five parts,
and then seven parts, one should fashion the tip at the end.
The best [measure] is nine cubits by means of the *avāma* measurement;
the middle is five cubits, and the lowest is six cubits.
Having thus prepared the three types of cloth according to the rule, one should likewise proceed with the silk (*paṭṭa*).
The supreme five-beat rhythm, as well as the middle and the fourth.
And having fashioned the lowest [mandala] in three ways, joined with five plantain leaves,
shaped like a triangle, and provided with excellent flowers;
The width at the top, the middle, and combined with the width of the tail—
endowed with these characteristics, the installation of the banner is proclaimed.
On the northern side of the tree, having been smeared with cow dung...
One should place eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice and half that amount of husked *taṇḍula* grain upon it.
Having spread a cloth over that and having drawn [the deity] upon bulls and other [emblems],
as well as a club, a *khaḍvāṅga*, a noose, and likewise a trident;
An umbrella and a pair of lamps, with two chowries on either side,
as well as a bull and a lotus seat, all adorned with every kind of ornament.
Having depicted a white bull, its horns are proclaimed to be red;
likewise, all the donkeys should be adorned with the splendor of the rising sun.
One should likewise cause a bull to be drawn setting out toward the [desired] direction,
along with the respective mounts of Indra and the other guardians of the eight quarters of the world.
It is joined with nine banners and has the form of Mount Aindrakūṭa and Japā.
One should place a goat in the region of Agni and a buffalo in the region of Yama.
One should place a swan in the region of Nirṛti, and likewise a crocodile in the west;
a deer in the northwestern region, and a horse is proclaimed for the north;
and a bull in the northeast, each on its respective right side.
Having written it as before and performed the rites, one should worship it with the beginning of one's own name;
specifically, the auspicious arrangement of the root deity should be performed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should perform a special worship of the wonderful Dakṣiṇeśvara.
The supreme teacher should perform the worship according to the extent of his resources.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus four finger-breadths in size with a white rice-powder line, he should prepare eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice.
Having prepared an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds, one should draw [the mandala] starting from the four corners;
having installed the ritual brush and the offering materials, one should worship the auspicious sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should place the pitcher—made of gold, silver, or copper, or even made of clay—upon the *kūrca* grass mat; it must be very firm and possess an excellent mouth-opening.
One should wrap the silver door-frame with a golden thread;
alternatively, one should encircle the pillars and other parts with a pure cloth.
Having sprinkled it with scented water and filled it completely,
[one should place] rubies, pearls, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and coral.
One should place these five jewels into the bull and the pitcher;
one should deposit them with the seed-syllable of the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) and the mantra of Īśa.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra, while mentally recollecting the mantra of gold, one should cast [them].
And one should place there a tuft of grass adorned with mango sprouts.
Having spread flowers upon the seat so that it is beautifully adorned,
and having wrapped it with fine cloth, one should offer incense and flowers.
In the pair of fire-positions [the southeast and southwest] of the bull, one should recite the root mantra;
having placed the cloth and the trident on the banner to the south, and the banner-staff to the north,
one should worship the world-protectors of the eight directions according to what was previously stated.
Having performed the circumambulation slowly, one should take refuge in the temple.
Having established the pavilion as before, one should cause fragrances and flowers to be offered.
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the sequence of circumambulation.
Between the sacrificial pedestal and the door, the location for the banner should especially be two cubits,
three cubits, or even one cubit in measure.
One should draw [the thread] with the weapon-mantra and likewise establish the water-pot;
one should fix the staff-thread upon the head of reality with the staff-mantra.
It should be smooth, well-joined, three cubits in length, and encircled by a sacrificial altar-cloth;
its height and width should especially be half of that [length].
For all [of these], the girdle (mekhalā) must likewise be continuous and square.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the supreme-of-the-supreme altar, the wise practitioner should,
upon that [altar],
fashion a shape— whether circular, square, or lotus-shaped— that is endowed with color and has a height equal to its own measure.
Having smeared it with cow dung and adorned it with a bull, one should meditate upon it;
then, having adorned it with ashes, one should further adorn it with white flowers.
There, one should cause the Brāhmaṇas to proclaim an auspicious day;
the [image] should be joined with the top of a flagstaff and adorned with a garland for the ears.
One should cause eight flowers to be offered to the deities of the eight directions.
The binding of ropes should be performed in sequence with the ten-syllable mantra.
Having uttered the five-syllable mantra during the rite of erecting the banner,
one should worship the vehicle there, beginning with the first letter of its own name, as part of the various offerings.
Having raised the bull and the pitcher with the eight-syllable mantra,
one should direct them toward the temple and fasten the banner as well.
Furthermore, that which was previously described as beautiful for the banner (dhvaja) is likewise endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments.
Having donned white garments and anointed himself with white sandalwood paste,
having wrapped himself in a white cloth and put on a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
he should bind his head with a new cloth and tie a waist-string.
And having worshipped them in due order, one should sprinkle them with the Astra-mantra.
One should offer rice mixed with mung beans, rice with molasses, and rice with milk;
that food is honored for the sake of victory, sons, and nourishment.
Having likewise worshipped at the base of the banner, the wise man should place a bull and a water-pot there;
he should wrap the staff with cloth and bind it with *darbha* grass.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he should worship the deity at the conclusion of the *tīrtha* rite.
Having performed the worship of the three junctions (*trisandhi*), one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should also worship the two seed-syllables (*vīja*), the Vedas, Bhṛṅgīśa,
Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, Caṇḍeśa, and the altar (*vedikā*).
The two staffs have all the gods as their deities, and the two poles belong to Sarasvatī;
the five wooden planks have the Pārvas as their deities, as does the bottom.
The two chowries have the Moon and Sun as their deities, and the jars have the Bull (Ukṣan) as their deity.
One should worship the deities Bhṛṅgī, Vādī, and the others with their respective primary names.
Having erected banners in the eight directions, one should worship them there with mantras;
at the time of hoisting the banner, however, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara.
One should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara, the Lord of Gods and the deity of all deities;
beginning with the Bharī-tāḍana, one should perform this in the evening.
One should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of Maṅgapa;
once the mound has been prepared, one should place a drum (bherī) in its center and worship it.
The drum has Kunda as its presiding deity, while the act of striking it has Vāyu as its presiding deity.
And Śabdana, Pārvatī, as well as Carma and Pañceśvara.
Vālukī, Carma, Sūtra, Valaya, and Paricandraka;
the seven worlds of Kumāra, and Prabhaskanda as the presiding deity.
Having worshipped with fragrant substances and other offerings, the wise one,
having recited the Nandi-mantra, should strike [the drum] with the heart-mantra by means of the preceptor.
One should quickly purify [the site] with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
it should possess the Śiva-tāla, the Dhātṛ-tāla, and be joined with the Murāri-tāla.
With the *vṛṣatāla*, the *śūlatāla*, the *karatāla*, and the *dvitāla* (6th line),
accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and dances joined with conchs and *kāhala* horns.
At the village boundary, one should offer a bali-oblation to Brahmā and Īśāna;
with these substances— sesame, yellow turmeric powder, parched grain,
and flour soaked in curd— one should worship the divine horses from the northeast.

Having performed a circumambulation slowly, one should take refuge in the temple. From the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the ritual bath (*tīrtha*), one should worship the deity of the banner (*dhvajadaivata*) at the three junctions of the day, adorning it with all ornaments.
Furthermore, with reference to the *Uttara-tīrtha*,
it is proclaimed as having seven limbs (*aṅga*), seven secondary limbs (*pratyaṅga*), and the inclusion of the left limb (*savyāṅga*) along with its constituent parts (*sasāṅga*).
This [section on] the deity of the banner (*dhvajadaiva*), the trees, and the *balī* offerings established for all;

the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandha*) is proclaimed as a constituent part of the festival. Furthermore, there is the discourse on the mechanical devices (*yantra*) and the *kola*, as well as the internal components of the machine.
One should cause various diverse questions and various fans to be made;
likewise, one should have various wonderful banners and chowries fashioned with peacock feathers.
Having thus adorned the temple, both below and above, [one should perform the rites].
Having constructed a beautiful structure to the northeast of the temple,
it should be adorned above with strings of pearls and decorated in due order with flower garlands.
One should construct the sacrificial hall (yāgaśālā) toward the northeast or likewise toward the southeast;
there, one should have a pavilion (maṇḍapa) built, provided with sixteen pillars,
measuring ten cubits, nine cubits, or even seven cubits.
It is provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
furnished with garlands of *darbha* grass, and beautified by canopies and banners.
One should fashion the center of the altar by taking one part out of nine;
it should be one cubit in height and resemble the surface of a mirror. Likewise, in the middle of the altar, one should construct a small sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of rice flour.
Specifically with four, five, or six *droṇas* [of grain],
one should have the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) formula along with those who chant;
then, as before, the commencement of the festival and the ritual sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should take place.

Having established it in the center of the altar, one should place the Śiva-pitcher, endowed with the five jewels, in the middle, together with a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) wrapped in cotton. It should be provided with sandalwood paste and offerings of boiled rice, adorned with garlands, and situated upon a lotus seat.
He has four arms and three eyes, holds a trident in his hand, and wears matted locks.
The god bears the crescent moon and is adorned with serpent ornaments;
he wears a golden sacred thread and rings set with the nine gems.
Having performed these [rites] on the right, one should worship the Lord of Yogins;
the *vardhanī* vessel, together with the *kūrca*, is established on the left side.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a lotus, a noose, and a goad, he grants fearlessness and bestows primordial wisdom.
One should install Paritoṣṭi there, accompanied by Vidyeśvara;
and having likewise placed water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) consisting of gems and scented water,
one should place flower-water and immediately thereafter oil-water.
Likewise, water with barley, accompanied by fragrances and flowers—
[one should place these] from Indra up to Īśāna. One should worship the jars and the *kūrca*-grass bundles therein, specifically with their respective mantras, in the golden pitcher.
One should fashion ten weapons out of iron, wood, or clay;
one should place all the scriptures upon the heads of the images.
Having covered oneself with the *kalaśa* garments, one should worship the ten weapons;
one should establish the various [deities] beginning with Vajra and worship them starting from the east.
The deity of the wheel should be in the north, and likewise the lotus in the south;
one should worship the forms of the eight auspicious symbols in the outer intermediate directions.
Having established either the trident or the wind, one should worship the auspicious triple-junction;
first, one should generate the Śiva-fire and worship that which was previously described as auspicious.
One should offer [the oblation] to the one who has three eyes and four arms, whose crest is formed by the half-moon;
it should be given to the embodiment of sacrifice, and one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon the seven-tongued [fire].
Having offered the fuel-sticks with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, the clarified butter with the *Puruṣa-mantra*,
the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *Aghora-mantra*, and the parched grains (*lāja*) with the *Aghorāstra-mantra*.
Having offered groats with the Vāma mantra, milk with the Sadyojāta mantra, barley with the Hṛdaya mantra, and sugar-candy with the Sadyojāta mantra for the accomplishment of one's purpose,
Maheśvara [offered it] with the Śiva-gāyatrī mantra.
One should offer sesame with the Īśāna mantra and mung beans with the Mantraka mantra.
Having offered the Vyāhṛtis at the end of each substance, I shall now describe the Rudras;
listen to the sequence beginning with the fourteen Rudras on the fourteenth day.
Dhūmrarudra, Kalārudra, Nīlarudra who consists of the Kalās,
Pāśarudra, Nāśarudra, and Asthirudra in the center.
Dhānañcaya, Aghorarudra, Rudra whose nature is Vīrarudra,
Vāsaka, Keśarudra, and the great-souled Candrarudra.
Bhūtarudra, Bālarudra, Sparśarudra, and Rudraka;
(7th line) Īśānarudra, Nāmarudra, Galarudra, and Agnirudraka.
The Earth-Rudra, the Milk-Rudra, the Eye-Rudra, the Self-Rudra;
the Taste-Rudra, the Tongue-Rudra, the Sound-Rudra, and the Self-Rudra.
Tarūrudra, Śikhārudra, Jyotsnārudra, Kharudraka,
Sadyarudra, Manorudra, Śubharudrāṇī,
Rudraka, Kālarudra, Mahārudra, and Caṇḍarudrasya Rudraka.
One should offer oblations to Vedarudra, Śanirudra, Liṅgarudra, Aṅgarudraka, Rakṣārudra, Virārudra, Kṛpa, Bindurudraka,
Māṃsarudra, Medarudra, and Bhuvanarudra.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the names beginning with Puruṣarudra, Ghorarudra, Budharudra, Ātmarudraka,
and the hundred and twenty Rudras, starting with Sunāman.

One should perform the *vyāhṛti* following the *Rudra*, while recollecting the armor-mantra (*varmantra*). One should perform all the ritual actions regarding the materials as prescribed for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*).
One should offer oblations in the evening and in the morning; at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice, Maheśvara [is worshipped], first Vighnarātri and secondly Bhūtarātri.
The third is the Night of the Sages (Ṛṣirātri), the fourth is the Night of Indra (Indrarātri),
the fifth would be the Night of Brahmā (Brahmarātri), and the sixth is the Night of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇurātri).
The seventh would be the Night of Rudra (Rudrarātri), and the eighth is the Night of Maheśvara (Maheśvararātri).
One should worship the lamp for nine days as the night of Sadāśiva, for ten days as the night of Bindu,
for eleven days as the night of Giri, and for twelve days as the night of Tāṇḍava;
one should worship the supreme nights of Vighneśa and Ananta.
The Bhūtarātri [consecration] should end with Śiva; one should demonstrate it within seven houses. The Ṛṣirātri should end with Śiva; one should demonstrate it within five houses.

A devoted person should cause the auspicious festival of Bhava to be performed for three days, beginning with Śiva and ending with Sadāśiva; however, it is also said that one may perform the Śaiva festival for a single day.
Pure food mixed with curd, resembling sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka) and cakes (apūpa),
along with fruits mixed with jaggery, bestows auspiciousness upon the Gaṇas. (4th line) [Likewise,] fruit,
powdered turmeric, saffron-colored rice, and roasted barley flour (saktu).
Mixed with well-nourishing substances and transformed into curd, it is a pleasing strength.
(5th line) The five roots, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and *śāli* rice mixed with ghee, combined with plantain fruit, is called the offering for the sages. (6th line)
Indravallī, haridrā, and priyaṅgu, combined with ghee, should be offered on the fourth lunar day; this is called the bali-offering to Indra.
A lotus flower, turmeric, and milk-rice mixed with parched grain should be offered on the fifth day; this is auspicious and brings delight to Brahmā.
On the eighth day, one should offer bamboo, curd, and plantain fruit combined; this is auspicious and pleasing to Īśa.

Five types of food previously prepared, along with clarified butter (ājya), should be placed in nine vessels; this auspicious offering is dear to the one called Sāda. Gulānna, pāyasānna, and pure rice mixed with clarified butter [are also to be offered].
Ten measures should be offered, which are auspicious and pleasing to the Liṅga.
Even for all [deities], pure food may be given, but rice mixed with molasses and clarified butter should especially be offered,
presenting it with their respective mantras.
