One should offer the oblation separately, measuring either a *droṇa*, or half of that, or even half of that again, using the size of a hen’s egg as the standard.
Having especially adorned either a village or even a city,
[one should wear] a yellow sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) with a luster that is level despite its depressions and elevations.
Having performed the purification of the site, one should likewise decorate the doors with moving banners, plantains, and other lamps, as well as with jars, fresh sprouts, wheels,
and ancestral jars.
Then one should perform the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) at the conclusion of the festival day.
One should especially perform it just as the offering of the sprouts was performed previously,
accompanied by cymbals, *kāhala* drums, and the like, and filled with incense and lamps.
Having placed the trident and the linga upon a golden pedestal, accompanied by banners with peacock feathers and those reciting hymns and auspicious prayers.
Having established the ten weapons, one should place them within a golden tube;
wherever there is a deficiency, one should then support all those subjects with one's head.
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing a turban and an upper garment,
likewise endowed with noble splendor and decorated with every kind of jewelry.
One should especially offer the bali-oblation extending from Brahmā up to Īśāna;
having placed the books in the middle of the chariot, adorned with flowers,
above the Prajā and at its end, fully equipped with all ornaments.
Having relied upon the auspicious scripture (*maṅgalāgama*) endowed with various topics;
at its end, one mounted on a goat; at its end, one with a horse as a vehicle;
at its end, a mechanical device (*yantra*); and at its end, one attended by celestial women.
At the end of that is a horse-machine, and at its end an elephant-machine;
at its end is a pavilion-machine, and on its right side a clever machine. Between the machine and the temple, it is accompanied by dancing and singing.
First is the comfortable posture (sukhāsana), and the second is the axle-bearing (akṣavāha).
The third [form] destroys the three cities; the fourth is Candraśekhara;
the fifth is Ardhanārī; and the sixth is half-Hari.
The seventh is Bhaikṣamūrti, and the eighth is Kāmanāśana;
the ninth is Kāladahana, and the tenth is the auspicious Kalyāṇa.
The eleventh is situated in the *liṅga* as the auspicious *sādākhya*; the twelfth is the beautiful [form];
and the thirteenth is the dance (*nṛtya*), endowed with all ornaments.
Whether on a stage, or in a palanquin, or on a chariot, or even in a small litter—
First are the Pāśupatas, and at the end of them are those of the Great Vow (Mahāvrata).
After them are the Mahāśaivas, after them the Brāhmaṇas in due order,
after them all the Bhairavas, and at the end are the servants of the Siddhas.
At its end, all the singers [should go]; at its end, the female dancers.
Then the Lord, together with Śakti, should proceed slowly and in due order, surrounded by those wearing blue garments and endowed with all auspicious marks.
With various flowers and variegated banners, joined with various chowries,
accompanied by various beings, and with various players of the kāhala drum;
(7th line) and with trident-lamps, and especially with mechanical lamps.

Adorned with eight lamps and [eight] lamps made of flour, and beautified by all the ritual implements; accompanied by priests who have duly performed their worship and are adorned with all auspicious ornaments;
he proceeds from behind, following the deity Caṇḍanāyaka on every side.
In front of that, one should cause it to be proclaimed there, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments:
with *paṭahas*, *maddalas*, *tālas*, *bherīs*, *paṭahas*, and *ḍuṇḍubhas*;
with *jhallarīs* and *jharjharas*, as well as *vīṇās*, flutes, and *kinnaras*.
One should especially cause it to be proclaimed both in front and behind;
at the end of that, one should shout out for the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others with sounds accompanied by water;
at the end of all the castes, however, there should be figures of elephants.
The elderly, the children, the youth, the eunuchs, women, men, those with physical disabilities, and those who come and go— after them, the servant-slaves shall inherit in due order.
Thus following [the path],
at every step a human being obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice for that particular interval of time.
They are liberated from all sins and shall attain the supreme state of Śiva.
Thus one should perform the circumambulation of either a village or a city;
having slowly completed the circumambulation of the temple, one should offer an oblation upon the pedestal of power (balapīṭha).
Having performed the washing of the feet,
we worship the supreme Śiva, who is present within the pavilion and other structures together with all the hosts of gods,
while great sounds of mṛdaṅga drums and other instruments resound.
The dancers and drummers were stationed on the right,
while the singers and flute players were situated on the left.
The Ācārya is in the northeastern direction, and the five kings are in the west;
outside both of these, at the outer edge, the courtesans of the Lord are prescribed.
In the presence of the deity, one should especially perform dance and song accompanied by rhythmic clapping (*tāla*).
One should perform the *nīrāñjana* rite and hold flowers of cloth in the hands of the divine women. Furthermore, one should carry ashes, flowers, a lamp, a sword, an umbrella, and chowries.
A mirror and a golden pitcher, both placed upon a three-legged stand.
One should offer water for the feet and water for sipping, place a flower upon the head,
and having applied the syllable [Om] to the head, one should especially offer fragrant perfume.
One should first offer water for sipping (ācamana) and worship with incense and lamps;
then, one should place the Vaiśyas as lamps upon the circumambulatory chariot.
At the conclusion of that, the wise man should cause ashes to be offered and show a mirror;
then the courtesan, having sung a song accompanied by the sound of musical instruments,
should place it before the pedestal or cast it outside the enclosures.
Even during festive rites, it should be done in this very same manner day after day.
On the morning of the eighth day, however, one should engage in hunting;
at the commencement of battle, by its power, one should circumambulate the village clockwise.
The wise one should tie the protective amulet (kautuka), especially on that night,
using a thread of gold, silver, or cotton.
Having placed the trident upon the sacrificial mound and circumambulated it clockwise,
one should perform the heart-bath either in a river, a lake, or even at home.

In the center of the sacrificial pavilion, one should encircle [the area] with the trident-thread while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra; there, one should proclaim the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). At the beginning of the festival night, one should apply the protective amulets (*kautuka*) for all [participants].
At the beginning of the festival, during the night, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
One should offer oblations of five colors and cause them to be given to the five faces.
To the east, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and likewise, to the south, ghee.
In the west, however, there is rice with jujube and rice with turmeric;
in the north, pure rice; and for the upward-facing [deity], the food offering consists of these five combined.
One should perform worship at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhyārcana*), which bestows prosperity upon the king and the kingdom.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the ritual fire-offering (*karmahoma*), followed by the offering of oblations (*bali*) into the hand and the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*).
[One should offer] water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), respectful offerings (*arghya*), as well as perfumes (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), and incense (*dhūpaka*).
Worship should be performed at the three times of day with lamps and food offerings. First, there is the pedestal of the trident, followed by betel and the form of Rudra;
both the Sakala (with parts) and Niṣkala (partless) forms, as well as the deities beginning with Indra and the sages.
One should worship Śrīdevī at the palace gate, Naṭeśvara in the assembly hall,
Āditya and Mahendra, as well as the deities of the village and its eastern directions.
The Gandharvas, Devas, and Siddhas are the deities of the southern gate;
Sugandhī and Śoṣṇī are the deities of the western gate;
and Mukhyā and Khaḍvāṅgī are the deities of the northern gate.
In the garden, O Great Goddess, and likewise in the cow-pen, is Gomukhī;
at a difficult crossroads (durgāsthāṇu), specifically, are the deities of the Egg-ornament (aṇḍābharaṇa);
Śiva in the form of Rudra is at a shrine of Śiva, and Vaiṣṇavī is indeed at a shrine of Viṣṇu.
Sarasvatī is in the place of Brahmā; Manonmanī is in the place of the Guru.
Candradeva is in the pond, and likewise Śiva is in the well.
At Vallīka he worshipped Nārada, at Parvata the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara),
at Citrasthāna the Gandharvas, and at Nadīsthāna Kāruṇā;
at Gajasthāna Vighneśa, and at Aśvasthāna Arkānī.
Pārvatī is at the site of the fire-oblation, and the Piśācas are at the ash-bath.
Thus, one should offer bali to all these deities with the first syllables of their respective names,
using mung beans, flowers, boiled rice, parched grain flour, fried grains, and sesame seeds.
One should offer all those substances for everyone under their respective names:
the mango, the kelī fruit, and the plantain fruit as well.
One should offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍū), cakes (pūpa), rice with jaggery (gulānna), and betel leaf;
this bestows freedom from poverty and sorrow, and grants the fulfillment of all desires.
By the measure of a mere *bali* offering, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the sequence of the Cūrṇotsava festival:
on the western side of the temple, a square area should be prepared with rice.
One should wash both the mortar and the pestle with the Astra-mantras.
In the center of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place a mortar while reciting the Praṇava;
it should be adorned with fresh flowers and embellished with all kinds of flowers.
Having worshipped them in due order, one should prepare the sprouts:
turmeric, usīra, saffron, camphor, and excellent stone.
One should place the yellow pigment (haridrā) in the center of the mortar according to the sequence;
having recited the Sadyojāta mantra and worshipped Maheśvara,
one should then cause the preceptor to perform the application of the powder immediately thereafter.
At the conclusion of that, he should feed the Brahmins; at the conclusion of that, the devoted person [should feed] the people.
Rudra and the Gaṇikās, adorned with new garments, should be present.
He should fashion an elephant-goad (aṅkuśa), adorned with perfumes and flowers.
Having repeatedly performed the *cūrṇa* rite with dances, songs, and instrumental music,
[the attendants] should perform it before the Liṅga, the Mirror-Spear, and the Image.
Having smeared himself with oil, he approached the Lord of the South;
he should overcome the obstacles of the teacher, the king, and his devotees.
One should cause it to be performed by all classes of people and have the *pūrṇatāla* rhythm played;
it should be accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and the like, as well as the resonance of kettledrums and other instruments.
Having caused the Brahmins to proclaim auspicious blessings and benedictions,
he should quickly proceed clockwise around the village or the city.
Or, one should cause that divinity to be installed in a river, the Sindhu, or a lake.
There, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared, and it should be an eight-petaled lotus with a lamp.
Having placed a trident there, one should then deposit the Kalās upon its tip.
Having established Maheśvara, the deity of sacrifice, to the north of the trident,
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and present betel-leaf. One should then place [the image] facing the idol, or [perform the rite] upon a sand altar.
Having firmly gathered nine auspicious vessels with a resonant sound,
one should again perform the purification of those vessels in the northern part of the sacrificial ground.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited with hymns of praise and benedictory verses, [the officiant] should,
in the midst [of the assembly], proceed in due order with scented water from the mouth of the preceptor (*ācārya*).
One should place [the mantras] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin around the jars;
one should worship them, cast [the offerings] therein, and perform the placement of the limbs and sub-limbs.
Having clothed the image in fine garments, one should cause *tulasī* to be offered;
having worshipped it in due order with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth,
one should worship the Trident— the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution— as the image itself.
One should worship with water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering, as well as with fragrances and flowers.
At the time of the *balivācana*, one should worship all the deities.

One should perform the ritual bathing (*snāpana*), and then offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *Sadyojāta* mantra. The water for sipping (*ācamana*) is offered with the *Puruṣa* mantra, and the respectful offering (*arghya*) is said to be given with the *Īśāna* mantra.

One should cause the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *arghya* offering to be presented to the Five Brahmās. [The ritual bath] mixed with ghee is the "ghee-bath" (*ghṛtasnāna*); curd is for the "curd-bath" (*dadhisnāna*); milk-porridge (*pāyasa*) is for the "milk-bath" (*kṣīrasnāna*) accompanied by the mantra; and likewise honey is for the "honey-bath" (*madhusnāna*) with the *madhuvātā* mantra.
In the midst of the rivers, one should first perform the bath;
then, having performed the "spear-bath" (śūlasnāna), [one performs] the auspicious thread (kautuka) and the two holy sites (tīrthaka).
The sacred ford (tīrtha) is a great means of subjugation, a protection that destroys enemies;
it is the remover of all diseases, a being, the auspicious-throated one (Śrīkaṇṭha), and the bestower of all perfections.
Having taken refuge in the temple of the deity, one should perform the rite for an auspicious day there.
The *liṅga*, the image, and the trident [should be worshipped] according to the sequence of complete propitiation;
joined with the sacrifice as before, it brings about the new flow of the city-sacrifice (*puryāga*).
Then one should perform the sacrifice of silence (*maunayāga*), immediately following the sacrifice to the deity (*devayāga*).
Then, immediately after the Gandhayāga, one should perform the Mṛgayāga.
One should perform the sacrifice exactly as previously described and shall obtain all fruits;
one should cause the auspicious sacrifice of Caṇḍeśvara to be performed according to the prescribed rules.
One should worship the jar situated in the sacrificial hall with the primary image,
as well as the deities Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Vikrānta, and Caṇḍeśa.
One should worship the pure deity Caṇḍa, the destroyer of all enemies;
having performed the concluding rite for the banner, one should avoid the ritual bathing of the banner.
One should cause offerings of food (bali) to be presented from Brahmā to Īśāna.
One should perform the dismissal of the excellent pedestal with the Astra-mantra accompanied by sound.
Having offered the oblation upon the offering-pedestal, one should worship it especially;
then, having washed the feet, one should worship the preceptor in due order.

One should worship the preceptor with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and a golden sacred thread, as well as with perfumes, flowers, and incense. (5th line) Now, listen to the procedure for the festival of the devotees, following the festivals of the preceptor.
One should sequentially tie the protective thread (kautuka) upon the devotees and the image,
accompanied by ornaments, dance, and song as previously described,
with Vedic chants resounding from those stationed in front.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should cause [the image] to enter the temple;
within the temple, one should establish the form of the devotee through consecration and other rites.
Having performed the worship as before, one should cause garments to be given to the devotees;
then, having performed circumambulation, one should worship the perfected deities.
Thus, the supreme power (Paramaśakti), having performed the festival according to the prescribed rites and having uplifted her own family lineage, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
For the sake of increasing the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, one should celebrate a festival for Maheśvara.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the festival to be performed in due order.
A wise person should cause the festival to be held; he should arrange the festival of Śiva.
This sequence of expiatory rites has been declared as ending with the festival of Śiva; now hear [the following].
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for festivals in the Makuṭāgama.]
Written by my own hand in the month of Tulā, O Noble Lady, Svāminī.
The word *prāyaścitta* means the destruction [of faults]; "citta" refers to the heat of the mind. Since they destroy these heats, it is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta*.
I shall now declare the expiation for that [omission] regarding plowing and other such acts, as well as for worship;
specifically, for the time when worship is omitted and likewise for the failure of the two *sandhyā* rites.
Thus, when the twilight worship (sandhyārcana) is omitted, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *hr̥nmant*ra;
having presented milk-rice (pāyasānna), one should worship again as before.
If the worship for a single day is omitted, one should perform a ceremonial bath with nine new jars and offer an oblation of rice mixed with jaggery;
then, as before, one should perform the auspicious worship.
Having performed this special worship, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
If the worship is omitted on the fourth or fifth day, it may occur;
one should perform the ritual bath with fifty water-pots (*kalaśa*).
For six days up until the tenth day, [the rite is performed] with jars (*karaka*) and cool-water pots (*śītakuṃbhaka*).
If the worship from the eleventh up to the fiftieth [day] is omitted,
one should establish the Śiva-fire and perform the worship as before with fifty-one sets of eight [offerings]; the food offering (naivedya) shall be twofold.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Śivā-mantra, one should present milk-rice as an offering.
But if the worship is deficient, one should offer seven hundred auspicious jars and,
having performed a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra, present an offering of milk-rice.
If worship has been omitted for two months, one should perform the rite with a thousand jars in due order;
if worship has been omitted for six months, one should then perform the sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa).
If the *bali* offering is omitted at one twilight (*sandhyā*), two *balis* must be offered at the next twilight;
if it is omitted at two twilights, one should then perform the ritual bath (*snapana*).
Furthermore, if there is an interruption of the *bali* for two days up until the end of the month, [the same penance applies].
Having performed the purification with the Śivāgni as before, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) one hundred and eight times.
If [the period] is deficient by more than one month from the *bali*, the preceptor should worship the Śiva-fire in due order,
having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Śiva-mantra.
One should perform an auspicious consecration with one hundred and eight water-pots;
furthermore, for a single day's auspicious festival, there should be two *bhāra* of food offerings (*naivedya*).
Upon touching a woman or a Śūdra, and likewise upon touching a Caṇḍāla,
one should perform twenty-five ritual ablutions and offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and worship the devotees; however,
at the time of the circumambulation of the offerings (*balibhramaṇa*), the *liṅga* may indeed fall,
or it may become cracked, displaced, broken, or even destroyed.
In that very place, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa), or else in the center of the temple;
having first offered the bali-offering and performed circumambulation there,
or else, having acted as before, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
There, one should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
or, whether it is forbidden or permitted, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra one hundred times.

If at that time the lamp is extinguished, one should remain there and offer the *bali* in due order; then, having re-invoked the lamp and performed the remaining rites, including the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*),
one should present double the amount of food offerings (*naivedya*) if they are deficient in liquid substances.

If the cow-products are lacking, however, it is double; if the daily worship of Maheśa is lacking, [it is likewise]. If the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*) is lacking, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *hṛnmantra*.
Now listen to the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) specifically regarding a festival (*utsava*).
But if the bull-sacrifice is omitted, or if the hoisting of the banner is omitted,
or if the banner-altar is omitted, or if the sacrificial pit-altar is omitted;
But [an image] that is devoid of the banner and bell, fallen, or inferior;
that is devoid of the eight auspicious symbols, or lacks divine weapons.
If it is devoid of the offering of the sprouts, or lacks the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga),
or is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or lacking the encircling of *darbha* grass;
If the ritual placement of the water-pot (kalaśasthāpana) is deficient— lacking the jar, lacking water,
devoid of gems and gold, or lacking the grass-bundle (kūrca) and the thread; (7th line) or if it lacks the grass-bundle, the enclosing fence, and likewise the cloth.
But when it is devoid of food offerings and the like, and lacking incense and lamps;
If the sacrificial materials are lacking, or if the offering of the bali-oblation is omitted,
or if the characteristic signs of the bali are absent, or if the trident and other implements have fallen;
If the vessel for the bali offering is missing, or if one steps over the chariot,
or if the festival lacks a sacrifice, or during a quarrel at that time,
or if the materials for worship have become stale for the two Śaṅkaras— the Liṅga and the Bimba— [the following applies].
If a statue falls while being carried in a procession with its limbs broken,
or if there is a festival in that village, or if a human being dies;
(3rd line) [then] the sprinkling of water at night and the two terrifying fire-sticks of the Agnīdhra priest [are required].
If [the practitioner] is devoid of the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) and lacks the preliminary bath (*kautukasnāna*),
and having commenced with another tantra, performs the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayāga*) in the body;
and if the mantras are [deficient], and likewise the sugar-candy (*śarkarā*) is lacking, and the *dvāḍārya* is missing on the right.
When such things as these arise, they cause harm to the villages and other settlements;
moreover, when the bull-sacrifice is abandoned, the cattle will undoubtedly perish.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of the bull, one should adorn it with perfumes and flowers;
one should offer mung-bean rice and cause a peace-offering oblation (*śāntihoma*) to be performed.
If the hoisting of the banner is deficient, the king shall incur invincibility;
therefore, the wise man should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa) and cause it to be planted according to the prescribed rite.
However, if it is devoid of the banner and altar, it is terrifying for the practitioners of mantra;
therefore, having performed a pacifying homa, one should again achieve the re-establishment [of the site].
If the rope is lost, the banner is severed, or if it is destroyed or fallen,
as well as when the flagstaff is missing, there is the destruction of the king and his queen.
One should perform the rites as before and have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited there.
Having finally performed the peace-offering (śānti-homa), one should indeed worship the devotees.
If the bell is damaged or falls, there will be a loss of fruits;
therefore, having had the Puṇyāha recited, one should mutter the root mantra one hundred times.
Having consecrated it with the Ghaṇṭā-weapon mantra, one should perform the re-consecration and worship.
However, if the striking of the drum is omitted, there will be fear from the enemy's army.
One should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed there; previously, one should strike Śambhu.
When the time for the proclamation has arrived, one should recite [the mantra] over a cloth that is torn or deficient.
At the time of cutting the hide, one should declare an immediate destruction;
having recollected the Svarṇa-mantra, one should recite it four times and then repeat it a hundred times.
Having grasped [the weapon] according to the very final rite, one should strike Śiva with the *tāḍa*.
If, however, the sacrificial hall is lacking, there is a certainty of the destruction of the crops.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should recite the root mantra one hundred times;
having prepared the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to the ritual rule, one should likewise bathe [it] in due order.
If the sacrificial fire of the ritual hall is established upon a staff or on a cloth, there will be fear from a hostile army; if it is placed on the ground, the king will meet with invincibility.
As before, one should certainly begin [the rite] in the sacrificial hall as if it were a jar;
having commenced the festival anew, from that day onwards, one should proceed as previously.
In cases of negligence and so forth, as well as regarding punishment, one should determine the sequence as before.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should offer a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
If the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are lacking, or if they have been excessively worn out by fire,
great diseases will constantly afflict the inhabitants of the village.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Tryambaka mantra;
if the garland of darbha grass is absent, a drought will prevail.
Having offered the root mantra one hundred times, one should then apply a garland of *darbha* grass.
If the sacrificial materials (*homadravya*) are lacking, there will undoubtedly be drought.
Having offered the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) one hundred times, one should then perform the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblation.
The wise one should offer that substance according to the previously mentioned procedure.
When the weapons have been stolen by a thief, which causes great fear,
he should perform oblations with the three-syllable mantra, having first worshipped it with the prescribed number of offerings.

Having performed the sprinkling with auspicious water according to the prescribed marks, [one should know that] if it is devoid of the eight auspicious signs, there will surely be the destruction of the people.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the mantra of Īśa, one should have [the image] fashioned according to the prescribed characteristics;
having sprinkled it with the five substances, one should install the completed work as before.
If the planting of sprouts is omitted, or if the seed-pots (*pālikā*) and other vessels are lacking, a great disease will arise and the crops will perish; of this there is no doubt.
One should perform oblations with the *sahasramūla* mantra and worship with offerings of cooked rice.
One should perform the offering of the sprouts of beauty, characterized by the *pālikā* vessels and other such items.
And when the ritual of the weapons (*astrayāga*) has been omitted, and a great pestilence (*mahāmārī*) breaks out,
one should then perform the *mūrtihoma* and the consecration (*snapana*) with nine jars.
There, one should perform the consecration of the sacrifice according to the previously mentioned method;
having recited the root mantra a hundred times, one should then apply a garland of *darbha* grass.
If there is a deficiency in the sacrificial substances, there will undoubtedly be drought.
If the placement of the *kumbha* is lacking, or if the *vardhanī* is devoid of jewels; if it is devoid of the *sūtra*, or if it lacks the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*);
if it lacks the *kurca* grass, the canopy (*vitāna*), and likewise the weapon (*astra*).
If offerings such as the food-oblation (*naivedya*) are lacking, a famine will certainly arise.
Therefore, having performed the *mūrti-homa*, one should offer oblations while worshipping with the root mantra.
In the absence of sacrificial lamps, and especially through negligence,
the crops will certainly be destroyed and become insane.
Having offered oblations consecrated with the Aghora mantra, one should again perform the re-consecration (*sandhāna*).
Furthermore, if the materials for the *bali* offering are deficient, one should then light a lamp;
otherwise, famine arises due to the interruption of the sacrificial offerings (*havis*) and other such faults.
Having entered that ash-house and established the fire, one should worship it;
then, having prepared fuel-sticks according to the prescribed knowledge, one should offer oblations with the root mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations for each [verse], one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* at the end of the substances.
If trade falters or declines, fever and disease arise;
one should then offer with the *astra-mantra* a hundred oblations and perform half as many again.
If the mantra is deficient, mental suffering and ailments such as abdominal tumors arise.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra, one should recite the *haṃsa* mantra a hundred times;
then, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the prescribed rite with the stated substances and mantras.
If the darbha grass is lacking as a boundary or has especially fallen away,
it causes the destruction of wealth and the loss of cattle.
One should perform the sacrifice there; as for the substance, one should employ the nine substances.
However, if the *bali* is devoid of its characteristic marks, or if it has moved or fallen, [one must act accordingly].
Furthermore, if the wall [of the temple] should likewise collapse, destruction will certainly occur.
Having performed a propitiatory *homa*, one should offer oblations a hundred times with the root mantra.
One should first perform the rite for a movable linga, and afterwards perform the *bali* offering.
When the *śūla* weapon falls, or likewise when the banner is destroyed or lost,
one should predict danger from weapons and the like for that specific village or kingdom.
Having performed [the rites] for the fallen [banner], one should cause a propitiatory *homa* to be performed.
One should offer oblations with the Astra-mantra while reciting the Śiva-mantra;
having offered the bali-offering in the remaining place, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
When the staff of the trident is broken, one should avoid using the ocean-vessel;
having taken up that weapon, one should perform the remainder of the sacrifice.
Having purified the weapon-mantra once again, one should install it according to the prescribed rite;
by means of that distinction from the other fire, one should perform the re-conjunction.
Furthermore, there is the consecration with water and the differentiation according to the time of installation.

If weapons are lost, or if they are broken or even fallen, great pestilence (mahāmārī) breaks out; [one should pacify it] with grains and herbs. Having offered a hundred oblations of the Aghora mantra, one should take possession of a new vessel.
If the *balitāla* is omitted, all the deities become displeased;
having offered a hundred oblations with the *mūrtimantra*, one should then offer a hundred oblations with the *mūlamantra*.
If the offering of bali and lamps is omitted, there is no doubt that Lakṣmī will perish;
one should recite each of the Pañcabrahma mantras and the Ṣaḍaṅga mantras one hundred times.

Having offered double the number of lamps, one should perform the remaining rites of the *bali* offering. If the time for the presentation of the *bali* to the leader (*nāyaka*) is exceeded, the destruction of that village is proclaimed; one should therefore offer a hundred oblations with the armor-mantra (*varmamantra*).
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited according to the ritual of the *balitantra*,
[if there is] a festival devoid of sacrifice, the king will meet his death.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *varma* mantra, the auspicious rite of the protective thread (*kautuka*) and the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) [should be performed].
Furthermore, one should perform the circumambulation of the village in the very same order as the procession;
otherwise, at that time and in that manner, there will be fear from an enemy army.
Having recited the root-mantra one hundred times, he should enter the supreme abode;
[he should do so] as Śaṅkara [enters] the linga-image with materials remaining from the previous worship.
There is fear from enemy armies, and the kingdom increases its afflictions by disease;
having offered thirty oblations with the Aghora mantra, one should perform the ablution with twenty-five.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should mutter the *Pāśupata* mantra a hundred times.
At the time of moving the image, however, if it moves while being deficient in its limbs,
the destruction of the presiding deities of the site (*vāstu*) and the king would occur in an instant.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing there, and then have the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited.
Then, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should again perform the reconnection;
however, one should avoid the head, the arms, and likewise the feet.
If [the image] is devoid of jeweled rings, it is a defect; if it lacks ornaments or clothing, it is a defect.
If it is devoid of the binding of the garment or lacks matted locks, O Maheśvara, having performed the re-joining, perform the sprinkling there.
Likewise, when a *śūdra* has been initiated, if he transgresses the word of his guru,
he will undoubtedly fall from his station and be cast out from the village.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the image and offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra a hundred times.
If the rite is devoid of the water-offering and the collyrium, there will indeed be fear.
Having especially recited the seed-syllable of Mūlaprakṛti a hundred times, [one should proceed].
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should carry out the previously mentioned procedure.
If, through negligence, the fire-brand [is dropped] into the eye, there is danger for the village dwellers;
by reciting the *sadyo-mantra* one hundred times, the auspicious bathing of the image [is accomplished].
If [the wheel] is devoid of the commencement of battle, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the crops;
having offered a hundred oblations with the wheel facing upward, one should proceed with the commencement of battle.
Thereafter, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed and likewise carry out the consecration (abhiṣecana).
In the absence of the hoisting of the banner (dhvajārohaṇa), there is the provocation of great sin (mahāpātaka).
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *praṇava* as before, and likewise a *droṇaka*,
if the ritual bath is omitted, there will undoubtedly be drought.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *puruṣasūkta*, one should then perform the ceremonial bathing.
In the morning and other times, there will be great suffering and the destruction of the warrior's strength and wealth.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the armor-mantra (*varmamantra*), one should then perform the ritual bathing;
likewise, for the sprinkling of water, one should employ the previously mentioned sacred formula (*pūrvatīrtha*).
Likewise, in the event of a deficiency or a separation [of the components], the destruction of the village will occur in due course.
On that day, having performed a hundred oblations (*homa*), one should bathe the Supreme Lord;
one should perform everything as previously described according to the former ritual procedure.
If the deities of accomplishment are not pleased, they do not meditate upon the seat and are devoid of joy.
Having offered oblations to the one worshipped with the root mantra, one should thereafter establish the eastern seat;
for if the Caṇḍa-sacrifice is omitted, there will be fear from a hostile army.
One should cause the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) to be performed for Śambhu and carry out the *caṇḍanāga* rite;
otherwise, through the fault of mixing different tantras (*tantrasāṅkarya*), pestilence and disease shall arise.
Having offered oblations with *samidh* sticks, *palāśa* leaves, clarified butter, and cooked rice,
consecrated by the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*), one should begin the recitation (*japa*) that many times.
One should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara, who brings all peace.
Now listen to the rule for expiation regarding that very [act]:
having touched one initiated by his own caste, one should perform a bath with ashes.
Upon touching a woman or a Śūdra, one should perform the aforementioned bath.
Among the intermediate castes, one should perform two baths upon touching them.
However, when in close proximity to a Caṇḍāla, one should recite the mantra a hundred times while avoiding physical contact.
Having seen [the food], at the time of eating, the wise one should discard the remainder of the meal.
Likewise, two baths are prescribed; one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If a foul odor should come with the wind, one should turn away even at the tip of the nose;
likewise, having touched cow dung, one should quickly recite the five-syllable mantra.

Having offered oblations for the sake of Sujānyā and others, the wise one should indeed recite the Īśa-mantra for the body that pervades the sky; even by day, he should recite it. The learned man should feed the king’s food and recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
Having eaten the food of a Vaiśya in this manner, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times in sequence.
Having eaten the food of a Śūdra out of desire, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
for by eating continuously for a month, that [sin] arises in the Śūdra.
If he is joined with a Śūdra, he should always behave like a Śūdra;
having formed an association with a Śūdra woman, he should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
Upon touching a woman during her menses, one should offer oblations, bathe, and recite the *varma* mantra one hundred times;
having recited it one hundred times, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara.
At the time of eating, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times without a lamp;
but having eaten, at the time of looking [at the deity], one should recite the Hṛdaya-mantra according to one's ability.
One should remember the Lord of the gods; by bathing in ashes, one becomes purified.
One should avoid garlic, fish, meat, and other forbidden things.
However, if one should consume them through negligence, one should recite the *varma* mantra one hundred times.
And one should feed the remnants of the food of the eldest preceptor, which bestows all accomplishments.
In the midst of each salt [grain], while drinking water in a vessel,
if one recites the Heart Mantra, all defects are destroyed.
Having abandoned harsh words while eating, one should recite the heart-mantra;
and upon hearing of those who are uninitiated or of a [female] consort (*śakti*), one should recite the heart-mantra.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Listen now to the rule for atonement regarding great afflictions such as sins:
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise the theft of gold.
Jumping over [a cow], speaking harsh words to a guru, and the killing of a cow—these constitute the five great sins.
Then, having meditated upon the Lord of the South in that great region,
one should consume meat as enjoyed by the Guru, or half of that, and observe silence.
Having drunk the water of the Supreme Lord, one should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day;
having always recited the three-syllabled mantra while standing in water reaching up to the neck.
Having meditated, one should cause [the disciple] to dwell there for three nights and always worship the Guru as a deity;
thus they are liberated from all sins and shall reach the Southern Gate.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in order the impurity (*āśauca*) resulting from birth (*sūtaka*) and death (*preta*):
purification for a Brāhmaṇa occurs on the tenth day, for a Kṣatriya on the twelfth day,
for a Vaiśya after half a month (fifteen days), and for a Śūdra it is said to be after one month.

A man who possesses true knowledge should immediately abandon the impurities of those who have died; at that very moment, both the knower and the ignorant are purified on the aforementioned day. However, in the Ūrdhva-tantra, due to the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), there is neither birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) nor death-impurity (*pretaka*).
Therefore, with every effort, one should initiate [them] into the Upper Śaiva [tradition].
For kings who have been initiated, there is indeed no impurity regarding birth or death.
Having committed all faults, one is liberated by means of the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
Having meditated upon and recited [the mantra], and having performed the worship, one should always mutter the root-mantra.
O Maheśvara, listen as I shall now describe the defects of the *liṅga* and so forth.
The *liṅga* may be made of crystal or stone; if it is old or worn out, one should likewise fashion a new *liṅga* and install it, but not a mere fragment (*vīyaka*).
One should perform its consecration (*snapana*) there according to one's means and as prescribed.
Whether it has moved or fallen, the cloth has not been dropped by him;
one should know that even if it has passed away in this manner, or even if the substance has been taken by thieves who are like the end of all things,
having established [the deity] there with its characteristic marks (*talliṅgaiḥ*), one should perform the worship of Śiva as before.
Having established [the deity] with a thousand jars, one should then perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
In a deep river current, one should join it with a hundred staffs (*śatadaṇḍāya*).
When the primary liṅga (*mūlaliṅga*) is no longer visible, one should worship the new liṅga.
Established in that place, it quickly brings about all prosperity and is auspicious.

Having offered a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). In the event of damage during the protection rite, the sanctuary should be restored as before.
One should install an auspicious *prāmārca* linga as before;
having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
A linga previously fashioned for his temple-linga should be understood as an *āliṅga*; it brings about invincibility and prosperity in the kingdom.
Furthermore, a fragment from that [original] may become a new earthen linga, free from defects.
One should place the Mahāmārī and others at the side according to the prescribed ritual.
Having offered oblations consecrated with the Varma-mantra, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
If a Liṅga has been installed by one who is not a deity [of the lineage], the king shall attain invincibility.
Therefore, O Maheśvara, with every effort, one should cause the aforementioned *liṅga* situated at the side to bestow garments and other gifts upon the devotees and attendants. Now,
for the sake of removing defects, I shall describe [the rite] for those whose faces are distorted.
And also when the color has appeared on the linga, or during the consecration of an image.
One should perform the snapana rite twenty times and then carry out a single oblation;
one should offer fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, consecrated with the Varma mantra.
Having performed the *triḥ-haraṇa* rite, it shall remove defects of color;
one should also perform the *pratimā-rodhana* rite and the preceding *homa*. One should offer a thousand *samidh* sticks of *udumbara* wood at the three junctions of the day.
One should perform the *śānti* and *māyā* rites, and hold a festival for the mantra itself.

Having installed a thousand-pitcher (*sahasrakalaśa*), one should prepare double the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). [This applies] when the temple has fallen or is deficient, or at the root of the sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*).
When a row of lamps appears on an anthill at the time of the planetary conjunction (*lagna*), or when there is the entry of fragrance [into such places],
and when such signs as these arise, there will be fear for the king and the kingdom.
For the purpose of pacifying those defects, one should perform a fire oblation (*homa*) in the northeast;
with *aśvattha* fuel-sticks, one should offer oblations while reciting the *varma* mantra.
One should perform a three-day festival and worship the devotees during an earthquake,
a solar eclipse, or the appearance of a mock sun.
If the constellation Puṣya arises at night during the Dhanasammita [period],
there will be a great battle involving egg-shaped fish that brings destruction to the people. To pacify that evil influence, the preceptor should be fully adorned.
One should perform ten thousand oblations with the mantra "Tryambaka," using the previously mentioned sacrificial materials, as well as fuel-sticks and bull-dung.

One should perform the *māsapūrṇaka* rite to pacify [the site] and remove defects. If an anthill (*valmīka*) is seen on the foundation or at the base of the temple, or if a rat's nest (*ratnakanyāsa*) has arisen within the temple that is supported by honey, [one must act].
Then, having entered the interior of the palace while assuming a tawny appearance,
one should blow the conch shell and fill it with pure rays of light.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
To the northeast of the altar, one should construct an auspicious pavilion;
having offered a thousand *apāmārga* fuel-sticks daily,
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) three times a day for either seven days or three days.
Uttering the mantra of the South, "Namo namo bhagasya," one should perform the worship with the auspicious mantra that pacifies all defects;
having made the oblation twice as much, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara.
One should cause a hundred pitchers to be placed above the heads according to the prescribed rite;
specifically, there should be an ablution with ghee and milk as much as possible.
One should perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and worship as previously described;
having offered oblations one hundred times with the Īśa-mantra, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
Whether the mirror is moving, worn out, fallen, broken, or [otherwise damaged], one should cast it into water or upon the ground;
then, using a new mirror, one should have it consecrated with the armor-mantra (varmamantra).
One should worship as before; thus Śambhurāja shall attain invincibility.
In the four directions, beginning with the east, the study of the four Vedas is likewise performed; and the daily ritual bathing is carried out according to the rule with yellow water alone.
One should perform daily consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), including ghee and the rest;
and especially, one should perform consecration with the waters of the coconut.
One should always worship the Lord with the consecration of the pure *nāda*,
as well as with constant, pure water-offerings or consecrations using fruits and other such items.
One should purify [the vessel] with turmeric, myrobalan, and ashes;
having collected pure water, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara.
At the end of that, milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered constantly, and it should be double the amount.

Thus, peace has been proclaimed, which destroys all misfortunes. Wherever this peace is performed, there shall be wealth, grain, sons, long life, strength, health, and the constant increase of victory.
For the supreme welfare of the king and the kingdom, I shall always declare the penance;
having explained the procedure for penance, now hear the procedure for the ripening of its fruit.
Through recitation, praise, meditation, salutation, and worship,
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having completed the circumambulation, he reaches the auspicious abode of Śiva on the right;
by taking refuge in that hair-tuft (*keśa*), he attains the supreme goal.
Just as there is reverence for the deity, so too is he worthy of worship among the worlds.
Furthermore, whoever performs a circumambulation during the time of the festival offering shall undoubtedly obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step.
[He who offers] a flower on land, a flower in water, and a flower from a tree— [all these] are equally pleasing.
The person who desires to perform the worship of the deities and the viewing of the Lord shall,
in this world, become wealthy, illustrious, and honored.
He should bestow ten thousand [gifts] upon the yogis and destroy the obstacles to the welfare of the three classes of listeners.
By bathing in the water of my feet, one shall obtain the fruit thereof.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with the five products of a tawny cow mixed with kuśa-water; one shall obtain the merit of giving ten million cows.
One should dwell for three nights in the presence of the Guru or in the vicinity of a deity;
endowed with various enjoyments, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whoever should offer incense and a bell is liberated by these three mantras;
whoever especially offers garments, ornaments, and the like—
various garments combined with various ornaments.
Venerable in the worlds of Śiva, he shall attain the state of Śiva.
He who gives land even the size of a cow’s ear, dedicated to Jyeṣṭhā as the presiding deity,
shall become the lord of villages and a protector against adversaries.
He who gives a lamp in the house of the teacher at times when the lamps have gone out,
attains a divine splendor like that of a lamp and reaches a state of formal similarity [to the deity] in this world.
The man who likewise undertakes these yogic practices for the sake of Śiva is always honored in the world of Śiva by means of a celestial chariot, having bestowed all manner of gifts.
Having attained perfection in the land of the Guru according to the prescribed rite and the path of ritual,
one reaches the world of Śiva, where one is eternally honored by the gods.
One situated near a temple shall attain a form similar to that of a calf;
having gone to the world of Śiva, one should know that one attains the state of proximity.
Having arrived there and worshipped Dakṣiṇeśvara, the Lord of Gods,
he shall enjoy all pleasures endowed with youth in the city of Śiva; after exhausting those enjoyments, he shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
If one should give even as much gold as a single masha, or even if it has fallen [on the ground], [the merit is great].
Having uplifted seven generations on both sides of his family, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, one who serves and is devoted to his gurus and the teacher residing in the city [attains the same].
Having enjoyed vast pleasures endowed with all objects of desire,
one shall become the sole ruler of the earth upon the exhaustion of merit for the sake of [further] enjoyment.
One should offer a single collyrium to the image and thereby obtain the fruit of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
for, having recited and offered oblations with the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*), one attains Sadāśiva.
Having enjoyed pleasures in the city of Śiva, one shall become the sole ruler of the earth;
having constructed a sacrificial pavilion, a hall, and a temple for the deity, one attains that station.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures and desired objects amidst a multitude of sons,
he meditated upon the true nature of his seat and the Lord Dakṣiṇa.
One should worship for the sake of all attainments; one should always speak thus in my world:
"I shall make the renunciation of all my life-breaths for the sake of [your] cutting."
Sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, and siddhi—
these [attainments] are found on the further side, near the sacred field of Śiva (śivakṣetra).
Having developed a sense of belonging right there, one goes to the world of Śiva.
Having performed the propitiation with sacrificial fees, one attains the supreme goal of sacrifice.
Therefore, one should always propitiate Śiva with every effort.
Now hear the prescribed rite for the ripening of the fruit, known as the Kṛttikā-lamp.
[Thus ends the chapter on the rules for penance in the *Āgamasangraha*. Hariḥ Om.
Written by the venerable master’s own hand. (5th line) Homage to the glorious Gurus. Hariḥ Om.
(P.168a, 1st line) The ritual for the many rites, including the belly, mouth, eyes, and the two with feet.
At the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head, [one places] rice, grain, *śāli* rice, sesame, mung beans, *dhātrī*, salt, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
This offering of seeds is here described for the purpose of increasing medicinal herbs— [the seeds] produced from Śiva and Śakti, which are the cause of the world's origin.
The gift of salt is said to bestow happiness and bring about the creation of one’s own self;
daughters and the like should be given away, as well as gold and the gift of garments.
Gold is for the protection of the world, and clothing increases one’s progeny.

[Side Heading: The Ritual Procedure for the Initial Filling] Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure for the filling; listen!
In the month of Āṣāḍha, there shall likewise be a full moon and also an Aśvattha full moon.
It is the most excellent performer of all pacification, auspiciously bestowing all accomplishments,
serving for the protection of villages, and providing total protection through its blessings.
For nine days, seven days, five days, or three days;
on the night preceding that day, one should cause the ritual planting of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) to be performed.
One should begin the consecration (adhivāsana) under the Maghā constellation;
it should be performed in the evening, adorned with all ornaments.
One should bathe [the deity] with the Manonmanī mantra and wrap it in a white cloth;
it should be adorned with all ornaments and anointed with all fragrant unguents.
Taking all the garlands, one should worship the Supreme Goddess in the pavilion,
in a pure place, or especially in the northeast;
or alternatively, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the north of the pavilion.
In a vessel containing eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, one should also place half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice;
half of that again for sesame seeds, and half of that for parched grain (*lājaka*).
Having surrounded this upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place it atop *darbha* grass and flowers.
One should prepare a seat there and commence the yogic posture;
having placed Gaurī above that, one should worship Manonmanī.
One should worship [the deities] together with the nine powers, worshipping each by its own name;
having thoroughly worshipped the deity of the weapon, one should indeed encircle it with a cloth.

Taking up a garland of flowers, one should especially perform worship upon a small platform or a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), with the thread-protector situated in its center. Having respectfully removed the attendant, one should circumambulate the temple.
Having remained for the day sacred to the gods, he should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Relying upon the *vṛta-homa*, he should perform the *kautuka* ceremony;
he should specifically offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and parched grain (*lāja*) into the fire.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the five Brahmans and the six limbs,

and one should offer twenty-five oblations with the Gaurī-gāyatrī mantra. Thereafter, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) and worship the form of the Weapon-mantra (astramūrti) thoroughly.
Having thoroughly worshipped Manonmanī, one should cause a protective thread to be made.
One should cause Manonmanī to be offered milk-rice mixed with fruits;
one should present betel-leaf and perform the ritual of the waving of lights (ārātrika).
Afterwards, one should cause [the disciple] to apply ashes and show him a mirror with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
then, by means of the parasol and fly-whisk, one should worship Manonmanī.
Having established a new *vardhanī* vessel, one should worship it with the nine Śaktis.
Five *bhāras* of mung beans is proclaimed as the best;
three *bhāras* is said to be the middling, and two and a half *bhāras* is the lowest.
With pure water alone, one should cleanse the sprout and the mud itself;
having prepared double the amount of salt, the procedure is ordained.
Now listen to the rules of conduct beginning from the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
And on the second day, one should bathe the supreme preceptor;
having sprinkled him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should likewise enter the temple.
For the rite of one's own benefit, one should perform worship and observe a fast;
having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, one should worship Manonmanī.
Having performed the preliminary rites during the first part of the night, one should sequentially establish the *vardhanī* vessel,
adorning it with new cloths and anointing it with all types of fragrant unguents.
Taking all the garlands and equipped with all ornaments,
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva measuring sixteen droṇas,
as well as half that amount of rice, or half of that again in sesame seeds;
The best of preceptors should place half of that, combined with parched grain (lāja).
Having stated the measurement in this way, one should gradually fashion the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*);
having drawn a lotus in its center, one should place [the vessel] upon it, wrapped in cloth.
In the center of that, there should indeed be a plantain leaf filled with salt;
it should be well-adorned and strewn with parched grain, flowers, sesame seeds, and darbha grass.
Having established Gaurī upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the supreme preceptor should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa);
he should worship her and place the nine Śaktis in the nine directions. In the center of that, however, Manonmanī should be placed facing the east.
To the west of the western gate and to the south of the southern gate.
On the northern side of the north gate, among the eight Śaktis,
the preceptor should perform worship with their respective names together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
One should worship Vighneśa in due order on the southern side of Gaurī;
on the left side of Durgā, however, one should worship [the deities] by their respective names.
Having taken recourse to green [plants], one should fill the peak and the surrounding area;
the rice should be filled with *śiva*, and the preceptor should place it upon the tip of *dūrvā* grass.
Indeed, it should be completely filled with cow-dung powder mixed with salt.
Having performed it according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should leave it overnight.

Having gathered the tips of *dūrvā* grass into a single vessel— the vessel of the body— and remaining composed with a focused mind, one who is fair-complexioned (*gaurī*) should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
The Goddess, having taken up the foot that bestows the abundance of mung-bean sprouts, [placed it] in a new vessel;
that vessel should be a container, and the vessel consists of two novices.
That vessel should be filled with mung beans; it is called the "new vessel.
At dawn, midday, and evening, the best of preceptors should perform the circumambulation three times while reciting the *vratācāpa* mantra. He should then set down the water-vessel.
One part of feces, one-fourth part of powder, and rice at the navel.

Having placed the night (the *rajani* herb) upon the heart and salt upon the throat, one should place *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon the head; this is indeed the morning ritual procedure.
With the sounds of conchs and drums, and with those reciting hymns and auspicious verses,
there shall indeed be three kinds of beings, [consisting of] nine, seven, and ten maidens.
One should worship [the deity] with garments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and she shall become a maiden;
thereafter, one should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel leaf.
According to one's ability, one should worship a maiden who is well-endowed with auspicious qualities;
and the Brāhmaṇas, those who recite benedictions, should likewise gaze upon the maiden.
The preliminary rite (pūrva-karma), accompanied by song and dance, is prescribed.
In the center of the pavilion, however, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is prepared.
Taking all the garlands and provided with all the ornaments, [the ritual proceeds].
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva, one should provide sixteen droṇas [of grain],
half of that in straw, half of that again in sesame seeds,
and half of that combined with parched grain (lāja); thus the ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed there.
Then, having prepared one hundred and eight [pots], one should perform the ceremonial bathing;
likewise, eighty-one, and then nineteen.
Alternatively, one should bathe the goddess Umā with twenty-five [substances],
having adorned her with new garments and decorated her with all ornaments;
taking all manner of garlands, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before Śiva with eight *droṇas* of rice,
one should wrap it above with cloth and place salt in its center.
Having established Gaurī upon that, one should worship her with the nine powers (*navaśakti*).
Then one should worship Vighneśa in the southern direction from Gaurī;
moreover, one should especially worship Durgā on her left side.
Having likewise prepared green blades of grass and placed them in the presence of Umā,
one should place a measure (prastha) full of rice together with the tips of dūrvā grass.
Having taken cow dung powder mixed with rice, turmeric, and salt in a single vessel, and likewise *dūrvā* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
he should then place it in the right hand of Gaurī and circumambulate her three times while pouring water.
The most excellent preceptor should cause a measure full of husked rice to be given;
then, taking a new cloth, he should offer milk-rice that bestows prosperity.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should perform the rite of moistening with water (*ārdrāvṛta*).
Taking hold of the hand of the preceptor (*deśika*), one should cause the Guru to drink water.
Having applied green [herbs] to the rice, one should apply the supreme *darśana* [mantra];
then, applying powdered dung to the feet, *vrīhi* [grain] to the region of the navel,
*rajanī* to the heart, and salt to the throat.
One should place *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon the head and cause [the disciple] to pierce through *Manonmanī*.
There, one should worship the Teacher according to one’s means;
one should especially perform the ritual bathing and worship of the Lord of the Gods.
After that, one should then cause milk-rice and betel-leaf to be given;
there, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
He should cause the devotees and attendants to receive gifts according to their capacity—
salt and a gift of mung beans— at every single house.
Having performed [this rite], one should cause it to be given to all; it bestows abundance of wealth and grain, increases the king and the kingdom, and is auspicious, bringing about total peace.
They are liberated from all evil by means of this single fruitful [rite].
Whether on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha or during the month of Aśvayuja,
it serves for the purpose of all auspicious rites and is the protector of all that is auspicious.
Having joined the preliminary rite (*pūrakarman*) with the fruit of all accomplishments,
[this concludes] the chapter on the festival procedure for the initial preliminary rite in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* concerning the cause.
Hariḥ Om. Om. Written by my own hand. (Side heading) (The festival of the Goddess and the circumambulation of Kukkuṭanaṭeśa). (Line 4)
At the time of the festival of the God of Gods, one should perform the festival of the Goddess as well.

On the day prior to the pilgrimage site (tīrtha), one should remove the previous marriage-thread (kautuka);

Ācārya Śiva himself would be thus; for there is indeed no difference between these two.

The guide, those ascending the palanquin, the descent of the obstacle-creating deity,
the destruction of the village and the kingdom, and the arrival of a royal command from another region.
Standing together with the Lord on the right side of the palanquin,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the Aghora weapon-mantra to pacify a thousand faults.

One should apply black-scented sandalwood for pacification... [in the middle of the site]. Taking the fragrance of *yakṣakardama* for the sake of fresh butter, one should smear it upon Gaurī at the region of the ear.
Having anointed the Lord Tāṇḍava with the pigment of the rose-apple fruit (*jambūphala*),
one should provide for all the proportions during the time of the festival procession;
at the times of Naṭeśa’s circumambulation, he should arrange them by his side.
Whether it be a guide, a leaf, a disciple, or a palanquin seat—
having recited the Aghora weapon mantra, which is the destroyer of Asuras,
one destroys the Rākṣasas and brings prosperity to the king and his kingdom.
Creation is moving to another place; maintenance is the binding of curiosity;
withdrawal is indeed the smelling of agaru; and concealment is the act of smearing.
The departure at the time of dawn, the witnessing of the *tāṇḍava* dance,
the chariot, the curiosity, the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and the grace— these are thus described.
When he assumes a non-terrible form and performs a dance, then,
for the sake of attaining a gentle nature, with joy Girijā applies black ointment to the forehead and the staff of Maheśa.
By the mere sight of it, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
by merely wearing its fragrance, the sins of seven lifetimes are destroyed.
In the Uttarakāmika [Tantra]: Whatever was previously [stated] and of whatever kind it may have been, that should be performed in that same manner;
one should carry out the practice according to the tantra in both cases alike.

All the devotees of Śiva should strike [the drums] with great clamor.

It shall be for the sake of pleasing all the gods and for the purpose of protecting the world. When the sun is in transit through Virgo, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, if that [lunar day] extends into the evening, one should worship Kedāreśa.
Thus [ends the account of] Aṃśumān.
"When both new-moon days or both full-moon days have arrived,
one should perform the ritual worship by combining them within the preceding month," so it is stated in the Raurava Āgama.
The supreme Kedāra-vrata should especially be observed in the month of Kanyā;

It must be performed in the preceding month and not in the subsequent one.

If the number of days [of the lunar month] is exceeded by the causal [period], it is not said to be a fault; however,

From that time forward, one should observe the vow during the day of the increase or the day of the waning of the moon. In the *Candrajñāna*,

The weapon, the sword, the power of Śamīśrī, and the supreme energy that bestows victory—

[Navarātri Festival Ritual]
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of the Navarātra rite;
one should perform the worship beginning with the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
The daily worship, according to the prescribed ritual, extends up to the stage of the first bliss (*prathamānanda*).
[The mandala] is square, with four doors and adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*).
In the center, upon a nine-square altar for Durgā between two new jars,
one should worship Aṣṭalakṣmī in the northern or northwestern direction.
One should worship Sarasvatī in the southwestern or western direction.
In the northeast, one should especially worship the Guru;
thereafter, one should install the Ācārya, wrapped in a pure cloth and provided with garments and ornaments, along with the ritual offerings for the Ācārya.
First is the gathering of the clay, second is the placing of the seed-sprouts,
and third is the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) ceremony performed by the preceptor together with the Goddess.
Beginning from the first day, one should perform the worship of Durgā and other rites.
There, one should worship Durgā; that is the worship of the Nine Durgās.
Beginning from the fourth day, one should worship the Eight Lakṣmīs;
beginning from the seventh day, there is the ritual adoration of Sarasvatī.
Thus it has been declared regarding the teachers; the wise one should worship them according to the rule, beginning with the *yonikuṇḍa* in accordance with the previously stated procedure.
Having meditated especially upon the Goddess in the midst of the fire, one should worship her;
having offered ten oblations to the Goddess, one should offer eight hundred for each [subsequent deity].

With the Mātṛgāyatrī mantra, one should offer twenty-five oblations for each [deity]; furthermore, one should offer one hundred oblations for each, accompanied by the sacrificial substances and other requirements. Alternatively, one may offer one thousand, half of that, or even one hundred.
Or one hundred and eight, or twenty-five, or sixteen;
when joined with these days, it bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
One should worship [the deities] in due order, beginning from the first bliss (ānanda).
One should worship Vijaya in the temple of Durgā, the worship of Lakṣmī with Śrīhṛdaya, and the worship of Sarasvatī; this is said to bestow the fruit of all branches of knowledge.
Thus, in this threefold worship which accomplishes all desired aims,
one should offer everything, beginning with fire, on the tenth day according to the prescribed ritual.
In another village, to the east and north in a region of fuel-wood,
at an auspicious moment and under a favorable conjunction, the Goddess, together with her chariot, [was established].
One should perform the installation of the Śaiva-ācārya, Danti, and the Goddess in due order.
The Goddess is seated upon a comfortable throne situated in the southern quarter.
With a four-square footed pedestal, there is the sounding of dance and musical instruments.

Or the son of the king of kings should cause [the victim] to enter the region of the *śamī* tree. He should then remove the goat and the man according to the procedure prescribed by the scripture. Having worshipped the Asuras and Rākṣasas with their respective names, he should offer the oblation (*bali*) in due order.
In the consecration of a *śamī* tree, one should worship Dharmadeva;
one should also worship the seat and the covering according to the prescribed ritual.
Thus it was proclaimed that when the weapons were joined with the hand of the preceptor,
the king’s entire army and all the weapons of the Rākṣasas were destroyed.

Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, and having adorned the central part with archways made of garlands of *darbha* grass and plantain trees facing eastward,

one should reach the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), which contains a square altar (*vedikā*) in the middle and a principal lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) to the east, graced by the *jayā* oblation.

Having performed the dismissal by the artisan, and having had the artisans give their permission, preceded by the propitiation of Vighneśvara, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited. Having performed the ritual of the six limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*) and having set out the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should consecrate [the site] with the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and sprinkle the pavilion. [Then, at] the gateway arch of the eastern door...

Having sprinkled [it] with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Maṅganī-toraṇa. Thus, having sprinkled the toraṇas at the four gates with the Astra-mantra and enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kuṃbhinī-toraṇa" [at the eastern gate]; "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Nikuṃbhī-toraṇa" at the southern gate. At the northern gate: *oṃ hrīṃ bhṛṅginītoraṇāyai namaḥ*. At the western gate: *oṃ hrīṃ maṅginītoraṇāyai namaḥ*.

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mahākālī. To the south: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Śaṅkhinī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vijayā. To the west: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vāruṇī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Siṃhavaktrī. To the north: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Dākṣāyaṇī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Haladhāriṇī.

Having thus invoked [them] and offered the *arghya*, one should [invoke] the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their respective positions from the east to the northeast: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadrā. To the southeast, Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. To the northeast, Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.
Having thus [recited], and having gazed upon the pavilion, one should worship the lion-throne of Dharma and the others upon the four pillars of the inner altar and the four pillars of the platform.

Having performed worship and meditated upon [the deity] as consisting of the power of *māyā*, one should then place eight jars— made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, provided with threads, gold, jewels, *nālīkera* (coconut), *kūrca* (grass-bushes), fruits, and sprouts— in the center of the altar. Having adorned the preceptor with new garments and ornaments,

and having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* and the special *arghya* offering while facing north, one should apply a sandalwood tilaka on the forehead and [place the deity] upon the jar-seat in the center of the altar.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Durgā-śakti. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī-siṃhāsanā. Oṃ, obeisance to Nirmokṣī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Yogāsanā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Padmāsanā. Having meditated upon that [lotus] as possessing five seed-syllables as its filaments and six petals; at the seed-syllables: Oṃ haiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Navadurgā, who wears a garland of severed heads and trunks. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍadurgā, the bearer of the conch and discus. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ...

Salutation to Rudradurgā, to Bhavatī. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Daṃṣṭrībhīṣaṇadurgā, the power (śakti) of Mātaṅgī. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Vaitālakhaḍginī, the Durgā of the upward-facing camel. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Saptamātṛ, the eighth Durgā.
Having worshipped with "Salutation to the Yoginī," [one should worship] on the filaments: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Umā in the form of the Bhaga; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī;
(third line) Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Gāyatrī; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Lakuleśvarī; Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ...
Salutation to Medinīdevī. Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to Vasundharā. Having thus worshipped her, [perform] the meditation (dhyāna).
One-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed, adorned with a crown;

Having meditated thus and having arrived [there], one should subsequently worship eight pitchers from Indra up to Īśāna. In the east: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ indraśaktyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ maheśvarīśaktyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*...
Homage to Kaumārī-śakti. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, homage to Brāhmī-śakti. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, homage to Vaiṣṇavī-śakti.

Having thus worshipped the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-śakti), having led [the deity] forth, and having worshipped the enclosure, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations into either a lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (padma-kuṇḍa) or a water-pot (kumbha). Having joined [the deity] within the pot, having led [it] forth, and having consecrated the dance, musical instruments, and so forth, one should bestow the benediction (āśīrvāda).

In the *Kāmika*, regarding the festival of Śiva: one should arrange the limbs such that the head of the dwelling is in the northeast (Īśāna), the feet in the southwest (Nirṛti), and the belly in the center (Brahman). One should thus fashion the auspicious parts.
Having bowed to Śiva, the supreme object of knowledge, who is eternally manifest and non-dual,
I shall describe the path of this Great Festival according to the scriptures.
Now, the procedure for the festival (utsavavidhi): [it concerns] the hoisting and lowering of the banner (dhvaja).
The ritual activities contained within that [period] are called the "festival" (utsava). In this regard, there are [festivals] lasting one day, three days, or five days.
On the seventh day, the ninth day, the eleventh day,

the twelfth day, the fourteenth day, or after a fortnight— these are the nine types [of rites]. Among them, in the three lower categories consisting of the third and fifth days, one should omit the hoisting of the banner.

Only the ritual complex beginning with the beating of the drum and ending at the sacred ford (tīrtha) is to be performed on the seventh, ninth, and eleventh days, as well as during the three intermediate periods,
and on the twelfth day.
On the fourteenth day, the eighth day, and during the three superior [periods], all the ritual sequences, including the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajārohaṇa*),

must be performed. In these two festivals— the intermediate and the superior— one should perform [the rites] starting from the hoisting of the banner, multiplied by the number of days [of the festival].
