[The festival] is doubled for that day. Preceded by the beating of drums (bherītāḍana), and preceded by the offering of the *aṅkurārpaṇa* on that same day—thus is the threefold festival. In this very way, among the many varieties of festivals, one should perform whichever festival is desired.

Therein is the procedure for the offering of nine sprouts: then the collection of earth, the offering of the flag-sprout, the consecration of the flag, and the offering of the festival-sprouts; (second line) the striking of the drum, the hoisting of the flag with the mantra of the World-Protectors, the offering of the sacred-site sprouts, the tying of the protective thread, the sacrifice for the site of the pavilion, and the purification of the pavilion. (third line)

The propitiation of Yāgeśvara; the worship of Utsaveśvara; the fire-oblation (homa) and the offering of oblations (bali) to the village deities and others; the procession of Utsaveśvara; the ceremonial bathing for the purpose of the festival; special worship; the viewing of diversions; and on the night preceding the final day, the re-tying of the sacred thread (kautuka) and the pilgrimage to the sacred site (kautukatīrtha).
The powder festival, the great pilgrimage site, the dismissal of the sacrifice,
the giving of sacrificial fees at the root-liṅga, the special worship with the consecration of the pitcher for the Lord of Sacrifice, the hoisting of the banner, the worship of Caṇḍa,
and the dismissal of the world-protectors.

These are the thirty constituent parts of the festival. Then follows the collection of clay. Having worshipped Vighneśvara at the time of evening, having offered an oblation such as a coconut, and having requested that there be no obstacles, one approaches the vicinity of the primary *liṅga* and worships it with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), including the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth.

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with joined palms, [he said]: "O Blessed One, the performer of all fruits, the great festival is now being commenced. Therefore, the Blessed One must be present in person. Having thus requested that the ceremony be completed without obstacles from the palace, and having received permission for that flower-offering, he went outside to Caṇḍeśvara and Gaṇapati of the festival.

Having worshipped the offering, having worshipped the King of Weapons (the Trident) upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) preceded by the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*), and having honored the constituent parts beginning with Rudra, and having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth; having consecrated the spade with the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*); having approached a site such as a mountain peak that has been purified by those [mantras]; and having performed the worship of Vighneśvara there and made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having sprinkled that place with water mixed with [the five] products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should arrange a nine-square grid (*navakoṣṭha*) upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there. Having worshipped the Brahmin in the central square as the embodiment of the seat (*āsana-mūrti*) with the root mantras,
[one should worship] in the four squares starting from the east.

Having worshipped the bees and others, and having offered oblations (*bali*) to Brahmā and the rest in due order with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*, having presented betel-leaf, and having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*), one should not remove the offering; then, having sprinkled that place with water while reciting the site-mantra (*taddeśamantra*), [one should place] *darbha* grass consecrated with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

Having spread [the ritual grass] and worshipped the ground in its center with roots as a seat, having offered incense and lamps, and having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) surrounding it; having dug three kinds of earth with the mantra of the "digger" weapon (*khanitrināstra*), and having placed it in a vessel made of gold or other materials;
having dismissed the world-protectors, and having worshipped the earth from the site with perfumes and other offerings, [he should cover it] with silk cloths and the like.

Having covered [the image] and performed a circumambulation of the village, one should enter the temple. Then, having approached a pleasing spot for the purpose of installing the flag-staff (*dhvajāṅkura*), one should perform the worship of Gaṇapati there, make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and sprinkle [the site]. Having fashioned a square of sixteen compartments with five lines upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place the Soma-vessel in the four central compartments.

Having established [the deity] therein, having worshipped Soma with the seat, the form, and the root-mantra along with its limbs, and having placed the *pālikās*, *ghaṭikās*, and *śarāvas* in order around the surrounding compartments starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), one should scatter earth previously collected in the *pālikās* and other vessels and sprinkle them with the *astra-mantra*.

Having worshipped the twelve Ādityas, beginning with the *pālikā* situated in the northeast corner; having soaked substances such as sesame, mung beans, and black gram in milk; having sown the seeds—beginning with the principal seed—among the small ants and other insects; and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items placed in the water-pot (*kuṃbha*).

Having sprinkled water from that [vessel] over the *pālikās* and other items, and having offered incense and lamps, one should arrange the *pālikās* and so forth with the *drupada* mantra and the *praṇava*. Having worshipped Soma until the completion of the ritual, one should protect the *pālikās* and the rest. Then, for the purpose of consecrating the banner (*dhvajādhivāsana*), [one should proceed] in front of Śiva, in the pavilion, or elsewhere.

Or, in an auspicious and well-prepared location, having arranged the ritual jars (*kalaśa*) for the consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and having prepared four sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) within the pavilion; having installed the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*) on the western altar, and having placed a banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa*) on the altar in front of that, a bull and water-jars (*vṛṣakumbha*) in front of that, and a kettle-drum (*bherī*) in front of that; and having performed the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) to be recited.

Having worshipped the Sun-god in the solar pitcher, having honored the gatekeepers of the archway, and having entered within by performing the worship of the western door; having worshipped the canopy, the *darbha* garlands, and the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgalāni*) in the directions starting from the east in the sacrificial pavilion;

(third line) having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) as in the daily rite, having prepared the special *arghya* water, and having performed the purification of the ritual substances and the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); having consecrated the pavilion in the southwest and having scattered the ritual offerings (*vikāra*), one should worship Vāstunātha and Lakṣmī.

Having worshipped Śiva and the Pāśupata weapon according to the procedure for the movable seat (*calāsana*) at the *yāgeśvara*, the *kumbha*, and the *vardhanī*; having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokeśas*); having performed the circumambulation of the *kumbha*; and having again fully worshipped the *kumbha* and *vardhanī* according to the procedure for the fixed seat (*sthirāsana*), one should worship Gaṇapati in the wind-vessel (*vāyukuṃbha*) and the Gurus in the northeast vessel (*aiśānyakuṃbha*). Then, having drawn the [mandala] lines and so forth with materials possessing the characteristics as prescribed, and subsequently having drawn the circle of light (*jyotirmaṇḍala*) within the circle of vision (*dṛṣṭimaṇḍala*) using a stylus and a suitable leaf.

Having performed the satiation rite with honey and clarified butter, having displayed the vessels of ghee, honey, and so forth, and having sprinkled the image with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for the purification of the idol;

(second line) having sprinkled it with the *arghya* water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) for the preliminary consecration (*jalādhivāsana*), having worshipped the bull according to the rules, and having bound the protective thread (*kautuka*); having placed the five types of earth upon the fivefold bed on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*); (third line)

First, having worshipped the bull-seat (*vṛṣāsana*) arising from the six [syllables] of the bull-mantra; having sprinkled the form of the bull (*vṛṣamūrti*); having manifested the bull by means of the body, eyes, base, and limbs of the Brahma-knowledge (*brahmavidyā*); having offered a handful of flowers with the *Vṛṣagāyatrī*; and having worshipped the bull with scents and other offerings—(4th line)—one should invoke and worship the three principles (*tattvatraya*) known as Ātman, Vidya, and Śiva, extending from the knees to the neck and ending at the head, which include their presiding deities and the Lord of the Form (*mūrtīśvara*), and then cover it with a red cloth. (5th line)

One should restrain [the bull] with firmness. Having first performed the ritual of the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated before that, one should invoke Vṛṣa as before into the central jar (*kuṃbha*). Then, in the surrounding jars, starting from the east in due order:
[offerings] to Dakṣa, Gopati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Tīkṣṇaśṛṅga, Nandin, Viṣāṇin, Paśupati, and Mahodara.

Having thus worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), having offered a handful of flowers with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra to the bull situated within the central pitcher, having presented mung-bean rice (mudga-anna), and having offered betel, incense, and so forth up to the end of the sequence,

one should inform [the deities] of the rite of fire-oblation (homakarma). For the purpose of the oblation, having performed the rites beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)— whether in a pit, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or between the pitcher and the drum— up to the naming of the Fire (Agni), and having dismissed the other two [deities], [one should proceed].

Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having divided the fire for the sake of the *caru* and clarified butter with the *akarādi* [mantras], and having thus performed the *homa*, one should meditate upon the fire and pray to it. Having worshipped that bull in the center as before, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of satisfying the mantras, and one-tenth as many for the Brahma-aṅgas. Then, having offered the final oblation—

Having performed the expiation according to the place, time, and other circumstances, having carried out the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantras, and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should purify the *caru* by means of inspection and other rites. Having prepared it together with the mantras, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations— or half of that— with the five substances consisting of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), *caru*, parched grain (*lāja*), and sesame seeds, or else with the three [substances] using the root of the *vṛṣa* [mantra].

Or, having offered a *vyāhṛti* at the end of each substance and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should gaze upon the *śāntikumbha* (the vessel of peace), purify it through rites such as *nirīkṣaṇa*, perform the *saṃpātāhuti*, and then cause the *pūrṇāhuti* to be offered. Then, having worshipped *Ādhāraśakti* in the fire, having offered three oblations, and having worshipped the principle of *Vṛṣātmatattva* along with its presiding deity (*īśvara*), one should offer three oblations for each of the *mūrttīśvaras* after worshipping them, offering three oblations for each.

For the sake of purifying the portion of Brahmā, one should offer twenty-five oblations with the root-mantra of the bull (*vṛṣamūla*), and having offered a tenth part for the limbs of Brahmā, one should give the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, having gone near the bull, one should sprinkle it with water from the *śānti*-pitcher, touch it with the root of *kuśa* grass and the root of the bull, and perform a recitation (*japa*) equal in number to the oblations. Finally, one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having meditated upon the *ātmatattva* as having become one with the *vidyātattva*, one should worship with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the Bull *ātmatattva* and the Bull *vidyātattva*. Having offered three oblations ending with *svāhā*, and having worshipped the *vidyātattva* together with its presiding deity, one should offer three oblations to each [deity] and worship the *mūrtis* and their respective lords (*mūrtīśvaras*) with individual oblations.

For the sake of purifying the middle portion, one should offer twenty-five oblations with the *vṛṣamūla* mantra; having offered a tenth part of the oblations for the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*), and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sprinkle the middle portion with the *śānti* water. Touching the middle of the bull with the middle of the *kuśa* grass, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) equal in number to the oblations. Then, having gone to the fire-chamber and meditated upon the *vidyā-tattva* as having become one with the *śiva-tattva*, one should recite: *oṃ hīṃ hūṃ namaḥ to the *vidyā-tattva* and *śiva-tattva*.
Having worshipped in this manner and offered three oblations, and having worshipped the Śiva-tattva along with its presiding deity,

he should satisfy each with oblations. Having performed the worship of the Mūrti and Mūrtīśvara and the fire-offering (*homa*) according to the previous procedure, and having held [the vessel] as before for the sake of purifying the upper portion, he should go near the bull and sprinkle [it] with the *śānti* water.

Having touched its tip with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass and recited [the mantra] as before, he should go to the fire-chamber and offer [oblations] as previously described. Then, having gone near the *astra* (weapon-mantra) located on the cloth, he should sprinkle it with water using the *astra-mantra*. Having performed the sixfold arising and the seat (*āsana*), he should worship Rudra and the others presiding over its constituent parts. Having manifested the *Śivāstra* with the root and limb mantras, he should worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
In the fire as well, having thus worshipped the weapon (*astra*),

one should offer twenty-five oblations with the weapon-mantra for the purpose of mantra-satiety (*mantratarpaṇa*). Having offered oblations to each of the Brahma-limbs (*brahmāṅga*) with their respective mantras, and having given the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), or with clarified butter alone, using the weapon-mantra.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having worshipped the *Ādhāra-śakti* in the fire and offered three oblations; (line 5) having worshipped the *Astra-tattva*, *Astra-vidyā-tattva*, and *Astra-śiva-tattva*, presided over by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra respectively, and having gratified each with three oblations; (line 6) having offered ten oblations for each to purify the three parts, and having gone to the cloth [the painting] and sprinkled it with *śānti* water; (line 7) [one should perform the purification] with the roots, middles, and tips of *kuśa* grass upon the root, middle, and tip of the *astra*.

Having touched [the vessel], performed the recitation according to the number of oblations, and gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), having offered full oblations with the *astra-mantra*, he should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root-mantra of Vṛṣa for the sake of expiation.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) for the sake of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), and having performed twenty-five oblations together with the final *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items to the Bull and the Weapon residing in the fire, and having worshipped them; having offered the *arghya* for turning away (*parāṅmukha*); and having saluted the ashes;

one should unite the Bull and the Weapon residing in the fire with the Bull and the Weapon on the cloth, dismiss the fire, and [dispose of] the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*).

Having offered the *bali*, having presented the *arghya* water, and having dismissed them; having moved past the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*), and having offered the inner *bali* and the outer *bali*; having washed his feet, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), and applied the sacred ashes (*bhasman*);

(4th line) having performed the ritual of complete protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), he should cause perfumes, flowers, and other offerings to be presented to the deity residing in the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) and the deity residing in the jar (*ghaṭa*). Then, for the sake of the festival sprouts (*utsavāṅkura*), [he should proceed] in the northern or north-western direction of the sacrificial hall. (5th line)
Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the purpose of offering the sprouts of the festival (*utsavāṅkurārpaṇa*),

and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should perform the offering of the festival sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure. Then, for the purpose of striking the drum (*bherītāḍana*), one should go before the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*), worship Vighneśvara, make the formal resolve, cause the proclamation of an auspicious day, and sprinkle both the King of Weapons and the drum with consecrated water.

(7th line) Having worshipped the sixfold seat at the base of the weapon (*astra*) with the mantra: *astrāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ* and *astramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, one should contemplate the form of the seat. Then, having worshipped Rudra and the others upon the petals starting from the middle petal and in the intermediate directions: (P.183, b1st line) [End].

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the Śivāstra mantra and the ancillary mantras, having worshipped [the drum] with perfumes and other offerings, and having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth, one should go near the drum. On the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated upon the drum, one should worship the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*). Having meditated upon and worshipped the form of the drum as consisting of the *praṇava* (OM), one should worship Rudra in the center, Brahmā on the right, Viṣṇu on the left, Sūrya on the right ring (*valaya*), and [Gaurī] on the left ring.

Having worshipped the seven *kīla*-Mother deities at the *soma* [corner], the nine *kīla* deities at the *graha* [corner], the eleven *kīla-Rudras* at the leather-thread, and the *Vāsukis* at the blow (fourth line); having invoked the root-mantra of Bharikā in the form of Parā, worshipped her with the ancillary limbs (*aṅga*), rendered her nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*, offered the *arghya* with face turned away, and fully honored her with food offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth; while reciting the *astra-mantra*, taking the blow-stick in the right hand, one should first deliver one blow upon the eastern plank of the drum (*bherī*).

Having struck [the drum] a second time with two blows or a third time with three blows—or even all three as a single blow—one should place that blow upon the head [of the disciple]. Having performed the invocation of the deity according to the ritual procedure, one should thereafter cause the disciple to recite the five-syllable mantra while sprinkling him with water. Having given him an upper garment and a sacred thread (*upavīta*), and having placed water and flowers in his hand, he too, according to the rite of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), should offer the flower upon the drum. Then, having placed the drum upon his shoulder...

One should play various musical instruments. Then, having performed the rites for the hoisting of the banner as prescribed, having fashioned and installed the staff, the secondary staff, the shoulder-piece, and the rings, and having constructed the altar according to the stated method,
one should smear the base of the staff with flour-paste and decorate it with colorful powders.

Having placed the flag-cloth, the tree, and the bamboo at the base of the staff, and having tied the staff-rope, the [flag-]tassel, the beard-fringe, the bell-garland, and so forth, one should lead it toward the flag. Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle the staff with water. Having worshipped the king [of the quarters] with [offerings] such as flowers, and having worshipped the sixfold throne (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) at the base of the staff, one should divide the staff into three parts and [proceed] from the top in sequence.

Having worshipped the principles beginning with Śivatattva along with their presiding deities; likewise, having worshipped the five constituent parts (*skandha*) and the staff (*daṇḍa*); having fully honored the Sun in the ring, Śakti in the rope, and Śiva in the staff; and having displayed the bull-seat and so forth upon the cloth-bull according to the ritual options, one should take the seed-syllable from the bull-pitcher and join it to the cloth. Then, having joined its retinue to that bull in that place, one should perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of its limbs.

Having offered incense and lamps, at that time having given [gifts] to the twice-born according to one's ability, and having bowed to the Lord of Festivals (Utsaveśvara), one should quickly hoist the cloth by means of the base of the bull. Having wound the rope around the staff clockwise and tied it to the base of the staff,
one should sprinkle the water from the bull-pitcher upon the base of the staff, and sprinkle the various pitchers in their respective places.

Having adorned the base of the staff with garments, garlands, and so forth, and having offered mung-bean rice (*mudgānna*) to the preeminent bull (*vṛṣendra*), one should present the oblation (*bali*) to both Vṛṣa and Vidyeśvara, and cause incense and lamps to be offered. Then, for the invocation of the guardians of the directions and worlds, [one should worship] the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) along with Liṅga, Caṇḍeśvara, and the ten weapons.

Having gathered the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the offering (*bali*), one should invoke the respective world-protectors (*lokapāla*)— beginning from Brahmā’s station up to Indra’s station, or from Varuṇa at the western door up to Nirṛti— at their respective locations by describing their specific attributes. Then, having worshipped those respective world-protectors at their respective places, accompanied by their respective *tāla* rhythms and *rāga* melodies.

Having offered the *bali* with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*, and having entered the temple, one should offer the *bali* as usual upon the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*). (Line 7) Thereafter, for the sake of the sacred water (*tīrtha*) and the ritual sprouts (*aṅkura*), one should perform the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) in the previously mentioned location within the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*) as described before. Immediately following that, for the purpose of binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*), one should go into the presence of the Lord of the Festival (*utsaveśvara*) together with the appropriate materials. Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and caused the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, [one should worship] Ādhāraśakti on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and the Self (*ātman*) within the yantra. (P.185a, Line 1)

Having worshipped the three principles consisting of Śiva within the vessel, *prakṛti* in the rice grains, the *saṃhitā-mantras* in the ash-receptacle, the *māyā-tattva* in the ashes, and Lakulīśvara and Nanda in the thread;

(second line) having worshipped the God and Goddess with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*); and having tied the thread upon the left hand of the Goddess with the *tryambaka* mantra and the *Gāyatrī* of the Goddess; (third line) [with the mantra] "bṛhatsāma... [etc.]
Having offered the oblation consisting of parched grain, cakes, and other such items, and having presented the incense and lamps, one should make this request:

"May the Blessed One, for the sake of the festival, grant his grace through this specific sacrificial offering to the Goddess. Then, one should perform the *kautuka* (auspicious binding) upon the central leaf within the *astrarāja* (the King of Weapons), as well as upon the images of the ten weapons and other figures suitable for the vehicle.
One should bind [the thread].

Then, having worshipped the Sun in the pitcher situated between the Śakra and Nala [pillars] in the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), and having sprinkled the door with the general *arghya* water using the Astra-mantra, one should worship the four arches (*toraṇas*) in the directions starting from the east—namely, the arches of Peace (*śānti*), Prosperity (*bhūti*), Strength (*bala*), and Health (*ārogya*). Furthermore, in the pitchers at the doors starting from the east, one should worship Peace (*śānti*), Knowledge (*vidyā*), Cessation (*nivṛtti*), and so forth.

(7th line) Having worshipped the doors of the installation, [one should worship] two by two at the eastern and other doors, on their respective right and left sides: Nandi and Kāla, Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka, Vṛṣa and Skanda, Devī and Caṇḍa. Having worshipped the vajras and so forth on the door-panels starting from the east, [one should worship them] on the banners starting from the east.

"Salutation to Kumuda, to Kumudākṣa, to Puṇḍarīka, to Vāmana, to Śaṅkukarṇa, to Sarvanetra, to Sumukha, and to Supratiṣṭha. Having thus worshipped, and having performed the worship of the door as usual in the west, one should enter within and stand to the south of the altar.

One should worship the essence of earth in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), the essence of water in the grasses, the essence of fire in the binding cords, the essence of air in the bamboo beams, and the essence of space in the pillars.

(4th line) Having worshipped the Moon in the canopy and Vāsukī in the garland of *darbha* grass, one should worship the Sun in the eight auspicious objects (*aṣṭamaṅgala*)—specifically in the mirror—and Varuṇa in the water-pot (*kuṃbha*). (5th line) In the bull [statue], [one should worship Śiva].
Having worshipped the bull on the *āmara*, Māraṇī on the horse, Śrī on the *śrīvatsa*, Bhāratī on the *svastika*, Vimala on the conch, and the fire (*havyavāha*) on the lamp;
having honored the pavilion pervaded by Sadāśiva to the south of the altar; having sat there;
having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites as in the daily practice; and having prepared the special *arghya* water—

Having performed self-worship and the purification of the mantra, having consecrated the *śivahasta* (the hand of Śiva), and having placed it upon one's own head; having taken up the thirty-six-fold *darbha*-grass as the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), and having realized "I am Śiva" (*śivohaṃ*); having set out the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and having sprinkled the pavilion with the *pañcagavya* using the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*); having gone to the southwest direction (*naiṛtadeśa*), [one should perform] there the rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four paths (*catuṣpatha*).

Having consecrated [the materials] with the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), having placed parched grains (*lāja*) upon them, and having scattered *kuśa* grass and *kurvīkā* grass, one should pour water from the *vardhanī* vessel into the *yāgeśvara* vessel with the root mantra. Having worshipped Vāstunātha in the southwest jar and Lakṣmī in the western jar, one should worship the bull, the seat of Śiva, in the northeast jar using the sixfold rising throne (*ṣaḍutthāsana*).

Having manifested the Mūrti-Brahmavidyā through its body, eyes, root-mantra, and limbs; having worshipped the serpent-throne (*vyālāsana*) upon the *vardhanī* vessel; having worshipped the Pāśupata weapon together with its form, root-mantra, and limbs; and having fully honored the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the jars within the pavilion;
[the officiant] entrusted them with the burden of protecting the sacrifice.

Having rotated the pitcher following the stream from the *vardhanī* while recollecting the *astra-mantra* and the fortress (*durga*) with the root mantra, and having placed those two in their respective positions;

having worshipped Śiva, together with his limbs (*aṅga*) and enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), upon the stable seat in the pitcher; having worshipped the *pāśupatāstra* and the form of the seat in the *vardhanī* with the root mantra and its limbs; and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth.

Having performed the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* by means of the *liṅgamudrā*, one should praise and rejoice [with the verse]: "Obeisance to you, Śaṅkara, who possesses the form of the *liṅga* and to Umā, who possesses the form of the *bhaga*. (7th line)
"For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this is your immovable form.
And these are the thirty-six deities of knowledge; seize your own weapons!"
Having thus bestowed the sword of consciousness (*citkhaḍga*), having recited the root mantra as many times as possible, having offered the tenth part and recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*),
and having worshipped [the deity] in the *vardhanī* vessel, [one should recite] the verse:
This sacrifice has been undertaken by me, a performer of rituals;
therefore, you must ensure its completion until it reaches its conclusion.
Having thus made this request and offered the *nirodhārghya* (the water of cessation), one should worship Gaṇapati in the air-vessel (*vāyukuṃbha*) and the lineage gurus in the northeast.
Then, for the propitiation of the Lord of the Sacrifice (*yāgeśvara*), having worshipped the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti in the central vessel on the altar,
and having worshipped the form of Śiva upon it, [one proceeds] by the method of the staff-bend (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *brahmans*, having produced the empowered body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) through the arrangement of the letters (*lipinyāsa*) according to the divisions of the thirty-eight *kalās* by means of the various aspects of the *muṇḍa-vaktra-kalās*, and having assigned the eyes; having performed the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*); having conceived the seat (*āsana*) and so forth for Manonmanī in the *vardhanī* vessel and worshipped her together with her limbs (*aṅgas*) and enclosures; having worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*) in the eight jars starting from the east; one should perform the complete worship up to the offerings of food (*naivedya*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and so forth, ending with the recitation (*japa*). Then, having entered the temple of the Lord of the Festival (*utsaveśvara*), one should consecrate the water of honor (*arghya*) with the ritual of the *kalaśas*.

(6th line) Having performed the worship of the door according to the ritual procedure for Maheśa and having entered within, one should offer flowers with the Maheśvara-gāyatrī. Having removed the previously offered floral remains (*nirmālya*) and so forth, and having performed the purification of the image (*bera-śuddhi*) in the prescribed manner, one should resolve upon the seat (*āsana*) by means of the entire path of worship (*sakalārcana-mārga*).

Having worshipped that [image] with the Mūrti-mantra, having performed the thirty-one-fold *kalā*-nyāsa and the arrangement of the letters (*lipivinyāsa*), having worshipped it with the Vidyā-body, the eyes, the root-mantra, and the limbs, having worshipped the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), and having worshipped the Goddess Skanda according to the prescribed method, one should worship with offerings of food (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth.

One should announce, "I shall perform the fire-sacrifice rite (*homakarma*). (Side heading) Then the Guru, having received permission, takes the vessel of honor-water (*arghyapātra*), gazes upon the sacrificial hall with divine vision, circumambulates it, and sitting near the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), should perform the consecration of the pit. Therein, with the thumb and ring finger, he should [touch] the base with the root-mantra while looking with his eye.

Having performed the inspection of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), its sprinkling with the *Astramantra*, and its striking with the tips of *kuśa* grass using the *Astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; and having performed the digging, filling of what was scattered, leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and smearing with the *Kavaca-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ* using the *Astra-mantra*; one should then assign the *kalā-mantras* beginning with *Śāntyatītā* to the center and other parts of the pit.

Having fashioned [the altar] out of *kalā* and having encircled it with three threads, one should worship it with: "Obeisance to the pit (*kuṇḍa*) consisting of *kalā*. Then, with three blades of *kuśa* grass, one should form a thunderbolt (*vajra*) shape upon the four intersecting lines—drawn both ways with their tips pointing east and north—which constitute the cross-lines. Furthermore, within the interior of the pit, one should form a four-way junction (*catuṣpatha*) using two blades of *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing east and north, while reciting the *astra-mantra*.

Having fashioned a protective enclosure with *kuśa* grass rising up on all sides as armor, and having offered in the center a seat in the form of a tuft of grass (*kūrca*) or a ritual mat (*viṣṭara*), saying:
"Obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvara. (8th line) Thus it is given.
In that [lotus], one should meditate upon Vāgīśvarī, who possesses living beings, is adorned with garlands of moonlight, and has four arms;
and one should also meditate upon the four-armed, three-eyed Vāgīśa.
Thus, *namaḥ* to Vāgīśvarī;

*namaḥ* to Vāgīśvara. Having worshipped those two with perfumes and other offerings, having brought fire into a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or similar vessel and placed it in the southeast, having abandoned the demons (*rākṣasa*), and having purified it by means of the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, [one should say]: "Obeisance to the form of Fire (*vahnimūrti*) with the flower-arrow mudrā. Thus, having seized the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), having united it with the fire of the navel and the fire of the seed-syllable, and having expelled it by means of exhalation (*recaka*), [one says]: "Obeisance to the consciousness of fire (*vahnicaitanya*)."
Having thus placed [the fire] in the *pātirastha* fire, having worshipped it with the *saṃhitā*,

and having performed the rites such as the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), one should take [the fire], cast it upward three times into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and contemplate the union of the *vit* and *tṛs*. (Fourth line) Having placed it facing oneself with the root of the knee resting on the ground, and having contemplated the gathering at the region of the navel as the act of donning the garment, one should offer a drop of water for the purpose of cleansing.

(5th line) Having fashioned a wooden [image] with the *kavaca* mantra and ignited it with the *astra* mantra, one should worship it with "Obeisance to the fire of the womb" (*garbhāgnaye namaḥ*). Then, for the protection of the embryo, having tied a bracelet consecrated with the *astra* mantra upon the hand of the Goddess, (6th line) one should worship with the *sadyojāta* mantra for the purpose of conception (*garbhādhāna*), and offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the *astra* mantra.
For the sake of *puṃsavana*, in the third month, having worshipped with the *vāmadeva* [mantra],
one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the head [of the deity], and having offered a drop of water; for the *sīmanta*, in the sixth month, having worshipped with the *aghora* [mantra],
one should offer [oblations] as before with the crest-lock (*śikhā*), for the purpose of fashioning the faces and limbs.

Having likewise offered oblations, and having worshipped the person at the tenth month of birth, and having donned the armor as before, [one should act] for the sake of bathing the newborn who removes the impurity of the womb. Having kindled the fire with *darbha* grass and other materials, and having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra*, one should remove the bracelet from the hand of the Goddess, meditate upon and worship the golden binding, and sprinkle the site with the *kuṇma-astra* to terminate the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Having struck it with the *darbha-astra* and sprinkled it with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should spread *darbha* grass with tips pointing east and north using the *astra-mantra*.

Having established the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, and having offered five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the *Śastra-mantra* to remove the saliva from the [deity’s] faces; having worshipped Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara on the enclosing sticks in the directions starting from the east; and having fully honored the world-protectors (*lokeśa*) upon the seats according to their respective positions—one should request the fire to protect the child. There, taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles along with *kuśa* grass, sprinkling them with water while reciting the *Astra-mantra*, heating them in the fire, and touching their tips with the tip of a *kuśa* blade—

Having again rotated [the vessel] through the middle with the middle [finger] and touched the base with the base [finger], one should worship the Śiva-vidyā, known as the three principles (tattvas) together with the Lord (Īśvara), in the places touched by the *kuśa* grass. Having placed the *śrucī* as Śakti and the *sruva* as Śambhu, and having encircled them with the *kavaca* mantra using *kuśa*, one should place [the ladles] on the left side and take up the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having purified [the clarified butter] by means of inspection and other rites, having meditated upon it as consisting of Brahman together with its limbs (*sāṅga*), and having taken it up and placed it above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) within the range of the fire that has been turned three times;

then, taking a drop of clarified butter with a blade of *kuśa* grass and having offered it with the mantra "Svāhā to Brahman," one should meditate upon one's own body as the form of Viṣṇu. Having placed the clarified butter in the northeast, one should offer it with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, saying "Svāhā to Viṣṇu. [Then one should meditate upon] one's own body...

Having meditated on the form of Rudra, having placed [the sacrificial grass] in the *yoni*, and having offered the oblation with the mantra "Svāhā to Rudra," he should withdraw it. Then, taking the purifier (*pavitra*)—which is one span long and has a knot in the middle—with the thumb and ring finger, he should perform three splashes of clarified butter toward the fire while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra, and likewise perform a splash toward himself. Having loosened that knot and cast it into the fire, [he should proceed] with the staff-like *darbha* using the *Astra* mantra.

Having touched the light and cast it into the fire, one should expel [the impurity] with the staff and the *kuśa* grass while reciting the *kavaca* mantra, and having cast it into the fire, one should touch the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the staff and a *darbha* blade while reciting the *vara* mantra, and burn it in the fire. (4th line) Then, having placed a *pavitra* made of two *darbha* blades—one span in length with a knot in the middle—into the clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava*, one should [visualize] the two fortnights, white and black, as the *piṅgalā* and *iḍā* [nāḍīs] in right and left order respectively. (5th line)

Having visualized the *suṣumnā*, and having taken clarified butter from the left side with the ladle, one offers it into the right eye, saying: "Svāhā to Agni. Having taken [butter] from the left side, one offers it into the left eye, saying: "Svāhā to Soma.
Having taken [butter] from the middle, one offers it into the middle eye, saying: "Svāhā to Agni and Soma. Again, having taken [butter] from the middle...

Having offered "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" and having taken a small portion [of the oblation] into the mouth of the Fire, one should cast the remaining clarified butter into the respective portions for the Ājyabhāgas with the mantra "Svāhā. In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), however, following the sequence beginning from the left side: "Svāhā to Soma," "Svāhā to Agni," "Svāhā to Soma and Agni," and "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"—these are offered into the left, right, and middle eyes of the Fire respectively.

Having offered clarified butter with the *saṃhitā* [mantra] and performed the worship, as well as the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth, one should perform the purification of the other clarified butter by casting drops of it from the heart-mantra. Then, by means of the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, one should perform the consecration of the faces with a single oblation for each exhalation (*recaka*). Next, one should effect the connection of the faces with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta. By the simultaneous utterance of the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, [the fire] proceeds from the fire toward the wind.

One should perform the unification of the faces by merging Nirṛti with Īśāna. Then, having worshipped [the fire] with Īśāna for the purpose of naming, one should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the Astra mantra. Having given the name "Śivāgni" or "Svam Hutāśana," and having dismissed the other two [deities], one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the fulfillment up to the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*).
One should divide the fire intended for the sacrificial pap and clarified butter among the other sacrificial pits.

Having divided the fire situated in each of those directions and preserved it in another place for the purpose of increasing the Śiva-fire, one should offer fuel-sticks with the sixteen vowels beginning with ‘A’. [Then one should meditate on] the form of Brahmā, seated upon a lotus throne, five-faced, four-armed, with a long beard, adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Having meditated thus: "Her lotus-like hands are busily occupied with a sacrificial ladle, a water-pot, a staff, and a rosary," one should pray:
"O Agni, you are the supreme, purifying splendor of Īśvara."

"Therefore, having established [the deity] within the lotus of your heart, I shall satisfy him. Having thus entered the middle channel (*madhya-nāḍī*) into the form of Agni, and having worshipped Śiva together with his seat and his retinue in its center, one should perform the libation with the root mantra one hundred and eight times, or a tenth part thereof, and likewise offer oblations for the Brahma-aṅgas.

Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and having performed oblations according to one's capacity with the root mantra for each [deity] to pacify ill omens related to place, time, and descent, and to bring about auspicious omens;
then, with the root mantras and the limb-mantras (*brahmāṅga-mantra*) ending in *svāhā*, one performs libation (*tarpaṇa*) with each individual oblation: *oṃ hūṃ maṃ hauṃ hūṃ śivāyā hūṃ phaṭ*;
*oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ īśānamūrdhne hūṃ phaṭ*.

"Oṃ hūṃ heṃ hūṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ aghorahṛdayāya hūṃ phaṭ |" Having performed the kindling with three oblations for each mantra, beginning with these and ending with the weapon-mantras (*astramantra*), one should proceed. Then, the image-protectors (*mūrtipāḥ*), having performed the consecration of their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) in their own pits, [should take] the fire from the principal pit...
Having joined each respective [substance] with its corresponding fire located in its respective direction; having placed the wood with the *kavaca* mantra; having kindled it with the *astra* mantra;

having strewn [the grass] around and established the *paridhi* and *viṣṭara* seats; having worshipped Brahmā and the others, as well as Indra and the others, situated upon those *paridhi* and *viṣṭara* seats; and having consecrated the *sruk*, *sruva*, and clarified butter (*ājya*) as before.

Having gratified the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having worshipped Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta in the eastern, southern, northern, and western sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) respectively; and having worshipped Sṛk, Śiras, Śikhā, and Kavaca in the pits of Agni, Īśāna, Nairṛta, and Vāyu respectively—(8th line)—having offered twenty-five oblations with their respective mantras for the purpose of mantra-satiation (*mantratarpaṇa*), and having offered half of the principal portion or half of that again with materials such as fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should offer oblations according to one's capacity with the [specific] mantra for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). (P.190a, 1st line)

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and worshipped each respective deity, and having joined [the fire] from each respective vessel into the principal jar at its proper place; having removed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the grass mats (*viṣṭara*) situated around each respective hearth (*kuṇḍa*), and having spread out the coverings (*paristaraṇa*) around the perimeters; they should join the fires situated in each respective hearth into the principal hearth at their respective places. Having prepared the sacrificial porridges (*caru*) according to the procedure for the teacher’s *sthālīpāka*, [they should offer] the fuel sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having offered one hundred and eight, or half of that, or a tenth part of each of the seven substances— namely parched grain (*lāja*), sesame (*tila*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), green gram (*mudga*), black gram (*māṣa*), *āḍhaka*, barley (*yava*), and bamboo (*vaiṇava*)— or of the five substances ending with sesame, beginning with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and ending with green gram, using the root mantra; and having likewise offered for the Brahma-aṅgas, and then having given the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) one hundred and eight of each using the root mantra, the Aghora mantra, and the Astra mantra.

Having offered one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, or twelve oblations, he should present the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having presented the food offering (*naivedya*), sandalwood paste, betel leaf, and so forth to the Blessed One residing in the fire, and having worshipped him with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), he should prostrate.

Having offered the *arghya* water for the deity facing away, and having taken up his seat and other implements, he should cause [the deity] to rise with the *nārāca-mudrā* and perform the ritual union (*saṃyoga*).
Having joined [the fire] into the Śiva-vessel and offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*,

having confined the fire and given the *bali* offering to Brahmā and the others seated upon the enclosures and the *viṣṭara*, having confined them and given the internal *bali* and the external *bali*, and having given the *bali* to the *dyurape*s (?), one should wash one's feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and carry out the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa*. Then, for the purpose of giving the *bali* to the village and so forth, [one should proceed] as before with the *tāstarāja*, the *anna-liṅga*, and so on.

Together with the banners and other [emblems], or [the ritual] from the banners up to the great seats (mahāpīṭha), or from Brahmā up to the seats, or from the wheels (cakra) up to the seats—as before—accompanied by their respective rhythmic beats (tāla), melodies (rāga), and musical instruments, and provided with the offerings for the world-protectors (lokapāla) and the daily offering (dinabali), one should enter the temple and cast the offering according to the regular procedure for the great seat. As for the daily offering: therein, from the first day until the ninth day...

(3rd line) One should offer oblations (*bali*) every day, both morning and evening, to the lords of the obstructing spirits (*vighna-bhūtṛṣīndra*), namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, one deity at a time in each of the eight directions. Regarding the specific materials for those oblations:
(4th line) sweetmeat balls (*laḍḍuka*), cakes (*apūpa*), fruits, molasses (*gulam*), curd, and rice.

Mung bean porridge mixed with the powder of *phala-rajanī*, ghee, curd, and parched grain; rice mixed with lotus roots, tips of *kuśa* grass, fruits, and ghee; yellow rice mixed with *indravallī*, *priyaṅgu*, and ghee;
and milk-rice mixed with turmeric, full-blown lotuses, flowers, and parched grain.

One should offer the oblation in due order: rice mixed with *gulā* and clarified butter from the *brahatī* fruit; rice mixed with curd and clarified butter from coconut, plantain, and jackfruit; and pure rice mixed with parched grain (*lāja*), flowers, curd, and clarified butter.
Having adorned the vehicle for the Lord of the Festival, one should sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra* and worship it with the respective mantras of its seat.

Having placed [the deity] upon each respective consecrated seat and having adorned him with all ornaments, one should lead the deity— along with the Viṣaya-yantras, Maṇi-yantras, and so forth in front of the god, and the Goddess Cañjā and others behind the god— into the purified and decorated pathway. Having caused them to perform a circumambulation of the village in due order, one should enter the temple and remain in the assembly pavilion (*āsthāna-maṇḍapa*).

One should cause water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth, to be presented. Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the presence of Utsaveśvara for the purpose of the procession and the ceremonial bath, one should—according to one’s wealth and means—resolve upon the various types of bathing, such as that with nine jars (*navakalaśa*). Having set out the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and performed the *śānti* oblation, one should consecrate [the deity] according to the prescribed procedure. Now, [the fourth line...]

For the sake of a special worship, having adorned the deity with various garments, flowers, and so forth, and having performed the worship from the seat and the form up to the final secondary enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), one should offer a great food offering (*mahā-naivedya*) together with fruits, cakes, and the like, as well as betel-leaf; then, one should cause incense and lamps to be presented, accompanied by song, instrumental music, rhythm, and melody for the purpose of providing entertainment.

Having performed the dance according to the sequence of the circumambulation and offered it to the God, he enters the interior of the temple. For the Goddess’s joint residence [with the God], he shall satisfy the divine couple with appropriate worship. Day and night, having performed the morning rites for his guru and entered the sacrificial pavilion, [he attends to] the Sūrya-arch, the gatekeepers, and so forth.

Having performed the purification of the pavilion up to the Guru-prajānanta, the worship of the Lord of the Sacrifice (*yāgeśvara*), the ritual of the jar (*kumbha*), and the worship of the pavilion of song (*gīta-maṇḍapa*); having worshipped the *nirmālya* in the altar-jar (*vedikā-kumbha*) with water for sipping and the seat along with its coverings as before;

having worshipped the *vardhanī* and the five [deities] beginning with Vidyeśvara; and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items to the Blessed One residing in the jar; one approaches the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having sprinkled [the wood] with the Astra-mantra and placed the fuel-wood with the Kavaca-mantra; having kindled it with the Astra-mantra; having worshipped the locations for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*); and having consecrated the *sruk*, *sruva*, and clarified butter as before—(third line)—having offered oblations into the Śiva-fire with the Vyāhṛtis; having worshipped Śiva in its center as before; and having offered the mantra-satisfaction (*mantratarpaṇa*) oblations appropriate to the place, time, and so forth; and having given the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to the Lord of All—(fourth line).

Having performed the morning worship, having conducted the entry into the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the offering (*bali*), the planting of the *radhāprarohaṇa*, and the feeding (*dhāna*) according to the previous procedure;

having stayed in the assembly pavilion (*āsthānamaṇḍapa*), having presented offerings such as coconuts and the like, and having performed the midday daily rites; [one performs] the ceremonial bathing for the procession (*yātrārthasnapana*), the special worship (*viśeṣārcana*), and the special viewing (*viśeṣadarśana*).

One should perform the offering of food (*naivedya*) to the Lord every day, both morning and evening; this constitutes the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-sandhyārcana*) and so forth. However, during the festival (*utsava*), there are sixteen rites for the Lord, beginning with the morning [rites] and ending with the evening. Following that, there is the oil massage (*tailābhyaṅgana*) and the circumambulation of the temple grounds (*deśabhramaṇa*). Having performed the hunting expedition (*mṛgayātrā*) according to the prescribed rule, one should visit the sacred sites (*tīrthāni*) during the early part of the night.
At the time of the ceremonial bath, having removed the previous *kautuka* (sacred thread),
and having specifically performed the binding of the *kautuka* once again with the *nasamadhetīr* [mantra],

one should, on the following day before sunrise, install the King of Mountains (*Svarāja*) in a place such as a riverbank. Having placed nine water-pots (*kalaśa*) before it, one should [invoke] Manonmanī in the central pot and [the other deities] in the eight pots surrounding it.

Having worshipped the holy fords such as the Śuṣagaṅgā and others, and having honored the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), he leads [the deity] into the midst of the water. Having consecrated [him] with jars of water and immersed him in that water, he invokes the holy fords, beginning with "O Goddess Gaṅge,
Yamune," and so forth, until sunset.
For as long as that time lasts, O wise one, one should cause this garland of sword-kings to enter.

(5th line) Having performed the morning salutation and worship of Utsaveśvara, and having completed the fire-oblation, the offering, and the procession according to the prescribed rite, [one should place it] first before Śambhu, who is seated in the assembly pavilion. (6th line)

Having worshipped with offerings such as coconuts and the like, and having prepared three sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) before the Lord following the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*), one should place a trident on one of them, a pestle (*musala*) in front of it, a mortar (*ulūkhala*) in front of that,
and a kettle-drum (*bherī*) in front of that.

Having performed the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should worship the King of Sounds (*svarāja*), present the food offering (*naivedya*) and other gifts, and worship the seat (*āsana*) placed upon the mortars.
Having worshipped the three principles beginning with Śivatattva, together with the Lord (Īśvara), upon the mortar divided into three sections;

having adorned the pestle with a tuft of grass, a garland, and so forth; having worshipped those same three principles together with the Lord upon that [pestle]; having worshipped Vāgīśvarī in the mortar and Vāgīśvara on the pestle with perfumes and other offerings; and [having placed] oil, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) surrounding the mortar—

Having repeatedly offered betel leaves and *kūra* into the vessels and worshipped them with their respective names, and having worshipped the drum upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated before them, one should strike the drum for the purpose of expelling the Rākṣasas who cause harm through [the use of] powder. Then, having summoned the drummer (*pādaka*), one should have him play the rhythmic beats (*tālāni*).
Thereafter, having cast the powder of *avaṭī*, turmeric (*rajanī*), and so forth into the mortar (*ulūkhala*)—

Divide the *musala* into three parts with the ten-syllable mantra. Have the Māheśvara singers of the *Śivagīta* and the Rudra-maidens pound it according to the procedure for offering *dūrvā* grass. Taking that powder to another place, add a little oil, worship it with the *Māyā-śakti* mantra, and [use it] for the sake of the Liṅga, the Goddess, and the festival image.

Having removed the spit and the entrails, one should go before each respective deity, worship them with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and offer betel leaf. Having applied oil, turmeric powder, and sprouts while reciting their respective mantras, and having offered incense and lamps, one should cause the distinguished powder and sprouts to be given to the devotees. Then, having gone to a place such as a riverbank—a site of great pilgrimage—one should install the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) to the northeast, and place the ritual jars (*kalaśa*) upon the mound situated in front of it.

Having worshipped the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*) and the jars (*kumbha*) as before, and having bathed, one should release the *kautuka* [thread] and, having entered the water and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should cause [the deity] to enter the temple. There, having released the *kautuka* from either the Lord of the Festival (*utsaveśvara*) or the vessel, and having consecrated [him] with the bathing rites and other ceremonies, one should have the offerings (*naivedya*) and so forth sung. Then the Guru, having entered the sacrificial hall through its northern door and having worshipped the jars of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), [should proceed].

Having worshipped the Yāgeśvara and the Kumbha, and having performed the ritual acts beginning with the sprinkling of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and ending with the libation of mantras (*mantratarpaṇa*), and having offered the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*);

having offered the *jayādi*, the *abhyādhāna*, the *rāṣṭrabhṛt*, the *kuśmāhuti*, the *indāhuti*, and the oblations with the *mahāvyāhṛti*s and others according to one's capacity; and having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), [one should proceed] to the fire-stand (*agnisthāya*).

Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and other items to the Blessed One, having worshipped with the *iṣṭapuṣpikā* (desired flowers), and having offered the *nirodhārghya* (the water of cessation), one should unite [the deity] within the *kumbha* (vase) and dismiss the fire. Having dismissed those who were seated upon the enclosures and the sacrificial grass (*paridhiviṣṭara*), and having performed the propitiation (*praṇuti*) of *Paritvā* and the others, one should draw three circles of four finger-breadths each in the portion of the pit for digging. Then, in the western [circle], on the first circle, starting from the east...

(Second line) In the directions: *namaḥ* to the Rudras; *namaḥ* to the Mothers; *namaḥ* to the Gaṇas; *namaḥ* to the Yakṣas; in the [directions] beginning with Īśāna: *namaḥ* to the houses; *namaḥ* to the Daityas; *namaḥ* to the night-stalkers; (Third line) *namaḥ* to the Nāgas; within the mandala, in the [corners] beginning with Īśāna, Agni, and Nṛti: *namaḥ* to the constellations (*nakṣatras*).

Salutation to the zodiac signs; salutation to the Viśvedevas. (4th line) Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the eastern mandala—with Varuṇa and Vāyu in the middle—to the Lord of the Field (kṣetreśa), salutation. (5th line) In the center of that mandala, salutation to Nīlalohita.
Outside of that mandala, salutation to Vāghasāda and the others who know the covenant (samaya).

Having thus worshipped, and having offered the *bali* with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*, one should invite them— having invited those [deities] residing in the pitchers of the pavilion, beginning with the Sun— and wash one's feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, having worshipped the Guru seated upon a seat on pure ground as if he were Śiva,
and having given gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth;

Having performed the purification of the liṅga through the worship of Tvaṣṭṛ and other rites, and having worshipped according to the prescribed method, one should consecrate the jars of the Lord of Sacrifice (Yāgeśvara). Then, having worshipped and consecrated the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) in the vardhanī vessel and on the pedestal, in their respective locations starting from the east; and whatever [vessels] such as the jar of the Lord of Sacrifice there may be, one should sprinkle them in their respective places.

Then, for the sake of special worship, having prepared the bathing rites, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and so forth; having consecrated [the deity] in due order and anointed [him] with sandalwood paste and other substances; having offered various food offerings (*naivedya*) and the like, one should burn incense, lamps, and so forth. Then, having gone to the staff and other implements for the lowering of the banner, and having placed a new water-pot (*navakumbha*) upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), [one should place it] in the central pot.

Having worshipped the bull and the eight jars, and having consecrated the bull-jar at the base of the staff; having consecrated and worshipped the eight jars in their respective positions starting from the east, and having offered the food oblation (*naivedya*) and so forth, and having placed the sacrificial offering (*bali*) upon the bull and others;
one should then address the locations of the staff, the sub-staff (*upadaṇḍa*), the shoulder, and the ring.

Having lowered the cloth, one should join it to the bull situated at the front. Then, having gone to the Mūla-caṇḍālaya and performed the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited.

Having established the *vardhanī* vessel together with nine jars upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should install Caṇḍeśa in the central jar, Yamanī in the *vardhanī*, and Rudra and Bharga in the eight surrounding jars. One should then assign Pracaṇḍa, Mahābala, Vikrānta, and Ṭaṅkapāṇi [to the remaining positions]. Having thus worshipped the eight Caṇḍas, [one should worship] Marula and Caṇḍa with the Caṇḍeśa-gāyatrī.

(Second line) Having offered flowers, having sprinkled the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*) with water, and having performed an ablution with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances according to one's means, and having performed an ablution with the water from the ritual jar (*kuṃbha*) at their respective places, and having adorned [the deity] with garments, perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
(Third line) having presented an offering of food (*naivedya*) such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and cakes (*apūpa*), one should worship with incense, lamps, and other articles.

Then, for the purpose of dismissing the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*), having summoned a certain celibate student (*brahmacārin*) and invoked Caṇḍeśa into him, and having fed him with cakes, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and other foods,

and having placed the *iṃkāra* weapon into his hand; together with him, having approached the eastern gate in the same manner as before, accompanied by the Thousand-King [mantra] and the ten weapons beginning with the *liṅga*.

(6th line) Having worshipped each respective world-protector together with their corresponding rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), melodies (*rāga*), and so forth, using their respective mantras; and having offered an oblation (*bali*) of turmeric rice with those same mantras ending in *svāhā* (7th line);

having dismissed those respective world-protectors to their respective places and entered the sanctum (*ālaya*); and having offered an oblation of pure food upon the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*) as a daily rite, [one should worship] the food-liṅga (*annaliṅga*).
Having dismissed Caṇḍeśa, one should establish the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) and the others in their respective places. [This concludes] the procedure for the food-offering and the liṅga.
The ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the worship of the bali-vessel, the worship of the sandals (pādukā), the procedure for the food-liṅga (annaliṅga), the method for Aṃśumān,
and the cooking of one *prastha* of rice for the sake of the food-liṅga: having washed the vessel (*sthalikā*) there with the Astra-mantra— (third line).

Having set aside that cooked rice, one should mix it with plantain fruits and curd, and then fashion a *liṅga* measuring ten fingers in width and twenty-four fingers in height. One should fashion its navel; the tip of the *liṅga* should be one finger [in diameter]. From the base to the tip, it should gradually taper. There should be a *kūśa* [protrusion] in the middle of that *liṅga* for the sake of the *Pāśupatāstra*.

"Namaḥ"—with these words one should worship, and then cover the liṅga with a cloth. Having worshipped in this manner, one should worship the banner at the top of the flagpole. On the first day, for the four [deities]:
Gaṇeśvara, Veṇukubali, Dravyakośca, and Paruryatoścatṛya—[one should offer] a portion of the food as an oblation. One should cause the bali-offering to be made from that food.

The *piṇṇaippu* (flower-offering): Having offered the cooked flowers as a regular *bali* to the deities beginning with Indra and ending with Brahmā; having offered the *bali* at the tip of the sacrificial grass (*dvijāgra*) with the mantra "To the Bull, Svāhā" (and so on for the ten directions); having offered the *bali* at the two sides of the gateway (*gopura*) with "To the Supporter, Svāhā"; [reciting] "Oṃ Hāṃ, to the Serpent, Svāhā"; [and offering] to Brahmā in the station of Brahmā with "To Brahmā, Svāhā"; [then] to the Lord of the Gaṇas through the principle (*tattva*).

Having offered the *bali* with "Svāhā!", one should offer it everywhere in this same manner. As before, there is the dancing, rhythmic beating (*tāla*), singing, and so forth. To Indra, Svāhā! To Gaṇeśvara, Svāhā! To Agni, Svāhā!
(Third line) To Gaṇeśvara, Svāhā! To Yama, Svāhā! To Gaṇeśvara, Svāhā! To Niṛti, Svāhā! To Gaṇeśvara, Svāhā!
To Varuṇa, Svāhā! To Gaṇeśvara, Svāhā! (Fourth line)
Svāhā to Vāyu; svāhā to Gaṇeśvara; svāhā to Soma; svāhā to Gaṇeśvara; svāhā to Īśāna;
svāhā to Gaṇeśvara. There, for the sake of satisfying all the gods and others, [offer] svāhā to the Weapon (*astra*).
Having thus offered the *bali*, wash one’s feet at the eternal great seat (*nityamahāpīṭha*).

One should offer the *bali* oblation. Having thus offered the *bali*, one should cast it into the water, install the *baliberā* and other items in their proper places, offer the *pādya* and other services, worship, and after bowing to the primary *liṅga*, one should conclude [the rite]. One should perform the preliminary services (*upacāra*) and so forth as before.
Thus ends the procedure for the festival (*utsava-vidhi*).
The Procedure for the Festival Procession:

On the chariot or in the palanquin, on the first day, there is the adornment of Maheśvara; the adornment of Gaurī; the adornment of Gaṇapati mounted upon his mouse-vehicle; and the adornment of the deities belonging to the devotees.

The Ornament of Caṇḍeśvara. (Second line) One should perform the worship of each of these by their respective names. Then one should proceed with the procession. At the time of the procession, the ritual service is performed on the right side of Maheśa. The preceptor stands together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās).
(Third line) In front of Maheśa.

Singing, dancing, rhythmic clapping, and instrumental music [take place] there. In front of that are the great Śaivas; in front of them, the Masuras; in front of them, the Rudra-prostitutes; in front of them, the kings and the king’s men. In front of them is the great musical instrument; in front of that is the Subrahmaṇya priest; in front of that is Vināyaka. On both sides are banners and flags; and at the side of Maheśa’s bull is Caṇḍeśvara.

To his side [are] the devotees behind; such is the sequence of the procession: flowers, *vellāviyu*, *semparutti*, sacrificial offerings (*balidravya*), milk-rice (*pāyasa*), *mañjalpoḍi*, *tāmarai*, *pūnūl* (6th line), *pori*, *āka*.

Beginning from the right of the door, one should offer the sacrifice (*bali*) to those beginning with Nandi and ending with the serpents. Various regional stories and sayings; the witnessing of a righteous battle at that time (7th line).
The preceptor stands on the left side of the king’s body.

On the left side of the king is the ritual bathing for the journey (*yātrārtha-snapana*), the ritual of complete consecration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and the worship of Vināyaka. [This concludes] the sequence for the ritual bathing for the journey. [Then follows] the consecration with water-jars (*kalaśābhiṣeka*). [Section headings: Second, Third, Fourth; Desirable [rites], 81, line 1.]

Cleaning with a white cloth; offering scents and flowers; the worship consisting of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, food offerings (*naivedya*), incense (*dhūpa*), and lamps, along with the remaining rites of the twilight worship (*sandhyā*); likewise at the time of dawn; the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth, as well as the sequence of offerings (*balikrama*); the procession (*yāna*); the ceremonial bath for the purpose of the journey (*yātrā*); and the festivals of the first day. The commencement of the second day occurs only at night, after completing all the rites beginning with the worship of the pavilion.

The specific offerings for the second day: the deities are Brahmā, Karuttūmattampū, Nākappū, Mallikaippū, and Āka. The offering materials are sesame-rice (*tilānna*), *neyi*, and *vālappalam*. (4th line) The sequence of the offering (*balikrama*) for Āka begins from the right side of the entrance and extends as far as the gate of the *gopura*, starting from the station of Brahmā as before. "To Brahmā, Svāhā! To the spirits (*bhūta*s), [Svāhā! (5th line).

*svāhā*, and so forth, as before. Instrumental music, singing, and so on, up to [the end], as before. Then the mounting (*yāna*) upon the vehicle of the Bhūtas, adorned with the moon-crested Lord (*candraśekhara*). The mounting is as before. *Mañjalpoḍi*. *Teṅgāy*.

Beginning from the right of the gate, up to the offering at the gate of the *gopura*, proceed as before. At the station of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*), offer "Svāhā to Brahmā," "Svāhā to Gandharva," and so forth, including the musical instruments and other items, as before. Then follows the procession.
Upon the bull-vehicle (*vṛṣabhavāhana*), there is the adornment of Maṅeśvara.

The vehicle is as before. It is the same at dawn. Thus, it is like the festival of the fourth day. For the deities of the fifth day, [the offerings are]: Indra; the flower is *campaka*; the *utpala* lotus; the materials for the *bali* offering are *tinai*, *neyi*, and *indravalli* (*āga*). Starting from the right side of the entrance, up to the *bali* at the gate of the *gopura*, it is as before: "To Brahmā, Svāhā! To Indra... (third line).

*Ya svāhā*. Also in the place of Indra: *Indrāya svāhā*, and so forth for the musical instruments and other offerings, as before. Then the mounting: the ornamentation of Candraśekhara in the flower-palace (*puṣpavimāna*). The mounting is for the sake of [providing] the capacity for [the ritual] action. Śakti and Śiva remain in the middle of the path.

The deities remain by looking at one another. The preceptor stands before the deity; the image-guardian stands before the goddess. Having performed the *kapūra* rite and having received the words of the preceptor, one should speak to Gaurī.

There, having heard the purification of the image in the presence of the Goddess, one should speak before the deity. Again, in this manner, one should perform the *sandhāna* (reconciliation/union) in the presence of the Goddess. At that time, Rambhā, the servant of the Goddess, takes the central handle of the leaves and strikes those who have gathered for the sake of the *sandhāna*—the ritual workers (*karmiṇaḥ*), our initiate (*samayī*), the reciters (*pāṭhakāḥ*), and the scribes (*lekhyākāḥ*). After that, there is a petition before Īśāna. Following that, everything given by the Lord—including the villages and other property—is [offered] to the Goddess.

(Second line) One should offer [the oblation]. Then follows the diversion of the dialogue between the God and the Goddess. They remain seated upon a single throne. At dawn, they descend; their journey is by means of a flower-palace alone.
(Third line) [This is] for the purpose of the Goddess drinking breast milk and for the purpose of the withdrawal of the ascetic practice (*kṣapaṇa*).

The decoration of the Lord of Relations (Sambandhanātha) upon the palanquin; the decoration of the other devotees; the offering of breast milk to the Goddess [at the temple of] Devīlaya; therein, the recitation of the Tamil hymn (Dramiḍastotra); the offering to the devotees of the remainder of the breast milk;
before Maheśa—

The standing of Saṃbandhanātha; then the standing of those reciting hymns before him; the offering of garments, perfumes, and so forth to them; the hearing of the *purāṇa* (the sixth line); the hymn; at the conclusion of the hymn, the restraint of the mendicants (*kṣapaṇa*); then the distribution of sacred ashes (*bhasman*) to the devotees; the departure of Saṃbandhanātha toward the presence of Maheśa; there (the seventh line).
The hymn and the dance. Then, the departure to their respective abodes and so forth, as before. The festival of the fifth day. For the deities of the sixth day:
the Ṛṣis. The flower is *kaḍambu*. [Under the heading of the sixth day: *utpala* (blue lotus). The offering materials for the *bali*: *mūṅgilarici* (mung bean rice).

The *śalāyya* (a type of rice preparation), the *māṃpala* (mango); on that day, at night, following the conclusion of the *homa*, there is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and adornment of Naṭeśvara and his Śakti. (Second line) The tying of the *kautuka* (sacred thread); the entry of the Dancing Form (*nṛttamūrti*) into another pavilion or into that [same one];
or, in the sacrificial hall (*yāgaśālā*), the perfuming with black fragrance (*kṛṣṇagandha*) and other substances—the sequence for the perfuming with black fragrance and so forth. (Third line)

The ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the worship of Vināyaka, and the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the perfuming of Naṭeśvara with black sandalwood (*kṛṣṇagandha*) and other substances. [Recite] the two *puṇyāha* mantras. On the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should fashion nine compartments. Thus, having placed black sandalwood in the central vessel, one recites the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. In the eastern vessel, one places camphor (*karpūra*).

The mantra "Salutation to Tatpuruṣa"—this [is for] the southern vessel. The application of saffron [is performed]. The mantra "Salutation to Aghora"—this [is for] the western [vessel], where the application of musk scent [is made]. The mantra "Salutation to Sadyojāta"—this [is for the northern vessel].

In the north, [place] snow-water with the mantra: "Vāmadevāya namaḥ. In the southeast, [apply] perfume with "Hṛdayāya namaḥ. In the southwest, [apply] *gorocanā* with "Śirase namaḥ. In the northwest, [apply] musk with "Śikhāya namaḥ. In the northeast, [apply] the eight perfumes (*aṣṭagandha*) with "Aṣṭagandhattukku."

Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *bāmbāla* (musk), *jālaka* (nutmeg), *kuṅkuma* (saffron), *vilāmicca* (ver), and *ceṅkadunīrakoṭṭa* (uśīra)—these, combined with *koṣṭha*, are known as the eight fragrances (*gandhāṣṭaka*). [The items are: sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *paccikla* (inuveliver), saffron, *vilāmicca* (ver), *ceṅkadunīrakoṭṭa*, and *āga* (uśīra). 8. The arrangement: "Salutation to the Armor" (*kavacāya namaḥ*)—this is the mantra. (Third line) Having thus worshipped, one should cover it with a cloth.

Covering that with *darbha* grass; as before, the fire offering (*homa*) during the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*). The materials for the fire offering: equal portions of clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), barley (*yava*), sesame (*tila*), and the *jayā* mantras and so forth. Musical instruments and the like for Naṭeśvara; the food offering (*naivedya*), betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), incense (*dhūpa*), and lamps (*dīpa*). Thus ends the section on black fragrances (*kṛṣṇagandha*).

The ritual of dwelling (adhivāsa) is completed. Following that is the sequence of offerings (balikrama). Beginning with the offering at the gate up to the offering at the city-gate (gopura), it is as before. "Svāhā to Brahmā! Svāhā to the Ṛṣis! and so forth, including the [offerings] to Āgādi and others, as before. Then follows the procession (yāna). On the elephant-vehicle, there is the adornment of Maheśvara; the procession is as before. Even at dawn, this is done without the perfuming with black incense and other substances. At the conclusion of the festival, there is the bathing of Naṭeśvara with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

(First line: The consecration with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), betel, incense, and lamps, and having gratified [the deity] with [these] waters, one should conclude the remainder of the twilight ritual and pay homage.
