Thus ends the festival of the sixth day. (Second line: [The heading for the application of black ointment (*kṛṣṇagandhalepana*)].

It is completed. That night, at the conclusion of the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), one should then, during an auspicious moment of the night, apply black fragrant paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*). With a well-pleased mind, the preceptor (*ācārya*), wearing a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) and an upper garment (*uttarīya*), having performed the ritual protection (*sakalīkṛtya*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), having sprinkled [the object] with the sprinkling-mantra (*saṃprokṣya*), and having concealed it with the armor-mantra (*varmaṇā*), he places the fragrant substance that has been infused [with mantras] upon a small pedestal (*sthalikā*) and consecrates it with the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*).

Having recited the mantra, displayed the *dhenumudrā*, and offered the nine substances beginning with black fragrant paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*), and having led [the image] in a circumambulation for one watch of the night, one should place the tripod (*tripādyā*) before Naṭeśa. There, having performed the ritual of the six limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*) and worshipped Vināyaka, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall apply the black fragrant paste to Naṭeśa. Then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) and performed the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).

Having established the peace-vessel (*śāntikuṃbha*) and having offered oblations with the seven substances— namely, fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), barley (*yava*), and sesame seeds (*tila*)— having performed the offerings with the seven mantras beginning with *Sadyojāta*, and having united the form residing in the fire with black fragrant incense, he should sprinkle it with the water from the peace-vessel.

Having performed the rites of protection (*rakṣā*), the drawing of the boundary (*avakuṇḍana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should bestow the gift of Śiva, dedicating it to Śiva.

First, having given gifts of perfume, a cow, gold, a bronze vessel filled with gold, and sesame seeds; then, having sought out an auspicious moment and gone into the presence of Naṭarāja, he should worship him with the invocation and other rites using the mantra of Naṭarāja: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ānandatāṇḍaveśvara; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Ānandatāṇḍava."

Having released [the thread] with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should thereafter apply black fragrant paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*). Taking the black fragrance, [one applies it] to the right arm: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. On the head: *oṃ hīṃ śirase namaḥ*. On the forehead: *oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai namaḥ*. On the throat: *oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. On the heart: *oṃ hauṃ*... (7th line).
Salutation to the eyes. To the feet of the one who stands firm.

*Oṃ haṃ*, salutation to the weapon (*astra*). Having taken the substances starting from the east, one should offer them in the previously mentioned places with: *Oṃ hoṃ*, salutation to Īśāna. Then, having offered the coconut and other fruits as the food offering (*naivedya*), and having given betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should present incense and the lamp.

One should offer all the ritual services (*upacāra*). For all the images as well, having caused black fragrant paste (*kṛṣṇagandha*) to be offered, one should subsequently present it to the devotees and then distribute the sacred ashes (*bhasma*). The sequence for the offering (*bali*) on the seventh day: the materials for the offering have already been mentioned previously. [The fruit]—in this manner, having reached the lunar day (*tithi*), having given the molasses (*gula*), by means of the vehicle of Naṭeśa, one should cause Maheśa’s vehicle to move. After Naṭeśa, on the side, [place] the mṛdaṅga drum and the kāhala trumpet.
Having caused the sound of conchs, lutes, and flutes to resound with various musical instruments according to the path taught by Bharata, and having gratified Naṭeśa;

having placed [the deity] in the assembly pavilion, offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should conclude [the rite]. Having performed the ceremonial bathing of Maheśa for the sake of his procession, and having completed the remainder of the twilight rituals.

(6th line) One should perform the worship with offerings of enjoyments and limbs. Then, at the time of dawn, at the conclusion of the morning twilight, one should wrap Naṭeśa in a white cloth and, according to the prescribed rite, devoutly smear him with sandalwood, cool water, and pieces of camphor. [One should offer] vellera-kampū, veṇtāmara, nandyāvarta, and go-nama-dhuma-dhuku-kkiragu.
